title: Master Guide for Clinical Psychology — Amit Panwar
text: Master Guide for Clinical Psychology — Amit Panwar A cheat-map of exactly what the MPhil / MA Clinical Psychology entrances test, lifted straight from Amit Panwar's Master Guide for Clinical Psychology and folded in clean. Four parts: the exam pattern analysis (what CIP, IHBAS, RML and NIMHANS hammer every year, plus the questions that actually repeat), an A–Z terminology glossary , 24 named therapies with founder + key concepts + techniques, and 25 landmark experiments with who/when/where/what. Read it once for the map, then drill the glossary and experiments cold. Source Amit Panwar, Master Guide for Clinical Psychology (Power Within Psychology). Transcribed verbatim; only obvious scan slips were cleaned. Marketing/contact pages dropped. Two of the experiments (Harlow's monkeys, the Darley "Good Samaritan / bystander" pair) appear twice in the original numbering — both kept as the guide lists them. In this guide Exam pattern analysis & repeated questions Why revising UGC-NET JRF papers pays off A–Z terminology glossary 24 important therapies (founder · concepts · techniques) 25 landmark experiments (who · year · where · what) 1. Exam pattern analysis: what actually gets tested Admission into CIP Ranchi, IHBAS, RML and NIMHANS (for MA/MPhil, PGDCP/PDCP, PsyD and PhD Clinical Psychology) is competitive, but the entrances recur in shape. The structure across institutes is similar: MCQs dominate , covering theoretical concepts, psychological tools, research methods, psychotherapies and clinical diagnosis. 1.1 Sections that show up Area What they ask General Psychology Classical theories — Freud, Jung, Adler, Skinner, Bandura; cognition, memory, sensation, perception, learning. Clinical Psychology Disorders, diagnosis, defense mechanisms, therapeutic approaches. Psychological Testing & Assessment Intelligence (Binet, Wechsler, Bhatia Battery, Performance tests), personality, projective tests; test construction. Psychotherapy & Counselling CBT, DBT, psychodynamic, client-centred; applied / case-based. Research Methods & Statistics Design, hypothesis testing, ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, factor analysis. Developmental Psychology Lifespan, stage theories, attachment. Biopsychology Brain anatomy and its link to psychological function. 1.2 Commonly asked topics, with real stems A. General & Clinical Psychology. Foundational theories of Freud, Jung, Adler, Skinner, Bandura come up constantly. "Psychoanalytic theory about human personality was proposed by?" (CIP) "Insight learning is studied by?" (CIP) B. Psychometric Testing & Intelligence. Binet, Wechsler, Bhatia Battery / Performance tests — components and Indian-context applications. "The prototype of the modern intelligence test was developed by?" (CIP) "Bhatia Battery of Performance Test includes which test?" (CET) Key tip Go deep on test theory and application; drill test-construction concepts ( reliability, validity ) — they're commonly tested. C. Research Methodology & Statistics. Design, hypothesis testing, and stats. Know ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, factor analysis cold. "Degrees of freedom in a chi-square 3×4 table?" (CIP) "What is Cronbach's Alpha used for?" (RML) D. Clinical Diagnosis & Disorders. DSM-5 criteria, especially schizophrenia, OCD, PTSD, depression; defense mechanisms; therapy approaches. "Which defense mechanism is most common in Borderline Personality Disorder?" (RINPAS) "Which therapy focuses on changing negative thought patterns?" — CBT (CIP) E. Neuropsychology & Biopsychology. Brain structures — hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, hypothalamus — and their functions. "Which structure allows communication between the hemispheres?" (RINPAS) "What is the role of the hippocampus in memory?" (NIMHANS) F. Therapies & Treatment Approaches. CBT, DBT, psychodynamic, client-centred — and applying them. "Functional Analysis is considered under which therapy?" (RINPAS) 1.3 Repeated questions across exams (use this to sharpen the mocks) Many items recur near-verbatim across papers. These are the highest-value drills. Theme Repeated stem Seen in Psychological theories "What are the basic types of defense mechanisms according to Freud?" (Id/Ego/Superego, displacement, repression) IHBAS, CIP, RML MPhil Psychometric tests "Which intelligence test includes the Pattern Drawing Test?" CET, RML Neuropsychology "Damage to the hippocampus affects?" RINPAS, NIMHANS, IHBAS Clinical disorders "Which disorder is characterised by repetitive intrusive thoughts?" (OCD) IHBAS, NIMHANS Defense + BPD "Which defense mechanism is most commonly associated with borderline personality disorder?" IHBAS, CIP, NIMHANS (first via UGC-NET) 1.4 Strategy for cracking the MPhil entrances Focus on core areas: master psychoanalytic, behavioural and cognitive theories; DSM-5 categories, criteria and treatments for common disorders; brain anatomy tied to cognition and memory. Practise previous-year papers: they expose recurring themes and question patterns — drill MCQs on the Bhatia Battery, CBT techniques and brain functions. Master psychometrics & research: intelligence tests, methodology and statistical tools are tested heavily; command of them is a real edge. Stay current: DSM-5 revisions and emerging trends in psychotherapy and neuropsychology. Time management: front-load high-yield topics (research methods, clinical disorders, brain functions); revise and take timed mocks to build speed and accuracy. 2. Why revising UGC-NET JRF papers pays off One of the strongest levers for these entrances: revise UGC-NET JRF papers. The overlap with MPhil Clinical Psychology entrances is large and well-documented. High overlap of topics & questions. Clinical and abnormal psychology (schizophrenia, OCD, personality disorders and their DSM-5 criteria), psychoanalytic theory and research methodology all recur in both. "What are the key diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia?" turns up across UGC-NET, GATE and MPhil papers. Theorist items — e.g. "Which theorist proposed the collective unconscious?" — appear in MPhil exams after first showing in UGC-NET JRF. Strong focus on research methods & statistics. ANOVA, t-tests, chi-square, validity and reliability are repeated. "Degrees of freedom in a chi-square 3×4 table?" appears across UGC-NET and GATE with slight variations in MPhil papers. Psychometric & intelligence tests. WAIS, Binet, and the Bhatia Battery are frequent. "Bhatia Battery of Performance Test includes which test?" has appeared across CIP Ranchi, UGC-NET and GATE — high repetition. Direct repeats in MPhil exams. Items on cognitive distortions, memory systems and CBT techniques carry over from UGC-NET into IHBAS, CIP and NIMHANS papers (e.g. shortlisting rounds). High-utility shared topics. Neuropsychology (hippocampus, amygdala, neurotransmitters; serotonin in depression), cognitive psychology and clinical diagnostics overlap heavily across UGC-NET JRF, GATE and MPhil. Bottom line UGC-NET JRF papers cover the same foundational topics and carry repeated questions and terminology. Folding them into your practice strengthens concepts, drills the repeats, and lifts your odds across the board. 3. A–Z terminology glossary Quick definitions for the key terms the guide flags. Searchable — type any term in the library search and this entry surfaces. A Agraphia The partial or complete inability to write, usually caused by brain damage. Aphasia Partial or complete loss of the ability to speak or comprehend language, typically caused by brain injury or neurological conditions. Aphonia The inability to produce vocal sounds due to damage to the larynx or related structures. Apraxia A disorder where an individual struggles to produce normal movement or speech despite intact muscles and comprehension. Anorexia Nervosa An eating disorder marked by an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted body image, leading to extreme restriction of food intake. Amygdala A structure in the brain's limbic system involved in emotion regulation, particularly fear and aggression. Anterograde Amnesia The inability to form new memories following brain damage, with preserved recall of past events. Attachment Theory Developed by John Bowlby; explains how early relationships with caregivers shape emotional bonds, with types such as secure, anxious and avoidant. Attention Span The length of time an individual can concentrate on a task without becoming distracted. Autosome Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome, carrying genetic information unrelated to sex determination. B Behavioural Theories Theories such as classical and operant conditioning that explain learning through associations, reinforcements and punishments (Pavlov, Skinner). Borderline Personality Disorder A disorder of unstable moods, relationships and behaviour, often marked by impulsive actions and intense fears of abandonment. Broca's Area A frontal-lobe region responsible for speech production; damage results in Broca's aphasia. Brute Force A problem-solving strategy that tries all possible solutions until the correct one is found. C Catharsis The release of pent-up emotions and psychological tension through expression, resulting in emotional relief. Chi-Square Test A statistical test used to examine the association between two categorical variables. Chunking A memory strategy where information is grouped into larger, meaningful units, making it easier to recall. Classical Conditioning Learning where a neutral stimulus becomes associated with a meaningful one, eliciting a conditioned response (Pavlov). Client-Centred Therapy A humanistic approach by Carl Rogers emphasising unconditional positive regard, empathy and client autonomy. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) A widely used therapy focused on altering negative thought patterns and behaviours to treat psychological disorders. Cognitive Dissonance The discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs or behaviours, motivating people to reduce the inconsistency (Festinger). Cognitive Distortions Irrational thought patterns (all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophising) that lead to emotional distress (CBT framework). Cognitive Psychology The study of mental processes like memory, problem-solving, perception and decision-making. Conformity The tendency to change behaviour or beliefs to align with group norms, often under social pressure. D Defense Mechanisms Unconscious strategies that protect the ego — e.g. repression, displacement, projection (Freud). Degrees of Freedom (df) The number of values free to vary when calculating a statistic. Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) An offshoot of CBT by Marsha Linehan, aimed at borderline personality disorder via mindfulness and emotion regulation. Displacement A defense mechanism where negative emotions are redirected from the original source to a less threatening target. Down's Syndrome (Trisomy 21) A congenital condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, leading to developmental and intellectual delays. E EEG (Electroencephalogram) A method for recording electrical activity in the brain using electrodes on the scalp. Extinction In classical conditioning, the weakening and disappearance of a conditioned response when the CS is no longer paired with the US. Eclectic Therapy An approach combining elements from different therapeutic techniques to best meet the client's needs. Empiricism The belief that knowledge comes primarily from sensory experience and observable evidence. Epigenetics The study of how environmental factors influence gene expression without changing the DNA sequence. Ethnocentrism Viewing one's own culture as superior and judging other cultures by its standards. F Factor Analysis A statistical method to identify underlying relationships between variables, often used in psychometrics. Flashbulb Memory Vivid, detailed memories of significant, emotionally charged events, often resistant to decay. G Gate Control Theory A theory of pain perception: a neural "gate" in the spinal cord modulates pain by controlling signal flow to the brain. Gene A unit of heredity composed of DNA carrying genetic information that influences traits and characteristics. Genotype The genetic makeup of an individual, including dominant and recessive genes. Groupthink A phenomenon where group members prioritise consensus over critical thinking, leading to poor decisions. H Halo Effect A general impression of a person (positive or negative) influencing judgements about their other, unrelated traits. Hallucinations Sensory perceptions occurring without external stimuli, common in psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. Hippocampus A brain structure crucial for forming new memories, particularly long-term memory processing. House-Tree-Person Test A projective test in which individuals draw a house, tree and person to assess personality traits. Hypothesis A testable prediction made by researchers, usually formed before an experiment. I Illusion A misperception or distortion of a sensory experience where perception does not match reality. Implicit Memory Memory that influences behaviour unconsciously, without intentional retrieval (e.g. procedural memory, riding a bike). Insight Learning A problem-solving process where understanding arises suddenly (Köhler's chimpanzee experiments). Insight-Oriented Therapy Psychotherapy aimed at helping clients gain awareness of unconscious thoughts, emotions and behaviours. Internal Locus of Control The belief that one controls one's own life events and outcomes, vs. external factors like luck or fate. J Just Noticeable Difference (JND) The smallest change in sensory stimulation a person can detect 50% of the time. Just-World Hypothesis A bias where people believe the world is fair, assuming individuals get what they deserve even in misfortune. K Klüver-Bucy Syndrome A disorder from temporal-lobe and amygdala damage, causing hypersexuality, visual agnosia and reduced fear responses. Klinefelter Syndrome (XXY) A genetic condition in males caused by an extra X chromosome, leading to developmental delays and specific physical traits. L Lateralisation of Brain Function Certain mental processes are specialised to the left or right hemisphere (e.g. language is typically left-hemisphere). Learned Helplessness Feeling unable to control or change a situation after repeated failure, leading to passivity and depression. Limbic System Brain structures regulating emotion, memory and motivation — includes hippocampus, amygdala and hypothalamus. Linguistic Relativity Hypothesis (Sapir-Whorf) Language influences thought and perception; speakers of different languages may experience the world differently. M Memory Systems The categorisation of memory into short-term, long-term and working memory, with subtypes like episodic and semantic. Null Hypothesis A statistical hypothesis stating there is no effect or difference; the baseline assumption in hypothesis testing. N Narcolepsy A sleep disorder of excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep attacks, often with muscle weakness (cataplexy). Neurotransmitters Chemical messengers across synapses — e.g. serotonin (mood), dopamine (reward), GABA (inhibitory). Neuroplasticity The brain's ability to reorganise and form new neural connections, especially after injury or during learning. Nomothetic Approach Seeking general laws that apply to all individuals (vs. the idiographic focus on the unique individual). Nurture Assumption The hypothesis that development is largely shaped by environment (nurture) rather than genetics (nature). O Object Permanence Understanding that objects continue to exist when unseen — Piaget's sensorimotor stage. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) Intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours (compulsions) performed to reduce anxiety. Operant Conditioning Skinner's theory of how behaviour is shaped by consequences, through reinforcement and punishment. Overgeneralisation A cognitive distortion: applying a single event or experience to an entire range of situations. P Phenotype The observable traits of an individual, influenced by both genetics and environment. Premack Principle In operant conditioning, high-probability behaviours reinforce low-probability ones ("games after homework"). Priming Exposure to one stimulus influences the response to a later stimulus, often outside conscious awareness. Projection A defense mechanism: attributing one's own unacceptable thoughts or motives to another person. Prosocial Behaviour Voluntary behaviour aimed at helping others, motivated by empathy or social norms. Psychoanalysis Freud's approach exploring unconscious thoughts and desires via free association and dream analysis. R Reinforcement In operant conditioning, increasing a behaviour by adding a positive outcome (positive) or removing an aversive stimulus (negative). Reciprocal Determinism Bandura's view that behaviour, environment and cognition all influence one another bidirectionally. Regression to the Mean Extreme data points tend to move closer to the average on subsequent measurements. Regression Analysis A statistical method to predict the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables. Reliability The consistency of a test or measure in producing stable, repeatable results (e.g. test-retest reliability). Retrograde Amnesia The inability to recall memories formed before the onset of amnesia. S Scaffolding In Vygotsky's theory, support from more knowledgeable others that helps a learner reach a higher level of understanding. Schemas Mental frameworks used to organise and interpret information, shaping perception and memory. Schizophrenia A severe disorder with hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech and impaired functioning. Short-Term Memory (STM) Temporary storage lasting ~15–30 seconds, with limited capacity. Social Learning Theory Bandura's view that learning occurs through observation, imitation and modelling, with reinforcement and punishment. Somatoform Disorders Disorders with physical symptoms lacking a medical cause — e.g. conversion disorder, hypochondriasis. Standardisation Establishing uniform procedures for administering and scoring tests to ensure consistency across situations. Stereotypes Oversimplified, generalised beliefs about groups of people, often based on race, gender or ethnicity. Stroop Test Naming the ink colour of a word, hardest when the word names a different colour (e.g. "red" printed in blue). T Temperament Biologically based tendencies to feel or act a certain way, present from early childhood; the foundation of personality. Transference In psychotherapy, clients projecting feelings and attitudes from past relationships onto the therapist. Transactional Analysis Eric Berne's theory examining interactions (transactions) based on Parent, Adult and Child ego states. T-Test A test comparing the means of two groups to see whether the difference is statistically significant. Turner Syndrome (XO) A condition in females from partial or complete absence of one X chromosome, with delayed development and infertility. U Unconditional Positive Regard Rogers' term for a therapist's non-judgemental acceptance and support of a client, regardless of what they say or do. Unconscious Motivation Desires, urges or thoughts that influence behaviour but exist outside conscious awareness (Freudian). Universal Emotions Per Paul Ekman, basic emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger and fear are recognised and expressed similarly across all human cultures. V Validity The degree to which a test measures what it is supposed to. Types: construct, criterion and content validity. Variable Ratio Schedule A reinforcement schedule rewarding behaviour after an unpredictable number of responses, giving high response rates (e.g. gambling). Visual Agnosia A disorder where a person can see but cannot recognise or interpret visual information, due to brain damage. W Working Memory Short-term memory that actively holds and manipulates information; crucial for reasoning, learning and comprehension. Wernicke's Area A region involved in language comprehension; damage causes Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but nonsensical speech). X Xenophobia An irrational fear or dislike of people from other countries or cultures. X-Linked Disorders Genetic disorders from mutations on the X chromosome, often affecting males more severely (e.g. colour blindness, haemophilia). Y Yerkes-Dodson Law Performance improves with arousal up to a point, after which further arousal hinders performance. Youth Bulge A demographic phenomenon where a large share of a population is young, often linked to social instability. Z Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) Vygotsky's gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can achieve with guidance or collaboration. Zeigarnik Effect The tendency to remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed ones — tension aids memory. 4. 24 important therapies Founder · key concepts · techniques for each. NIMHANS/MET love "Therapy X was founded by?" and "Technique Y belongs to which therapy?" — drill both directions. Therapy Founder Key concepts Techniques 1. Animal-Assisted Therapy (AAT) No single founder (various psychologists & animal therapists) Uses animals (dogs, horses) to improve emotional well-being, enhance cognition and reduce stress; used for PTSD, anxiety, depression. Structured interaction with animals to build rapport and reduce anxiety. 2. Attachment Therapy Based on John Bowlby's attachment theory Building and repairing attachment bonds, often in children with trauma, neglect or inconsistent caregiving. Activities to build trust and strengthen the caregiver–child relationship. 3. Bibliotherapy No specific individual (used as an adjunct) Reading material that relates to the person's struggle to support healing and growth. Reading and discussing books, poetry or essays that give insight. 4. Cognitive Analytic Therapy (CAT) Anthony Ryle (1980s) Integrates cognitive and analytic approaches to understand problematic patterns of thinking, feeling and relating. Mapping behaviour patterns, identifying maladaptive thinking, reformulation letters to build insight. 5. Coherence Therapy Bruce Ecker & Laurel Hulley Symptoms arise from learned emotional responses; therapy uncovers and resolves them. Emotional uncovering, experiential work, creating moments of change. 6. Dance Movement Therapy (DMT) Marian Chace and other dance therapists (1940s) Movement as a form of expression to enhance emotional, cognitive and physical well-being. Movement exploration, body mirroring, expressive dance. 7. Developmental Needs Meeting Strategy (DNMS) Shirley Jean Schmidt Unmet childhood developmental needs drive adult emotional and psychological issues. Healing attachment wounds by meeting unmet developmental needs. 8. Dramatherapy Influenced by Jacob L. Moreno & Peter Slade Drama and theatre techniques to facilitate emotional expression, self-awareness and conflict resolution. Role-play, improvisation, storytelling, guided imagery. 9. EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation & Reprocessing) Francine Shapiro (1987) Treats trauma by processing distressing memories and reducing their impact; client recalls trauma while focusing on bilateral stimuli. Eye movements, bilateral tapping, cognitive restructuring of traumatic memories. 10. Functional Analytic Psychotherapy (FAP) Robert Kohlenberg & Mavis Tsai Uses the therapeutic relationship to change problematic interpersonal behaviours as they emerge in session. Reinforcing adaptive behaviour in the relationship, in-vivo exposure, emotional validation. 11. Hypnotherapy Modern form attributed to Milton Erickson (roots in Franz Mesmer, 18th c.) Hypnosis to create focused attention, heightened suggestibility and deep relaxation; used for phobias, addictions, chronic pain. Trance induction, suggestion therapy. 12. Integral Therapy Ken Wilber Integral theory integrating multiple perspectives — internal/external, individual/collective — into a holistic whole. Working across four quadrants to create a holistic approach to therapy and development. 13. Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP) Habib Davanloo Active therapy to overcome resistance and access repressed emotions; tackles deep-rooted problems in a short time. Emotionally focused interventions, unlocking the unconscious, working through defenses. 14. Logotherapy Viktor Frankl Existential therapy centred on finding meaning in life, even amid suffering; humans are driven by a "will to meaning." Socratic dialogue, dereflection, paradoxical intention. 15. Metacognitive Therapy Adrian Wells Modifies dysfunctional metacognitive beliefs that maintain anxiety and depression. Detachment from thought processes, attention training, challenging metacognitive beliefs. 16. Multimodal Therapy (MMT) Arnold Lazarus Evaluates seven dimensions of personality — the BASIC ID: Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal relationships, Drugs/biology. Tailored interventions for each modality based on the person's specific needs. 17. Narrative Therapy Michael White & David Epston Sees people as separate from their problems; clients "re-author" their lives with empowering narratives. Externalising problems, identifying unique outcomes, re-authoring personal stories. 18. Play Therapy Virginia Axline & Carl Rogers (influences) Play as a medium for children to express emotions, resolve conflicts and process difficult experiences. Sand tray, role-playing, art-based activities, storytelling. 19. Positive Psychotherapy Nossrat Peseschkian Emphasises inherent capacities for growth and healing; focuses on strengths rather than pathology. Balancing techniques, active goal-setting, identifying personal strengths. 20. Rational Living Therapy (RLT) Aldo R. Pucci A cognitive-behavioural approach building on REBT to replace irrational beliefs with more logical ones. Cognitive restructuring, disputing irrational beliefs, a rational-living plan. 21. Reality Therapy William Glasser Based on choice theory: clients take control of their lives by making better choices; emphasises personal responsibility and the present. Action planning, focusing on current behaviour, exploring new choices. 22. Sexual Identity Therapy No single founder Addresses sexual orientation, identity and gender identity in a supportive, affirming way. Exploratory discussion, psychoeducation, supportive counselling. 23. Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT) Steve de Shazer & Insoo Kim Berg Short-term, goal-oriented; finds solutions in the present rather than dwelling on past problems. Miracle question, scaling questions, identifying exceptions. 24. Structural Family Therapy Salvador Minuchin Looks at family hierarchies, boundaries and subsystems and how they shape individual behaviour and mental health. Joining, restructuring family interactions, boundary setting. 5. 25 landmark experiments The classic studies, with who ran them, when, where and what they showed. The entrances ask these as "Experiment X was conducted by?" and "Which study demonstrated effect Y?". Experiment Conducted by Year Where What it showed 1. Hawthorne Studies Elton Mayo 1924–1932 Western Electric, Hawthorne Works, Chicago Productivity rose when workers knew they were observed — the Hawthorne effect . 2. Little Albert Experiment John B. Watson & Rosalie Rayner 1920 Johns Hopkins University A baby was classically conditioned to fear a white rat; fear generalised to similar stimuli. Now a landmark in research ethics. 3. Halo Effect Experiment Edward Thorndike 1920 Case Western University A positive impression of one quality (e.g. attractiveness) led people to overestimate other qualities. 4. The Monster Study Wendell Johnson 1939 University of Iowa Attempted to induce stuttering in orphan children through negative speech therapy — one of the most unethical studies in psychology. 5. Robbers Cave Experiment Muzafer Sherif 1954 Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma Intergroup conflict arises between groups and is resolved through superordinate goals . 6. Asch Conformity Experiment Solomon Asch 1951 Swarthmore College Participants conformed to clearly wrong answers given by a group — the power of social pressure. 7. Cognitive Dissonance Experiment Leon Festinger 1957 Stanford University Discomfort when behaviour conflicts with belief; participants justified their behaviour by changing their beliefs. 8. Harlow's Monkey Experiment Harry Harlow 1961 University of Wisconsin-Madison Infant monkeys preferred a cloth "mother" (comfort) over a wire one (food) — contact comfort drives attachment. 9. Fantz Looking Chamber Experiment Robert Fantz 1961 Case Western Reserve University Infants preferred looking at human faces over patterns — innate visual preferences. 10. Bobo Doll Experiment Albert Bandura 1961 Stanford University Children who watched an adult act aggressively toward a doll imitated it — observational / social learning. 11. Milgram Obedience Experiment Stanley Milgram 1961 Yale University Participants administered what they believed were painful shocks when told to by an authority — obedience over morality. 12. Schachter & Singer Experiment on Emotion Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer 1962 Columbia University Supported the two-factor theory of emotion (arousal + cognitive labelling); participants misattributed arousal based on others' behaviour. 13. Ainsworth Strange Situation Mary Ainsworth 1969 Johns Hopkins University Assessed infant attachment via reaction to a caregiver's absence/return; three styles — secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant. 14. Split-Brain Experiment Roger Sperry 1968 California Institute of Technology Studied severed-corpus-callosum patients; showed the two hemispheres have specialised functions (Nobel Prize). 15. The Good Samaritan Experiment John Darley & C. Daniel Batson 1973 Princeton University Situational factors (being in a hurry) drove helping more than values — even among theology students. 16. Stanford Prison Experiment Philip Zimbardo 1971 Stanford University A simulated prison showed the extreme psychological effects of perceived power; guards turned abusive, prisoners traumatised — ended early. 17. Marshmallow Test Walter Mischel 1972 Stanford University A longitudinal study of delayed gratification in children; those who waited for a larger reward had better later outcomes. 18. Bystander Effect (Good Samaritan study) John Darley & Bibb Latané 1968 Columbia University People are less likely to help in distress when others are present — responsibility is diffused. 19. Ross's False Consensus Effect Study Lee Ross 1977 Stanford University People overestimate how much others share their beliefs, attitudes and behaviours — the false consensus effect . 20. Selective Attention (The Invisible Gorilla) Daniel Simons & Christopher Chabris 1999 Harvard University Counting basketball passes, many viewers missed a gorilla walking through — inattentional blindness . 21. Car Crash Experiment Elizabeth Loftus & John Palmer 1974 University of California, Irvine The misinformation effect : question wording ("smashed" vs "hit") altered recalled speed of the cars. 22. A Class Divided Jane Elliott 1968 Riceville, Iowa After MLK's assassination, Elliott split her class by eye colour, treating one group as superior then reversing it — showing prejudice is arbitrary and damaging. 23. Learned Helplessness Experiment Martin Seligman 1967 University of Pennsylvania Dogs given unavoidable shocks stopped trying to escape even when they could — learned helplessness , a model for depression. 24. Surrogate Mother Experiment (Harlow's monkeys) Harry Harlow 1961 University of Wisconsin-Madison Monkeys offered a wire mother (food) and a cloth mother (comfort) chose comfort — contact comfort over feeding. 25. Visual Cliff Experiment Eleanor Gibson & Richard Walk 1960 Cornell University Infants placed on a glass surface over an apparent drop avoided the "cliff" — depth perception develops early.

title: Biopsychology (Pinel & Barnes), in full depth
text: Biopsychology (Pinel & Barnes), in full depth The whole of Pinel's Biopsychology , all eighteen chapters, rewritten as real explanatory prose instead of bullet fragments. Every concept is built from scratch in full sentences, every mechanism is walked through step by step, the experiment or the patient behind each claim is named, the theorist is named wherever there is one, and worked examples are given where a concept only clicks once you push a number or a case through it. Read a chapter cold and you should finish it understanding the concept, not merely recognising the words. How to read this The chapter order is Pinel's own, so it doubles as a map of the book. Chapters 1 to 5 are the foundations (what the field is, where the machinery came from, how it is built, how it signals, how we study it). Chapters 6 to 8 are sensation and movement. Chapters 9 to 11 are plasticity and memory. Chapters 12 to 15 are the motivated behaviours. Chapters 16 to 18 are the higher functions and the clinic. Nothing in a later chapter assumes you skipped an earlier one, but Chapters 3 and 4 are the load-bearing ones: if the action potential and the synapse are solid, everything downstream reads easily. The artwork is the book's own. Every numbered figure in Biopsychology is here, all 310 of them, plus all nine numbered tables, cropped straight out of the source and dropped at the paragraph that explains it rather than collected at the end of a chapter. Nothing has been redrawn or summarised. If you open a chapter and a picture you remember from the book is not there, it is a bug: screenshot it and it gets fixed. The eighteen chapters Biopsychology as a neuroscience Evolution, genetics and experience Anatomy of the nervous system Neural conduction and synaptic transmission The research methods of biopsychology The visual system Mechanisms of perception: hearing, touch, smell, taste and attention The sensorimotor system Development of the nervous system Brain damage and neuroplasticity Learning, memory and amnesia Hunger, eating and health Hormones and sex Sleep, dreaming and circadian rhythms Drug use, addiction and the brain's reward circuits Lateralisation, language and the split brain Biopsychology of emotion, stress and health Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders How the eighteen chapters fit together 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour. That one-line definition hides the thing that makes the field distinctive, so it is worth unpacking slowly. Neuroscience as a whole is the study of the nervous system, and it is enormous: it includes people who study how a single ion channel folds, people who model networks mathematically, and people who develop drugs. Biopsychology is the branch of neuroscience that keeps behaviour at the centre of the question. A biopsychologist does not ask "what does this structure do" in the abstract; the question is always "what does this structure do to what the organism thinks, feels, or does". Pinel's phrase for the discipline's contribution is that biopsychologists bring to neuroscience a knowledge of behaviour and of the methods of behavioural research, which the other neurosciences do not supply on their own. You can know everything about a receptor and still have no idea what an animal will do, because behaviour has its own laws and its own measurement problems. The name was not always this. Earlier labels included psychobiology, behavioural biology and behavioural neuroscience, and you will still meet all of them. Pinel prefers biopsychology precisely because the word order carries the argument: bio is the adjective and psychology is the noun, so the discipline is a kind of psychology that uses biology, not a kind of biology that happens to notice behaviour. The founding text: Hebb, 1949 Biopsychology has a reasonably clean origin date. In 1949 Donald O. Hebb published The Organization of Behavior , and this is generally taken as the first comprehensive theory of how complex psychological phenomena (perception, emotion, thought, memory) could be produced by ordinary activity in the brain. Why that mattered is easy to miss now that it is obvious. Before Hebb, the widespread assumption among psychologists was that complex mental events were simply too complex to be traceable to neural activity, so the honest thing was to study behaviour and leave the brain alone. Hebb's move was to show that you could actually specify a mechanism. The human brain: Appearances can be deceiving! Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.1 His mechanism was the Hebb synapse , usually compressed into the slogan "cells that fire together wire together". Stated properly: if a presynaptic neuron repeatedly participates in firing a postsynaptic neuron, some growth process or metabolic change occurs at that synapse so that the presynaptic neuron's later ability to fire the postsynaptic one is increased. Chain those strengthened synapses together and you get a cell assembly , a set of neurons that has been wired into a functional unit by experience and can now be re-activated as a whole by any part of it. Chain assemblies in sequence and you get a phase sequence , which is Hebb's account of a train of thought. Notice the structure of the argument: a single local, plausible, physical rule, applied repeatedly, yields something that looks psychological. That is the template for essentially every biopsychological explanation that follows in this book. Hebb built his theory from a genuinely mixed evidence base, and this is the second thing he established as normal practice: experiments on laboratory animals, clinical case studies of human patients, and logical argument all counted. He did not privilege one. High-yield Hebb (1949), The Organization of Behavior = the founding of biopsychology as a discipline, and the first real theory of how psychological phenomena arise from brain activity. Hebbian learning: co-active neurons strengthen their synapse. Cell assembly (a wired-together group) then phase sequence (a chain of assemblies, i.e. a thought). Nobel prizes specifically related to the nervous system or behavior. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 1.1 Human subjects and animal subjects Biopsychology studies both humans and non-human animals, and each has real advantages, so the choice is a research-design decision rather than a matter of taste. Human participants have three obvious advantages. They follow instructions, which means you can run a task instead of waiting for a behaviour to occur spontaneously. They report subjective experience, which is the only direct access anyone has to conscious content. And they are cheaper: no purpose-built housing, no colony maintenance. There is a fourth advantage that is easy to overlook: they have a human brain, and if the question is about a specifically human capacity such as syntax, only a human brain will do. Animal subjects have a different and equally real set of advantages. Their nervous systems are simpler, so the effect you are looking for is not buried under the extra machinery. The comparative approach becomes available: studying the same system across species lets you separate the general biological principle from the local human quirk, and it is usually only across species that you can see what a structure is for . It is possible to run genuinely invasive experiments, meaning lesions, direct stimulation, single-cell recording, and selective breeding, which are the only methods that establish causation cleanly. And practically, you can control genetics, rearing, and history in ways that are simply not possible with people. The six divisions of biopsychology Pinel divides the field six ways. The division is by method and subject , not by topic, which is the single most common thing students get wrong here. Two people can both be studying memory and belong to different divisions. The six divisions of biopsychology, and how they overlap. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.4 Division The defining question Method and subjects Physiological psychology What neural mechanism produces this behaviour? Direct manipulation of the brain: lesions, electrical stimulation, surgery. Almost always laboratory animals. Pure research. Psychopharmacology How do drugs change behaviour and the brain? Manipulation by drug rather than by scalpel. Animals and humans. Strongly applied: it is where therapeutic drugs come from. Neuropsychology What are the psychological effects of brain damage? Human patients with existing brain damage. Case studies plus standardised test batteries. Never experimental brain damage. The most applied division. Psychophysiology How does physiological activity relate to behaviour in intact people? Non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy human volunteers: EEG, heart rate, blood pressure, skin conductance, pupil diameter, EMG, EOG. Cognitive neuroscience What is the neural basis of cognition? Predominantly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in healthy humans performing cognitive tasks. Highly collaborative and interdisciplinary. Comparative psychology How and why did this behaviour evolve? Comparison across species , including ethology (behaviour in the wild) and evolutionary/behavioural genetics. Visual tracking of a pendulum by a healthy control participant (top) and three participants with schizophrenia. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.5 Functional brain imaging is the major method of cognitive neuroscience. This image—taken from the top of the head with the participant lying on her back—reveals the locations of high levels of neural activity at one level of the brain as th… Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.6 Trap Three of these six names are routinely confused, and papers exploit it. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation, animals, pure research. Psychophysiology = non-invasive measurement, healthy humans, no manipulation of the brain at all. Neuropsychology = pre-existing brain damage in human patients. The give-away words in a question stem are "lesioned rats" (physiological), "skin conductance in volunteers" (psychophysiology), and "patient with left temporal damage" (neuropsychology). The six major divisions of biopsychology with examples of how they have approached the study of memory. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Table 1.2 Converging operations: why one method is never enough Every method in the list above is flawed, and each is flawed in its own particular direction. Lesion studies establish that a structure is necessary but tell you nothing about what it contributes when intact, and a lesion inevitably damages fibres that are merely passing through. Imaging shows correlated activity but cannot show that the activity is doing any work. Human case studies are rich but uncontrolled, since the damage was not assigned to the patient by a researcher. Animal experiments are controlled but raise the question of whether the finding generalises. The field's response is the strategy Pinel calls converging operations : attack a single problem with several methods whose weaknesses do not overlap, and trust the conclusion only where they agree. The classic worked example is Korsakoff's syndrome . Human case studies of chronic alcoholics showed a devastating amnesia, which invited the conclusion that alcohol is the cause. But converging evidence changed the answer. Some patients with the syndrome had no history of alcohol at all, but did have severe malnutrition. Alcoholics eat badly and alcohol interferes with the absorption of thiamine (vitamin B 1 ). Giving thiamine to Korsakoff patients halted progression, and thiamine-deprived animals developed comparable brain damage without alcohol. The conclusion that survives all the methods is that Korsakoff's syndrome is caused by thiamine deficiency , with alcohol as the usual route to that deficiency and an additional independent toxin in its own right. No single method could have got there. Scientific inference: how you study something you cannot see The brain's workings are not directly observable, so biopsychology relies on scientific inference : you measure something you can observe, and reason back to the invisible mechanism that must have produced it. This is not a weakness peculiar to the field. It is what physics does with subatomic particles. What matters is that the inference is disciplined. President Calvin Coolidge and Mrs. Grace Coolidge. Many students think the Coolidge effect is named after a biopsychologist named Coolidge. In fact, it is named after President Calvin Coolidge, of whom the following story is told. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.2 The textbook illustration is the perception of movement during eye movement. Your eyes are constantly making rapid saccades , so the image of the world sweeps across your retina many times a second, yet the world does not appear to jump. Two competing inferences are available. Either the brain tracks the eye's position by monitoring feedback from the eye muscles, or it uses the motor command it has just issued to the eye muscles, that is, it knows where it told the eye to go. You cannot see which. But you can design an observation that separates them. If the eye is prevented from moving while the command to move is still issued, a feedback account predicts the world will look stationary (no movement occurred, no feedback), whereas a command-based account predicts the world should appear to jump (a command was issued, so a compensation is applied that nothing cancels). The world does appear to move. The inference is therefore that the visual system compensates using the outgoing motor signal , a copy of the command, rather than sensory feedback from the muscles. Note the form: an unobservable mechanism, two rival accounts, and one observable consequence on which they disagree. Lester and Gorzalka (1988): the design and the result that ruled out fatigue as the explanation of the Coolidge effect. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.3 The perception of motion under four different conditions. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.7 Critical thinking about biopsychological claims Pinel closes the chapter by teaching a habit rather than a fact, and he does it with two cautionary cases. The habit is to separate what was observed from what was concluded , because the gap between them is where bad science lives. The right and left prefrontal lobes, whose connections to the rest of the brain are disrupted by prefrontal lobotomy. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.8 Case one: Delgado and the bull. José Delgado implanted an electrode in the caudate nucleus of a bull, entered the ring, and stopped a charging bull by radio stimulation. The claim built on it was that the caudate contains a mechanism that inhibits aggression, and by extension that human violence might be treated by stimulating it. What was actually observed is narrower: the stimulation stopped the charge. But the bull did not stop in a way that looked like a loss of aggressive motivation. It turned consistently in circles in one direction. A far more parsimonious reading is that the stimulation elicited a motor response, a forced turning, which happens to be incompatible with charging straight ahead. The observation is real; the conclusion about aggression was never licensed by it. Case two: the prefrontal lobotomy. Egas Moniz introduced the prefrontal leucotomy as a psychiatric treatment and received a Nobel Prize in 1949; tens of thousands of operations followed, including Walter Freeman 's transorbital version, which was fast enough to be performed outside an operating theatre. The evidential base was startlingly thin. It rested substantially on Carlyle Jacobsen 's report that a chimpanzee named Becky, who had been extremely upset by errors on a delayed-response task, became placid after frontal-lobe lesions. One primate, one behaviour, in a laboratory task. Against that, another chimpanzee in the same work, Lucy, showed no comparable calming, and the follow-up evaluation of human patients was for years essentially anecdotal and conducted by the surgeons themselves. The lesson is not that psychosurgery is inconceivable; it is that the evidence, the sample, and the outcome measure must be examined before a mechanism is believed, and that the enthusiasm of the person making the claim is not evidence. The prefrontal lobotomy procedure developed by Moniz and Lima. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.9 High-yield Delgado's bull = caudate stimulation, the turning-response reinterpretation, the warning about over-reading a dramatic demonstration. Moniz = prefrontal lobotomy, Nobel 1949, built on Jacobsen's chimpanzee Becky; Freeman = transorbital lobotomy. Korsakoff's = thiamine deficiency, and the standing example of converging operations. The transorbital procedure for performing prefrontal lobotomy. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 1.10 Worked example A researcher records skin conductance and heart rate in undergraduates while they view emotional photographs, and concludes that the amygdala generates the arousal. Which division is the study, and what is wrong with the conclusion? The methods are non-invasive surface measures in healthy humans, so the study is psychophysiology . The conclusion is not licensed: nothing in the study measured the amygdala, and no structure was manipulated. Skin conductance indexes sympathetic activation, which many structures could drive. To get to the amygdala you would need converging evidence, for example fMRI showing amygdala activation in the same task (cognitive neuroscience), plus patients with selective amygdala damage failing to show the response (neuropsychology), plus amygdala lesions abolishing the response in animals (physiological psychology). Once the three agree, the claim stands. 2. Evolution, genetics and experience This chapter exists to dismantle a question rather than answer it. The question is "is this behaviour due to nature or to nurture", and Pinel's position is that it is not a hard question with a subtle answer, it is a malformed question that cannot have an answer. Understanding why it is malformed is the whole chapter. The two flawed dichotomies The first flawed dichotomy is physiological versus psychological , sometimes phrased as brain versus mind. This is Cartesian dualism , from René Descartes , who proposed a material body governed by physical law and a non-material mind, interacting at the pineal gland. It has an appealing tidiness and it is false in a way that matters practically: if some behaviour is caused by a non-physical mind, then that behaviour is permanently outside biological explanation, and the research programme stops. Biopsychology proceeds on monism : there is one kind of stuff, and thinking is something that brains do. A schematic illustration of the way in which most biopsychologists think about the biology of behavior. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.3 The second flawed dichotomy is nature versus nurture , the assumption that behaviour can be partitioned into an inherited portion and a learned portion. Two historical camps set this up. European ethologists such as Konrad Lorenz and Niko Tinbergen studied instinctive behaviours in the wild and emphasised inheritance; North American behaviourists such as John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner studied learning in the laboratory and emphasised experience. Both were describing real phenomena. Both were generalising from a method that could only see one of the two. Pinel's replacement model has three terms rather than two. Behaviour is the product of the interaction between (1) the organism's genetic endowment , which is a product of its evolution, (2) its experience , and (3) its perception of the current situation . Genes and experience do not contribute separate portions of a behaviour; genes build a nervous system that develops in an environment, and the resulting brain then responds to a situation as it perceives it. Asking which of the two produced the behaviour is like asking whether the area of a rectangle is due to its length or its width. The one-sentence version Genes and experience are not two additive sources of behaviour; genes specify how development responds to experience, so every behaviour is 100% genetic and 100% environmental at the same time, and the only sensible questions are about how the interaction works. Natural selection, and what it actually says Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, presenting three lines of evidence: the fossil record's documented change over time, the striking structural similarities among living species (a bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a human hand share a bone plan), and the effects of selective breeding by humans, which showed that heritable variation plus selection produces change within a few generations. Asomatognosia often involves damage to the right frontal and parietal lobes. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.1 The mechanism, natural selection , needs only three ingredients: individuals vary, some of that variation is heritable, and variants differ in how many offspring they leave. Anything meeting those three conditions will evolve. The unit of accounting is fitness , which in evolutionary biology does not mean health or strength; it means the number of offspring an individual contributes to the next generation relative to others. A frail animal that reproduces more is fitter, in this technical sense, than a magnificent one that does not. The reactions of chimpanzees to their own images suggest that they are self-aware. In this photo, the chimpanzee is reacting to the bright red, odorless dye that was painted on its eyebrow ridge while it was anesthetized. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.2 Two refinements matter for behaviour. First, sexual selection , also Darwin's: traits can evolve because they improve mating success even at a cost to survival, which is how you get peacock tails and the general pattern of intrasexual competition (males competing for access) and intersexual selection (choosiness, typically female). Second, evolution is opportunistic and does not design. It works on whatever is already there, so structures often get repurposed: a feature that arose for one function and was later co-opted for another is an exaptation , and a feature that is a structural by-product of something else and was never selected for at all is a spandrel . This is the standing corrective to lazy adaptive storytelling: not everything is for something. Four kinds of evidence supporting the theory that species evolve. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.4 Trap Evolution is not a ladder and humans are not at its top. Living species are all contemporary end-points of separate branches, not rungs. We did not evolve from chimpanzees; chimpanzees and humans share a common ancestor. Evolution has no goal, "more complex" is not the direction of travel, and most species that ever existed left no descendants. Also: individual differences within a species are typically far larger than the average difference between related species. Two massive bull elephant seals challenge one another. Dominant bull elephant seals copulate more frequently than those lower in the dominance hierarchy. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.5 The course of human evolution, and the brain The lineage runs, in the order the textbook uses, from early multicellular water-dwellers to chordates (animals with a dorsal nerve cord), then vertebrates (chordates with a spinal bone casing), then the first vertebrates, the bony fishes, then amphibians , which added life on land while still returning to water to lay eggs, then reptiles , which solved reproduction on dry land with the shelled egg and dry skin, then mammals , which added internal gestation and milk, then primates , and within primates the apes and then the hominins . The genus Homo is recent, and anatomically modern Homo sapiens is very recent indeed on this timescale. A recently discovered fossil of a missing evolutionary link is shown on the right, and a reconstruction of the creature is shown on the left. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.6 Species from five different groups of primates. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.7 A comparison of the feet and hands of a human and a chimpanzee. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.8 ). Hominins include six sub-groups including Australopithecus and Homo. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.9 Three things happened to the brain along the way and they are separable. Overall size increased, but size on its own is a poor index because it scales with body size, which is why comparisons use the ratio of brain to body weight, and better still the size of the brain relative to what a body of that size would predict. Second, the increase was not uniform: it was concentrated in the cerebrum and specifically in the neocortex , the structures involved in complex adaptive processes, while the brain stem, which handles reflexes and basic regulation, changed comparatively little. Third, and this is the elegant engineering point, cortex increased in area far more than the skull increased in volume, and it accommodated this by convolution : folding into gyri and sulci. Folding lets you pack a large sheet into a small box, which is why cortical surface area, not brain mass, is the number that tracks capability. The remarkably complete skull of a 3-yearold Australopithecus girl; the fossil is 3.3 million years old. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.10 Fossilized footprints of Australopithecine hominins who strode across African volcanic ash about 3.6 million years ago, leaving a 70-meter trail. There were two adults and a child; the child often walked in the footsteps of the adults. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.11 Hominin evolution. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.12 The brains of animals of different evolutionary ages—cerebrums are shown in pink; brain stems are shown in orange. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.13 Fundamental genetics, built up Gregor Mendel got the foundations right in the 1860s by making three good methodological choices: he studied dichotomous traits (either/or, such as brown versus white seeds, with no intermediates), he began from true-breeding lines , and he counted offspring across generations instead of describing them. Crossing brown-seed with white-seed true-breeding lines gave an all-brown first generation, and crossing those offspring with each other gave brown and white in a 3:1 ratio. Whiteness had vanished for a generation and returned unchanged, so it could not have been diluted or blended. Mendel's inference was that inheritance is carried by discrete particles, now called genes , that each organism carries two of them for a trait, and that where the two differ one may be expressed ( dominant ) and the other not ( recessive ). Two copies of the same version make a homozygote , two different versions a heterozygote . What is expressed is the phenotype ; what is carried is the genotype . The 3:1 ratio falls straight out: one homozygous dominant, two heterozygotes and one homozygous recessive, and only the last shows the recessive phenotype. How Mendel’s theory accounts for the results of his experiment on the inheritance of seed color in pea plants. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.14 Genes sit on chromosomes , which come in matched pairs. Ordinary cell division, mitosis , copies every chromosome so each daughter cell gets the full set. The production of gametes uses meiosis , which halves the number, so that egg and sperm each contribute one chromosome of each pair and the offspring is a genuinely new combination. Meiosis also includes crossing over , in which paired chromosomes exchange segments before separating. Crossing over is the reason inheritance is not simply reshuffling of whole parental chromosomes, and it is why genes physically close together on a chromosome tend to be inherited together, a phenomenon called linkage . Sex is determined by one pair: XX develops as female, XY as male, and the traits carried on the X alone are sex-linked , which is why recessive X-linked conditions appear far more often in males, who have no second X to mask them. During fertilization, sperm cells attach themselves to the surface of an egg cell; at least one must enter the egg cell to fertilize it. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.15 Watson and Crick in 1953 identified the structure that makes all this physical: DNA as a double helix of two complementary strands, with adenine pairing to thymine and guanine to cytosine. Complementarity explains replication in one step: unzip the helix and each strand specifies its partner, so two identical copies result. The structure of DNA, with the complementary base pairs that make replication possible. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.16 DNA replication. As the two strands of the original DNA molecule unwind, the nucleotide bases on each strand attract free-floating complementary bases. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.17 Expression runs in two steps and the vocabulary is worth getting exactly right. In transcription , the DNA sequence of a gene is copied into a strand of messenger RNA , which leaves the nucleus. In translation , a ribosome reads the mRNA in three-base units called codons , each codon specifying one amino acid, and assembles the amino acid chain that folds into a protein . Proteins are the point: they are the enzymes and channels and receptors and structural elements, so "a gene does something" always cashes out as "a gene specifies a protein". The human genome contains on the order of twenty thousand protein-coding genes, strikingly few, and most of the genome is not protein-coding but regulatory, which is the modern answer to how so few genes build something so complicated: the same parts, controlled differently. Gene expression: transcription of DNA into mRNA, then translation of mRNA into a protein. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.18 Control is where epigenetics enters. Every cell has the same DNA but expresses a different subset of it, and expression is regulated by chemical marks that do not change the sequence: DNA methylation , which typically silences a gene, and histone modification , which changes how tightly the DNA is spooled and therefore how accessible it is. These marks respond to experience, and some are transmitted through cell division and in some cases across generations. Epigenetics is the concrete mechanism that makes the nature-nurture dichotomy untenable: experience physically regulates genes. High-yield Mendel: dichotomous traits, true-breeding lines, 3:1 ratio, dominant/recessive, genotype/phenotype. Meiosis halves and includes crossing over (source of linkage); mitosis copies. Watson and Crick 1953, double helix, A-T and G-C complementarity. Transcription (DNA to mRNA) then translation (codons to amino acids to protein). Epigenetics: methylation and histone remodelling change expression without changing sequence. Behavioural genetics: the experiments that settle the interaction Two studies carry this section, and both are designed so that the interaction is not merely asserted but measured. The two epigenetic mechanisms that do most of the work: DNA methylation and histone remodelling. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.19 Selective breeding, Tryon. Robert Tryon bred rats for maze performance, mating the best learners with the best learners and the worst with the worst over successive generations. The two lines separated cleanly, which established that maze-learning ability is heritable. That is a real and non-trivial result, and it is also exactly where naive interpretation goes wrong. Selective breeding of maze-bright and maze-dull strains of rats by Tryon (1934). Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.20 Cooper and Zubek (1958). This is the study to remember, because it takes Tryon's maze-bright and maze-dull lines and asks what environment does to them. Rats from both lines were reared in one of three conditions: an enriched environment (large, complex, full of objects), an impoverished environment (bare cage), or a normal laboratory cage. The finding is a textbook interaction. In the impoverished condition, both lines performed poorly and the difference between them shrank to nothing. In the enriched condition, both lines performed well and again barely differed. The genetic difference between "bright" and "dull" rats appeared in full only in the ordinary environment. The heritability of the trait was real, yet whether it made any difference at all depended entirely on the environment. There is no fixed quantity of genetic influence to be measured; the size of the genetic effect is itself a function of the environment. Tryon's maze-bright and maze-dull rats did not differ when both strains were reared in an enriched environment. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.21 The same logic gives the cleanest single illustration of gene-environment interaction in humans: phenylketonuria (PKU) . PKU is caused by a single recessive gene that leaves the child unable to make the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, so phenylalanine accumulates and, in the developing brain, causes severe intellectual disability. It is unambiguously a single-gene disorder with a known biochemistry. And its principal consequence is entirely preventable by an environmental manipulation: a low-phenylalanine diet begun early in life. The gene is not the destiny; the gene specifies a vulnerability to a particular dietary environment. Trap Heritability estimates are the most misread statistic in psychology. A heritability estimate is a proportion of the variation in a trait within a particular population in a particular set of environments that is attributable to genetic variation. It is not the proportion of the trait in an individual that is due to genes, that quantity is meaningless. It does not tell you the trait is unmodifiable (PKU is highly heritable and fully treatable). And it does not transfer across populations or environments: change the range of environments and the estimate changes, as Cooper and Zubek showed directly. The human tools are twin and adoption studies . Monozygotic twins come from one zygote and are genetically near-identical; dizygotic twins come from two zygotes and share about half their genes, like ordinary siblings. Comparing the two, and comparing twins reared together against twins reared apart, is the standard way of estimating heritability in humans. The known confound is that monozygotic twins are also treated more alike, so the design overestimates genetic contribution to the extent that it does. Note too that a small amount of DNA, the mitochondrial DNA , is inherited from the mother only, since mitochondria come with the egg. Epigenetic research suggests that the common practice of referring to monozygotic twins as “identical twins” is no longer appropriate. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 2.22 Worked example A paper reports that the heritability of a cognitive test score is 0.70 in a sample of middle-class children, and concludes that educational intervention is largely futile. Take it apart. First, 0.70 refers to variance in that sample, not to any individual's score. Second, and decisively, that sample has a narrow range of environments: if nearly everyone is in a similar decent environment, environmental variance is small, so genetic variance must account for most of what is left, and heritability is pushed up. Broaden the sample to include deprived environments and the estimate will fall, because there is now real environmental variance to account for. This is Cooper and Zubek's point in human form: a high heritability inside a narrow environmental range says nothing about what happens when you change the environment. Third, heritability is silent about modifiability in any case. PKU is the counter-example that ends the argument. 3. Anatomy of the nervous system Anatomy is the chapter students try to memorise and should instead try to organise. Almost everything here follows from two facts: the nervous system is built as a tube that swells at the front end, and it is described using a coordinate system borrowed from four-legged animals. Get those two and the names stop being arbitrary. The coordinate system, and why it bends in humans Directions are given in three axes. Anterior means toward the nose and posterior toward the tail, so these are also called rostral and caudal. Dorsal means toward the back surface and ventral toward the belly. Medial means toward the midline and lateral away from it. The catch is that these terms were fixed for an animal whose spinal cord and brain lie along one straight horizontal line. Humans stand upright, so the axis bends about ninety degrees at the top of the brain stem. The practical consequence: in the human brain, dorsal means superior (toward the top of the head) and ventral means inferior , whereas in the human spinal cord dorsal still means toward the back. This single bend is responsible for a large share of confusion, so read the term as belonging to a structure rather than to the body. (a) Anatomical directions in representative vertebrates, my (JP) cats Sambala and Rastaman. (b) Anatomical directions in a human. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 3.15 Three cutting planes: the sagittal plane runs front to back down the vertical midline (the mid-sagittal section splits left from right), the horizontal plane cuts top from bottom, and the coronal or frontal plane cuts front from back, like a slice across the face. Finally ipsilateral means on the same side of the body and contralateral on the opposite side, which is the phrase you will need constantly once movement and sensation are crossed. Horizontal, frontal (coronal) and sagittal planes. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 3.16 The major divisions The whole nervous system splits into the central nervous system (CNS) , meaning brain and spinal cord, encased in bone, and the peripheral nervous system (PNS) , everything else. The PNS then splits functionally. The human central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS is represented in red; the PNS in orange. Notice that even those portions of nerves that are within the spinal cord are considered to be part of the PNS. Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology , 11th ed. · Fig 3.1 The somatic nervous system (SNS) deals with the external environment and the skeletal muscles. It has afferent nerves carrying sensory signals inward from skin, muscles, joints and the special senses to the CNS, and efferent nerves carrying motor commands outward to the skeletal muscles. Afferent means arriving, efferent means exiting, and the mnemonic worth keeping is that afferent a rrives and efferent e xits. The autonomic nervous system (ANS) deals with the internal environment: smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands. Its afferents carry interoceptive signals inward. Its efferents divide into two antagonistic branches. The sympathetic branch mobilises: heart rate and blood pressure up, bronchi dilated, blood shunted to skeletal muscle, pupils dilated, digestion suspended, adrenal medulla triggered. This is the fight-or-flight arm, and its fibres leave the CNS from the thoracic and lumbar segments of the spinal cord.
