title: Biopsychology & Neuroscience
text: Biopsychology & Neuroscience The biology of behaviour from first principles: how neurons fire and talk, how the nervous system is built and mapped, the transmitter systems and their drugs, and the circuits behind sensation, movement, memory, hunger, hormones, sleep, stress, emotion, addiction and psychiatric disorders, anchored to Pinel & Barnes and deepened with Carlson, prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical neuropsychology. In this book Biopsychology as a neuroscience Evolution, genetics & experience Anatomy of the nervous system The cranial nerves (I–XII) Neural conduction & the action potential Synaptic transmission & neurotransmitter systems Research methods of biopsychology The visual system Audition & the other senses The sensorimotor system Development of the nervous system Brain damage & neuroplasticity Learning, memory & amnesia Hunger, eating & health Hormones, sex & the HPA axis Sleep, dreaming & circadian rhythms Reward, drugs of abuse & addiction Lateralisation, language & the split brain Emotion, stress & health Biopsychology of psychiatric disorders Clinical neuropsychology: syndromes & batteries Genetic, chromosomal & metabolic disorders Landmark studies, walked through Extended concept bank Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience The one idea behind the whole field. Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour : how the nervous system produces what we think, feel and do. It is the branch of neuroscience (the larger study of the nervous system) that keeps behaviour at the centre. The recurring lesson is that mind and brain are not two things: every thought is a physical event in tissue. The six divisions of biopsychology The field is split by what you study and how . Learn each by its defining method, because the paper tests "which division does X?". Division What it studies Typical method Physiological psychology Neural mechanisms of behaviour Direct manipulation of the brain in controlled experiments (lesions, stimulation), usually in lab animals Psychopharmacology Effects of drugs on behaviour and the brain Manipulate behaviour with drugs; develop therapeutic drugs Neuropsychology Psychological effects of brain damage in human patients Case studies + standardised tests; the most applied division (NIMHANS leans here) Psychophysiology Relation between physiology and behaviour using non-invasive body measures in healthy humans EEG, heart rate, skin conductance (GSR), pupil size Cognitive neuroscience Neural bases of cognition (thought, memory, attention) Mainly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in humans Comparative psychology Behaviour across species, evolution, genetics, ethology Cross-species comparison, naturalistic + lab study Trap Psychophysiology vs physiological psychology. Both have "physiolog" in the name. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation of the brain, usually in animals . Psychophysiology = non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy humans . And neuropsychology = the study of human brain-damaged patients. Kinds of research, kinds of inference Pure vs applied. Pure = curiosity-driven knowledge; applied = solving a practical problem. Most real work is a blend. Experiments vs non-experiments. Only a true experiment (the researcher manipulates an independent variable and randomly assigns) can support a causal claim. Quasi-experiments and case studies cannot fully rule out confounds. Converging operations. Because every single method is flawed, biopsychology trusts a conclusion only when several different methods point the same way . This is the field's signature methodological value. Morgan's Canon / law of parsimony: prefer the simplest explanation that fits; do not attribute a higher mental process when a lower one will do. High-yield Human brain-damaged patients = neuropsychology ; drugs = psychopharmacology ; non-invasive measures in healthy humans = psychophysiology ; imaging of cognition = cognitive neuroscience ; animal brain manipulation = physiological psychology ; across species = comparative . Causation needs a true experiment; trust the conclusion many methods agree on. 2. Evolution, genetics & experience The problem this fixes. The old "nature versus nurture" question is a false dichotomy. Genes and experience are not rival causes adding up to 100%; they interact continuously. A trait is a genetic program read out in an environment. You cannot say a behaviour is "60% genetic" for an individual, only how much variation in a population is associated with genetic variation (heritability). Evolution of the brain Natural selection (Darwin): heritable traits that improve fitness (reproductive success) spread. Behaviour evolves too. Larger brains are not automatically "better"; what matters is brain size relative to body size and the expansion of specific regions, especially the cerebral cortex in primates. Convergent evolution = similar traits arise independently (analogous structures). Homologous structures share a common ancestor. Do not read similarity as shared ancestry. Spandrels & exaptations: not every trait is a direct adaptation; some are by-products later co-opted for new uses. Mendelian genetics & the molecular layer Gene = a stretch of DNA on a chromosome. Humans have 23 pairs; the 23rd is the sex pair (XX female, XY male). Dominant vs recessive alleles; homozygous vs heterozygous ; genotype (the genes) vs phenotype (the expressed trait). Dizygotic (fraternal) twins share ~50% of genes (like ordinary siblings); monozygotic (identical) twins share ~100%. Comparing them is the classic heritability tool. Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein. Epigenetics: experience changes which genes are read Epigenetics is the mechanism that finally dissolves nature-versus-nurture. The DNA sequence does not change, but experience can switch genes on or off via chemical tags, especially DNA methylation (silences genes) and histone modification . These marks can

title: Cognitive Psychology — the whole domain, explained cold
text: Cognitive Psychology — the whole domain, explained cold Built from Eysenck & Keane, Cognitive Psychology: A Student's Handbook , the book you listed for cognitive. This is the full-depth version : for every named model you get what it claims, who proposed it, the key experiment (what was done and what was found), and the contrast with its rival in a red trap box. Tables stay as quick-reference, but read the prose around them first. Cognition spans perception, attention, memory, knowledge, language and thinking, so this single page walks the book chapter by chapter. Rebuilt to full depth 2026-05-29. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How cognitive is tested. (1) Name the model from its claim ("we store info in three stores" = multi-store). (2) Pin the model to its author (working memory = Baddeley & Hitch). (3) Tell rival models apart — that's where the distractor lives: Gregory vs Gibson, early vs late selection, episodic vs semantic, prototype vs exemplar, Broca vs Wernicke. Learn each in its contrast pair, and learn the one experiment that decides between them. Jump to: 1. Approaches 2. Visual perception 3. Object & face recognition 4. Attention 5. STM & working memory 6. Long-term memory 7. Forgetting & everyday memory 8. Concepts & knowledge 9. Language 10. Problem solving & expertise 11. Judgement & decision making 12. Reasoning ★ At-a-glance compare ★ MCQ traps ★ Key studies ★ Glossary ★ Self-test 1. Approaches to human cognition Eysenck & Keane open by saying cognitive psychology is not one method but four converging approaches , each with its own logic and limits. The point of knowing all four is that an exam stem will describe a technique and ask which approach it belongs to. Experimental cognitive psychology What it claims: you can infer the hidden stages of mental processing in healthy people by measuring behaviour under controlled conditions — chiefly reaction time (RT) and accuracy/error rate . It is the oldest strand and the historical core of the field. If a manipulation slows people down, that stage must require processing. Key logic: the subtraction/additive-factors idea — compare two tasks differing in one operation, and the RT difference estimates that operation's duration. Limit: behaviour alone is ambiguous about the underlying architecture (many models predict the same RT), and lab tasks may lack ecological validity. Cognitive neuropsychology + modularity What it claims: studying brain-damaged patients reveals the normal architecture of cognition, because damage can knock out one ability while sparing another. The bedrock assumption is modularity (Fodor): the mind contains specialised, domain-specific, informationally encapsulated modules that can be independently impaired. Key logic — the double dissociation : patient A is impaired on task X but fine on Y, while patient B is fine on X but impaired on Y. That pattern is strong evidence the two tasks rely on separate systems (one alone could be explained by task difficulty). Example: H.M. lost the ability to form new long-term memories yet had normal short-term span; other patients (e.g. K.F.) show the reverse — together a double dissociation of STM and LTM. Limit: damage is rarely clean, the brain reorganises, and single cases generalise poorly. Cognitive neuroscience methods What it claims: by measuring the living brain we can locate where and time when cognition happens. The methods trade off spatial against temporal resolution, and the exam loves to ask which method gives which. Method Measures Strength fMRI Blood-oxygen (BOLD) — indirect metabolic signal Excellent spatial resolution (mm), poor temporal (seconds); shows where . PET Radioactive tracer, blood flow/metabolism Good spatial, very poor temporal; needs injected tracer. EEG / ERP Scalp electrical activity; ERP = signal averaged to an event Excellent temporal resolution (ms), poor spatial; shows when . TMS Magnetic pulse that briefly disrupts a region Creates a "virtual lesion" → tests if a region is necessary (causal, not just correlational). Spatial vs temporal mnemonic: fMRI/PET = WHERE (great space, poor time). EEG/ERP = WHEN (great time, poor space). TMS = whether it's NECESSARY (causal). fMRI and EEG are merely correlational; only TMS and lesions establish that a region is causally required. Computational cognitive science & connectionism (PDP) What it claims: if a theory is precise enough, you can implement it as a running computer program; a model that actually reproduces human performance (including human errors ) is a strong test of the theory. The dominant style is connectionism / parallel distributed processing (PDP) : networks of simple, neuron-like units connected by weighted links, where knowledge is distributed across the pattern of weights rather than stored in one location, and learning happens by gradually adjusting weights (e.g. back-propagation). NIMHANS tests harder — connectionism. Be ready for the contrast with classical "symbolic" models. Symbolic (e.g. Newell & Simon's physical-symbol-system) manipulates discrete rules and symbols, processing serially. Connectionist/PDP uses distributed sub-symbolic representations and parallel processing; its hallmarks are graceful degradation (partial damage = partial loss, not total crash), generalisation, and learning from examples. NIMHANS may ask which framework explains prototype effects or developmental error patterns (e.g. the U-shaped curve in learning the past tense) — that's connectionism. Bottom-up vs top-down; serial vs parallel Two cross-cutting distinctions run through the whole book. Bottom-up (data-driven) processing starts from the stimulus and works up. Top-down (concept-driven) processing brings expectations, context and stored knowledge to bear. Information processing (the frame Broadbent founded) treats the mind as stages from input → encoding → storage → retrieval → output. Within that frame, processing can be serial (one stage at a time

title: Developmental Psychology
text: Developmental Psychology The lifespan story of how mind, behaviour, and relationships unfold, told through the theorists MET 2026 and NIMHANS love to test: Piaget and Vygotsky on cognition, Bronfenbrenner on context, Erikson, Freud, Marcia on identity and psychosocial growth, Kohlberg and Gilligan on morality, Bowlby, Ainsworth, Main, Harlow on attachment, Baumrind on parenting, Thomas and Chess plus Rothbart and Bates and Kagan on temperament, plus prenatal development, language, adolescence, and aging. Read top to bottom once, then revise off the tables and the red Trap boxes. In this book Foundational principles Prenatal development and teratogens Piaget: cognitive development Vygotsky: sociocultural theory Bronfenbrenner: ecological systems / bioecological model Erikson: psychosocial stages Marcia: identity statuses Freud: psychosexual stages Kohlberg and Gilligan: moral development Attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth, Main, Harlow Baumrind: parenting styles Temperament: Thomas & Chess, Rothbart & Bates, Kagan Language development Adolescence Aging and late adulthood Theorist hooks (one line each) Top MCQ traps and 30-second recall 1. Foundational Principles Principle Meaning Example Cephalocaudal Head to toe Head control before walking Proximodistal Center to periphery Trunk control before fine finger movement Continuity vs Discontinuity Gradual growth vs stage jumps Vocab growth (continuous) vs Piaget stages (discontinuous) Nature vs Nurture Genes vs environment; modern view = interactionist Twin studies, behavioral genetics Critical period Rigid window; miss it and the capacity is lost Lorenz imprinting in geese Sensitive period Flexible window; learning easier but still possible later L1 acquisition, depth perception Stability vs Change Do traits persist or shift across life? Temperament (mostly stable), IQ (some plasticity) Active vs Passive child Does the child shape their own development? Bidirectionality (Bronfenbrenner, Bell) Trap Critical = rigid biological window (lost if missed). Sensitive = optimal but flexible. Lorenz's imprinting = critical. Language learning = sensitive (you can still learn L2 at 30, just harder). 2. Prenatal Development and Teratogens Three prenatal stages Stage Duration Key event Germinal 0-2 weeks Zygote to blastocyst to implantation Embryonic 2-8 weeks Organogenesis; most vulnerable to teratogens Fetal 8 weeks to birth Growth and refinement; viability ~24 weeks Teratogens (high-yield) Alcohol — Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD); FAS = facial anomalies, growth restriction, CNS damage. Most common preventable cause of intellectual disability. Tobacco — low birth weight, prematurity. Thalidomide — limb malformations (1950s-60s, classic teratogen exam case). Rubella — heart, eye, ear defects in 1st trimester. Lead, mercury — CNS damage. Zika — microcephaly. Trap The embryonic period (weeks 2-8) is most vulnerable, not the fetal period. Organs are forming. By the fetal period, organs already exist and growth is the main task. 3. Piaget: Cognitive Development The 4 stages Stage Age Achievements Limits Sensorimotor 0-2 Object permanence (~8mo), goal-directed action, deferred imitation (end) No symbolic thought early on Preoperational 2-7 Symbolic thought, language, pretend play Egocentrism, animism, centration, no conservation Concrete Operational 7-11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation, decentration Tied to concrete reality; abstract is shaky Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive, propositional logic Adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable) Sensorimotor: the 6 substages Reflexive schemes (0-1mo) Primary circular reactions (1-4mo, on own body) Secondary circular reactions (4-8mo, on objects) Coordination of secondary schemes (8-12mo, intentional, object permanence , A-not-B error) Tertiary circular reactions (12-18mo, experimentation) Mental representation (18-24mo, deferred imitation, symbolic thought) Key concepts Schema — mental framework for understanding the world. Assimilation — fitting new info into an existing schema (a horse = a "doggie"). Accommodation — modifying the schema for new info ("ok, that's a horse, not a doggie"). Equilibration — the drive to balance assimilation and accommodation; the engine of cognitive change. Egocentrism — preoperational; can't take another's perspective. Three Mountains task. Animism — preoperational; attributing life to objects. Centration — focus on one feature at a time; blocks conservation. Conservation — quantity stays the same despite a change in form (number, mass, volume). Order: number then mass then liquid then length then area then weight then volume (last, ~11). Trap Object permanence (sensorimotor, ~8mo) is NOT conservation (concrete operational, ~7yr). Different stages, different concepts. Also: "egocentrism" in dev psych is a cognitive limit, not narcissism or a personality trait. Critiques of Piaget Underestimated infants (modern habituation studies show object permanence earlier). Stages less discrete than he claimed ( horizontal décalage = uneven performance within a stage). Underplayed culture (Vygotsky's main attack). Not everyone reaches formal operational, especially for unfamiliar content. 4. Vygotsky: Sociocultural Theory ZPD (Zone of Proximal Development) — the gap between what a child can do alone vs with help from a more knowledgeable other (MKO). Scaffolding — temporary, tailored support, withdrawn as competence grows. This is Bruner's term , applied to Vygotsky's framework. Private speech — kids talk to themselves while problem-solving. It becomes inner speech and guides cognition. Piaget called this "egocentric speech" and dismissed it; Vygotsky said it is central. Tools of thought — language is the master tool, internalized from social interaction. Higher mental functions are socially mediated . Cultural specificity — cognitive development depends on the cultural tools available (counting systems, writing, schooling). Trap "Sca

One entry per concept, every unique detail kept. Read once for coverage, then revise off the tables and the red Trap boxes. Defining abnormality (the 4 Ds) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation. Distress — subjective suffering. Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning. Danger — risk to self or others. Trap Deviance alone is not abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. You always need at least distress or dysfunction alongside it. High-yield Some textbooks list a 5th D, Duration , used for chronicity criteria (the recurring duration thresholds like ≥ 6 months, ≥ 2 years, etc. that define many disorders below). 2. Historical models & conceptions Era Model Key name(s) Prehistoric / Ancient Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek / Roman Biological, four humors Hippocrates, Galen Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum (1487) Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (Bicêtre, "moral treatment"), Tuke (York Retreat) 19th c. Biological, classification Kraepelin ( dementia praecox ), Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia , 4 As) Early 20th c. Psychological Freud (psychoanalysis), Watson (behaviorism) Mid 20th c. Cognitive-behavioral Beck (depression / CBT), Ellis (REBT) 1980s+ Biopsychosocial integration Engel (1977) Trap Kraepelin coined dementia praecox (emphasising early onset and a deteriorating course). Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia ("split mind", referring to fragmented thought, not split personality). Do not confuse with DID. 3. Approaches to psychopathology Approach Cause Treatment Biological Genes, neurotransmitters, brain Meds, ECT, psychosurgery Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early experience Psychoanalysis, free association, transference Behavioral Maladaptive learning Conditioning, exposure, reinforcement Cognitive Distorted thoughts, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring (Beck), REBT (Ellis) Humanistic Blocked self-actualization Person-centered (Rogers), Gestalt (Perls) Sociocultural Family, culture, stigma, oppression Family therapy, community psychology Biopsychosocial All three interact ( Engel, 1977 ) Integrative Diathesis-stress Predisposition × stressor Reduce both load 4. The ICD: WHO's classification (full breakdown) Definition The ICD (International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems) is the WHO's global classification of all diseases, not just mental ones. Mental disorders occupy a single chapter of it. DSM (American Psychiatric Association) covers mental disorders only. So: ICD = whole-body, global, free, used for official health statistics; DSM = mental-only, US, paywalled, research-heavy. NIMHANS / India officially codes on ICD . 4.1 What ICD is & who owns it Question Answer Full name International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems Publisher WHO (World Health Organization). DSM is APA, the contrast examiners love. Scope All diseases and health conditions, every body system. Mental & behavioural disorders are just one chapter . Purpose Global standard for mortality & morbidity statistics , billing, epidemiology. Official tool for cause-of-death and disease reporting worldwide. Cost Free , multilingual. DSM is copyrighted and sold by APA. Used where ~194 WHO member states, including India . DSM dominates US clinical research. 4.2 Version history (the dates they ask) Version Year Note ICD-6 1949 First edition to include a section on mental disorders. Common MCQ. ICD-8 1965 ICD-9 1975 US used a clinical modification, ICD-9-CM , for decades. ICD-10 1990 endorsed, 1992 in use Still tested. Mental disorders = Chapter V (F-codes) . Alphanumeric coding introduced here. ICD-11 Adopted 2019, in force 1 Jan 2022 Fully digital "foundation" architecture. Mental disorders = Chapter 06 . High-yield Lock the three dates: ICD-6 (1949) = first mental-disorder section · ICD-10 (1992) = F-codes · ICD-11 (in force 2022) = current. 4.3 Where mental disorders live ICD-10 ICD-11 Chapter Chapter V Chapter 06 Title Mental and Behavioural Disorders Mental, Behavioural or Neurodevelopmental Disorders Code prefix F (F00–F99) Alphanumeric 6 -codes (e.g. 6A20 for schizophrenia) Companion text "Blue Book" (Clinical Descriptions & Diagnostic Guidelines) + "Green Book" (research criteria) CDDR (Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements) High-yield Why "F"? No mnemonic meaning, it is simply the letter assigned to the mental-disorders chapter (Chapter V) in ICD-10's alphanumeric scheme. If asked "F-codes refer to," the answer is mental and behavioural disorders . 4.4 ICD-10 F-codes — the F00–F99 blocks (memorise the ranges) Range Block Examples F00–F09 Organic, incl. symptomatic, mental disorders Dementia (Alzheimer's, vascular), delirium F10–F19 Mental/behavioural due to psychoactive substance use Alcohol, opioids, cannabis dependence F20–F29 Schizophrenia , schizoty

title: Abnormal Psychology — the integrative approach, disorder by disorder (Barlow & Durand + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11)
text: Abnormal Psychology — the integrative approach, disorder by disorder (Barlow & Durand + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11) The Abnormal section built the way Barlow & Durand, Abnormal Psychology: An Integrative Approach teaches it: every disorder opens with a clinical case , then runs the book's four-beat frame — (1) clinical description · (2) statistics (prevalence, onset, sex ratio, course) · (3) causes , read through the multidimensional integrative model (biological × psychological × emotional × social × developmental) · (4) treatment . On top of the book, every disorder's classification is cross-checked against the current criteria so nothing is outdated: DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) and ICD-11 (WHO, in force Jan 2022), shown side by side where they differ (the ICD-11 reclassifications are exactly what MET/NIMHANS/RCI fish for). Look-alike distinctions MCQs live on are in red trap boxes; where NIMHANS pushes past the book it's in purple . This is the companion to the Ahuja full-book page — same disorders, the integrative/case lens instead of the Indian-psychiatry lens. Built 2026-06-07. Abnormal (Barlow & Durand) Abnormal (Ahuja, full book) Abnormal cheatsheet ICD breakdown High-yield sheet Counselling (Sharf) Lookalikes What is "Barlow & Durand" and why a second abnormal page. The Ahuja page reads the field as Indian psychiatry: definitions, criteria, drugs, fast and exam-tight. Barlow & Durand reads it as integrative science : it refuses any single cause and forces every disorder through a multidimensional model , and it teaches from cases . That's the angle this page adds. Same syllabus, deeper "why does it happen" answers (causes), plus the triple vulnerability theory (Barlow's own) for the anxiety block and the equifinality / multifinality developmental ideas — both pure B&D, both testable. Use Ahuja for the cut-offs and drugs, use this for the model questions ("which approach / what causes it / which dimension"). Two ideas hold the whole book together. (1) The multidimensional integrative model. No disorder has one cause; each is the product of biological (genes, brain circuits, neurotransmitters), psychological (learning, cognition, conditioning), emotional , social/cultural and developmental dimensions interacting. (2) Diathesis-stress run forward in time. A vulnerability (diathesis) only becomes a disorder when life delivers the stress; genes and environment are not separate but reciprocal (your genes shape the environments you pick), and experience switches genes on and off ( epigenetics ). Hold these two and you can reconstruct almost every "what causes X / which model" answer. Jump to: 1. Defining a disorder (the 3 components) 2. The integrative model 3. Assessment & diagnosis 4. Anxiety disorders + triple vulnerability 5. Panic disorder & agoraphobia 6. Specific & social phobia 7. Trauma- & stressor-related (PTSD) 8. OCD & related 9. Somatic symptom disorders 10. Dissociative disorders 11. Mood disorders 12. Suicide 13. Eating disorders 14. Sleep–wake disorders 15. Sexual, gender & paraphilic 16. Substance-related & addictive 17. Personality disorders 18. Schizophrenia spectrum 19. Neurodevelopmental 20. Neurocognitive DSM vs ICD at a glance All the MCQ traps Names & studies roster Fast glossary (A–Z) Self-test (active recall) Part One · Foundations & the integrative model Ch 1. What makes behaviour a disorder, and the three traditions Barlow & Durand do not use a "4 Ds" list. Their working definition of a psychological disorder has three components , and all three usually travel together: (1) psychological dysfunction — a breakdown in cognitive, emotional or behavioural functioning; (2) distress or impairment — it hurts the person or wrecks their day-to-day functioning; (3) an atypical or culturally unexpected response — it deviates from what the culture expects (and is not merely a deviant act society dislikes). They lean on Wakefield's "harmful dysfunction" : a disorder is a failure of an internal mechanism to do what it evolved to do ( dysfunction ) and that failure is harmful to the person by their culture's standards. B&D's 3 vs Ahuja's 4 Ds. If a question cites " dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected ," that's the Barlow & Durand definition (3 components). The "Deviance, Distress, Dysfunction, Danger" 4-D list is the more common Indian-text framing. Danger is NOT one of B&D's three. Both agree dysfunction/impairment is the indispensable core and distress alone is neither necessary nor sufficient (a person in mania feels great). Tradition Core claim · key names Treatment it implies Supernatural Possession, sin, the moon, witchcraft; Malleus Maleficarum (1487); the "mass hysteria"/St Vitus dances Exorcism, prayer, shunning Biological Hippocrates' four humours (imbalance = illness); Galen ; Kraepelin (classification, dementia praecox ); the discovery that general paresis = late-stage syphilis cemented "mental illness can be physical" Rest, drugs, ECT, psychosurgery Psychological Moral therapy (Pinel at Bicêtre, Tuke's York Retreat — humane treatment); Freud & psychoanalysis (unconscious, defences); Watson/Pavlov/Skinner behaviourism (learning); humanism (Rogers) Talk therapy, conditioning, person-centred B&D frame the modern clinician as a scientist-practitioner : a consumer and producer of research who treats each case as testable. The whole book is then an argument that the three traditions are not rivals but dimensions of one integrative explanation. Recap Ch 1. B&D disorder = psychological dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected (3 components, NOT 4 Ds; "harmful dysfunction," Wakefield). Three historical traditions — supernatural, biological (humours → Kraepelin → general paresis), psychological (moral therapy → Freud → behaviourism) — converge in the integrative model. The clinician is a scientist-practitioner. Ch 2. The integrative (multidimensional) model — the signature of the book This is the chapter the rest of the book runs

title: Personality — the full book, chapter by chapter
text: Personality — the full book, chapter by chapter Not a summary. This is your Schultz & Schultz, Theories of Personality walked through in the book's own order, one chapter per theorist, with the book's signature recurring frame kept intact for each: the life (how the theorist's own biography shaped the theory), the theory unpacked in full, the book's Questions About Human Nature scorecard, Assessment , Research , and Reflections (the criticisms). After the book's chapters come the four domains the book underweights but NIMHANS tests hard, flagged in purple: object relations & self · existential · type theories · Indian / Triguna · assessment in depth . Built 2026-05-22 · Rewritten as a teaching chapter 2026-05-24 · Poured out to full-book, chapter-by-chapter depth 2026-05-24 . Expanded to full depth 2026-05-24 (added the key studies walked through, an extended concept bank, an A–Z glossary, and a by-chapter self-test). How to read this page. Read it like the textbook, top to bottom, once; then revise off the coloured boxes. Each chapter follows the book: amber = the intuition / why it matters, amber "Human nature" = where the theorist lands on the book's six recurring issues. Green = the line to lock. Red = the MCQ trap. Purple = NIMHANS-specific (clinical / Indian / rival-theory swaps). Grey recap = the chapter in one breath. The one-line testable list lives in Rapid Recall ; the personality tests in depth (MMPI/16PF/NEO/projectives, scoring) are on the tests deep-dive . Jump to: 1. What personality theory is 2. Freud 3. Jung 4. Adler 5. Horney 6. Erikson 7. Allport 8. Maslow 9. Rogers 10. Kelly 11. Skinner 12. Bandura 13. The trait approach & Five-Factor Model 14. Facets of personality 15. Personality in perspective S1. Object relations & self S2. The other neo-Freudians S3. Existential S4. Type theories S5. Indian psychology / Triguna S6. Assessment in depth At-a-glance compare All the MCQ traps Key studies, walked through Extended concept bank Fast glossary (A–Z) Self-test (active recall) The one frame that organises the whole book. The book ends every chapter by scoring the theorist on six recurring Questions About Human Nature . Hold these six and you can predict any theorist's "view of the person" answer: (1) free will vs determinism · (2) nature vs nurture (heredity vs environment) · (3) past vs present (does childhood fix us, or does the here-and-now/future drive us) · (4) uniqueness vs universality · (5) equilibrium vs growth (is the basic motive to reduce tension and stay balanced, or to grow ) · (6) optimism vs pessimism . Freud is the dark end of all six; the humanists are the bright end. Everyone else sits between. Part One · The study of personality Ch 1. Personality: what it is, and how the book studies it Personality is the relatively enduring, distinctive pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviours that characterises a person and how they adapt to the world. The word comes from the Latin persona , the mask the Roman actor wore, which already hides the book's central tension: is personality the mask we show, or the real face behind it? Every theory in the book is one answer to four questions: what is personality made of , where does it come from , why do people differ , and can it change . The book groups the theorists into approaches , and that grouping is the spine of the table of contents: the psychoanalytic (Freud); the neopsychoanalytic (Jung, Adler, Horney); the life-span (Erikson); the genetics/trait pioneer (Allport); the humanistic (Maslow, Rogers); the cognitive (Kelly); the behavioural (Skinner); the social-learning (Bandura); the trait approach (Cattell, Eysenck, the Five-Factor Model); and the facet / limited-domain theories (Rotter, Zuckerman, Seligman). How the book assesses and researches personality The book insists every theory must answer two practical questions, and the recurring "Assessment" and "Research" sections grade each theorist on them: Assessment = how do you measure this theory's constructs? The methods recur: self-report inventories (objective, scored against norms, e.g. MMPI, 16PF, NEO), projective techniques (ambiguous stimuli, e.g. Rorschach, TAT), clinical interviews , behavioural assessment , and idiographic personal documents (diaries, letters). A good test must clear three bars: reliability (consistency), validity (measures what it claims), and standardised norms . Research = how was the theory tested ? Three designs recur: the clinical method (case studies, the dominant psychoanalytic tool, rich but unreliable and unrepresentative), the experimental method (manipulate a variable, the only route to cause and effect), and the correlational method (relate two measured variables, covariation only, never causation). TRAP — method by camp. Case study / clinical method = the psychoanalysts (Freud, Jung, Adler). Correlational + factor analysis = the trait theorists (Cattell, Eysenck, FFM). Controlled experiment = the behaviourists and social-learning theorists (Skinner, Bandura) and Rogers, who pioneered experimental psychotherapy research. The method usually tells you the camp. Recap Ch 1. Personality = the enduring, distinctive pattern of how a person thinks, feels and behaves. The book is organised by approach and grades every theorist on six human-nature issues plus Assessment and Research. Nomothetic (general laws, trait research) vs idiographic (the unique individual, case studies) is the master methodological split. Part Two · The psychoanalytic approach Ch 2. Sigmund Freud — psychoanalysis The life (1856–1939). Born in Moravia, raised in Vienna, the adored eldest son of a young mother (the book notes this shaped his Oedipal theory). Trained as a neurologist; studied hysteria under Charcot in Paris and worked with Josef Breuer , whose patient Anna O. coined the "talking cure". A flirtation with cocaine, a long self-analysis after his father's death (the engine of The Interpretation of Dreams , 1900), decades of jaw cancer, and finall

title: Social & General Psychology
text: Social & General Psychology One consolidated revision chapter for the whole domain: the foundational ("general") psychology of perception, attention, memory, learning, emotion, motivation, intelligence, cognition, personality, development, consciousness and stress, and the full social-psychology arc from research methods through social cognition, attribution, the self, attitudes, prejudice, attraction, influence, prosocial behaviour, aggression and groups, closing with the landmark experiments walked through and a fast A–Z glossary. Anchored to Baron & Branscombe's Social Psychology and standard general-psychology texts; every named effect, theorist, date, table, mnemonic and MCQ trap from both source sets is preserved. The dominant question type NIMHANS and MET test is which name goes with which effect , so the lookalike pairs are flagged throughout in trap boxes. Read it like a textbook, then drill the traps and glossary. In this book Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives Sensation & perception Attention Memory Learning Cognition: thinking, language & social cognition Emotion Motivation Intelligence Personality Developmental psychology Consciousness & sleep Stress, coping & health Social perception & attribution The self Attitudes & persuasion Stereotyping, prejudice & discrimination Attraction, relationships & love Social influence: conformity, compliance, obedience Prosocial behaviour (helping) Aggression Groups & individuals Landmark studies, walked through Schools & history of psychology The MCQ traps, collected Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Psychology as a science: methods & perspectives What the field claims. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others (Allport's classic definition). The key word is scientific : it settles questions by study, not intuition. The governing insight, repeated throughout, is the power of the situation : ordinary people help, conform, obey and aggress far more because of where they are and who is around than because of fixed traits. That theme, situation over disposition, returns in obedience (Milgram), bystander apathy (Latané & Darley) and attribution (the fundamental attribution error is precisely our failure to see it). The role of theory. A theory is an integrated set of principles that explains and predicts observed events. Good science runs a loop: a theory generates a falsifiable hypothesis ; a study tests it; results refine or refute it. A theory is never "proven", only supported or disconfirmed. The core research methods Method What you do Strength / limit Experimental Manipulate one factor (the independent variable, IV ), hold all else constant, measure the effect on the dependent variable, DV . Use random assignment to conditions. The only method that establishes cause and effect . Limit: artificiality, low external validity if over-controlled. Correlational Measure two or more variables as they naturally occur and see if they covary (correlation coefficient, −1 to +1). Good for real-world variables you cannot ethically manipulate. Limit: correlation ≠ causation (direction problem + third-variable problem). Survey Ask a representative sample questions to describe a population's attitudes/behaviour. Cheap, broad. Limit: sampling bias, wording effects, social-desirability responding. Systematic / naturalistic observation Watch and record behaviour as it occurs without intervening (e.g. counting jaywalkers). High realism. Limit: no control, observer effects, no causal claim. High-yield The IV is the cause you dial (the knob), the DV the effect you read off (the dial). Random assignment is what lets you claim the knob, not pre-existing differences between people, moved the dial; correlational work has no knob, so it cannot tell you which dial drives. A mediator is the mechanism between cause and effect, explaining why (frustration → anger → aggression: anger mediates). A moderator changes the strength or direction of a relationship, telling you when / for whom it holds (heat raises aggression more for provoked people). A meta-analysis statistically combines many studies to estimate the true effect size. Ethics, deception and replication Because the true purpose can change behaviour, social psychology often uses deception (a cover story), permitted only under strict safeguards: informed consent , the right to withdraw, minimising harm, and a thorough debriefing that reveals the true purpose and removes any after-effects. An Institutional Review Board / ethics committee must approve the study first. The field also takes its replication crisis seriously: a finding is trusted only when independent labs replicate it, which is why classics (Milgram, marshmallow studies) are now discussed alongside their replications and failures. The four perspectives Baron uses Perspective Core claim Cognitive To explain social behaviour, study how people think : notice, store, recall, interpret. The dominant modern lens (schemas, heuristics, attribution live here). Evolutionary Some tendencies (mate choice, helping kin, fear of strangers) were shaped by natural selection for survival/reproduction. Social neuroscience Links social behaviour to brain and biology (fMRI, hormones): amygdala in out-group fear, oxytocin in trust. Cultural / multicultural Many findings hold differently across cultures; must test whether an effect is universal or culture-bound (individualist vs collectivist). High-yield The researcher is also a thinker prone to the very biases the field studies, so methods (random assignment, double-blind procedures, pre-registration, replication) exist partly to fence out the researcher's expectancy bias / experimenter effects. NIMHANS asks methods crisply: name the only method that proves causation (experimental), say why correlation cannot (third-variable + directionality), and distinguish mediator (the why ) from moderator (t

title: Psychological Assessment & Testing
text: Psychological Assessment & Testing A psychological test is a measuring instrument, and like any instrument it must be (a) consistent and (b) accurate. Consistent = reliability . Accurate = validity . Everything in this chapter is either a way to estimate reliability, a way to estimate validity, a way to interpret scores against norms, or a real-world test built on those foundations. We measure things we cannot see directly (anxiety, intelligence, personality) by building instruments out of items, like a thermometer made of questions, then deciding things with them: special education, army fitness, diagnosis. This chapter locks the psychometric theory first, then the major intelligence, personality, projective, and clinical instruments, with every author, year, item count, scale, score range, and exam trap in one place. In this book Item analysis & test construction Reliability (the consistency story) Validity (the accuracy story) Norms & standard scores Intelligence theories & IQ mechanics Stanford-Binet family Wechsler family Raven’s Progressive Matrices Kaufman, Cattell CFIT & special-purpose scales Group & infant/developmental scales Indian intelligence tests IQ classification & intellectual disability Objective (self-report) personality tests Projective tests Adjustment, clinical & Indian inventories Aptitude, attitude & interest scales Psychiatric & cognitive rating scales Educational measurement basics Master reference tables & trap list 1. Item analysis & test construction Each test item is a single sensor reading. If a sensor is too easy (everyone passes) it tells us nothing; too hard (no one passes) it tells us nothing; and if it disagrees with the rest of the test, something is wrong with it. That is why every well-built test goes through item analysis. Difficulty index, p The difficulty index is the proportion who got an item right. p = (number correct) / (total attempting) , range 0 to 1. p = 0.50 is the sweet spot for a free-response item because it discriminates the most. For a 4-option MCQ the optimal p is ~0.625 , halfway between chance guessing (0.25) and ceiling (1.00). p above 0.80 = too easy; p below 0.20 = too hard. Both are revision candidates because they cannot separate strong from weak students. Discrimination index, D Do high-scorers on the whole test do better on this item than low-scorers? D = p_upper − p_lower , where p_upper = proportion correct in the top 27% of scorers and p_lower = proportion in the bottom 27%. Range −1 to +1. D above 0.40 = item agrees with the test, a good signal. D near zero = random noise; both groups perform alike. Negative D = the bottom group out-performed the top group: the item is mis-keyed, ambiguous, or has a trick strong test-takers over-think. Trap Read negative discrimination as a mis-keyed / flawed item to discard immediately , NOT as a merely “hard” item. This is asked every cycle. 2. Reliability (the consistency story) Reliability is not about whether a test is correct; it is about whether it is consistent . A bathroom scale that reads 75 kg every time is reliable even if your true weight is 70 (that is a validity problem). A scale bouncing between 60, 90, 80 is unreliable, full stop. If a test is unreliable you cannot trust any single score: the same person retested gives a different answer for reasons unrelated to the trait. You are measuring noise. Definition Classical Test Theory: Observed Score = True Score + Error . Reliability is the proportion of observed-score variance that is true variance, not error. A reliability of 0.80 says 80% signal, 20% noise. There are several reliability methods because there are several ways to think about “consistency”: Across time: test the same person twice (test-retest). Across forms: give two equivalent versions (parallel/alternate forms). Within one administration, across items: check items hang together (split-half, Cronbach alpha, KR-20). Across raters: check two judges agree (Cohen kappa for categorical, ICC for continuous). Test-retest (time stability) Give the test, give it again later, correlate the two scores. High correlation = stable over time. The standard window is two to four weeks . Too long and the trait itself can change (correlation drops, but the test is not at fault); too short and memory carryover inflates the correlation. Split-half + Spearman-Brown Give the test once, split into two halves (often odd vs even items), correlate the halves. By splitting you have halved the test length, and shorter tests are less reliable, so the raw split-half correlation under estimates full-test reliability. Spearman-Brown corrects this: r_full = 2 × r_half / (1 + r_half) . Example: r_half = 0.60 → r_full = 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75 . Always apply Spearman-Brown after any split. Cronbach alpha Imagine doing every possible split-half and averaging the result: that mean is Cronbach alpha. It is the most common internal-consistency measure for tests with multi-point (e.g. Likert) items. Alpha rises with item count, item homogeneity, and trait variance. Trap Alpha is NOT a measure of unidimensionality. A test can have high alpha and still measure two distinct constructs. The MET loves this. KR-20 (Kuder-Richardson 20) When items are right-or-wrong (dichotomous, 1/0), Cronbach alpha simplifies to KR-20: same idea, adapted for 0/1 items. So “30-item right-wrong vocabulary test, one administration, which reliability?” → KR-20 . Inter-rater: kappa and ICC When humans do the scoring (Rorschach protocols, clinical interviews, essay grades), reliability is about rater agreement. Cohen kappa for categorical decisions (OCD: yes/no), corrects for chance agreement. Kappa ≥ 0.81 = almost-perfect; 0.61–0.80 = substantial. Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous ratings (a 0–100 severity score); different ICC forms exist depending on whether raters are random or fixed. Trap Kappa is NOT an internal-consistency measure. If a question describes a one-administration internal-structure tes

title: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics
text: Therapy, Counselling & Ethics One consolidated chapter for everything the MET / NIMHANS paper tests on treatment: the learning principles that behaviour therapy is built on, the major schools of psychotherapy & counselling (Sharf's frame, school by school, with the third-wave and integrative models folded in), the common therapeutic factors that cut across schools, and professional ethics . Each concept lives in exactly one place. The exam tests four moves: name the theory from its claim; pin the theory to its founder; pin the named technique to its theory; and tell rival theories apart, because that is where the distractor always hides. Learn every technique in its contrast pair . In this book Learning & conditioning: the foundation How to read any theory (the master frame) Psychodynamic approaches Humanistic & existential approaches Behavioural & cognitive approaches Constructivist, feminist & systemic approaches Third-wave, integrative & specialised models Group therapy (Yalom) Common factors & the therapeutic frame Indications quick-map (what to recommend) Professional ethics Master trap list, rosters & glossary High-yield The single most-tested skill is telling near-identical pairs apart: REBT (Ellis) vs Cognitive Therapy (Beck) , systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) vs flooding , ERP (OCD) vs EMDR (trauma) , cognitive triad (Beck) vs ABC (Ellis) , DBT modules (4) vs ACT hexaflex (6) , and the four family-therapy founders (Bowen / Minuchin / Haley / Satir). And in learning: shaping vs chaining , fading vs extinction , VR vs VI , latent vs insight learning . Master these pairs and most of the section answers itself. 1. Learning & conditioning: the foundation of behaviour therapy Behaviour therapy is applied learning theory, so the vocabulary below is tested both as 1-mark definition traps and as the mechanism behind clinical techniques. Read this orientation once: classical (Pavlovian) conditioning is about stimulus pairings ; operant (Skinnerian) conditioning is about consequences shaping voluntary behaviour ; priming is about one stimulus making a later one easier to process ; and habituation / sensitization are non-associative (a single stimulus, no pairing). When a question mixes the families, the answer is almost always the term whose family matches the stem. Family Terms inside Classical (Pavlovian) phenomena Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, habituation, sensitization Operant (Skinnerian) shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant reinforcement schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social learning Latent learning (Tolman), insight learning (Köhler), observational learning (Bandura) Implicit / cognitive priming Priming (semantic, perceptual, affective) 1.1 Operant shaping tools — shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Shaping (Skinner): reinforcing successive approximations of a target behaviour the organism does not yet emit . Train a rat to press a lever by reinforcing facing it, then approaching, then touching, then pressing. The defining feature is that the reinforcement criterion changes across trials . Clinically: skill acquisition, autism intervention. Chaining : linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours into a longer chain, where each behaviour is the discriminative stimulus (S D ) for the next and only the final link is reinforced (brushing teeth: pick up brush → wet → paste → brush → rinse → put away). Forward chaining teaches step 1 first; backward chaining teaches the last step first, so the learner always reaches the reinforcer at the natural endpoint (often preferred clinically). Used heavily in ABA / ADL skills training. Prompting : an added antecedent stimulus (verbal, gestural, physical, modelled, visual) that helps the learner emit the right response in the presence of the natural cue. Prompt hierarchy, most → least intrusive: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual/positional . "Least-to-most" vs "most-to-least" prompting are classic vignette distractors. Fading : gradually removing the prompt while transferring stimulus control to the natural cue (teach "ball": full model "say ball" → partial "say buh…" → just holding up the ball). Trap Shaping vs chaining: shaping builds a new behaviour ; chaining links existing behaviours . Fading vs extinction: fading removes the prompt (an antecedent) and transfers stimulus control; extinction removes the reinforcer / UCS and eliminates the behaviour. Prompts are antecedents; reinforcement is a consequence — that distinction has been tested directly. 1.2 Classical conditioning phenomena Extinction : reduction and disappearance of a conditioned response when reinforcement (operant) or the UCS (classical) is no longer presented — Pavlov's dog stops salivating to the unpaired bell; the ignored tantrum fades. Watch for the extinction burst : a temporary increase in frequency/intensity right after reinforcement is withdrawn, before decline. Extinction does not erase learning. Spontaneous recovery : reappearance of a previously extinguished response after a rest period, with no new conditioning trials — proving extinction is suppression, not unlearning . The recovered response is typically weaker , and re-extinction is faster the second time (savings effect). Distinguish from reinstatement (re-emergence after UCS-alone presentation) and renewal (re-emergence in a new context). Generalization vs discrimination. Generalization = responding similarly to stimuli that resemble the CS / S D (Little Albert, conditioned by Watson & Rayner to fear a white rat, also feared a white rabbit, cotton wool, a Santa beard). The generalization gradient : response strength drops with distance from the original CS. Discrimination = responding only to the specific stimulus, taught by differential reinforcement (reinforce in presence of S D , withhold for S Δ ). One-liner: generalization is the default; discrimination is trained. Failure to discriminate underlies many phobias. Note: stimul

title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics One consolidated, exam-ready treatment built from A. K. Singh ( Tests, Measurements and Research Methods in Behavioural Sciences — strong on measurement, test construction, item analysis) and Coolican ( Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology — design, the logic of inference, which test to run). Read the prose and understand why each statistic does what it does; the tables are then just reminders. Trap boxes flag the exact confusions MCQs are built on. Coverage runs MET 2026 depth with NIMHANS M.Phil clinical extensions where the entrance pushes harder. In this book Research design & methodology Variables, confounds, mediation & moderation Validity & threats in a study Sampling Levels of measurement Reliability & validity in measurement Scaling (attitude measurement) Item analysis & test construction Descriptive statistics Distributions, z-scores & the Central Limit Theorem The logic of inference Parametric tests Non-parametric tests Correlation, regression & special coefficients Degrees of freedom — from scratch Qualitative & mixed methods Clinical trials & reporting standards Research ethics Decision table: which test do I use? Collected MCQ traps Worked intuition Fast glossary Research design & methodology Only an experiment (manipulate the IV and randomly assign participants) can establish causation, because randomisation balances out unknown confounds. Everything else can describe and relate, but not prove cause. Experimental hierarchy — by degree of control Design Manipulate IV? Random assignment? Control group? Internal validity True experimental (RCT) Yes Yes Yes High — gold standard for causation Quasi-experimental Yes No (intact/pre-existing groups: classes, wards) Usually yes Moderate — confounds remain Pre-experimental Loosely No Often none Low — e.g. one-group pretest-posttest; many threats Non-experimental (correlational) No — — No causal claim Between- vs within-subjects (and factorial) Between-subjects (independent groups): different people in each condition. No carry-over, but between-person variability is noise and groups may differ to start. Within-subjects (repeated measures): the same people in every condition. Each is their own control, so it is powerful and economical, but risks order/carry-over effects (practice, fatigue) — fixed by counterbalancing . Factorial: two or more IVs crossed, so you can test their interaction (a 2×2 has 4 cells). Specific designs to know Pretest-posttest control group: the classic two-group RCT. Posttest-only control group: avoids pretest sensitisation entirely. Solomon four-group: combines both. Two groups get a pretest, two do not; half of each get treatment. It detects and separates pretest sensitisation (the interaction of pretest and treatment) from the treatment effect itself. Resource-heavy but the most rigorous design for ruling out testing effects. Crossover design: every subject receives both conditions in different order. Single-case designs (ABA, ABAB, multiple baseline): used in behaviour analysis. Non-experimental & epidemiological designs Correlational: measure variables as they are and relate them; no manipulation, so no causal claim. Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time; reports prevalence . Cheap, but cannot show temporality or change. Longitudinal: the same people followed over time; can show change and causal order, but slow, costly, and bleeds participants through attrition . Cohort study: follow exposed and unexposed groups forward in time; reports relative risk . Case-control: start with cases and controls, look back at exposure; reports odds ratio . Case study: deep dive into one person/unit (rich, hypothesis-generating, not generalisable). Observational: watch behaviour in situ — naturalistic vs structured; participant vs non-participant; covert vs overt. Controlling confounds Randomisation — random assignment spreads unknown confounds evenly across groups (the most powerful control). Counterbalancing — vary the order of conditions across subjects to cancel order effects in within-subjects designs. Matching — pair subjects on a key variable (e.g. IQ) before assigning, removing that variable as a confound. Single-blind (participant unaware of condition) and double-blind (participant and experimenter/assessor unaware) — control expectancy and experimenter effects. Trap Random sampling vs random assignment . Random sampling = who gets into the study (drives external validity/generalisability). Random assignment = which condition they go to (drives internal validity/causation). A study can have one without the other. Trap Counterbalancing (fixes order effects in within-subjects designs) vs matching (controls a specific confound variable in between-subjects designs). Variables, confounds, mediation & moderation Independent variable (IV): what the experimenter manipulates or groups by — the presumed cause. Dependent variable (DV): the measured outcome — the presumed effect. Control variable: a variable deliberately held constant. Confound: a variable tied to both the IV and the DV, creating a spurious link and offering a rival explanation. Controlled by randomisation, matching, or statistical adjustment. Extraneous variable: any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV; it becomes a confound only if it also correlates with the IV. Operationalisation: defining a fuzzy construct in concrete, measurable terms (e.g. "anxiety" = score on the GAD-7). Bad operationalisation sinks construct validity. Mediator vs moderator — the high-frequency trap Both are "third variables," but they do opposite jobs: Mediator explains HOW / WHY the IV affects the DV — the mechanism in the causal chain: IV → Mediator → DV . Stress → cortisol → poorer immunity: cortisol mediates. If you control the mediator, the IV–DV link weakens or vanishes. Tested with Baron-Kenny steps or Hayes PROCESS. Moderator changes WHEN / FOR WHOM / HOW STRONGLY the IV affects the DV — it alters the strength or directio

title: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction
text: Unit 3 – Psychometrics & Test Construction The science of measuring the mind: how a psychological test is built, scored and judged. This book teaches the four scales of measurement, the anatomy of a good item and how to analyse one, the full reliability and validity families with their formulae, the meaning of norms and standard scores, and the major families of real tests – intelligence, neuropsychological, personality, interest and aptitude – together with where and why each is applied (education, occupation, military, clinic). It closes with the M.Phil-style exam questions folded in. Sourced from Rodrick Prashanth's Unit 3 decks (Areas of testing, Applications of testing, Interest & aptitude tests, Item writing & item analysis, Reliability/Validity/Norms, Scales) and the M.Phil question bank, deepened to NIMHANS clinical depth. In this book Scales of measurement & attitude scaling Item writing & item analysis Reliability Validity Norms & standard scores Areas of testing: intelligence & creativity Areas of testing: neuropsychological assessment Areas of testing: personality assessment Interest & aptitude tests Applications of testing Structured personality-test construction M.Phil exam questions 1. Scales of measurement & attitude scaling The one idea. Before you can measure a psychological attribute you must decide what kind of number you are assigning. S. S. Stevens' four levels of measurement – nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio – form a ladder: each rung adds one mathematical property and therefore unlocks one more legitimate statistic. Choosing the wrong scale is the commonest hidden error in test interpretation: you cannot average ranks, and you cannot say one IQ is "twice" another. The four levels Level Allows categorising Allows ranking (order) Equal intervals True (absolute) zero Example Nominal Yes – – – Diagnosis codes, gender, jersey numbers Ordinal Yes Yes – – Rank in class, Likert agree/disagree, race finishing order Interval Yes Yes Yes – Temperature in °C, IQ scores, calendar years Ratio Yes Yes Yes Yes Reaction time, weight, number of errors, age Why each property matters. A nominal scale only labels – the numbers are names, so the only legitimate operations are counting frequencies and the mode. An ordinal scale adds order, so you can take a median and percentiles, but the gaps between ranks are unequal (the difference between 1st and 2nd is not the same "amount" as between 2nd and 3rd). An interval scale adds equal spacing, so you can finally add, subtract and compute a mean and standard deviation; but its zero is arbitrary (0°C is not "no temperature"). A ratio scale adds a true zero meaning total absence of the attribute, so ratios become meaningful: 40 errors is genuinely twice 20 errors. High-yield Memorise the ladder of properties: N ominal = categorise; O rdinal = + order; I nterval = + equal intervals; R atio = + true zero. Each level permits everything the levels below it permit, plus one more. Mnemonic NOIR (French for "black") gives the order of increasing power: N ominal → O rdinal → I nterval → R atio. Trap Interval vs ratio. Both have equal intervals; only ratio has a true zero. IQ and Celsius temperature are interval – an IQ of 0 does not mean "no intelligence," so you cannot say IQ 140 is "twice as smart" as IQ 70. Kelvin temperature and reaction time are ratio. Attitude scales Attitude measurement applies these principles to subjective opinion. The deck names four classic formats: Scale Structure Key feature Likert scale Five ordered responses on an agree/disagree or approve/disapprove continuum (e.g. Strongly Agree → Strongly Disagree) Summative; the most widely used attitude format. Strictly ordinal, though usually treated as interval in practice. Guttman scale Items ordered by intensity; a respondent who endorses one statement also endorses all milder statements on the same continuum Cumulative / unidimensional. "Check the statement from each group that is most true of you." Semantic differential (Osgood) A set of bipolar adjective scales (Healthy – Unhealthy, Pleasant – Unpleasant) anchoring a 7-point line Measures the subjective meaning and affective reaction to a concept; classic dimensions are Evaluation, Potency, Activity. Stapel scale A single ( unipolar ) adjective with 10 categories from −5 to +5, no neutral zero A one-adjective alternative to the semantic differential; forces a direction. Trap Semantic differential vs Stapel. Semantic differential uses bipolar adjective pairs with a neutral midpoint; the Stapel scale uses a single (unipolar) adjective on a −5 to +5 line with no neutral point . Guttman is cumulative (endorsing a strong item implies endorsing the weaker ones); Likert is summative. 2. Item writing & item analysis The one idea. A test is only as good as its items. Item construction is part craft (writing clear, unambiguous questions) and part statistics (keeping the items that actually discriminate among people and dropping those that do not). Item analysis is the set of empirical methods for that pruning. Guidelines for item writing (DeVellis, 2012) Define clearly what you want to measure before writing anything. Generate an item pool larger than the final test, so weak items can be discarded. Avoid exceptionally long items – length adds reading load, not information. Keep reading difficulty appropriate to the intended respondents. Avoid "double-barrelled" items that pack two ideas into one statement ("I feel anxious and depressed") – the respondent cannot answer cleanly. Mix positively and negatively worded items to counter acquiescence (yea-saying) response bias. Item formats & correction for guessing The dichotomous format scores an item 0 or 1 (true/false, right/wrong). The polytomous format gives each item more than two alternatives. In a multiple-choice item, the incorrect alternatives are called distractors ; it is usually best to write three or four good distractors per item, and three distractors are about as effectiv

title: Unit 4 — Biological Basis of Behaviour
text: Unit 4 — Biological Basis of Behaviour The full biological machinery of behaviour, built from the ground up: how a single neuron is wired and how it fires, the chemical languages it speaks, how those neurons are assembled into the brain and the rest of the nervous system, and the circuits that drive movement, every sense, hunger and thirst, emotion, the hormones and glands, sleep, heredity, and the methods scientists use to take the whole system apart. Anchored to Carlson & Pinel-level neuroscience and prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology. In this book Neurons: structure, types & the neural impulse Neurotransmitters Structure & functions of the nervous system Divisions of the nervous system (CNS, PNS, ANS) Divisions of the human brain & their functions The motor (sensorimotor) system Sensory systems — vision Auditory & somatosensory systems Chemical & vestibular senses Hunger & thirst Emotions Hormonal regulation of behaviour The glandular (endocrine) system Sleep & biological clocks Genetics & behaviour Invasive & non-invasive research methods 1. Neurons: structure, types & the neural impulse The neuron is the information-processing and information-transmitting element of the nervous system. Everything else in this unit is about how neurons are built, how they fire, how they talk to each other, and how billions of them are wired into the brain. Master the neuron first and the rest of the unit becomes mechanism rather than memorisation. The four regions of a neuron Part What it is Function Cell body (soma) Contains the nucleus and most of the cell's life-support machinery; shape varies widely between neuron types. Keeps the cell alive; integrates incoming signals. Dendrites Branching projections; the major receivers of messages. Receive neural messages transmitted across the synapse (the small gap between a terminal button and the dendrite). Axon A long slender tube, often myelinated; works like an electrical cord. Carries the action potential away from the soma toward the terminal buttons. Terminal buttons Little knobs at the ends of axon branches. When an action potential arrives, they secrete a chemical messenger, the neurotransmitter . Definition Action potential — a brief electrical event that starts at the axon end nearest the cell body (the axon initial segment) and travels toward the terminal buttons. It is the basic message the axon carries. Axoplasmic transport Terminal buttons need molecules that can only be made in the soma, so substances are moved along the axon along microtubule "tracks". This is an active process, separate from the action potential. Anterograde transport (soma → terminal): accomplished by the motor protein kinesin , which "walks" along microtubules carrying cargo. Remarkably fast, up to 500 mm/day. Retrograde transport (terminal → soma): accomplished by the protein dynein ; about half as fast as anterograde transport. Types (classes) of neurons Multipolar neuron — more than two processes extending from the cell body (the most common type). Unipolar neuron — one process extending from the cell body (e.g. sensory dorsal-root neurons). Bipolar neuron — two processes (e.g. in the retina). Interneurons — neurons with a short axon or no axon at all; they integrate neural activity within a single brain structure . Neuroanatomical gross structures Composed of In the CNS In the PNS Mostly cell bodies Nuclei Ganglia Mostly axons Tracts Nerves Trap Cell-body clusters are nuclei in the CNS but ganglia in the PNS; axon bundles are tracts in the CNS but nerves in the PNS. The paper loves to swap these. Glial cells There are roughly equal numbers of neurons and glia in the human brain. Four kinds matter: Oligodendrocytes — paddle-shaped processes that wrap myelin around axons in the CNS . A single oligodendrocyte produces up to 50 segments of myelin. Myelin is 80% lipid, 20% protein and speeds axonal conduction. Schwann cells — perform myelination in the PNS ; one Schwann cell wraps one axon entirely. After PNS injury they digest dead axons and form cylinders that guide axonal regrowth, which is why PNS axons regenerate and CNS axons largely do not (the difference is in the supporting cells, not the axons). Microglia — the brain's immune cells; multiply after injury, engulf debris and dead cells, and trigger inflammation. Astrocytes — the largest glia, star-shaped; provide physical support, clean up debris, supply chemicals neurons need, gate substances between blood and CNS neurons, and contract/relax blood vessels to match local blood-flow demand. The resting membrane potential Recorded with intracellular microelectrodes, the inside of a resting neuron sits at about −70 mV relative to the outside. The neuron is then said to be polarized . Four ions matter: organic anions (A−), chloride (Cl−), sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+). At rest there is more Na+ outside the cell and more K+ inside; organic anions are trapped inside (too big to cross the membrane). Na+ feels strong pressure to enter from both the concentration gradient and electrostatic (electrical) pressure, but Na+ channels are mostly closed at rest. Balance is held by: The sodium–potassium pump — actively pushes 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in . More open K+ channels than Na+ channels, but few K+ actually leave because the negative interior holds them in. Mnemonic Resting potential = "bow and arrow." The membrane has done its work in advance (taut bowstring) so the neuron can fire strongly and rapidly the instant it is stimulated. The action potential, step by step Depolarization to threshold: a stimulus reduces polarization toward zero. If it crosses the threshold of excitation (about −65 mV), voltage-dependent Na+ channels open wide. Rising phase: Na+ rushes in explosively (driven by diffusion + electrostatic pressure). Membrane potential shoots from −70 mV to about +40 mV , overshooting zero to a reversed polarity. Peak (~1 ms): Na+ channels become refractory (blocked) and cannot reopen until

title: Unit 5 — Attention, Perception & Memory
text: Unit 5 — Attention, Perception & Memory The cognitive core of the syllabus, built from Solso-style cognitive psychology and the classic learning systems: how attention selects a trickle from the flood of sensation (Broadbent, Treisman, Deutsch-Norman, Kahneman), how organisms learn by association and consequence (Pavlov, Skinner, Thorndike, Guthrie, Hull, Spence, Tolman, Bandura), how memory encodes, stores and retrieves (Atkinson-Shiffrin, Baddeley, Tulving, Craik & Lockhart), why we forget (decay, interference, retrieval failure, repression, motivated forgetting), and how the visual system builds a stable percept of form, depth and pattern (Gestalt, template/feature/prototype, Biederman, Selfridge) under uncertainty (signal detection theory). Each model is taught for its mechanism and its exam relevance, with theorists, dates and the traps that examiners love. In this book Attention: forms & models Classical & instrumental conditioning Fundamental learning theories Hull, discrimination, latent & observational learning Memory processes & systems Theories of forgetting Perception: approaches, illusions & pattern recognition Distance & depth perception Form perception Signal detection theory 1. Attention: forms & models Solso defines attention as "the concentration of mental effort on sensory or mental events." More fully (Duncan 1999; Motter 1999; Posner & Fernandez-Duque 1999), attention is the means by which we actively process a limited amount of information from the enormous amount available through our senses, stored memories and other cognitive processes. It is a concentration of mental activity that includes both conscious and unconscious processes. Definition Attention = selective concentration of finite mental resources on some stimuli at the expense of others. The central problem it solves is that the sensory world delivers far more information than the system can fully process. Forms of attention Divided attention — attending to several messages simultaneously, responding to each as needed. Performance typically suffers unless the tasks are well practised; practice alters the limits of attentional capacity. Selective attention — focusing on one task/stimulus while disregarding the others. It simplifies our lives because attentional capacity is limited. The Stroop effect is the classic demonstration of the cost of selecting against a dominant response. Sustained attention (vigilance) — the maintenance of selective attention to infrequent events over long periods. There is a reliable vigilance decrement : performance declines as time-on-task wears on, affected by the neurological and physiological state of the person. Filter / bottleneck models — early selection Everyday phenomena like the cocktail-party effect (you can follow one conversation in a noisy room, yet your own name spoken across the room captures you) are explained by filter theories . Early-selection means attention operates early in the information-processing sequence: only one source (the attended one) reaches meaningful processing; unattended information is actively filtered/blocked before it can compete for scarce higher-order resources. Broadbent's switch (filter) model (1958) Broadbent proposed a simple on-off switch : attention directs processing to one input channel, which is fully analysed for meaning and made available to consciousness. Because the switch is all-or-none, additional messages are completely blocked. Attention is attracted and maintained by sensory/physical attributes of messages (e.g., the voice qualities at a party). The switch does not allow unconscious processing: unattended signals left in sensory memory rapidly decay and never receive the extra processing needed for longer-term retention. A subject should therefore be able to report only the physical features of the unattended message, not its meaning. Cherry's dichotic listening & shadowing (1953) Colin Cherry created a paradigm to test early selection: dichotic listening (different messages to each ear at once) combined with shadowing (repeating one message aloud as it occurs). Shadowing forces the subject onto one message so they cannot switch. Findings that strain the strict switch: when the meaning of the shadowed sentence switches to the non-shadowed ear, shadowing is disrupted (Treisman 1960) — the subject follows the meaning rather than the physical cue of ear location, allowing determination of when attention shifts. Treisman's attenuator model (1964) Anne Treisman proposed a more flexible early-selection theory using a different mechanical metaphor: instead of an off/on switch, attention works like an attenuator (regulator) that allows gradations of energy through. Most of the attended message passes through; some unattended information may also reach the level of pattern recognition. Attention thus becomes a matter of degree . Physical cues tune the attenuator, but it can also be influenced by the meaning of previously analysed material, so control is exerted by both sensory and semantic information. It remains an early-selection theory because filtering still occurs prior to full meaningful analysis; partial analysis of all signals occurs. Late-selection models — Deutsch & Deutsch (1963), Norman (1968) Late-selection models propose that all information is recognised: every sensory input activates its corresponding meaning in long-term memory, but attention then selects among the activated meanings , allowing only a limited amount to reach consciousness. Selective attention operates on response output , not input. The non-shadowed information, requiring no overt response, may be rapidly forgotten before testing. The activation of meaning is unconscious; awareness itself is treated as a response . The activity decays quickly unless the activated meaning is selected for conscious processing.
