title: Unit 6 — Intelligence, Creativity & Thinking
text: Unit 6 — Intelligence, Creativity & Thinking The higher cognition syllabus from first principles: what intelligence is and the great factor theories that try to carve it (Spearman's g through CHC), how intelligence is tested, what creativity is and how it is produced and nurtured, and then the machinery of thought itself: how we form concepts and categories, how we reason and where reasoning breaks, how we solve problems and get stuck, and how we make decisions and judge probability with the heuristics Kahneman & Tversky exposed. Built to NIMHANS/MET clinical-psychology depth, reproducing every named theorist, model and term in the source notes. In this book Intelligence: definitions & theories Creativity Nurturing creativity at the workplace Thinking Concepts & categorization Reasoning Problem solving Factors influencing problem solving Decision making Decision-making styles Heuristics in decision making 1. Intelligence: definitions & theories The one problem behind the whole field. Everyone agrees intelligence exists; nobody agrees what it is . So the topic is really two arguments: (a) how to define intelligence, and (b) how it is structured : one general ability, a handful of group factors, or many independent ones. The factor theories below are best learned as a single conversation in which each thinker reacts to the last. The classic definitions (know the one-liners) Theorist Intelligence is… Spearman (1904, 1923) a general ability involving mainly the eduction of relations and correlates . Binet & Simon (1905) the ability to judge well, understand well, and reason well. Terman (1916) the capacity to form concepts and grasp their significance. Pintner (1921) the ability to adapt adequately to relatively new situations in life. Thorndike (1921) the power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact. Wechsler (1939) the aggregate or global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with the environment. Piaget (1972) the superior forms of organization/equilibrium of cognitive structuring used for adaptation to the environment. Sternberg (1985) the capacity to automatize information processing and emit contextually appropriate behavior in response to novelty. Eysenck (1986) error-free transmission of information through the cortex. Gardner (1986) the skill to solve problems or fashion products valued within one or more cultural settings. Ceci (1994) multiple innate abilities that develop, fail to develop, or atrophy depending on motivation and exposure. High-yield Match the phrase to the man: eduction of relations = Spearman; judge/understand/reason well = Binet & Simon; aggregate/global capacity = Wechsler; error-free cortical transmission = Eysenck; fashion products valued in a culture = Gardner. Galton and sensory keenness (the false start) The first theories came from the "Brass Instruments" era at the turn of the 20th century. Galton and Cattell promoted a sensory keenness theory: smarter people have sharper senses and faster reactions. This proved a psychometric dead end . (Curiously, Jensen (1980) later reported reaction-time and movement-time indices correlating as high as .50 with traditional IQ tests, partly rehabilitating the idea of mental speed.) Spearman and the g factor Charles Spearman proposed that intelligence consists of two kinds of factors: a single general factor g plus numerous specific factors (s1, s2, s3…). To test this he helped invent factor analysis : a statistical technique to discern how many underlying factors must exist to account for the observed correlations among many tests. Performance on any homogeneous test is determined mainly by two influences: g (pervasive) and s (specific to that test). Because s differs for every test and is usually weaker than g, Spearman cared little about it. Spearman (1923) held that individual differences in g show up in three principles of cognition : Apprehension of experience Eduction of relations (given two ideas, find the relation between them) Eduction of correlates (given an idea and a relation, find the matching idea) Eduction simply means the process of figuring things out. The hardest problem for his two-factor theory was the stubborn existence of group factors (clusters bigger than s but smaller than g), which the next thinkers seized on. Definition g = a single, pervasive general intelligence loading on all cognitive tasks. Factor analysis = the statistical tool Spearman built to find the latent factors behind a correlation matrix. Thurstone and the Primary Mental Abilities (PMAs) L. L. Thurstone (1931) refined factor analysis to search correlation matrices for group factors and concluded intelligence is not one thing but about a dozen relatively independent Primary Mental Abilities : Verbal Comprehension (best measure: vocabulary; also reading comprehension, verbal analogies) Word Fluency (anagrams; quickly naming words in a category) Number (speed/accuracy of simple arithmetic) Space (visualizing a 3-D object rotated or disassembled) Associative Memory (rote paired-associate learning) Perceptual Speed (clerical checking of visual detail) Inductive Reasoning (finding a rule, e.g. number-series completion) P. E. Vernon (1950) reconciled Spearman and Thurstone with a hierarchical group-factor theory : g sits at the top; below it two major group factors, verbal-educational (v:ed) and practical-mechanical-spatial-physical (k:m) ; below those, minor group factors resembling Thurstone's PMAs; specific factors at the bottom. Trap Spearman = one general factor (g + specifics). Thurstone = many coequal group factors (the PMAs), no dominant g. Vernon = a hierarchy that contains both (g on top, group factors beneath). Cattell–Horn–Carroll: fluid & crystallised, then CHC Raymond Cattell (1941, 1971) split g into two broad abilities: Fluid intelligence (Gf) : on-the-spot reasoning independent of acquired knowledge: drawing inferences, forming concepts, generating and testing hypothes

title: Unit 7 — Personality, Emotion & Motivation
text: Unit 7 — Personality, Emotion & Motivation The whole of personality from first principles — the psychodynamic founders (Freud, Jung, Adler) and the neo-Freudians, the trait and type measurers (Allport, Cattell's 16PF, Eysenck's PEN, the Big Five and beyond), the humanistic-existential self (Maslow, Rogers, May), and the behavioural / social-cognitive theorists (Bandura, Rotter, Mischel, Seligman, Kelly) — then how personality is assessed, and finally the affective and developmental engine behind it: theories of emotion, stress and the GAS, theories of motivation, attachment and emotional-social development, and the exploratory/sensation-seeking drive. Built from the Unit 7 source decks and taught to NIMHANS/MET depth, losing no named theorist or term. In this book Freud & the psychoanalytic approach Neo-Freudians: Jung, Adler, Horney, ego & object relations Erikson & lifespan identity Trait & type approaches Humanistic: Maslow & Rogers Existential: Rollo May Behavioural & social-cognitive: Bandura, Rotter, Mischel Cognitive approaches: Kelly, Lewin, Seligman, Kohlberg Assessment of personality Emotion & its physiology; theories of emotion Stress, the GAS & conflict Theories of motivation Emotional & social development Attachment Exploratory behaviour, curiosity & sensation seeking Fast glossary (A–Z) 1. Freud & the psychoanalytic approach The one idea. Freud saw the psychological world as a series of opposing tensions (for example the tension between selfishness and society). Underlying every tension were inner pressures that strive for relief. The motor of the whole system is instinct : the German term is Trieb — a driving force or impulse. Instincts are the basic elements of personality, the motivating forces that drive behaviour and determine its direction. Instincts and motivation Life instincts (Eros). Serve the survival of the individual and the species by satisfying needs for food, water, air and sex. They are oriented toward growth and development. The psychic energy of the life instincts is the libido (Latin for desire/lust). Cathexis. The libido can be attached to, or invested in, objects — Freud called this cathexis . Death instincts (Thanatos). In opposition to the life instincts, Freud postulated a destructive/death instinct. One component is the aggressive drive — the wish to die, turned outward against objects other than the self. Levels of personality (the topographic model) Level What it holds Conscious All sensations and experiences in immediate awareness. Preconscious / subconscious The storehouse of memories that can be brought to awareness. Unconscious The most important level and the major portion of personality; holds instincts, drives, desires and emotionally charged memories. The structure of the mind (the structural model) Id — operates on the pleasure principle ; strives solely to satisfy desires and reduce inner tension. It can only act through reflex or through wish-fulfilling hallucinatory/fantasy experience, which Freud called primary-process thought . Ego — based on the reality principle ; the structure that develops to deal with the real world using perception, recognition, judgement and memory ( secondary-process thought ). Superego — based on the morality principle ; represents society's demands. Through praise/punishment children learn good and bad: punished behaviours form the conscience ; praised behaviours form the ego-ideal . When the ego and especially the superego do not do their job, elements of the id slip out as parapraxes — mistakes that reveal the unconscious. Freudian slips (errors in speech or writing) are more common when a person is tired or distracted, because defences are down and unconscious impulses surface. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Erogenous zone / conflict Fixation outcome Oral 0–1 Mouth; pleasure from sucking; id dominant Oral-incorporative (optimism, dependency) vs oral-aggressive/sadistic (pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness) from painful teething Anal 1–3 Toilet training interferes with gratification from defecation Anal-aggressive (hostile, sadistic) vs anal-retentive (stubborn, stingy, hoarding, rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate) Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus/Electra complex; castration anxiety; superego develops Phallic character — strong narcissism Latency 5–puberty Sublimation of the sex instinct — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Sex-role identity, adult social relationships Genital type — finds satisfaction in love and work (work = acceptable sublimation of id impulses) Definition Fixation. An arresting of part of the libido at an earlier psychosexual stage because of excessive frustration or gratification, leaving a characteristic adult personality pattern. Anxiety and the defence mechanisms For Freud, anxiety is a feeling of fear and dread without an obvious cause. He proposed three types: reality anxiety (fear of tangible dangers), neurotic anxiety (id–ego conflict), and moral anxiety (id–superego conflict). When anxiety builds, the ego deploys defence mechanisms : Defence What it does Repression Unconscious denial of the existence of something that causes anxiety Denial Denying an external threat or traumatic event Reaction formation Expressing an id impulse that is the opposite of the true one Projection Attributing a disturbing impulse to someone else Regression Retreating to an earlier, less frustrating period and acting childishly Rationalization Reinterpreting behaviour to make it more acceptable, less threatening Displacement Shifting id impulses from a threatening/unavailable object to an available substitute Sublimation Diverting instinctual energy into socially acceptable behaviours Mnemonic Three anxieties map to the three conflicts: Reality = external world; Neurotic = id vs ego; Moral = id vs superego. "RNM = world, ego, conscience." 2. Neo-Freudians: Jung, Adler, Horney, ego & object relations Carl Jung — analytical psychology Jung divided the psyche into three parts: Cons

title: Unit 8 — Social Psychology
text: Unit 8 — Social Psychology How the presence, behaviour and existence of other people shape what we think, feel and do: the field's history and grand theories, how we read other people, how groups push us into conformity, obedience and compliance, what happens inside groups, how leaders lead, why we help and why we harm, the roots of prejudice and intergroup conflict, and how all of it is applied to health, the law and the environment. Built file-by-file from the Rodrick Prashanth source decks and deepened to NIMHANS / MET clinical-psychology depth, preserving every named theorist, study, term and proposition. In this book History of social psychology Theories of social psychology Social perception Group & social influence Group dynamics Leadership styles Prosocial behaviour Aggression Theories of intergroup relationship Applying social psychology 1. History of social psychology The one idea. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the actual, imagined or implied presence of others influences an individual's thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Its history is a chain of named "firsts" and named "founders", and the paper loves to test who did what, in what year. The foundation (late 19th to early 20th century) Figure Year Contribution Norman Triplett 1897–1898 Credited with the first research article in social psychology . He noticed cyclists raced faster against others than against a clock, and designed a careful controlled experiment to study it. This is the origin of social facilitation . Max Ringelmann 1880s (published 1913) Found individuals performed worse on simple tasks such as rope-pulling when working with others. This is the origin of social loafing (the "Ringelmann effect"). William McDougall 1908 Published an early social psychology textbook; helps establish the field. Edward Ross 1908 American who published a founding social psychology text the same year. Floyd Allport 1924 His textbook is taken as establishing social psychology as a distinct experimental field. Trap Triplett = social facilitation (first article, 1897–98). Ringelmann = social loafing (1880s, published 1913). Don't swap them. Establishing the field as a discipline is attributed to McDougall (1908), Ross (1908) and Floyd Allport (1924). 1930s–1950s: the field finds its problems 1936: Gordon Allport (younger brother of Floyd, the 1924 textbook author) and others formed the Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues (SPSSI) . Muzafer Sherif published groundbreaking experimental research on social influence (the autokinetic-effect norm-formation studies). Kurt Lewin fled the Nazis and emigrated to the US in the early 1930s. His central contribution: behaviour is a function of the interaction between the person and the environment (the interactionist perspective ), often written B = f(P, E) . 1950s: Gordon Allport (1954) published The Nature of Prejudice . Solomon Asch (1951) demonstrated how willing people are to conform to an obviously wrong majority. Leon Festinger introduced two landmark theories: social comparison (1954, how people learn about themselves by comparing to others) and cognitive dissonance (1957, how attitudes change through one's own behaviour). 1960s–1990s: crisis and pluralism Stanley Milgram's obedience research (early/mid 1960s) linked the post-WWII era to the coming era of social revolution, showing individuals' vulnerability to the destructive commands of authority. Strong disagreements of the period (the "crisis of social psychology") were largely a reaction against the dominant method of the day, the laboratory experiment . Mid-1970s onward = an era of pluralism: laboratory and field experiments used side by side; a "hot" perspective (emotion and motivation) alongside a "cold" perspective (cognition); and the rise of international, cross-cultural and multicultural perspectives. Social psychology in a new century Social cognition dominated the final quarter of the field's first century: the study of how people perceive, remember and interpret information about themselves and others. Social neuroscience emerged as a subfield studying the relationship between neural and social processes. Behavioural genetics (the study of how genes affect behaviour) triggered research on, e.g., whether aggression is heritable and the role of genes in sexual orientation. Evolutionary psychology uses evolutionary principles to understand behaviour (e.g., asking how the psychological mechanisms underlying jealousy may have evolved from natural-selection pressures). Increasing emphasis on testing the universal generality vs cultural specificity of theories via cross-cultural and multicultural research. High-yield Triplett (facilitation, first article) · Ringelmann (loafing) · McDougall/Ross 1908 + Floyd Allport 1924 (founding) · Lewin B = f(P,E) · Sherif (norm formation) · Asch 1951 (conformity) · Festinger 1954 social comparison / 1957 dissonance · Milgram 1960s (obedience) · Gordon Allport 1954 Nature of Prejudice . New century: social cognition, social neuroscience, behavioural genetics, evolutionary psychology, cross-cultural work. 2. Theories of social psychology The grand frameworks the field uses to explain social behaviour. Learn each by its core construct and its named author. Field theory (Kurt Lewin) Lewin, whose name is most associated with field theory , was a student of the founders of the Gestalt movement. Others (Tolman 1932, Wheeler 1940, Lashley 1929, Brunswik 1949) have been called field theorists, but none dealt specifically with social behaviour, so Lewin is taken as the best representative. Six principal attributes of field theory: (1) use of a constructive method ; (2) a dynamic approach; (3) emphasis on psychological processes; (4) analysis based on the situation as a whole ; (5) a distinction between systematic and historical issues; (6) a mathematical representation of the psychological situation (Lewin favoured topology ). title: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention
text: Unit 9 — Human Development & Intervention The arc of a human life and the clinical work built on top of it: how development proceeds from conception to old age across every domain and theory (Freud, Erikson, Piaget, Vygotsky, the learning and information-processing views), how language and motor skills unfold, what it means for behaviour to become abnormal and how disorders are described and classified, the full landscape of psychotherapies (psychoanalytic, person-centred, Gestalt, existential, behavioural, REBT/CBT, transactional, family/systems), and the biological and socioemotional theories of successful aging. Built from Rodrick Prashanth's MET source decks and taught to NIMHANS clinical depth, losing no named theorist, term, or stage. In this book Developmental processes, domains & periods Theories of development Piaget's cognitive stages Vygotsky & information-processing Sensorimotor & motor development Language: components, theories, periods The concept of abnormality Describing & assessing disorders Classification (DSM & ICD) & causes Psychoanalytic therapy Person-centred, Gestalt & existential Behaviour therapy REBT & Beck's cognitive therapy Transactional analysis Family & systems therapy Successful aging: biological theories Socioemotional aging & late-life disorders 1. Developmental processes, domains & periods The one idea. Developmental science studies change and stability across the lifespan. Scientists care not only about how people change but about the underlying stability or constancy of personality and behaviour over time. Two kinds of change Quantitative change — a change in number or amount : growth in height, weight, vocabulary, aggressive behaviour, or frequency of communication. Qualitative change — a change in kind, structure, or organisation . Not "more of the same" but a different form altogether. Three domains of development Change and stability occur in various domains (dimensions) of the self. Scientists discuss them separately but treat development as a single unified process . Domain What changes Physical development Growth of body and brain; change or stability in sensory capacities, motor skills, and health. Cognitive development Change or stability in mental abilities: learning, attention, memory, language, thinking, reasoning, and creativity. Psychosocial development Change and stability in emotions, personality, and social relationships. Periods of the lifespan The division of the lifespan into periods (infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) is a social construction : a concept about the nature of reality based on societally shared perceptions or assumptions, not a fixed biological fact. High-yield Quantitative = change in amount (height, vocabulary). Qualitative = change in kind/structure . Three domains: physical, cognitive, psychosocial. Lifespan periods are a social construction . 2. Theories of development The psychoanalytic viewpoint — Freud Freud concluded that human development is a conflictual process : as biological creatures we have basic sexual and aggressive instincts that must be served, yet society dictates that many of these drives be restrained. The ways parents manage these urges in the first few years play a major role in shaping personality. Freud held personality was fixed in childhood — essentially formed by age 5 or 6. Psychosexual stages of development Stage Age Characteristics Fixation outcomes Oral 0–1 Mouth is the primary erogenous zone; pleasure from sucking; id is dominant . Oral incorporative (taking in) — optimism, dependency. Oral aggressive/sadistic (during teething) — pessimism, hostility, aggressiveness. Anal 1–3 Toilet training (external reality) interferes with gratification from defecation. Anal aggressive — defecates to defy parents; basis for hostile/sadistic adult behaviour. Anal retentive — stubborn, stingy, hoarding; rigid, compulsively neat, obstinate, overly conscientious. Phallic 4–5 Incestuous fantasies; Oedipus and Electra complex ; castration anxiety; superego development. Phallic character shows strong narcissism . Latency 5–puberty Period of sublimation of the sex instinct. — Genital Adolescence–adulthood Development of sex-role identity and adult social relationships. Genital type finds satisfaction in love and work , work being an acceptable outlet for sublimation of id impulses. Erikson's theory of psychosocial development Erikson renounced Freud's idea of fixity, arguing that identity formation is a lifelong process . Personality (Erikson focused on identity ) develops through eight stages as life unfolds. The outcome of each stage depends on the outcome of the previous one, and successful negotiation of each ego crisis is essential for optimal growth. He used Freud's psychosexual stages as his basis; his first five stages reflect ego crises tied to Freud's stages. Trap Freud: personality fixed by age 5–6 , five psychosexual stages. Erikson: identity is lifelong , eight psychosocial stages built on Freud's first five. Don't merge the two. The learning viewpoint — Watson & the operant view Watson believed that well-learned associations between external stimuli and observable responses (called habits ) are the building blocks of development. From this perspective children do not progress through distinct biologically dictated stages; development is a continuous process of behavioural change shaped by each person's unique environment, and may differ dramatically from person to person. Operant learning theory claims development depends on external stimuli (reinforcers and punishers) rather than internal forces such as instincts, drives, or maturation. Modern developmentalists agree habits can emerge and disappear over a lifetime depending on their positive or negative consequences. The cognitive viewpoint — Jean Piaget Piaget (1950) defined intelligence as a basic life process that helps an organism adapt to its environment . As children mature they acquire ever more complex cognitive s

title: Unit 10 — Emerging Areas
text: Unit 10 — Emerging Areas The newer frontiers of applied psychology, built directly from the Unit 10 source: the psychology of gender and the schools of feminism , feminist psychology and feminist therapy with their critique of traditional treatment, the workplace barriers women face, the psychology of poverty , the positive-psychology science of wellbeing and self-growth (eudaimonia vs hedonia, the major wellbeing models, character strengths and post-traumatic growth), and cyberpsychology (online disinhibition and internet addiction). Every named area, model and theorist in the file is reproduced and taught to NIMHANS depth. In this book Issues of gender Types of feminism Feminist psychology Workplace barriers: glass ceiling & relatives Feminist therapy Issues in traditional therapies Empowerment & feminist techniques The psychology of poverty Wellbeing & self-growth Models of wellbeing Character strengths & virtues Post-traumatic growth Cyberpsychology 1. Issues of gender The one distinction to never blur. The whole topic rests on separating two words the public uses interchangeably. Sex is the biological distinction between male and female, fixed at conception by the chromosomes: the male karyotype is XY and the female karyotype is XX . Gender is the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness, that is, the social meanings of masculinity and femininity . Sex is given by biology; gender is built by culture. Definition Gender = the culturally constructed categorisation of maleness and femaleness (masculinity / femininity). Sex = the biological distinction of male (XY chromosome) and female (XX chromosome). Gender stereotypes A gender stereotype is a widely held belief about the abilities, personality traits, and social behaviour of females and males (the source attributes this definition to Weiten, 2001 ). Stereotypes are not the same as differences that actually exist; they are beliefs about the sexes, which may be exaggerated, inaccurate, or self-fulfilling. They feed the discrimination patterns described later in this book (glass ceiling, maternal wall, etc.). Minimalist vs maximalist views of gender differences How big are the psychological differences between men and women? The field splits into two camps: Maximalists believe in huge, fundamental differences between men and women. On this view the sexes are deeply, qualitatively distinct. Minimalists believe there are few fundamental differences between them. On this view the apparent gaps are small, situational, or socially produced rather than essential. Trap Maximalist = MAXimum difference; minimalist = MINimum difference. Maximalists emphasise large, fundamental sex differences; minimalists emphasise that the genuine fundamental differences are few. Do not confuse the camps because the names sound technical. High-yield Sex = biological (XY male, XX female). Gender = cultural construction of masculinity/femininity. Gender stereotype = widely held belief about males'/females' abilities, traits and social behaviour (Weiten, 2001). Maximalists = big differences; minimalists = few fundamental differences. 2. Types of feminism The source lists five branches of feminism . Each answers the same question, "what is the root of women's oppression and how do we end it?", in a different way. Learn them by their diagnosis and their strategy , because that is what is tested. Branch Core idea / diagnosis Strategy Liberal feminism Works within the structure of mainstream society. Its roots reach back to social-contract theory of government, the idea instituted by the American Revolution. Integrate women into the existing structure (equal access, equal rights) rather than overthrow it. Radical feminism Seen by many as the "undesirable" element of feminism, yet it is actually the breeding ground for many of the ideas that other branches shape and pound out. Holds that women's oppression is the deepest, original oppression. Tackle the root system of male domination (patriarchy) directly; the source ties consciousness raising to this branch. Socialist feminism The result of Marxism meeting radical feminism . Marxism recognises that women are oppressed and attributes the oppression to the capitalist / private-property system . The only way to end women's oppression is to overthrow the capitalist system . Cultural feminism Retreated to vanguardism , working instead to build a women's culture . Some of this effort has had real social benefit. Create and value a distinct women's culture rather than fight for integration. Eco-feminism Much more spiritual than political or theoretical in nature. May or may not be wrapped up with Goddess worship and vegetarianism . Its basic tenet: a patriarchal/hierarchical society will exploit its resources without regard to long-term consequences, as a direct result of the attitudes fostered in such a society. Link the domination of women to the domination of nature; resist both. Mnemonic " L iberals L obby (work within), R adicals R oot out patriarchy, S ocialists S mash capitalism, C ultural C reates a women's culture, E co links women & E arth." — L-R-S-C-E. High-yield Socialist feminism = Marxism + radical feminism , blames the capitalist/private-property system. Radical feminism is the "breeding ground" of feminist ideas and is the home of consciousness raising . Liberal feminism = integration within the system. Eco-feminism = spiritual, links patriarchy to environmental exploitation. 3. Feminist psychology Feminist psychology aims to understand the individual within the larger social and political aspects of society . Its defining move is to refuse to study a person in isolation: a woman's distress is read against the background of her social and political situation, not just her internal makeup. Key figures named in the source Karen Horney — Feminine Psychoanalysis. Horney challenged Freud from within psychoanalysis, replacing his "penis envy" account of female development with a social and c

title: Research Methods & Statistics
text: Research Methods & Statistics How psychological knowledge is made and judged: the philosophical paradigms beneath every study, the quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods that grow from them, the experimental and non-experimental designs that license (or block) causal claims, and the statistical tests that decide whether a result is real. This book moves from epistemology to inference, builds every parametric test (t, F) from the logic of sampling distributions, extends them to MANOVA and ANCOVA, and closes with the distribution-free family. It is prioritised for MET 2026 and NIMHANS clinical psychology, with assumptions, degrees of freedom and a "which test when" decision table you can recite under pressure. In this book Paradigms & methods of research Research designs & sampling Hypothesis testing & inference Parametric test: the t-test ANOVA & experimental designs MANOVA & ANCOVA Non-parametric tests "Which test when" decision guide 1. Paradigms & methods of research The one idea behind the section. Before any method is chosen, a researcher already holds a paradigm : a way of thinking about and conducting research, a philosophy that guides how the research might be done. Method is downstream of philosophy. Two scientists can study the same phenomenon and reach different designs because they answer two prior questions differently: what is real ( ontology ) and how can we know it ( epistemology ). Definition Ontology = the nature of reality (is there one objective reality, or many constructed realities?). Epistemology = the nature of knowledge and the relationship between the knower and what is known (can the researcher stand apart from what is studied, or are they entangled with it?). Together they shape both the data-collection process and the analysis. The four research paradigms Learn each by its stance on reality, on the researcher, and on the kind of knowledge it produces. Paradigm Ontology / epistemology Typical methods Goal Positivism One objective reality exists and can be measured directly; researcher is detached and value-free Experiments, structured measurement, statistics Discover universal laws; explain and predict Post-positivism Objective reality exists but can only be known imperfectly and probabilistically ; all observation is theory-laden Quantitative methods with a plan fixed before the study; falsification Approximate truth through repeated, fallible testing Constructivism / interpretivism Reality is socially and personally constructed ; multiple realities; knower and known are inseparable Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents kept in text form Understand meaning from the participant's perspective Critical / transformative Reality is shaped by power, history, economics; knowledge is political Critical ethnography, participatory and emancipatory designs Expose and change unjust structures; empower Trap Positivism vs post-positivism. Both are "objective-reality" paradigms and both drive quantitative work. The shift is that positivism claims we can know reality directly and with certainty, while post-positivism (the modern stance behind most quantitative social science) says we can only know it imperfectly : every measurement is fallible, theory-laden, and provisional, so we falsify rather than prove. In exam phrasing, "quantitative research = post-positivist approach" and "qualitative research = constructivist approach". Quantitative vs qualitative vs mixed methods The paradigm choice cascades into a whole research stance. The table is high-yield because the paper tests the cascade directly. Feature Quantitative (post-positivist) Qualitative (constructivist) Plan A specific plan is developed prior to the study; tight structure Less structure on specific guidelines; general guidelines only; emergent design Data "Objective": easily classified or quantified (age, gender, test scores, recovery time) "Subjective": interpreted differently by different people (perceptions of pain, feelings about work) Collection Structured interviews / questionnaires, observations, records; scored reliably with little training Open-ended interviews, observation, narrative documents (diaries); data kept in text form Analysis Inferential statistics to generalise from sample to population Coding of themes , assigning meaning to words or images Strength Results across many studies can be combined into a large body of evidence Depth; tools for data, analysis and interpretation that quantitative work lacks Mixed methods. When the two paradigms are blended so that one sets the stage for or leads to the other , the approach is mixed methods. It rests on the pragmatic approach, which focuses on methodological rather than philosophical concerns and combines qualitative and quantitative methods, using exploratory and confirmatory methods. This widens the options for data collection, analysis tools and interpretation. Trap Using two methods in the same study but discussing them separately is not mixed methods, it is just "two methods being used". Mixed methods requires genuine integration where one paradigm feeds the other. Qualitative methods of research, in depth NIMHANS expects you to name each qualitative tradition and its signature. Observation. Being present in a situation and recording one's impressions. The primary research instrument is the self , consciously gathering sensory data. Problems: the enormous complexity of human behaviour, the impossibility of a complete record, and the subjectivity of the researcher. Types: structured (schedules predetermine the categories of behaviour/talk to be observed, e.g. Flanders' Interaction Analysis Categories, FIAC), unstructured (broad decisions made in advance, seen through the researcher's own socio-culturally constructed values), shadow studies (tracking one participant), and participant observation (the researcher joins and participates, gaining unique insight but risking distraction from the research purpose). title: UGC NET Psychology — Past Papers & Syllabus
text: UGC NET Psychology — Past Papers & Syllabus A faithful reference pack for the UGC NET (subject code 04) Psychology paper: the complete official 10-unit syllabus reproduced as a clean outline, a plain-language guide to how the exam works distilled from the NTA FAQ, and three full past papers transcribed question-by-question. The December 2019 paper is reproduced with its official answer key; the June 2019 paper and the 2020 paper are reproduced verbatim from the source documents, and because no official answer key was supplied for them, every question there is marked "Answer: not in key" rather than guessed. Use this to learn the real shape, weight and wording of the exam. In this book The official syllabus (all 10 units) How the exam works December 2019 NET paper (with answer key) June 2019 NET paper 2020 NET paper 1. The official syllabus (all 10 units) This is the University Grants Commission (UGC) NET Bureau syllabus for Psychology, Code No. 04 , reproduced in full. The paper draws its questions from these ten units. Topics are listed exactly as in the official syllabus. High-yield Every NET Psychology question maps to one of these ten units. Knowing the unit a question belongs to is half the battle: it tells you which body of theory the examiner is testing. Units 1 (Emergence/systems), 2 (Methodology & Statistics) and 3 (Testing) are disproportionately heavy in the papers in this book. Unit 1. Emergence of Psychology Eastern systems: Psychological thought in major Eastern systems — Bhagavad Gita, Buddhism, Sufism and Integral Yoga. Academic psychology in India: Pre-independence era; post-independence era; 1970s (the move to addressing social issues); 1980s (Indigenization); 1990s (paradigmatic concerns, disciplinary identity crisis); 2000s (emergence of Indian psychology in academia). Issues: the colonial encounter; post-colonialism and psychology; lack of distinct disciplinary identity. Western: Greek heritage, medieval period and modern period. Structuralism, Functionalism, Psychoanalytical, Gestalt, Behaviorism, Humanistic-Existential, Transpersonal, Cognitive revolution, Multiculturalism. Four founding paths of academic psychology — Wundt, Freud, James, Dilthey. Issues: crisis in psychology due to strict adherence to the experimental-analytical paradigm (logical empiricism); Indic influences on modern psychology. Knowledge paradigms: Essential aspects — ontology, epistemology, and methodology. Paradigms of Western Psychology: Positivism, Post-Positivism, Critical perspective, Social Constructionism, Existential Phenomenology, and Co-operative Enquiry. Paradigmatic controversies. Significant Indian paradigms on psychological knowledge: Yoga, Bhagavad Gita, Buddhism, Sufism, and Integral Yoga. Science and spirituality (avidya and vidya). The primacy of self-knowledge in Indian psychology. Unit 2. Research Methodology and Statistics Research: Meaning, purpose, and dimensions. Research problems, variables and operational definitions, hypothesis, sampling. Ethics in conducting and reporting research. Paradigms of research: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed methods approach. Methods of research: Observation, Survey (interview, questionnaires), Experimental, Quasi-experimental, Field studies, Cross-cultural studies, Phenomenology, Grounded theory, Focus groups, Narratives, Case studies, Ethnography. Statistics: Measures of central tendency and dispersion. Normal probability curve. Parametric (t-test) and non-parametric tests (Sign test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Mann-Whitney test, Kruskal-Wallis test, Friedman). Power analysis. Effect size. Correlational analysis: Correlation (Product Moment, Rank Order), partial correlation, multiple correlation. Special correlation methods: Biserial, Point-biserial, tetrachoric, phi coefficient. Regression: simple linear regression, multiple regression. Factor analysis: assumptions, methods, rotation and interpretation. Experimental designs: ANOVA (one-way, factorial), Randomized Block Designs, Repeated Measures Design, Latin Square, Cohort studies, Time series, MANOVA, ANCOVA. Single-subject designs. Unit 3. Psychological Testing Types of tests. Test construction: Item writing, item analysis. Test standardization: Reliability, validity and norms. Areas of testing: Intelligence, creativity, neuropsychological tests, aptitude, personality assessment, interest inventories. Attitude scales — Semantic differential, Stapel, Likert scale. Computer-based psychological testing. Applications of psychological testing across settings: Clinical, Organizational and business, Education, Counseling, Military, Career guidance. Unit 4. Biological Basis of Behavior Sensory systems: general and specific sensations, receptors and processes. Neurons: structure, functions, types, neural impulse, synaptic transmission. Neurotransmitters. The Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems — structure and functions. Neuroplasticity. Methods of Physiological Psychology: Invasive methods (anatomical methods, degeneration techniques, lesion techniques, chemical methods, microelectrode studies); Non-invasive methods (EEG, scanning methods). Muscular and glandular system: types and functions. Biological basis of motivation: hunger, thirst, sleep and sex. Biological basis of emotion: the limbic system, hormonal regulation of behavior. Genetics and behavior: chromosomal anomalies; nature-nurture controversy (twin studies and adoption studies). Unit 5. Attention, Perception, Learning, Memory and Forgetting Attention: Forms of attention, models of attention. Perception: Approaches to the study of perception (Gestalt and physiological). Perceptual organization (Gestalt, figure and ground, laws of organization). Perceptual constancy (size, shape, colour); illusions. Perception of form, depth and movement. Role of motivation and learning in perception. Signal detection theory: assumptions and applications. Subliminal perception and related factors, information processing approach, culture and perception, perceptual styles, pattern recognition, ecological perspective on perception. Learning process: Fundamental theories (Thorndike, Guthrie, Hull). Classical conditioning: procedure, phenomena, related issues. Instrumental learning: phenomena, paradigms, theoretical issues. Reinforcement: basic variables and schedules; behaviour modification and its applications. Cognitive approaches in learning: latent learning, observational learning. Verbal learning and discrimination learning. Recent trends: neurophysiology of learning. Memory and forgetting: Memory processes (encoding, storage, retrieval). Stages of memory (sensory, short-term/working, long-term — declarative: episodic and semantic; procedural). Theories of forgetting (interference, retrieval failure, decay, motivated forgetting). Unit 6. Thinking, Intelligence and Creativity Theoretical perspectives on thought processes: Associationism, Gestalt, Information processing, Feature integration model. Concept formation: rules, types, strategies; role of concepts in thinking. Types of reasoning. Language and thought. Problem solving: types, strategies, obstacles. Decision-making: types and models. Metacognition: metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation. Intelligence: Spearman; Thurstone; Jensen; Cattell; Gardner; Sternberg; Goleman; Das, Kar & Parrila. Creativity: Torrance, Getzels & Jackson, Guilford, Wallach & Kogan. Relationship between intelligence and creativity. Unit 7. Personality, Motivation, Emotion, Stress and Coping Determinants of personality: biological and socio-cultural. Approaches to personality: Psychoanalytical, Neo-Freudian, Social learning, Trait and Type, Cognitive, Humanistic, Existential, Transpersonal. Other theories: Rotter's Locus of Control, Seligman's explanatory styles, Kohlberg's theory of moral development. Basic motivational concepts: instincts, needs, drives, arousal, incentives, motivational cycle. Approaches to motivation: Psychoanalytical, Ethological, S-R, Cognitive, Humanistic. Exploratory behavior and curiosity. Zuckerman's sensation seeking. Achievement, affiliation and power. Motivational competence. Self-regulation. Flow. Emotions: physiological correlates. Theories of emotion: James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, Schachter and Singer, Lazarus, Lindsley. Emotion regulation. Conflicts: sources and types. Stress and coping: concept, models, Type A/B/C/D behaviors, stress-management strategies (Biofeedback, Music therapy, Breathing exercises, Progressive Muscular Relaxation, Guided Imagery, Mindfulness, Meditation, Yogasana, Stress Inoculation Training). Unit 8. Social Psychology Nature, scope and history of social psychology. Traditional theoretical perspectives: Field theory, Cognitive Dissonance, Sociobiology, Psychodynamic approaches, Social Cognition. Social perception (communication, attributions); attitude and its change within cultural context; prosocial behavior. Group and social influence (Social Facilitation; Social Loafing). Social influence (Conformity, Peer Pressure, Persuasion, Compliance, Obedience, Social Power, Reactance). Aggression. Group dynamics, leadership style and effectiveness. Theories of intergroup relations (Minimal Group Experiment and Social Identity Theory, Relative Deprivation Theory, Realistic Conflict Theory, Balance Theories, Equity Theory, Social Exchange Theory). Applied social psychology: Health, Environment and Law; personal space, crowding, and territoriality. Unit 9. Human Development and Interventions Developmental processes: nature, principles, factors, stages of development. Successful aging. Theories of development: Psychoanalytical, Behavioristic, Cognitive. Various aspects of development: sensory-motor, cognitive, language, emotional, social and moral. Psychopathology: concept, Mental Status Examination, classification, causes. Psychotherapies: Psychoanalysis, Person-centered, Gestalt, Existential, Acceptance Commitment Therapy, Behavior therapy, REBT, CBT, MBCT, Play therapy, Positive psychotherapy, Transactional Analysis, Dialectical Behavior Therapy, Art therapy, Performing Art Therapy, Family therapy. Applications of theories of motivation and learning in school. Factors in educational achievement. Teacher effectiveness. Guidance in schools: needs, organizational set-up and techniques. Counselling: process, skills, and techniques. Unit 10. Emerging Areas Issues of gender, poverty, disability, and migration: cultural bias and discrimination. Stigma, marginalization, and social suffering; child abuse and domestic violence. Peace psychology: violence, non-violence, conflict resolution at the macro level, role of media in conflict resolution. Wellbeing and self-growth: types of wellbeing (Hedonic and Eudemonic), character strengths, resilience and post-traumatic growth. Health: health-promoting and health-compromising behaviors, lifestyle and chronic diseases (Diabetes, Hypertension, Coronary Heart Disease), psychoneuroimmunology (Cancer, HIV/AIDS). Psychology and technology interface: digital learning; digital etiquette; cyber bullying; cyber pornography (consumption, implications); parental mediation of digital usage. 2. How the exam works UGC-NET (the National Eligibility Test) is conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA) on behalf of the University Grants Commission. It determines eligibility for Assistant Professor only, or for Assistant Professor and Junior Research Fellowship (JRF) both, in colleges and universities. Below is the practical guidance distilled from the official NTA FAQ document. Format and mode Mode: Computer Based Test (CBT) only. Sittings: Two shifts on exam day — roughly 09:00–12:00 and 15:00–18:00. The date and slot are allotted randomly by computer (needed for the normalization process); a candidate cannot choose them. Two papers in one session: Paper 1 (general teaching/research aptitude, common to all subjects) and Paper 2 (the Psychology subject paper based on the 10-unit syllabus above). Both are attempted in the same sitting. Subjects: NET is conducted in roughly 80+ subjects; Psychology is subject code 04. High-yield There is NO negative marking in UGC-NET. The official FAQ states plainly: "No. There is no negative marking for wrong answers." So you should attempt every question — leaving a question blank can only cost you, never protect you. (This is the opposite of many other entrance tests, so do not carry a "skip if unsure" habit into NET.) Marking and result Negative marking: None. Every question carries positive marks only; wrong answers are not penalised. Qualifying criterion: Per UGC policy, the top 6% of candidates who appear in both papers and obtain the minimum qualifying marks (in aggregate of both papers) are declared NET-qualified. No all-India rank: The FAQ states "Rank is not assigned in UGC-NET." Results are pass/qualify based, with JRF allocated subject-wise and category-wise. Challenging the key: After the test, the question paper, recorded responses and the provisional answer key are released. Candidates may challenge an answer by paying a non-refundable fee (Rs 200 per question challenged) within the given window. The final result uses the answer key vetted by subject experts. No re-evaluation or re-checking is done after results. Eligibility and age Subject: Candidates should appear in the subject of their post-graduation. If their PG subject is not in the NET list, they may appear in a related subject. JRF age limit: Not more than 31 years (as on the first day of the month in which the exam concludes), with relaxations for reserved categories. There is no upper age limit for the Assistant Professor eligibility. Category concessions: Candidates in the non-creamy layer whose category is in the central OBC list, and SC/ST/PwD candidates, get fee and (where applicable) qualifying-mark concessions. Fees (as per the cited cycle) Category Fee General / Unreserved Rs. 1100 Gen-EWS / OBC-NCL Rs. 550 SC / ST / PwD / Third gender Rs. 275 Payment is online only (debit/credit card or net banking). Fees are non-refundable and applications cannot be withdrawn. Documents and most details can be edited later through the correction window. Mnemonic Remember the three numbers that define NET: 0 (zero negative marking), 6 (top 6% qualify), 2 (two papers in one session). Attempt everything, aim for the top slice, and budget time across both papers. Trap NET does not give you a "rank" or a "score out of 100" that ranks you nationally for admission the way a CET does. Qualifying is a percentile-style cut-off (top 6%). Do not confuse a NET qualification with an entrance-exam merit rank. 3.
