title: Statistics for Clinical Psychology Entrances
text: Statistics for Clinical Psychology Entrances Everything from scales of measurement to MANCOVA, factor analysis and item response theory, built from scratch, with a diagram on every idea that has a shape. This is a book, not a cheat sheet. Every concept is built from the ground up: what the thing is, why it exists, the formula with every symbol named, a worked example with real numbers, the assumptions it stands on, what breaks it, and who invented it. Read it cold and you will understand statistics, not just recognise the words. Twenty-seven diagrams are drawn from the actual functions, so the normal curve really is a normal curve and the F distribution really is an F distribution. 17 sections 27 diagrams 60+ named statisticians Every test with its assumptions Built for IHBAS · CIP · RML · JSS · DIMHANS · Amity · SGT · NIMHANS 1 · Variables and scales of measurement 2 · Frequency distributions and graphs 3 · Central tendency 4 · Dispersion 5 · Skewness and kurtosis 6 · The normal curve and standard scores 7 · Probability, sampling and the sampling distribution 8 · Hypothesis testing, errors, power, effect size 9 · The t tests 10 · ANOVA 11 · ANCOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA 12 · Correlation 13 · Regression 14 · Non-parametric tests 15 · Psychometrics 16 · Which test to use 17 · Formula sheet and who-did-what index How to use this book. First pass: read sections 1 to 8 straight through, because everything later is built on them. Second pass: sections 9 to 14 are the test family; do not memorise formulas, memorise the question each test answers and the assumptions it needs , because that is what entrance papers ask. Third pass: section 15 (psychometrics) is worth as many marks as ANOVA in most of these papers and is usually the least prepared. Section 16 is the decision tree; if you can walk it without looking, you can answer any "which test would you apply" item. Section 17 is the night-before page. 1 Variables and scales of measurement Statistics is a set of tools for one job: getting from what you observed in a handful of people to a defensible statement about people in general. Everything in this book is either describing what you have (descriptive statistics) or generalising beyond what you have (inferential statistics). Keep that split in your head; it is the first line of a hundred exam answers. 1.1 The vocabulary you cannot skip Term Meaning Symbol Population The entire set of people or observations you actually want to talk about. Usually hypothetical and never fully measured. N Sample The subset you actually measured. Statistics exists because samples are all you ever get. n Parameter A number describing the population . Fixed, unknown, written with Greek letters. μ, σ, ρ, π Statistic A number describing the sample . Known, varies from sample to sample, written with Roman letters. M or X̄, s, r, p Variable Any characteristic that takes more than one value. X, Y Constant A characteristic that takes only one value in your study. – Datum / data A single recorded observation / the set of them. Xᵢ The rule that generates half the notation questions: Greek letters are for populations, Roman letters are for samples. μ is the population mean, M (or X̄) is the sample mean. σ is the population SD, s is the sample SD. ρ (rho) is the population correlation, r is the sample correlation. β is the population regression weight, b is the sample one. Types of variable Independent variable (IV): the one the experimenter manipulates or selects. The presumed cause. Also called the predictor (in regression) or the factor (in ANOVA). Its values are called levels . Dependent variable (DV): the one you measure. The presumed effect. Also called the criterion or the outcome. Extraneous variable: anything else that could affect the DV. Controlled by randomisation, matching, holding constant, or statistically (ANCOVA). Confounding variable: an extraneous variable that actually varies systematically with the IV , so its effect is inseparable from the IV's. A confound is an extraneous variable that got away. Mediator: the variable through which the IV acts (X → M → Y). Explains how or why . Tested by Baron and Kenny's (1986) steps or by Sobel / bootstrapped indirect effects. Moderator: a variable that changes the strength or direction of the X–Y relation. Explains when or for whom . Statistically, a moderator is an interaction . Discrete variable: takes only separate whole values (number of children, number of hospital admissions). Continuous variable: can take any value in a range; between any two values another is possible (reaction time, IQ). Measured to a limit of precision, with real limits of ±half the smallest unit: a reported weight of 62 kg means 61.5 to 62.5. Trap: mediator and moderator are the single most confused pair in research-methods sections. Mediator = the mechanism, sits between IV and DV in the causal chain. Moderator = the condition, sits outside and changes the size of the effect. "Stress causes depression through rumination" is mediation. "Stress causes depression more strongly in people with low social support" is moderation. 1.2 The four scales of measurement (S. S. Stevens, 1946) Stanley Smith Stevens , Harvard psychophysicist, published "On the theory of scales of measurement" in Science in 1946. The four-scale taxonomy is his, and it is the single most examined single fact in the statistics section of every one of these papers. Learn it perfectly. Scale What it does Properties Examples Permissible central tendency Permissible statistics Nominal (categorical) Names / labels only. Numbers are arbitrary tags. Identity / difference only. No order, no equal intervals, no true zero. Gender, diagnosis, blood group, jersey numbers, marital status, religion Mode only Frequencies, percentages, mode, χ², phi, contingency coefficient, Cramér's V Ordinal (ranks) Orders cases, but the gaps between ranks are unequal and unknown. Identity + order. No equal intervals, no true zero. Socio-economic status, ranks in a class, Likert-type agreement, Mohs hardness, stage of illness, birth order Mode and median Median, percentiles, quartile deviation, Spearman ρ, Kendall τ, Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis Interval Equal units, but the zero point is arbitrary. Identity + order + equal intervals. No absolute zero. Temperature in °C or °F, calendar years, IQ scores, most psychological test scores, z scores Mode, median and mean Mean, SD, Pearson r, t test, ANOVA, regression, factor analysis Ratio Equal units and a true zero meaning "none of it". All four properties. Ratios are meaningful. Height, weight, reaction time, number of errors, income, age, kelvin temperature Mode, median, mean, geometric and harmonic mean Everything, plus coefficient of variation and ratio statements Mnemonic: NOIR (French for black), in order of increasing information: N ominal, O rdinal, I nterval, R atio. Each scale keeps all the properties of the ones before it and adds one. Any statistic legal at a lower scale stays legal at a higher one; the reverse is never true. The two traps that are asked every year. (1) Temperature in Celsius is interval, not ratio , because 0°C is the freezing point of water, not the absence of heat; 40°C is not "twice as hot" as 20°C. Temperature in kelvin is ratio. (2) IQ is interval, not ratio. There is no IQ of zero meaning "no intelligence", so a person with IQ 140 is not twice as intelligent as one with 70. Strictly, IQ is arguably only ordinal, but for exam purposes it is treated as interval. Why the scale decides everything downstream. The scale of your DV is the first branch of the which-test decision tree. Nominal DV means frequencies means chi-square. Ordinal DV means ranks means the non-parametric family. Interval or ratio DV means the mean and the SD are meaningful, which means the parametric family (t, ANOVA, Pearson, regression) becomes available. If you can name the scale you have already narrowed the answer to about four tests. Two more scales worth knowing Absolute scale: a counting scale where the unit is one and cannot be changed (number of children). Some texts treat it as a fifth, strongest scale. Interval-like ordinal (quasi-interval): Likert items are ordinal per item, but a summed Likert scale of many items is conventionally treated as interval. Say this explicitly if asked; examiners like the nuance. 2 Frequency distributions and graphs Raw data is unreadable. The first act of every analysis is to impose order on it, and the tool for that is the frequency distribution. 2.1 Building a grouped frequency distribution Find the range: R = highest score − lowest score (some texts add 1 for the "inclusive range"). Choose the number of class intervals: conventionally 10 to 20. Too few hides the shape, too many defeats the purpose. Find the class interval width (i): i = R / (number of intervals), rounded to a convenient number (2, 3, 5, 10). Set the intervals so they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and start the lowest interval at a multiple of i. Tally and count. Term Definition Example (interval 50–59) Apparent (written) limits The limits as printed. 50 and 59 Exact / real limits The true boundaries, extending half a unit each way. Used in all computation. 49.5 and 59.5 Class interval (i) Upper real limit − lower real limit. 59.5 − 49.5 = 10 Midpoint (lower limit + upper limit) / 2. Assumed to represent every score in the interval. 54.5 Cumulative frequency (cf) Running total of frequencies up to the top of that interval. – Relative frequency f / N, usually expressed as a proportion or percentage. – 2.2 The graphs Histogram bars touch: the variable is continuous Frequency polygon midpoints joined, anchored to the baseline 50% → median Ogive (cumulative frequency) always S-shaped; read percentiles off it Same grouped frequency distribution, three standard graphs. A bar diagram differs from a histogram in one way: its bars have gaps, because the variable is categorical. The three graphs of a frequency distribution. Graph Built from Used for Distinguishing feature Bar diagram Categories on X, frequency on Y Nominal or ordinal data Bars have gaps between them, because the categories are discrete Histogram Class intervals on X, frequency on Y Continuous, grouped data Bars touch , because the variable is continuous. Area is proportional to frequency Frequency polygon Midpoints joined by straight lines Comparing two or more distributions on one axis Anchored to the baseline at both ends; area under it equals the histogram's area Frequency curve A smoothed frequency polygon Showing the underlying shape Smooth, no corners; the theoretical limit as N → ∞ and i → 0 Ogive (cumulative frequency curve) Cumulative frequency plotted at the upper real limit Reading percentiles and the median straight off the graph Always S-shaped and never decreasing. The score at 50% cumulative frequency is the median Pie chart Proportions as sectors of a circle Parts of a single whole, nominal data Each 1% = 3.6° Stem-and-leaf plot (Tukey) Leading digits as stems, trailing as leaves Small datasets Shows the shape and preserves every original value Box plot (Tukey) Five-number summary Comparing groups, spotting outliers and skew Built entirely from ranks, so extreme scores cannot distort it Scatterplot / scattergram Paired X and Y values as points Correlation and regression The only honest way to see a relationship before computing r Lower whisker Q1 − 1.5×IQR Q1 (25th %ile) Median (Q2) Q3 (75th %ile) Upper whisker Q3 + 1.5×IQR Outliers Interquartile range, IQR = Q3 − Q1 (semi-interquartile range or quartile deviation Q = IQR/2) Tukey's box-and-whisker plot. Everything in it is a rank statistic, so it is unaffected by extreme scores , that is why it is paired with the median, not the mean. Box plot (John Tukey, 1977): the five-number summary drawn. Reading a box plot for skew: if the median line sits nearer the bottom of the box and the upper whisker is longer, the distribution is positively skewed. Nearer the top with a longer lower whisker means negative skew. A centred median with equal whiskers means symmetry. 3 Central tendency A measure of central tendency is a single value that best represents the whole distribution: the point around which the scores cluster. There are three you must know cold, and two more worth naming. 3.1 The mean (arithmetic average) Definition: the sum of all scores divided by the number of scores. The balance point of the distribution. Formulas. Ungrouped sample mean: M = ΣX / n . Population mean: μ = ΣX / N . Grouped data: M = ΣfXᵐ / N , where Xᵐ is the midpoint of each interval and f its frequency. Assumed-mean (short) method: M = A + (Σfd / N) × i , where A is any assumed mean, d = (Xᵐ − A)/i, and i is the class interval. Worked example Scores: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13. ΣX = 40, n = 5, so M = 40 / 5 = 8 . The six mathematical properties of the mean (each one is an exam item) The sum of deviations about the mean is exactly zero: Σ(X − M) = 0. This is what "balance point" means, and it is why you must square deviations to get a usable measure of spread. The sum of squared deviations about the mean is a minimum: Σ(X − M)² is smaller than Σ(X − any other value)². This is the least squares property , and it is the reason regression, ANOVA and the variance are all built on the mean. Adding a constant c to every score adds c to the mean. Multiplying every score by c multiplies the mean by c. The mean is affected by every single score , so one extreme score moves it. It is not resistant. The mean of a combined group is the weighted mean: Mᵗ = (n₁M₁ + n₂M₂) / (n₁ + n₂). The mean is the most reliable measure across repeated samples , that is, it has the smallest standard error, which is why inferential statistics is built on it. Trap: the mean cannot be computed from an open-ended distribution ("60 and above"), because the top interval has no midpoint. In that situation you must use the median. 3.2 The median Definition: the value that divides the ordered distribution into two equal halves. The 50th percentile, the 2nd quartile, the 5th decile. Formulas. Ungrouped, n odd: the ((n+1)/2)th score. Ungrouped, n even: the mean of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th scores. Grouped: Md = L + [(N/2 − cf) / f] × i , where L is the exact lower limit of the median class, cf the cumulative frequency below it, f the frequency of the median class and i the interval width. Worked example Scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 13 (n = 5, odd): the (5+1)/2 = 3rd score, so Md = 7 . Add a sixth score of 40: ordered 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, 40; median = (7 + 9)/2 = 8 , while the mean jumps from 8 to 13.3. That single comparison is the whole argument for the median. Properties The sum of absolute deviations from the median is a minimum: Σ|X − Md| is smaller than about any other point. (The mean minimises squared deviations; the median minimises absolute ones.) It is a positional average, so it is unaffected by extreme scores : it is robust or resistant. It can be computed for open-ended distributions and for ordinal data. It cannot be manipulated algebraically the way the mean can, so it is not used in inferential statistics. 3.3 The mode Definition: the most frequently occurring score. The point of maximum density. Grouped formula (crude vs. exact). Crude mode = midpoint of the interval with the highest frequency. Exact (King's) formula: Mo = L + [(f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × i . Empirical relation for a moderately skewed distribution (Karl Pearson): Mo = 3Md − 2M , equivalently M − Mo = 3(M − Md) . A distribution can have no mode, one mode ( unimodal ), two ( bimodal ), or many ( multimodal ). A bimodal distribution usually means two different populations have been pooled, and that is a substantive finding, not a nuisance. It is the only measure of central tendency usable with nominal data. It is the least stable across samples and the least used inferentially. A rectangular or uniform distribution has no mode at all. 3.4 Choosing between them Use the... When Because Mean Data are interval or ratio, distribution roughly symmetrical, and you intend to do further statistics on it Most reliable, uses all the data, algebraically tractable, required by t, ANOVA and regression Median Distribution is skewed, there are outliers, the distribution is open-ended, or the data are ordinal Resistant to extreme scores; still meaningful when the mean is misleading Mode Data are nominal, or you specifically want the most typical or most common case The only legal option at nominal level; identifies the actual peak Classic applied example: income. Income distributions are strongly positively skewed, so the mean income of a country is dragged up by a few very rich people, and the median income is the honest description of the typical person. Same logic for hospital length of stay, reaction times, and number of therapy sessions attended. Two extra means worth naming Geometric mean: the nth root of the product of n scores. Used for rates of change, growth rates and ratio data. GM ≤ AM always. Harmonic mean: n divided by the sum of the reciprocals. Used for averaging rates and, in statistics, for computing the effective sample size in unequal-n ANOVA and post hoc tests. HM ≤ GM ≤ AM always. 4 Dispersion Two distributions can have the same mean and be completely different. Central tendency without dispersion is half a description. Measures of dispersion (variability, scatter, spread) tell you how far the scores stray from the centre. 4.1 Range R = highest score − lowest score. Simplest, crudest, and completely determined by the two most extreme scores, which are also the two least reliable ones. Unstable across samples. Useful only as a quick indication. 4.2 Quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) Q = (Q₃ − Q₁) / 2 , where Q₁ is the 25th percentile and Q₃ the 75th. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q₃ − Q₁; the quartile deviation is half of it. It covers the middle 50% of scores, so it is unaffected by extreme values. It is the partner of the median : report Md and Q together, always. 4.3 Average deviation (mean deviation) AD = Σ|X − M| / N. The average distance of scores from the mean, ignoring sign. Uses all scores, which is a step up from the range, but the absolute-value operator makes it algebraically useless, so it disappeared from inferential statistics. It is minimised when taken about the median , not the mean. 4.4 Variance and standard deviation Definition: the standard deviation is the root-mean-square deviation from the mean. It is, quite literally, the typical distance a score sits from the mean, in the original units. The variance is its square. Formulas. Population variance: σ² = Σ(X − μ)² / N · population SD: σ = √[Σ(X − μ)² / N] Sample variance (unbiased estimate): s² = Σ(X − M)² / (n − 1) · sample SD: s = √[Σ(X − M)² / (n − 1)] Computational (raw-score) form: s² = [ΣX² − (ΣX)²/n] / (n − 1) The numerator Σ(X − M)² has its own name: the sum of squares (SS) . Remember that, because the whole of ANOVA is bookkeeping about sums of squares. Worked example Scores 4, 7, 7, 9, 13; M = 8. Deviations: −4, −1, −1, +1, +5. (They sum to 0, as they must.) Squared: 16, 1, 1, 1, 25. SS = 44. s² = 44 / (5 − 1) = 11.0 · s = √11 = 3.32 . If these five were the whole population: σ² = 44/5 = 8.8, σ = 2.97. Note that dividing by n gives a smaller , biased-downward answer. 4.5 Degrees of freedom: why n − 1 The idea. Degrees of freedom is the number of values in a calculation that are free to vary once the constraints are imposed. To compute the sample variance you must first compute M from the same data. That fixes one thing: the deviations must sum to zero. So if n = 5 and you know four of the deviations, the fifth is forced. Only 4 of the 5 are free. Hence df = n − 1. The consequence. Dividing SS by n gives a variance estimate that is systematically too small, because the sample mean is always closer to the sample's own scores than the population mean is. Dividing by n − 1 corrects the downward bias, and is called Bessel's correction . It makes s² an unbiased estimator of σ². Degrees of freedom for every test you will meet One-sample t: df = n − 1 · Independent t: df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 · Paired t: df = n(pairs) − 1 One-way ANOVA: df between = k − 1, df within = N − k, df total = N − 1 Two-way ANOVA: df A = a − 1, df B = b − 1, df A×B = (a−1)(b−1), df within = N − ab Repeated measures: df treatment = k − 1, df subjects = n − 1, df error = (k−1)(n−1) Pearson r significance: df = n − 2 · Simple regression: df = n − 2 · Multiple regression: df = n − k − 1 χ² goodness of fit: df = k − 1 · χ² independence: df = (r − 1)(c − 1) A general principle: df = number of observations − number of parameters you had to estimate from the data. 4.6 Coefficient of variation CV = (s / M) × 100. A relative, unit-free measure of dispersion, so it lets you compare the variability of two things measured in different units (heights in cm vs. weights in kg), or two groups with very different means. It requires a ratio scale with a meaningful zero, so it must not be used on IQ or on Celsius temperature. 4.7 Properties of the standard deviation Adding a constant to every score leaves the SD unchanged (the whole distribution shifts, the spread does not). Multiplying every score by c multiplies the SD by |c| and the variance by c². The SD is in the same units as the original scores; the variance is in squared units. That is why you report SD and analyse variance. Variances add; standard deviations do not. This is the reason ANOVA partitions variance . The SD is the most reliable measure of dispersion across repeated samples, and it is the one used in every inferential formula. It is affected by every score, including extreme ones. On badly skewed data, report the quartile deviation with the median instead. Recap of sections 1 to 4: Stevens's four scales (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) determine which statistics are legal. A frequency distribution and its graphs (histogram, polygon, ogive, box plot) show you the shape. Central tendency locates it: the mean is the balance point and minimises squared deviations, the median is the 50th percentile and resists outliers, the mode is the peak and the only option at nominal level. Dispersion measures how wide it is: range, quartile deviation (partner of the median), average deviation, and the standard deviation (partner of the mean), whose squared numerator SS and denominator n − 1 are the foundation of everything that follows. 5 Skewness and kurtosis Central tendency gives the location, dispersion gives the width. The third and fourth properties of a distribution are its shape : how lopsided it is (skewness) and how peaked it is (kurtosis). Formally these are the third and fourth moments about the mean; the first moment is zero by definition and the second is the variance. 5.1 Skewness Mo Md M Negative skew Mean < Median < Mode long tail to the LEFT Sk < 0 Mo = Md = M Normal (symmetrical) Mean = Median = Mode no tail Sk = 0 Mo Md M Positive skew Mode < Median < Mean long tail to the RIGHT Sk > 0 Skewness. Mo = mode, Md = median, M = mean. The name of the skew follows the tail, not the hump. The mean is dragged furthest because it is the only one of the three that uses every score's value. Definition: the degree of asymmetry of a distribution. A distribution is skewed when one tail is longer than the other. Positive (right) skew Symmetrical Negative (left) skew Tail Long tail to the right, towards high scores Both tails equal Long tail to the left, towards low scores Order Mode < Median < Mean Mode = Median = Mean Mean < Median < Mode Sk > 0 = 0 < 0 Bulk of scores Low; a few very high scores stretch it out Centred High; a few very low scores stretch it out Test example A very difficult test: most people score low A well-constructed test of average difficulty A very easy test: most people score high (a ceiling effect) Real examples Income, reaction time, number of psychiatric admissions, symptom counts in a normal population Height, IQ in the general population Age at death, scores on a mastery test, life satisfaction in a healthy sample The rule that unlocks every skew item: the skew is named for the tail , not the hump, and the mean is always dragged furthest into the tail , because the mean is the only one of the three that uses each score's actual value. So the mean is always on the tail side of the median, and the mode is always at the hump. Get the mean's position and the whole ordering falls out. Formulas. Pearson's first coefficient of skewness: Sk = (M − Mo) / s Pearson's second coefficient (used when the mode is unstable): Sk = 3(M − Md) / s Bowley's quartile coefficient: Sk = (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2Md) / (Q₃ − Q₁) , bounded between −1 and +1 Moment coefficient: g₁ = m₃ / s³ , where m₃ is the third moment about the mean = Σ(X − M)³/N Interpretation rule of thumb: |Sk| under 0.5 is approximately symmetrical, 0.5 to 1.0 is moderately skewed, over 1.0 is substantially skewed. Another common working rule: skew is a problem if it exceeds twice its own standard error. What causes skew, and what to do about it Floor effect: the measure cannot go below a limit and most people are at it. Produces positive skew. Common with symptom counts and error counts in healthy samples. Ceiling effect: the measure cannot go above a limit and most people are at it. Produces negative skew. Common with easy tests. Selection: studying only the extreme end of a population. Transformations to fix positive skew: square root (mild), logarithm (moderate), reciprocal (severe). For negative skew, reflect the variable first (subtract each score from the maximum + 1), then apply the same transformation. Or switch to a non-parametric test , which does not care about the shape. 5.2 Kurtosis Leptokurtic (Ku > 3, excess > 0) Mesokurtic (normal, Ku = 3, excess = 0) Platykurtic (Ku < 3, excess < 0) All three have the same mean and the same total area. They differ in peakedness and tail weight. Excess kurtosis = Ku − 3. Leptokurtic = tall and thin with fat tails; platykurtic = flat and broad. Kurtosis: the peakedness of the distribution. Definition: the degree of peakedness of a distribution relative to the normal curve, and equivalently the heaviness of its tails. Type Shape Ku (moment) Excess kurtosis (Ku − 3) Tails Leptokurtic Tall, thin, sharply peaked ("lepto" = slender, think a leaping narrow peak) > 3 Positive Fat: more extreme scores than a normal curve Mesokurtic The normal curve itself ("meso" = middle) = 3 0 Normal Platykurtic Flat, broad, blunt ("platy" = flat, think a plateau or a platypus) < 3 Negative Thin: fewer extreme scores; in the limit, a rectangular distribution Formula. Moment coefficient of kurtosis g₂ = m₄ / s⁴ , where m₄ = Σ(X − M)⁴/N. Percentile-based: Ku = Q / (P₉₀ − P₁₀) , which equals 0.263 for a normal curve. Most software reports excess kurtosis, so a printed value of 0 means normal, not flat. Trap: SPSS and most statistical software report excess kurtosis (already minus 3). So a reported kurtosis of 0.00 means mesokurtic (normal), while a reported 3.00 means strongly leptokurtic. Exam questions almost always use the raw moment version where normal = 3. Read the question for which convention it wants. Testing normality formally Test Who Use Read it as Shapiro–Wilk Samuel Shapiro and Martin Wilk, 1965 The most powerful normality test for small to moderate n (under about 50, usable to 2000) Non-significant (p > .05) = normal. You want it to fail Kolmogorov–Smirnov Andrey Kolmogorov and Nikolai Smirnov Compares the sample cumulative distribution to the normal one; better for larger n (with the Lilliefors correction) Non-significant = normal Skewness / kurtosis z tests – Divide the coefficient by its standard error |z| > 1.96 means significant departure at .05 Q–Q plot / P–P plot – Visual check Points on the straight diagonal = normal The large-n paradox. Shapiro–Wilk and K–S become so powerful with large n that they flag trivial, harmless departures from normality as significant. With n over about 300, trust the histogram, the Q–Q plot and the skew and kurtosis values instead of the p value, and remember that the central limit theorem has already protected you. 6 The normal curve and standard scores The normal curve was derived by Abraham de Moivre in 1733 as the limit of the binomial, developed by Pierre-Simon Laplace , and applied to measurement error by Carl Friedrich Gauss (hence "Gaussian"). Adolphe Quetelet was the first to apply it to human characteristics ("l'homme moyen", the average man), and Sir Francis Galton brought it into psychology, along with the words "regression", "correlation" and "percentile". 34.13% 34.13% 13.59% 13.59% 2.14% 2.14% 0.13% 0.13% z score -4 -3 -2 -1 0 +1 +2 +3 +4 Percentile 0.003 0.1 2.3 15.9 50 84.1 97.7 99.9 99.997 T score (M50, SD10) 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 90 Wechsler IQ (M100, SD15) 40 55 70 85 100 115 130 145 160 Stanford-Binet IQ (SD16) 36 52 68 84 100 116 132 148 164 Stanine (M5, SD2) 1 1 1 3 5 7 9 9 9 68.26% of all cases lie within ±1 SD · 95.44% within ±2 SD · 99.74% within ±3 SD (the ±1.96 SD band is exactly 95%, the ±2.58 SD band exactly 99% , those are the numbers used for confidence intervals) Mean = Median = Mode The normal probability curve. Area under the curve = 1.00. The percentages are fixed properties of the curve, which is why one z score converts into every other standard score. 6.1 Properties of the normal probability curve Bell-shaped and perfectly symmetrical about the mean. Skewness = 0. Mean = median = mode , all at the centre. Asymptotic: the tails approach the X axis but never touch it, so the curve extends from −∞ to +∞. Any score has a non-zero probability. Unimodal , with a single maximum ordinate at the mean. The maximum ordinate is 0.3989 (that is, 1/√2π) when expressed in z units. Mesokurtic: kurtosis = 3, excess kurtosis = 0. Total area under the curve = 1.00 (or 100%), which is why areas can be read as probabilities. Points of inflection (where the curve changes from concave-down to concave-up) lie exactly at ±1σ. It is completely defined by two parameters: μ and σ . Change μ and the curve slides; change σ and it widens or narrows. The standard normal curve is the special case with μ = 0 and σ = 1. The quartile deviation Q = 0.6745σ, and the average deviation AD = 0.7979σ. 6.2 The area percentages (memorise these exactly) Band Area inside Area in each tail μ ± 1σ 68.26% (34.13% each side) 15.87% μ ± 2σ 95.44% (adds 13.59% each side) 2.28% μ ± 3σ 99.74% (adds 2.14% each side) 0.13% μ ± 1.96 σ 95.00% exactly 2.5% (this is where α = .05 two-tailed comes from) μ ± 2.58 σ 99.00% exactly 0.5% (this is where α = .01 two-tailed comes from) μ ± 1.645 σ 90.00% 5% (the one-tailed .05 critical value) The three numbers that carry the most marks: 68 – 95 – 99.7 for 1, 2 and 3 SD, and 1.96 and 2.58 as the exact 95% and 99% cut-offs. Every confidence interval and every z test in the paper comes out of these. 6.3 z scores Definition: a z score expresses a raw score as the number of standard deviations it lies above or below the mean. z = (X − M) / s (sample) · z = (X − μ) / σ (population) · to go back: X = M + z·s Worked example A student scores 85 on a test with M = 70 and s = 10. z = (85 − 70)/10 = +1.5 . From the table, the area below z = 1.5 is .9332, so the student is at the 93rd percentile and beat 93% of the group. A second student scores 60: z = −1.0, area below = .1587, so the 16th percentile . Properties of a z distribution The mean of a set of z scores is always 0 and the SD always 1 . Converting to z is a linear transformation. Standardising does not change the shape of the distribution. A skewed distribution converted to z scores is still exactly as skewed. This is the most frequently missed point about z scores. z scores make scores from different tests comparable, which is the whole reason they exist. Roughly 99.7% of z scores fall between −3 and +3. Trap: "z transformation normalises a distribution." False. It standardises it (fixes M = 0, s = 1) but leaves the shape untouched. To actually change the shape into a normal one you need a normalised standard score , which is computed from percentile ranks via the area table, not from the linear z formula. Normalised T scores and stanines are of this second kind. 6.4 The derived standard scores Score Mean SD Formula from z Where you meet it z 0 1 – The base currency of all standard scores T score (McCall) 50 10 T = 50 + 10z MMPI, MCMI, most clinical inventories. Avoids negative numbers and decimals Wechsler IQ (deviation IQ) 100 15 IQ = 100 + 15z WAIS, WISC, WPPSI Stanford–Binet IQ 100 16 IQ = 100 + 16z Stanford–Binet (5th ed. now uses 15) Wechsler subtest scaled score 10 3 = 10 + 3z Individual WAIS/WISC subtests Stanine (standard nine) 5 2 = 5 + 2z, then rounded to 1–9 US school testing. Nine bands, each half an SD wide except the extremes Sten (standard ten) 5.5 2 = 5.5 + 2z Cattell's 16PF CEEB / SAT / GRE 500 100 = 500 + 100z Older SAT and GRE subscales NCE (normal curve equivalent) 50 21.06 = 50 + 21.06z US education, chosen so 1, 50 and 99 match percentiles Conversion recipe. Any standard score converts to any other by going through z. Example: a T score of 70 means z = (70 − 50)/10 = +2.0, so the Wechsler IQ equivalent is 100 + 15(2) = 130 , the percentile is 97.7 , and the stanine is 5 + 2(2) = 9 . That single chain answers a whole family of exam items. Percentile rank is not a standard score Percentiles are ordinal, not interval. A percentile rank says what proportion of the group scored below you. Because scores pile up in the middle of a normal distribution, percentiles are squeezed together at the centre and stretched at the extremes : the difference between the 50th and 55th percentile is a tiny difference in raw score, while the difference between the 94th and 99th is large. So you must not average percentiles or do arithmetic on them. Convert to z first. This is one of the most reliably examined points in the psychometrics section. 7 Probability, sampling and the sampling distribution 7.1 Probability basics Probability p(A) = number of favourable outcomes / total number of equally likely outcomes. Ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Addition rule (for "or"): mutually exclusive events, p(A or B) = p(A) + p(B). Non-exclusive, p(A or B) = p(A) + p(B) − p(A and B). Multiplication rule (for "and"): independent events, p(A and B) = p(A) × p(B). Dependent, p(A and B) = p(A) × p(B|A). Conditional probability p(A|B): the probability of A given that B has occurred. The basis of Bayes's theorem , and of sensitivity, specificity and predictive value in diagnostic testing. Binomial distribution: the probability distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials each with probability p. Mean = np, variance = npq. As n grows it approaches the normal curve, which is exactly de Moivre's 1733 result. 7.2 Sampling Simple random every case an equal chance Stratified random sample within each stratum Cluster whole intact groups sampled Systematic every kth case from a list Filled = sampled. All four are PROBABILITY methods, so sampling error is calculable. Purposive, quota, snowball, convenience and incidental sampling are NON-probability: cheaper, but no sampling error can be estimated and generalisation is unsafe. The four probability sampling designs. Method How Strength Weakness PROBABILITY sampling: every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, so sampling error is calculable and generalisation is defensible Simple random Lottery or random-number table; every case has an equal chance Unbiased, the theoretical ideal, the assumption behind every inferential formula Needs a complete sampling frame; may miss small subgroups by chance Stratified random Divide the population into strata (gender, diagnosis, SES), then sample randomly within each. Proportionate or disproportionate More precise than simple random , guarantees representation of every stratum, reduces sampling error You must know the strata in advance Cluster Divide into naturally occurring groups (schools, wards, villages), randomly select whole clusters, study everyone inside Cheap and practical when the population is geographically spread; no full frame needed Largest sampling error of the probability methods, because people within a cluster are alike Systematic Choose a random start, then take every kth case (k = N/n) Simple, spreads the sample evenly through the list Fails badly if the list has a periodicity matching k Multi-stage Cluster sampling applied repeatedly (state → district → school → class) The only feasible design for national surveys Error accumulates at each stage NON-PROBABILITY sampling: selection chance unknown, so sampling error cannot be estimated and inferential statistics are strictly not justified Purposive / judgemental The researcher picks cases judged typical or informative Efficient for expert or rare populations Wide open to researcher bias Quota Fill preset quotas per subgroup, but choose within them non-randomly Gets the demographic profile right cheaply; the non-probability cousin of stratified Selection within quota is biased Snowball / chain referral Participants recruit further participants The standard method for hidden populations: substance users, sex workers, undocumented migrants Heavily networked people are over-represented Convenience / accidental / incidental Whoever is available (the classic undergraduate subject pool) Cheapest and fastest Weakest external validity of all Definitions to be exact about: sampling error is the natural, unavoidable discrepancy between a sample statistic and its population parameter, caused by chance alone; it shrinks as n grows. Sampling bias is a systematic tilt caused by a faulty method; it does not shrink with n, and a bigger biased sample is simply a bigger wrong answer. 7.3 The sampling distribution of the mean This is the pivot of the whole book. Everything inferential rests on one imaginary object. The idea. Take a sample of size n and compute its mean. Put it back, take another sample of size n, compute its mean. Do this endlessly. You now have a distribution, not of raw scores, but of sample means . That is the sampling distribution of the mean . It is theoretical; you never actually build it. But you know its three properties exactly, and that is enough to say how surprising your one real sample is. Its mean equals the population mean: μ M = μ. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator. Its standard deviation is the standard error of the mean: SE M = σ / √n , estimated in practice by s / √n . Its shape approaches normal as n grows, whatever the shape of the parent population. That is the central limit theorem. μ Population (skewed, μ = 2.0, σ = 1.2) → μ n = 2 SE = σ/√2 = 0.85 → μ n = 10 SE = σ/√10 = 0.38 → μ n = 30 SE = σ/√30 = 0.22 Central limit theorem: whatever the shape of the population, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as n grows, centres on μ, and narrows by a factor of √n. n ≥ 30 is the working rule of thumb. The central limit theorem, the single result that lets you use z and t on non-normal data. The central limit theorem, stated properly Central limit theorem (CLT). As sample size n increases, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n, regardless of the shape of the population distribution . If the population is already normal, the sampling distribution is normal for any n. If it is not, n ≥ 30 is the conventional threshold at which the approximation is good enough. Why the CLT is the most important theorem you will be asked about. It is the licence to use z, t, F and every parametric test on real psychological data, which is almost never normally distributed. It says that the non-normality of the raw scores stops mattering once n is reasonable, because the tests are built on the sampling distribution of the mean, not on the raw scores.

title: Systems & Theories of Psychology
text: Systems & Theories of Psychology The whole history of psychology told as a single argument: how the discipline broke away from philosophy in 1879 and then spent a century fighting over one question, what is the right object of study, the mind, behaviour, the whole person, or consciousness itself. This book teaches every major school from the ground up, with the theorists inline, the dates the exam tests, and the traps it sets. Read it top to bottom once to see how each school is a reply to the one before it, then revise off the tables, the red Trap boxes, and the side-by-side comparison at the end. It is the companion notes to the 119-question Systems & Theories mock. In this book Before the schools: roots and the big questions Structuralism (Wundt, Titchener) Functionalism (James, Dewey) Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Köhler, Koffka, Lewin) Behaviorism (Watson, Pavlov, Thorndike, Skinner, Bandura) Psychoanalysis and the psychodynamic school (Freud and after) Humanistic and existential psychology (Maslow, Rogers) Cognitive psychology (the cognitive revolution) Indian psychology and Eastern systems The schools side by side: timeline, comparison, and traps 1. Before the Schools: Roots and the Big Questions Psychology did not appear from nowhere in 1879. For more than two thousand years its questions belonged to philosophy , and its tools, later, to physiology . The schools you are about to study are best understood as rival answers to a handful of very old questions that psychology inherited and then tried to settle with experiment. The philosophical inheritance Mind and body — are they two different substances or one? René Descartes' dualism (interactionism via the pineal gland) said two; the monists said one. This is the mind-body problem. Where knowledge comes from — the rationalists (Descartes, Leibniz, Kant) held that the mind brings innate structure to experience; the British empiricists ( John Locke's tabula rasa , the blank slate, plus Berkeley, Hume, and the Mills) held that all knowledge is written by experience. The empiricists also gave psychology associationism , the idea that complex ideas are built by associating simple ones, which became the raw material of both structuralism and behaviorism. Nature versus nurture — the same debate in modern dress, still alive in every school. The physiological inheritance In the nineteenth century, physiology made the mind measurable for the first time. Johannes Müller's doctrine of specific nerve energies, Hermann von Helmholtz's measurement of the speed of the nerve impulse and his work on vision and hearing, Ernst Weber and Gustav Fechner's psychophysics (Fechner's 1860 Elements of Psychophysics gave the first true mental measurement, relating stimulus intensity to sensation), and Paul Broca and Carl Wernicke's localisation of speech in the brain all showed that mental events have lawful, measurable physical correlates. Charles Darwin's theory of evolution (1859) supplied the other great engine: it made function and adaptation central and licensed the study of animals, infants, and individual differences (taken up by his cousin Francis Galton , founder of mental testing and the study of individual differences). High-yield Fechner (psychophysics, 1860) and Helmholtz made the mind measurable; Darwin (1859) made it functional and adaptive; Wundt (1879) made it a laboratory science. These four names are the bridge from philosophy to scientific psychology, and they explain why the very first quarrel, structuralism versus functionalism, was about structure versus adaptation. Memory hook Read the schools as a chain of rebellions: Structuralism (study the contents of consciousness) provokes Functionalism (no, study its purpose) and Gestalt (no, study organised wholes); Behaviorism throws consciousness out entirely; Psychoanalysis dives under it to the unconscious; Humanism answers both Freud and the behaviorists with the whole, free person; and the Cognitive revolution brings the mind back as an information processor. Indian psychology runs alongside the whole story with a different goal: not explaining the mind but transcending it. 2. Structuralism Psychology as we know it began on a single, much-tested date: 1879 , when Wilhelm Wundt founded the first formal psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig , Germany. This act is the conventional birth of psychology as an independent science : it stepped out from under philosophy (which had asked about the mind for centuries through reason and argument) and from under physiology (which studied the body but not experience as experience). Wundt's claim was bold: the contents of conscious experience could be studied with the same controlled, measured, repeatable methods that physics and physiology used. He thereby created experimental psychology and trained the first generation of psychologists, many of whom carried the lab model across Europe and to America. Wundt's program was to study the structure of conscious experience : to break down the mind into its basic elements and discover the laws by which they combine. His chosen method was introspection , but a disciplined, laboratory version of it. He distinguished immediate experience (the raw, direct datum of consciousness as it is happening, the proper object of psychology) from mediate experience (experience used as a means to know something else about the outside world, which is what other sciences study). A psychologist, for Wundt, reports the immediate experience itself, not the object it points to. Definition Introspection is the systematic self-observation and reporting of one's own conscious experience (sensations, images, feelings) under controlled conditions. In Wundt's lab it required trained observers giving standardized reports to a measured stimulus, not casual self-reflection. It is a common error to label Wundt a "structuralist." Wundt's own position is better called voluntarism : he held that the mind is active , not a passive mosaic of elements. Through a central process he called apperception , the mind selects, attends to, and creatively organizes elementary contents into a meaningful unified experience, an act of will ( voluntas ). Pure, systematic structuralism , the doctrine that consciousness is to be analyzed into static elements and nothing more, is really the creation of Wundt's student, Edward Bradford Titchener . Beyond his lab method, Wundt's experimental work included mental chronometry : using reaction-time measurements (an idea he took from the astronomer's "personal equation" and from Donders) to time mental operations such as discrimination and choice. Importantly, Wundt did not think introspection could reach the higher mental processes, language, myth, religion, social custom. These, he argued, must be studied historically and culturally in a second great enterprise he called Völkerpsychologie (folk, cultural, or "people's" psychology), to which he devoted ten volumes late in life. Titchener and the systematizing of Structuralism Titchener, an Englishman, took the Leipzig training to Cornell University in the United States, where he coined the term structuralism and radicalized the method into analytic introspection . Trained observers learned to report the raw elements of an experience while strictly avoiding the stimulus error , the mistake of describing the meaningful object ("I see an apple") rather than the bare sensory contents (a red, round, bright patch). For Titchener the mind contained three irreducible elements: Sensations , the elements of perceptions (from sense organs); Images , the elements of ideas (representing experiences not present); Affections , the elements of emotions (feelings such as pleasantness/unpleasantness). Each sensation could be described by its attributes : quality , intensity , duration , and clarity (attensity), with extensity added for some modalities. Titchener also offered a context theory of meaning : meaning is nothing mystical but simply the context of associated sensations and images that a core sensation calls up. The discipline set itself three questions: the what (analyze consciousness into its elements), the how (specify how those elements combine, via the laws of association and synthesis), and the why (explain the experience). Wundt allowed a causal "why," and physiological explanation entered through reaction time; Titchener was stricter, treating physiology only as the parallel substrate and resisting a functional "why." Dimension Wilhelm Wundt E. B. Titchener Place Leipzig, Germany (1879 lab) Cornell, USA School name Voluntarism (often miscalled structuralism) Structuralism (he coined it) View of mind Active; organizes elements via apperception Passive mosaic of elements; pure analysis Introspection Controlled self-observation + reaction time Rigorous analytic introspection; avoid stimulus error Elements Sensations and feelings (tridimensional feeling theory) Sensations, images, affections Higher processes Studied via Völkerpsychologie Largely set aside Trap Do not swap the two men. Wundt = Leipzig, 1879, founder of experimental psychology, a voluntarist . Titchener = Cornell, the man who coined and built structuralism . Exam items deliberately ask "who founded structuralism?" expecting you to wrongly answer Wundt. The system named "structuralism" is Titchener's; Wundt founded scientific psychology. High-yield 1879, Leipzig, Wilhelm Wundt is the single most-tested fact in the entire history-and-systems syllabus. Memorize the trio together: year, place, person. Why Structuralism died Structuralism was attacked and ultimately collapsed for several reasons. Its method was the central weakness: introspection proved unreliable and unreplicable , because different trained labs reported different elements for the same stimulus. The decisive blow was the imageless thought controversy : the Würzburg school under Oswald Külpe reported that thinking can occur without any sensory image, directly contradicting Titchener's claim that every conscious content reduces to sensations and images. Critics also found the school far too narrow : by limiting psychology to the introspection of the normal adult human mind, it excluded animals, children, and the abnormal , and it produced little of practical use, earning the charge of being sterile . When Titchener died in 1927, structuralism essentially died with him, but it had done its historic job: it established psychology as an experimental laboratory science. Memory hook "Wundt Won the lab; Titchener Titled the school." Wundt won psychology its first lab (1879); Titchener gave structuralism its title (and its three elements: Sensations, Images, Affections = "SIA" ). 3. Functionalism While German laboratories dissected consciousness into elements, a very different psychology grew up in the United States as a reaction against structuralism . Where structuralism asked what consciousness is made of, functionalism asked what consciousness is for : what does the mind do , and how does it help the organism survive and adapt? This shift was no accident. The deepest influence was Charles Darwin : if bodily organs evolve because they serve a function in adaptation, then so might mind and consciousness. The practical, problem-solving temper of American life reinforced the move; American psychologists wanted a psychology that worked , one applicable to schools, clinics, and industry. Trap The single most tested contrast in this unit: structuralism studies the WHAT (the structure / contents / elements of consciousness, analysis), whereas functionalism studies the WHY / WHAT-FOR (the function, purpose, and adaptive use of mental processes). Structure vs function; contents vs operations. Do not reverse them. William James, the forerunner William James is called the "father of American psychology." His monumental Principles of Psychology ( 1890 ) framed the questions a whole generation would pursue. James argued that consciousness is not a string of static elements but a stream of consciousness : continuous (no gaps), constantly changing , personal (belonging to a self), and above all selective , attending to some things and ignoring others, which is precisely its adaptive function. Among his lasting ideas are the James-Lange theory of emotion (we feel afraid because we tremble and run; bodily change precedes the felt emotion), his analysis of the self into the I (the knower) and the Me (the known, with its material, social, and spiritual aspects), his classic treatment of habit as the "flywheel of society," and his philosophy of pragmatism (an idea's truth lies in its practical consequences). James, however, founded no formal school; he was more an inspiring precursor than a system-builder, and he largely abandoned psychology for philosophy. The Chicago school, the formal founding Functionalism as an organized movement is usually dated to John Dewey's 1896 paper, "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology," the field's recognized founding document . Dewey attacked the reflex arc (the stimulus-response unit) for being artificially "chopped up" into separate stimulus, central process, and response. In real behavior, he argued, these form one continuous coordinated act : perception and movement are bound together in a single adaptive circuit, and the "stimulus" and "response" are only roles within an ongoing whole. James Rowland Angell then organized and championed the Chicago school; his 1906 APA presidential address, "The Province of Functional Psychology," laid out its program explicitly. Harvey Carr later consolidated and matured the school. The Columbia school A second center grew at Columbia University, more applied and individual-differences oriented. James McKeen Cattell (who had studied under Wundt yet rejected his approach) pioneered mental tests , in fact coined the term "mental test," and championed the study of individual differences . Robert S. Woodworth developed dynamic psychology and inserted the organism into the equation, expanding S-R into S-O-R (Stimulus-Organism-Response): the organism's drives and state determine the response. Edward L. Thorndike studied animal learning, formulated connectionism and the law of effect (responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in), and in doing so built a clear bridge to behaviorism . Center Key figures Signature contributions Forerunner William James Principles (1890); stream of consciousness; self (I/Me); James-Lange emotion; pragmatism Chicago school John Dewey, J. R. Angell, Harvey Carr Dewey's Reflex Arc (1896, founding paper); Angell's program; mental operations as adaptation Columbia school J. McK. Cattell, R. S. Woodworth, E. L. Thorndike Mental tests / individual differences; dynamic psychology (S-O-R); connectionism / law of effect The functionalist program, taken as a whole, studied mental operations rather than mental contents , treated the mind-body as one functioning whole serving adaptation, and prized individual differences, applied psychology, education (Dewey's lasting influence on schooling), and mental testing . Because it asked what mind is for rather than what it is made of , it had no reason to exclude anyone: it threw psychology's doors open to the study of animals, children, and the abnormal , and to the applied fields, clinical, educational, and industrial psychology, that define so much of the discipline today. High-yield Pin the two anchors: William James = forerunner, Principles of Psychology (1890). John Dewey = "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology" (1896) is functionalism's founding paper . Chicago = Dewey, Angell, Carr; Columbia = Cattell, Woodworth, Thorndike. Finally, note that functionalism did not "die" the way structuralism did. It had no single dramatic refutation; instead it dissolved into the mainstream of American psychology , becoming so widely accepted that it ceased to be a distinct school. In the process it gave birth to behaviorism (through Thorndike's animal learning and the focus on observable function) and seeded the entire enterprise of applied and clinical psychology . Its very success was its disappearance. Memory hook "Function = For." Functionalism asks what the mind is For , born For -Darwin (adaptation), and is remembered For opening psychology to applied fields. People hook: "James Dreamed, Dewey Arced, Angell Announced" (James inspired, Dewey wrote the Reflex Arc, Angell announced the program). 4. Gestalt Psychology In the opening years of the twentieth century, while Wundt's structuralists were busy dissecting consciousness into sensory elements and the behaviorists were preparing to throw consciousness out altogether, a third movement arose in Germany that rejected both . This was Gestalt psychology . The German word Gestalt has no exact English equivalent: it means roughly "form," "shape," "configuration," or "organized whole." The Gestaltists argued that the mind does not register a mosaic of separate sensations that are later glued together; rather, it grasps organized wholes directly and immediately. Their rallying cry was that the whole is different from the sum of its parts . Definition Gestalt: an organized whole or configuration whose properties cannot be derived from, or predicted by, the properties of its isolated parts. The melody survives transposition to a new key even though every individual note has changed: the form, not the elements, is what we perceive. A note of precision that examiners love: the popular phrase "the whole is greater than the sum of its parts" is a loose rendering. The more faithful translation of Wertheimer's claim is that the whole is different from the sum of its parts. The organized whole possesses emergent properties, qualities that simply do not exist at the level of the components and therefore cannot be predicted by adding them up. The founding demonstration: the phi phenomenon (1912) The movement is conventionally dated to 1912, when Max Wertheimer published his study of apparent motion , the effect he labelled the phi phenomenon . The set-up is simple: two stationary lights are flashed in rapid succession, first one and then, a fraction of a second later, the other. What the observer sees is not two separate flashes but a single light moving from the first position to the second (this is the same principle that makes a strip of still film frames look like continuous motion). The crucial point is that the motion exists only in the perceived whole . There is no movement in either light considered alone; movement is a property of the configuration. Elementism, which insists that experience is built up from independent sensory atoms, cannot account for this. Wertheimer's collaborators and observers in these experiments were Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka , and the three became the founders of the school. High-yield Phi phenomenon, Max Wertheimer, 1912 is the founding study of Gestalt psychology. Apparent motion proves that the organized whole has properties (here, motion) not present in its parts, refuting structuralist elementism. The three founders Founder Signature contribution Max Wertheimer Founder of the school; the phi phenomenon (1912); later productive thinking (genuine, insightful problem-solving versus blind reproduction of memorized routines). Wolfgang Köhler Insight learning in chimpanzees, reported in The Mentality of Apes (1925); the concept of isomorphism ; carried Gestalt psychology to the United States. Kurt Koffka Chief popularizer in the English-speaking world; Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935); applied Gestalt ideas to developmental psychology. The laws of perceptual organization The Gestaltists' most enduring legacy is their catalogue of the principles by which the perceptual system organizes a raw sensory field into coherent objects and groups. Presiding over all of them is the law of Prägnanz . Definition Prägnanz (the "law of good figure," "law of simplicity," or minimum principle ): of all the ways a stimulus could be organized, we perceive the one that is the simplest, most stable, most regular, and most economical. It is the master principle from which the other laws follow. Law / principle What it says Everyday example Prägnanz (good figure) We adopt the simplest, most regular, most stable organization available. Overlapping rings are seen as whole circles, not odd arcs. Proximity Elements close together are grouped as a unit. oo oo oo reads as three pairs, not six dots. Similarity Elements that look alike are grouped together. Rows of crosses among circles are seen as belonging together. Continuity (good continuation) We prefer smooth, continuous contours over abrupt changes. Two crossing lines are seen as two straight lines, not four bent segments. Closure We mentally fill in gaps to perceive a complete, whole figure. A broken circle is still read as a circle. Common fate Elements that move together are grouped together. A flock of birds turning in unison is seen as one flock. Figure-ground The field splits into a bounded "figure" standing out against a formless "ground." The Rubin vase/faces reversible image. Symmetry / good form Symmetrical, balanced regions are perceived as figures and as wholes. Symmetrical bracket pairs { } group as one unit. Definition Figure-ground organization: the most basic act of perceptual segregation, in which one part of the field is seen as a distinct, contoured object (the figure ) and the rest recedes into an undifferentiated background (the ground ). In reversible figures the two can spontaneously swap. Memory hook For the grouping laws remember "Pretty Cats See Clearly, Fully Content" = P roximity, C ontinuity, S imilarity, C losure, F igure-ground, C ommon fate. And keep Prägnanz at the top as the " P resident" of all the laws: simplicity rules. Insight learning (Köhler) Köhler, marooned on Tenerife during the First World War, studied chimpanzees, the most famous of whom was named Sultan . Placed in a cage with a banana hung out of reach and some boxes and sticks lying about, Sultan would, after a period of apparent contemplation, suddenly stack the boxes or fit two sticks together to rake in the fruit. Köhler called this insight : a sudden reorganization of the perceptual field in which the relations among the elements abruptly fall into place, the famous "aha!" moment. Crucially, once achieved, the solution was retained and could be transferred to new but structurally similar problems. Trap Köhler's insight learning vs. Thorndike's trial-and-error. Thorndike's cats in the puzzle box learned gradually and blindly , by random fumbling that was slowly stamped in by reward (a smooth learning curve). Köhler's apes solved problems suddenly and intelligently , by grasping relationships (an abrupt, all-or-none jump). Insight = perceptual reorganization, not incremental association. Exam items love to swap these two. Isomorphism To explain why we perceive organized wholes, Köhler proposed the doctrine of psychophysical isomorphism : conscious perceptual experience and the underlying processes in the brain share the same structural form . The organization we experience is not imposed on a chaotic brain; it mirrors a corresponding organization in the cortical "field." Perceived form and neural form are, in this sense, isomorphic (literally "same shape"). Kurt Lewin: field theory, the bridge to social psychology Kurt Lewin extended the Gestalt insight, that elements are governed by the whole field they belong to, from perception to motivation, personality, and social behavior . He is the bridge from Gestalt perception to modern social and organizational psychology. His central construct was the life space : the totality of all the facts (needs, goals, barriers, possibilities) that influence a person at a given moment. From this came his celebrated formula: High-yield B = f(P, E) — behavior is a function of the person and the environment , taken together as an interacting field. Memorize the formula exactly. Tension systems: an unmet goal creates a state of psychological tension that presses toward resolution. The Zeigarnik effect: Lewin's student Bluma Zeigarnik showed that uncompleted tasks are remembered better than completed ones, because the unresolved tension system keeps them active in memory. Conflict types: approach-approach (two desirable goals), avoidance-avoidance (two undesirable options, "between a rock and a hard place"), and approach-avoidance (one goal with both attractive and repellent features). Group dynamics and action research: Lewin founded the systematic study of groups and championed research conducted in real-world settings to produce social change, summed up in his maxim, "There is nothing so practical as a good theory." Legacy Gestalt psychology founded the scientific study of perceptual organization and its laws are still taught essentially intact. Its emphasis on holistic mental structure fed directly into the rise of cognitive psychology and into research on problem-solving and insight . Through Lewin it seeded much of modern social and organizational psychology . Trap Do not confuse the Gestalt psychology of Wertheimer, Köhler, and Koffka (a school of perception and cognition ) with Fritz Perls' Gestalt therapy (a humanistic-existential psychotherapy of the here-and-now, the empty chair, awareness). They share only the word "gestalt" and a loose holistic spirit. Perls was not one of the founders, and Gestalt therapy is not an application of the laws of perceptual organization. 5. Behaviorism Behaviorism dominated American psychology from roughly 1913 to the 1960s and remains, even now, the single most heavily tested school on Indian clinical entrances. It grew out of a frustration with structuralism and its method of introspection , which produced unreliable, unverifiable reports of private experience. The behaviorists' radical answer was to throw out the mind altogether as a subject matter and rebuild psychology as an objective natural science of behavior , governed by laws of learning that could be observed in a laboratory and applied to predict and control what organisms do. Definition Behaviorism is the school holding that psychology should study only observable, measurable behavior (stimulus-response relations), not the mind or consciousness. Its goal is to predict and control behavior, and its core mechanism is learning through conditioning . 5.1 The behaviorist manifesto: John B. Watson John B. Watson (1878-1958) is the founder of behaviorism as a formal school. In 1913 he published "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" in Psychological Review , a paper so programmatic it is simply called the "Behaviorist Manifesto." Watson declared that psychology is "a purely objective experimental branch of natural science," whose theoretical goal is the prediction and control of behavior . He rejected consciousness, mental states, and introspection as outside the bounds of science, and demanded that psychology deal only in observable stimuli and responses. Watson's stance is best labelled methodological behaviorism : he did not deny that inner events exist, but insisted they are scientifically useless because they cannot be publicly observed. He was a fierce environmentalist , denying that heredity shapes personality and ability. His most quoted line captures this radical environmentalism: "Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed, and my own specified world to bring them up in and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select... regardless of his talents, penchants, tendencies, abilities, vocations, and race of his ancestors." In 1920, with his student and later wife Rosalie Rayner , Watson ran the famous "Little Albert" experiment . A roughly 11-month-old infant ("Albert B.") was shown a white rat (initially a neutral stimulus he did not fear). Each time he reached for it, the experimenters struck a steel bar behind his head, producing a loud, frightening noise (UCS). After repeated pairings, Albert came to fear the white rat alone (a conditioned emotional response ), and the fear generalized to other furry white objects, a rabbit, a dog, cotton wool, even a Santa Claus mask. The study demonstrated that emotions like fear can be classically conditioned in humans, anchoring Watson's environmentalism. (It is also a standard ethics case study: there was no evidence Albert's fear was ever extinguished.) Watson left academia in 1920 after his affair with Rayner became a scandal and went on to a successful career in advertising , applying conditioning principles to consumer behavior. High-yield Three dates examiners love: Watson's 1913 manifesto ("Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It"), Pavlov's classical conditioning (work from the late 1890s-1900s), and Little Albert 1920 (Watson & Rayner). Watson = founder of behaviorism; goal = prediction and control . 5.2 Classical conditioning: Ivan Pavlov Ivan Pavlov (1849-1936) was a Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on digestion , not for psychology. While studying salivation in dogs, he noticed they began to salivate before food touched their mouths, at the sight of the feeder or the sound of footsteps. He called these anticipatory responses "psychic secretions" and turned to studying them systematically, founding classical (Pavlovian/respondent) conditioning . In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus (a bell, originally producing no salivation) is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus (food) that automatically triggers an unconditioned response (salivation). After enough pairings, the bell alone elicits salivation, now a conditioned response to a conditioned stimulus . Element Abbreviation In Pavlov's dog Unconditioned stimulus UCS Food (meat powder) Unconditioned response UCR Salivation to food (reflexive, unlearned) Conditioned stimulus CS Bell (after pairing with food) Conditioned response CR Salivation to the bell alone (learned) Several lawful phenomena follow: Acquisition — the building of the CS-CR association across pairings. Learning is strongest when the CS slightly precedes the UCS ( forward/delayed conditioning ); contiguity (close timing of CS and UCS) is essential, and short CS-UCS intervals work best. Extinction — presenting the CS repeatedly without the UCS weakens and eventually abolishes the CR. Spontaneous recovery — after extinction and a rest interval, the CR reappears (weakly) when the CS is presented, showing extinction suppresses rather than erases learning. Generalization — stimuli similar to the CS (a higher-pitched bell) also evoke the CR. Discrimination — the organism learns to respond only to the specific CS and not to similar stimuli (the opposite of generalization). Higher-order (second-order) conditioning — a well-established CS can itself act like a UCS to condition a new neutral stimulus (e.g., pairing a light with the already-conditioned bell so the light alone evokes salivation). Watson explicitly built on Pavlov : Little Albert is classical conditioning of a fear response in a human, with the loud noise as UCS and the rat as CS. 5.3 Edwin Guthrie: contiguity and one-trial learning Edwin Guthrie (1886-1959) offered the most economical learning theory: the law of contiguity . A stimulus pattern that accompanies a response will, on its recurrence, tend to be followed by that response, no reinforcement required. Crucially, Guthrie argued the full-strength S-R bond is formed in a single pairing ( one-trial learning ); apparent gradual learning is just the building up of many independent stimulus-response connections. His practical legacy is the idea that breaking a habit means attaching the old cue to a new, incompatible response. 5.4 Edward Thorndike: connectionism and the Law of Effect Edward L. Thorndike (1874-1949) studied how animals learn by placing hungry cats in a puzzle box from which they had to escape (by pressing a lever or pulling a loop) to reach food. Cats did not "reason" their way out; they thrashed about until they stumbled on the correct response, and over trials the time to escape steadily fell. He called this trial-and-error learning and his theory connectionism , because learning is the strengthening of bonds (connections) between stimuli and responses. Thorndike's laws: Law of Effect — responses followed by a satisfying state of affairs are "stamped in" (strengthened); responses followed by discomfort are "stamped out." This is the cornerstone law. Law of Exercise — connections are strengthened by use (repetition) and weakened by disuse. (He later softened this, recognising practice without feedback does little.) Law of Readiness — learning depends on the organism's preparedness to act; acting when ready is satisfying, being blocked is annoying. High-yield Thorndike's Law of Effect is the direct conceptual ancestor of Skinner's operant conditioning. "Satisfying consequences strengthen behavior" (Thorndike) becomes "reinforcement increases behavior" (Skinner). Note that Thorndike is sometimes classified under functionalism rather than behaviorism, because of his focus on the adaptive function of learning. 5.5 B. F. Skinner: radical behaviorism and operant conditioning B. F. Skinner (1904-1990) is the most influential behaviorist. Unlike Watson, his radical behaviorism did not deny private events (thoughts, feelings): it accepts they exist but treats them as behavior to be explained, never as inner causes of action. Causes always lie in the environment and the organism's reinforcement history. Skinner distinguished respondent behavior (reflexive, Pavlovian, elicited by stimuli) from operant behavior, which is emitted and "operates on" the environment, controlled by its consequences . He invented the operant chamber ("Skinner box") , in which a rat presses a lever or a pigeon pecks a key to obtain food. The unit of analysis is the three-term contingency or A-B-C : an Antecedent (discriminative stimulus that signals availability of reinforcement), the Behavior (response), and the Consequence (reinforcer or punisher) that changes the future probability of that behavior. Definition Reinforcement = any consequence that increases the future probability of the behavior it follows. Punishment = any consequence that decreases it. "Positive" and "negative" do not mean good/bad: positive = add a stimulus , negative = remove a stimulus . Positive (add stimulus) Negative (remove stimulus) Reinforcement (behavior up) Positive reinforcement: add something pleasant. Give a child praise/candy for studying, studying increases. Negative reinforcement: remove something aversive. Take a painkiller and the headache stops, pill-taking increases. (Seatbelt buzzer stops when you buckle up.) Punishment (behavior down) Positive punishment: add something aversive. A spanking or a scolding for misbehaving, misbehavior decreases. Negative punishment (omission): remove something pleasant. Take away phone/TV privileges for breaking curfew, curfew-breaking decreases. Trap Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. This is the most-missed item on these exams. Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus and therefore increases behavior (escape/avoidance). Punishment decreases behavior. If the behavior goes up, it is reinforcement, full stop, regardless of "negative." Memory hook Two questions decode the 2x2 every time: (1) Did the behavior go UP or DOWN? Up = Reinforcement, Down = Punishment. (2) Was something ADDED or TAKEN AWAY? Added = Positive, Removed = Negative. Solve them in that order and you can never confuse the cells. More Skinnerian machinery: Primary vs secondary reinforcers — primary reinforcers satisfy biological needs innately (food, water, warmth); secondary (conditioned) reinforcers acquire their power by association (money, tokens, grades, praise). Shaping (successive approximation) — reinforcing closer and closer approximations to a target behavior to build complex responses that would never occur spontaneously. Schedules of reinforcement — the rule for when responses are reinforced. Continuous reinforcement produces fast learning but rapid extinction; partial/intermittent schedules produce learning that is more resistant to extinction. Schedule Rule Response pattern Everyday example Fixed-ratio (FR) Reinforce after a set number of responses High rate; brief post-reinforcement pause Piece-rate pay (every 10 items) Variable-ratio (VR) Reinforce after a varying, unpredictable number of responses Highest, steadiest rate; most resistant to extinction Slot machines, gambling Fixed-interval (FI) Reinforce first response after a set time "Scalloped" pattern; responding rises near deadline Weekly paycheck; studying before a scheduled exam Variable-interval (VI) Reinforce first response after a varying time Slow, steady, stable rate Checking email; pop quizzes High-yield Variable-ratio (VR) produces the highest, most stable response rate and is the most resistant to extinction , which is exactly why gambling is so addictive. Mnemonic: ratio schedules give the higher response rates (you control the count), and variable schedules resist extinction (you never know when the next reward comes, so you keep going). Skinner's principles powered behavior modification : the token economy (institutional patients earn tokens, secondary reinforcers, for target behaviors, later exchanged for privileges), programmed instruction, and a wide range of clinical and educational interventions. In 1957 he published Verbal Behavior , arguing language too is learned operant behavior. In 1959 Noam Chomsky's scathing review demolished it, arguing the speed and generativity of children's language acquisition could not be explained by reinforcement and required innate cognitive structures. That critique is widely cited as a turning point that helped launch the cognitive revolution . 5.6 Neo-behaviorism: the S-O-R turn The neo-behaviorists kept the objective method but inserted the Organism (O) between Stimulus and Response, allowing unobservable intervening variables as theoretical constructs (S-O-R rather than bare S-R). Clark Hull (1884-1952) built a formal hypothetico-deductive system of learning expressed in equations. His drive-reduction theory held that learning occurs when a response reduces a biological drive (hunger, thirst), restoring homeostasis. His central formula, sEr (reaction potential) = sHr (habit strength) x D (drive) and further terms, treats habit strength and drive as intervening variables linking stimulus to response. Edward Tolman (1886-1959) championed purposive (or cognitive) behaviorism . His rats in mazes showed latent learning : rats that explored a maze without reward still learned its layout, showing a sudden drop in errors once reward was introduced, proving learning had occurred without reinforcement. He argued animals build internal cognitive maps of their environment. Tolman effectively cracked open the "black box," reintroducing internal representation and purpose, and prefigured cognitive psychology. Kenneth Spence (1907-1967), Hull's foremost collaborator, refined the Hull-Spence theory, especially work on the role of incentive motivation ( K ) and discrimination learning. 5.7 Social learning: Albert Bandura, the bridge to cognitive Albert Bandura (1925-2021) showed that much learning occurs without direct reinforcement , through observation and modeling . In the Bobo doll experiment (1961), children who watched an adult aggressively beat an inflatable Bobo doll later imitated that aggression, while those who saw a non-aggressive model did not. Children also learned vicariously : when a model was rewarded for aggression, imitation rose; when punished, it fell ( vicarious reinforcement/punishment ).
