title: Systems & Theories — Answer Explanations
text: Systems & Theories — Answer Explanations Every one of the 119 questions from the Systems & Theories mock, written out the way the test screen shows them: the correct answer and the theorist it belongs to up top, the concept built from scratch below, then each wrong option nailed to whose idea it actually is. Read it straight through to lock in who owns what, or jump to a school and skim the answer lines. Companion to the Systems & Theories teaching book and the mock itself. In this book History & Schools (19) Psychodynamic (36) Behavioural / Learning (13) Humanistic / Gestalt (21) Cognitive / Consciousness (12) Indian Psychology (18) History & Schools Q1 What do Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common? ✓ Answer: D · (a) and (c) The answer is option (d) because the question rewards seeing that two separate claims are each fully true of all three men, and stopping at one undersells what they share. To place this historically, all three belong to the late nineteenth-century emergence of psychology as a science, the era when the study of mind broke away from pure philosophy and physiology and began to use real methods. Hermann Ebbinghaus (Germany, memory research), Francis Galton (England, differential psychology), and Sigmund Freud (Austria, psychoanalysis) worked in different countries and traditions and never collaborated, yet each launched a brand-new line of inquiry on his own initiative, which is exactly what option (a) means by independent pioneers. None of them merely speculated; each invented a fresh observational method to make some part of the mind studyable, which is what option (c) adds. Ebbinghaus created the nonsense-syllable technique and used himself as sole subject to chart the forgetting curve , bringing the experimental rigour of Wundt 's new science to the higher process of memory. Galton pioneered the measurement of individual differences , devising questionnaires, twin studies, mental tests, and the statistical idea of correlation , seeding psychometrics and behaviour genetics. Freud developed clinical tools like free association and dream interpretation to probe the unconscious, opening the dynamic/clinical tradition that ran parallel to the academic labs. Because both the pioneer claim and the novel-method claim hold for every one of the three, the combined option is correct. Lock in: when two single options are each independently true and a 'both' choice exists, the 'both' choice usually wins, so never stop at the first correct-looking answer. Panwar key: Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud, all 3 of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology. And they developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works. Why the other options are traps A. Each of them worked independently and were pioneers in the field of psychology Option (a) names their independent, pioneering originality, which is genuinely true of Ebbinghaus, Galton and Freud, so it tempts you to stop early. But it captures only half of what they share and ignores option (c)'s equally true point that each invented a new observational method. Because (c) is also correct, the combined choice (d) is the complete answer, making (a) true but incomplete. B. Each of them founded a formal psychology laboratory Founding a formal psychology laboratory belongs to Wilhelm Wundt , who opened the first lab at Leipzig in 1879 ; it is the standard distractor in any history item about early figures. None of these three founded such a lab: Ebbinghaus did self-experiments, Galton ran an anthropometric measurement station, and Freud worked clinically. So this statement is simply false of all three and cannot be what they share. C. Each of them developed novel observational methods to study how the mind works Option (c), the invention of novel observational methods, is fully true of all three (nonsense syllables, correlation, free association), so it is tempting in its own right. The catch is that it describes only their methodological side and leaves out option (a)'s equally true point about independent pioneering. Since both single claims hold, the combined option (d) is the better and more complete answer. Q2 In which year the first mental hospital in the USA was opened? ✓ Answer: B · 1753 The answer is 1753 because that is when the Pennsylvania Hospital in Philadelphia, the first hospital in the United States, opened its doors and, crucially, admitted patients with mental illness from the very start. To see why this date matters in the history of psychology, separate a general hospital from a dedicated asylum, and place the event on the historical arc of how society moved from neglect toward treatment of the mentally ill. In the colonial era, before any organised system of care, people with mental illness were typically confined at home, jailed, or left to wander; there was no public institution to receive them, and explanations of madness were still heavily moral and supernatural rather than medical. The 1753 opening sits at the very beginning of the institutional and moral-treatment story that would later run through Philippe Pinel 'unchaining' patients in France, William Tuke 's York Retreat in England, and Dorothea Dix 's mid-nineteenth-century reform crusade across America. The Pennsylvania Hospital, championed by Benjamin Franklin and physician Thomas Bond , was founded to care for the sick poor of all kinds, and among its earliest patients were several suffering from mental illness. That detail is the whole point: organised institutional care for the mentally ill in America began not inside a separate asylum but within this general hospital in 1753. Purpose-built facilities such as the Williamsburg asylum (1773), often called the first American hospital devoted solely to the mentally ill, came later, but the recognised starting line for organised treatment is the 1753 opening. Lock in the pairing: first U.S. hospital equals 1753, Philadelphia, with mental patients among its first admissions, so the answer is this general hospital and not the later dedicated asylums. Panwar key: The first hospital in the U.S. opened its doors in 1753 in Philadelphia. While it treated a variety of patients, six of its first patients suffered from mental illness. Why the other options are traps A. 1693 1693 is far too early; the American colonies had no public hospital of any kind at that point, and the care of the mentally ill was still entirely informal (home confinement or jail). The number is a near-miss decoy designed to tempt anyone who only half-remembers a late-seventeenth-century date, but no American mental hospital existed then. C. 1793 1793 is a real and memorable Philadelphia date, but it marks the catastrophic yellow-fever epidemic that devastated the city, not the founding of any hospital. The question pairs the right city with the wrong event to bait you. The Pennsylvania Hospital had already been open for forty years by 1793, so this cannot be the founding year. D. 1547 1547 is the year London's Bethlem Hospital (the infamous 'Bedlam') was granted to the City and became a dedicated asylum, in England , not the USA. It is a tempting distractor because Bethlem is the most famous early institution for the insane. But the question asks specifically about the first American mental hospital, so an English date is wrong by country. Q3 Who established the first laboratory for experimental study of psychology? ✓ Answer: C · Wundt The answer is Wundt because Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory devoted to the experimental study of psychology, and that single act is conventionally treated as the founding moment of psychology as an independent science. To grasp why this is such a landmark, place it on the historical arc. Before 1879 the study of the mind belonged to two parent disciplines: philosophy , which reasoned about mind from the armchair, and physiology , which studied the body's sensory and nervous machinery (figures like Weber, Fechner and Helmholtz). There was no separate discipline that examined mental processes through controlled experiment. Wundt fused the two when he founded his laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879 , Germany, deliberately creating a space where conscious experience could be measured under controlled conditions, for instance by timing reactions to stimuli (mental chronometry) and training observers to report their sensations through introspection . Because he founded both the lab and a formal research programme with students (Titchener, Hall, Cattell and others) who then carried the method across Europe and America, Wundt is called the father of experimental psychology , and the school he launched is structuralism (later systematised by his pupil Titchener). He thus sits at the precise hinge between the pre-scientific philosophy of mind that came before and the procession of modern schools that followed: structuralism, then functionalism, then behaviourism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis and the cognitive era. Every later force in the history of psychology defines itself in part by how it agrees with or revolts against the experimental, consciousness-studying programme Wundt began in that room in Leipzig. The fact to lock in is the trio of name, year and place: Wundt, 1879, Leipzig. If a question asks who founded the first psychology laboratory or who made psychology an experimental science, the answer is Wundt, not the physiologists or differential-psychology figures who preceded or accompanied him. Panwar key: Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory of psychology in 1879, in Leipzig, Germany. Why the other options are traps A. Galton Francis Galton belongs to the same founding era and did pioneer mental testing, individual differences, and his 'anthropometric laboratory' for measuring people, which makes 'laboratory' a tempting word-match. But Galton's was a measurement station for collecting data on the public, not a research laboratory for the controlled experimental study of consciousness, and it came after Leipzig. He did not found experimental psychology. B. Weber Ernst Weber was a physiologist whose work on sensory thresholds (Weber's law, the just-noticeable difference) directly fed into the new experimental psychology, so he is a plausible-sounding 'early scientist of the mind'. However, Weber studied sensation as physiology and founded no psychology laboratory; he is a precursor to Wundt, not the founder of the discipline's first lab. D. Jung Carl Jung is a famous name in psychology, which makes him an easy lure, but he was a psychoanalyst who founded analytical psychology in the early twentieth century. He was born in 1875, only four years before the Leipzig lab opened, worked in the clinical/depth tradition rather than the experimental one, and founded no early experimental laboratory. Q4 American Psychological Association (APA) was founded in: ✓ Answer: A · 1892 The answer is 1892 because the American Psychological Association was founded in July of that year, and the place and people are worth fixing alongside the date. The APA was organised at Clark University in Worcester, Massachusetts, when a small group of psychologists met to create a national society to advance psychology as a science and profession. Its driving force and first president was G. Stanley Hall , himself a giant of early American psychology: he studied in Wundt's Leipzig tradition, is credited with opening one of the first U.S. psychology laboratories (at Johns Hopkins), founded the first American psychology journal, and trained many of the country's earliest psychologists, which is why he was the natural figure to convene the new body. To place this historically, the 1890s were the moment American psychology came of age and detached itself from philosophy and physiology. The discipline born in Wundt's Leipzig laboratory in 1879 had crossed the Atlantic; William James had just published his landmark Principles of Psychology (1890); structuralism and the emerging functionalism were competing for direction; laboratories were multiplying on American campuses; and practitioners needed a shared organisation for standards, communication and annual meetings. The APA filled exactly that role and has since grown into the largest professional psychology body in the world, marking the professional, institutional phase of psychology's becoming a science. The cluster to lock in is: APA, 1892, Clark University, G. Stanley Hall as first president. Watch the year carefully, because the 1892 founding is easy to blur with the dates of subsequent annual meetings, the first formal convention, or later expansions; the foundational year this question tests is 1892. Panwar key: The American Psychological Association was formed in July 1892 at Clark University, Worcester, Massachusetts, United States. Why the other options are traps B. 1893 1893 is a deliberate off-by-one decoy. It sits right next to the true founding year and is exactly the kind of near-miss that catches a candidate who recalls 'early 1890s' but not the precise digit. It is not the APA's founding year, which was 1892; treat the one-year gap as the whole trap. C. 1896 1896 is a genuinely important date in American psychology, which is what makes it dangerous: it is the year Lightner Witmer opened the first psychological clinic (at the University of Pennsylvania), launching clinical psychology. The question is counting on you to confuse two different 'firsts'. It is not when the APA was founded, so it is wrong here. D. 1897 1897 postdates the APA's 1892 founding by five years and is simply a later year offered to muddy the timeline. There is no major APA-founding event in 1897, so it functions purely as a distractor for anyone unsure whether the association formed in the early or late 1890s. Q5 What is true about Structuralism? ✓ Answer: A · Aim was to create a "periodic table" of the "elements of sensations" The answer is option (a) because the defining, signature ambition of structuralism was to build the mental equivalent of chemistry's periodic table, cataloguing the basic elements of sensation . To understand this, place the school on the historical arc. Structuralism, founded by Wilhelm Wundt in his 1879 Leipzig laboratory and systematised by his English-born American student Edward Titchener , was the very first formal school of psychology after the discipline became a science. Its core assumption was openly borrowed from the chemistry of the day: just as complex substances reduce to a finite set of chemical elements, complex conscious experience should reduce to a finite set of irreducible mental elements, namely sensations, images and affective feelings. The method for isolating these elements was trained introspection , in which disciplined observers reported the raw contents of their awareness (the quality, intensity and duration of an experience) under controlled conditions. The aim was thus both analytic and descriptive: dissect consciousness into its atoms and arrange them into an orderly table of sensory elements. Historically, structuralism was soon challenged by functionalism (which asked what the mind is for, not what it is made of) and then largely swept aside by behaviourism , which rejected the study of consciousness altogether. Historically this was the discipline's first attempt to look like a hard science, modelling itself on chemistry's success in reducing matter to elements; its eventual failure (introspective reports proved unreliable and irreproducible between laboratories) helped trigger both functionalism and the behaviourist revolt. While structuralists did also care about consciousness in a general sense, the answer the question rewards is the unique, signature goal: the periodic table of sensations. Lock this in: structuralism equals reducing consciousness to elemental sensations, which is why option (a) beats the vaguer option (b) and why the behaviourist-flavoured option (c) is simply wrong. Panwar key: Structuralism was the first approach to understanding psychology after the field was born. The aim was to understand and be able to well describe the structures of which the human mind is formed. It also aimed at creating a table of elements of sensations like the periodic table in chemistry. Why the other options are traps B. Aim was to understand the nature of consciousness Option (b), understanding the nature of consciousness, is loosely true of structuralism and so is a tempting 'safe' choice, but it is too broad and vague: it describes the general territory rather than structuralism's distinctive aim. The signature goal the key prefers is the 'periodic table of sensations' in option (a). And option (d) 'all the above' is impossible because option (c) is false, so (b) cannot be folded into a correct 'all' answer. C. Aim was to study the behaviour and not mind Studying behaviour and not the mind describes behaviourism (Watson, Skinner), the school that explicitly rejected introspection and consciousness, which is the direct opposite of structuralism. It is placed here precisely to bait a student who has not separated the schools. Structuralism studied the mind via introspection, so this statement is false of it, and its falsity is also what sinks option (d). D. all the above 'All the above' is a tempting catch-all, but it can only be correct if every component statement is true, and option (c) (behaviour not mind) flatly contradicts structuralism. Because one of the bundled claims is false, the whole 'all the above' option collapses; this is the classic rule that a single false member kills an 'all of the above' choice. Q6 According to John Dewey, ____ is the connection between sensory stimuli and motor responses. ✓ Answer: B · Reflex arc The answer is the reflex arc because in his famous 1896 paper The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology , John Dewey took the reflex arc, the supposed connection between sensory stimulus and motor response, as his explicit subject and target of criticism. To understand the concept, start with what a reflex arc means in physiology: a stimulus excites a sensory (afferent) pathway, which connects through the nervous system to a motor (efferent) pathway, producing a response, usually diagrammed as a one-way stimulus-then-response chain. To place this historically, Dewey's paper is a founding statement of American functionalism (the Chicago school) and an early shot against the emerging stimulus-response (S-R) psychology that would harden into behaviourism under Watson. The S-R view treated 'stimulus' and 'response' as two separate, basic building blocks of behaviour stitched together. Dewey argued that this carving is artificial: sensation and movement are not two detachable units but phases of one continuous, coordinated act of adaptation, in which the response loops back and reshapes how the next stimulus is even perceived (the child reaching for the candle flame is one organised act, not stimulus then separate response). Physiology, he said, implies a unity of coordinated action, whereas the old psychology wrongly treated stimulus and response as separable. This emphasis on the whole adaptive act, and on function over fixed elements, is exactly what makes the paper functionalist and a bridge toward later organism-centred and Gestalt-flavoured thinking. The fact to lock in: the term Dewey defined and then criticised is the reflex arc (the sensory-stimulus-to-motor-response connection), and his contribution was to reject its fragmentation in favour of a unified, functional act. Panwar key: John Dewey's Education theory based on his concept of functional psychology, focused on action and application. It went against the traditional concept of stimulus-response. Dewey through his theory argued that the neural circuitry of the reflex arc was being misinterpreted by behaviourist psychology which was using stimulus and response as basic units. Physiology implied a unity of coordinated action, but psychology was treating 'stimulus' and 'response' as separable. Why the other options are traps A. Efferent arc The 'efferent arc' names only the outgoing motor limb of the pathway (efferent meaning carrying signals away from the centre toward the muscles), which is genuinely part of the picture and so sounds technical and plausible. But it is just one half of the connection; the reflex arc is the whole afferent-to-efferent loop Dewey discussed. Picking the half-term misses the unified concept he was actually targeting. C. Association arc 'Association arc' is not a term Dewey used, and it borrows the respectable-sounding word 'association' (from associationist psychology) to seem like a real technical concept. There is no such named structure in Dewey's reflex-arc paper, so it is a pure fabrication distractor designed to tempt anyone who does not recall the exact phrase 'reflex arc'. D. Dynamic arc 'Dynamic arc' likewise is not a recognised Dewey concept; it sounds appealing because Dewey's whole point was that the act is dynamic and continuous rather than static. The examiner is weaponising the spirit of his argument to invent a plausible-but-false label. The concept he actually named and critiqued was the reflex arc, not any 'dynamic arc'. Q7 According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of ______ in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. ✓ Answer: D · Self observation The answer is self observation because that is precisely how Edward Titchener framed his trained method: introspection is a highly specialised form of self-observation in which the psychologist studies his own consciousness scientifically. To understand this, place Titchener and his project on the historical map. Titchener was Wundt's English-born student who carried the new German laboratory psychology to America and founded structuralism at Cornell in the 1890s, the school whose aim, inherited from Wundt's 1879 Leipzig programme, was to reduce mental life to its elemental sensations, images and affective states. Reaching those elements cannot be done by watching behaviour from outside; it requires a disciplined inward look, and Titchener characterised that look as a comparatively neutral, systematic act of observing the self , sharply distinct from casual everyday reflection. His trained observers (often called 'reagents') learned to report the raw qualities of an experience, its quality, intensity, duration and clearness, while avoiding the stimulus error , the mistake of naming the object instead of describing the bare sensation it produced (saying 'an apple' rather than 'a round red patch with these brightness and hue qualities'). So introspection for Titchener was self-observation made rigorous and scientific, a controlled report of conscious contents rather than ordinary thinking, perceiving or merely attending. Historically this very method became structuralism's fatal vulnerability: trained introspection proved unreliable and irreproducible between laboratories, with different labs reporting different 'elements', which is exactly what let behaviourism (Watson, 1913) dismiss the whole enterprise as unscientific and shift psychology to observable behaviour. The distinction to lock in: Titchener's introspection is defined as a specialised form of self-observation, the neutral scientific watching of one's own conscious contents, which is why the answer is self observation and not attention, self-perception or self-thinking. Panwar key: According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of self observation in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically. Self-observation is the relatively neutral approach to study the self and was used by Edward Tichener. Why the other options are traps A. Self perception 'Self-perception' is the term from Daryl Bem's 1960s self-perception theory, the idea that we infer our own attitudes by observing our behaviour, a social-psychology concept from a completely different era and tradition. It is a tempting near-synonym because both involve the self, but Titchener's structuralist method was about directly reporting the contents of consciousness, not inferring attitudes from behaviour. B. Self thinking 'Self thinking' is not a recognised technical term anywhere in structuralism's account of introspection; it is offered because it loosely echoes the idea of an inward mental act. Titchener's method was deliberately distinguished from ordinary thinking, since thinking is itself one of the conscious contents to be observed, not the act of observation. The fabricated phrase is there to catch a loose match. C. Attention 'Attention' is a real and central topic in early experimental psychology (the focusing of consciousness on a stimulus), which makes it a credible decoy. But attention is an object of study, a process the introspecting observer might report on, not the act of observing one's own consciousness. Titchener defined introspection as self-observation, so naming the studied process instead of the method is the trap here. Q8 The aim of Functionalism was to study ______ as it functions in adapting the ______ to its environment. ✓ Answer: B · Mind, Organism The answer is option (b), mind then organism , because the classic aim of functionalism was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. To understand this, place functionalism on the historical arc and contrast it with the school it reacted against. Structuralism (Wundt's Leipzig lab and Titchener at Cornell) was the first force, asking what the mind is made of and breaking consciousness into elemental sensations through introspection. Functionalism , the distinctively American second force, was led in spirit by William James at Harvard and developed by John Dewey and James Angell at the University of Chicago around the turn of the twentieth century; it asked instead what the mind is for . This shift was driven by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution: if every biological feature exists because it aids survival, then mental processes (perceiving, remembering, feeling, willing) must also serve an adaptive purpose. The guiding question therefore became practical and biological: how do mental processes help a living creature meet the demands of its surroundings and survive? In that formula the mind is the thing studied, and the organism is what the mind serves by adapting it to its environment. This adaptive emphasis is why functionalism is often described as importing Darwinian thinking into psychology, and why it later seeded evolutionary psychology downstream and the whole tradition of applied psychology (education, industry, mental testing). The order of the blanks is exactly what the question tests: study the mind as it adapts the organism, not the reverse. Lock in the phrasing precisely: functionalism studies the mind functioning to adapt the organism to its environment. Panwar key: Functionalism was an early approach after the idea of Cartesian duality was popular. The aim was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment. Why the other options are traps A. Organism, Mind Option (a) uses the right two words, 'organism' and 'mind', but in the reversed order, which is exactly the trap, since careless readers grab the familiar terms without checking the slots. Functionalism studies the mind as the thing that functions to adapt the organism; making the organism adapt the mind inverts the entire logic and contradicts the Darwinian, survival-serving role functionalism assigned to mental processes. C. Thinking, Organism Option (c) narrows the first blank to 'thinking', which is tempting because thinking is an obvious mental activity. But functionalism's declared object of study was the mind in its broad sense, the whole sweep of mental processes serving adaptation, not the single faculty of thinking. Substituting one narrow process for the general subject matter makes this both too narrow and historically inaccurate. D. Attention, Individual Option (d) offers 'attention' and 'individual', both real psychology terms, which lends it a plausible feel. Attention, however, is just one specific mental process, not the overarching subject matter functionalism set out to study, and 'individual' does not match the biological framing of 'organism' adapting to its environment. The mismatch on both blanks rules it out. Q9 ______ of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology. ✓ Answer: B · Division 38 The answer is Division 38 because that is the APA division designated for Health Psychology , now formally called the Society for Health Psychology. To understand the answer, you need to know how the American Psychological Association is organised. Rather than being one undifferentiated body, the APA (founded 1892, the institutional milestone in psychology's becoming a profession) is split into numbered divisions, each representing a distinct specialty or interest area; the numbers roughly track the order in which divisions were chartered, not any ranking of importance, so they function as essentially arbitrary labels. Division 38 is devoted to the psychological dimensions of physical health and illness: how behaviour, stress, beliefs and emotions influence the onset and course of disease; how to promote healthy behaviour; and how psychologists work inside the healthcare system to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability. As a field, health psychology emerged as a recognised force in the 1970s, alongside the rise of behavioural medicine, and rests on the biopsychosocial model articulated by George Engel (1977), which holds that health and illness arise from the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors rather than biology alone, a direct challenge to the older purely biomedical model that the discipline helped overturn. The APA recognises clinical health psychology as a professional specialty, and Division 38 is its organisational home. The fact to lock in is the simple pairing: Division 38 equals Health Psychology. Because division numbers are arbitrary chartering labels rather than meaningful codes, this is purely a memory item, so anchor it firmly as 38 for health and do not let it slide into the neighbouring numbered divisions. Panwar key: Division 38 of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology. Under APA (American Psychological Association) clinical health psychology is a professionally recognized specialty that investigates and implements clinical services across diverse populations and settings to promote health and well-being and to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability. Why the other options are traps A. Division 16 Division 16 is the Division of School Psychology , the specialty serving children and education systems. It is a real, well-known division, which is what makes it a strong decoy, but it has nothing to do with physical health and illness. Health psychology is Division 38, so 16 is simply the wrong number attached to a different (and easily confused) applied specialty. C. Division 47 Division 47 is the Society for Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology . It is a tempting trap because exercise and physical wellness sit close to the idea of 'health', and a hurried reader may equate sport/fitness with health psychology. But sport and exercise psychology is its own distinct division focused on athletic performance, not the biopsychosocial study of illness, which belongs to Division 38. D. Division 98 There is no Division 98 representing health psychology, or indeed any APA division numbered that high in this context; it is a pure fabrication distractor. The large, round-feeling number is offered to catch anyone with no firm recall who might gamble on a high number. The correct, real designation for health psychology is Division 38. Q10 Which of the following historical perspectives gave rise to the evolutionary perspective? ✓ Answer: D · Functionalism The answer is functionalism because the evolutionary perspective grew directly out of functionalism's central question, which was what mental processes are for . To understand the lineage, start with functionalism itself and its place on the historical arc. Founded in spirit by William James and developed by the Chicago school (Dewey, Angell), functionalism arose in late-nineteenth-century America as a reaction against structuralism. Where structuralism dissected the contents of consciousness, functionalism, deeply shaped by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, asked how consciousness helps an organism adapt to and survive in its environment. That made adaptation , purpose and survival value the heart of psychological explanation. Evolutionary psychology , a modern perspective that crystallised in the late twentieth century (associated with figures like Tooby, Cosmides and Buss), takes exactly this adaptive logic and pushes it further: it explains behaviours and mental traits as products of natural selection , asking how a given tendency would have improved survival and reproduction in ancestral environments. So the conceptual bridge between the two is the shared focus on function and adaptive value; functionalism interpreted thought and behaviour through their usefulness to the organism, and evolutionary psychology reframes that usefulness in terms of inherited, gene-based adaptations. The other schools, by contrast, centred quite different things and so could not have produced the adaptive logic: structuralism (Wundt, Titchener) catalogued what consciousness contains ; psychoanalysis (Freud) explained behaviour through unconscious drives and childhood conflict; and behaviourism (Watson, Skinner) reduced it to learned stimulus-response links forged by the environment in a single lifetime. None of these placed inherited adaptive function at the centre. Functionalism alone made 'what is this mental process for, and how does it aid survival' the organising question, and evolutionary psychology simply re-rooted that question in genes and natural selection. The distinction to lock in: it is functionalism, with its Darwinian adaptive emphasis, that seeded the modern evolutionary perspective. Panwar key: Functionalism paved the way for the understanding and interpreting human evolution and behaviour from a perspective that focused on the functionality aspect of thought and behaviour, the choices and the fears that people make and have. Why the other options are traps A. behaviourism Behaviourism (Watson, Skinner) studied observable conditioned responses and explicitly banned talk of inner mental states or adaptive 'purpose', leaning on learning rather than inherited function. It is a tempting distractor because it is biological-sounding and scientific, but its whole stance, environment-driven learning over inherited adaptation, is conceptually opposed to the evolutionary emphasis on naturally selected traits, so it did not give rise to it. B. Structuralism Structuralism (Wundt, Titchener) analysed consciousness into its elemental sensations and deliberately ignored questions of purpose, function or survival value. It is offered because it is an early foundational school, but its static, element-cataloguing aim is the exact opposite of the adaptive, functional thinking that fed evolutionary psychology. Structuralism actually provoked functionalism as a reaction, rather than seeding the evolutionary view. C. Psychoanalysis Psychoanalysis (Freud) explored unconscious drives, childhood conflict and instinctual energy. The word 'instinct' can make it feel biological and therefore evolutionary, which is the bait. But psychoanalysis explained behaviour through intrapsychic conflict and developmental history, not through the adaptive function of mental processes shaped by natural selection, so it is not the parent of the evolutionary perspective. Q11 Who is the most associated with the techniques of introspection? ✓ Answer: A · Wundt The answer is Wundt because Wilhelm Wundt is the figure most identified with the technique of introspection , having made it the signature method of the first scientific psychology. To understand this, recall what introspection meant in his hands and where it sits on the historical arc. It was not casual self-reflection but a trained, controlled, almost experimental procedure (sometimes called experimental self-observation ): observers were given a precise, repeatable stimulus and asked to report the immediate contents of their own consciousness, such as the quality, intensity and duration of a sensation, under standardised laboratory conditions, with trials repeated to check reliability. Wundt founded the first psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879 , Germany, the act conventionally treated as psychology's birth as a science, and built his school, structuralism , around this method, using it to break conscious experience into its elemental components on analogy with chemistry. His student Edward Titchener later carried introspection to America and refined it (including the concept of the stimulus error ), but the technique is most associated with Wundt as its originator within experimental psychology. The historical contrast worth holding is the cast of other founders, each tied to a different force: William James founded functionalism and was sceptical of rigid introspection; John Watson founded behaviourism (1913) and rejected introspection outright as unscientific, demanding the study of observable behaviour instead; and Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology, which studied whole perceptual forms. Indeed, introspection's eventual unreliability between laboratories is exactly what gave behaviourism its opening to dismiss the method. The fact to lock in: Wundt plus introspection plus the Leipzig 1879 lab plus structuralism form one tight cluster, so when introspection is named, the default answer is Wundt. Panwar key: Wilhelm Wundt, the founder of modern psychology, a proponent of the structuralist perspective, used the technique of introspection to understand and interpret the human mind. He started the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany. Why the other options are traps B. James William James is from the same founding generation and certainly used and discussed introspection, which makes him a credible choice. But James founded functionalism and was openly critical of the rigid, element-hunting introspection that Wundt and Titchener practised, favouring a more naturalistic study of the 'stream of consciousness'. He is not the figure most associated with the introspective technique ; that is Wundt. C. Watson John Watson is a strong trap precisely because his name is tightly linked to introspection, but for the opposite reason: in his 1913 behaviourist manifesto he explicitly rejected introspection as unscientific and unverifiable, insisting psychology study only observable behaviour. Choosing him reverses the relationship. He is the great opponent of introspection, not its proponent, so he is wrong here. D. Wertheimer Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology , which studied whole perceptual organisations ('the whole is greater than the sum of its parts') and reacted against the atomistic, element-by-element approach that introspection served. He is offered as a famous early-school founder to tempt the unsure, but his method and aims were about perceptual wholes, not the introspective reporting of elemental conscious contents. Q12 Which among the following branches of Psychology specifically studies behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance? ✓ Answer: A · Evolutionary Psychology The answer is evolutionary psychology because it is the branch that specifically explains behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance and the action of natural selection. title: Amity, MA Clinical Psychology: The Entrance, Built to the Exhaustive Syllabus
text: Amity, MA Clinical Psychology: The Entrance, Built to the Exhaustive Syllabus This is the whole RCI-regulated M.A. / M.Phil Clinical Psychology entrance in one book, built to the Ultimate Exhaustive Master Syllabus you sent and taught from the ground up. Not notes about the exam: the actual content, every micro-concept built from scratch to the depth you set (the Jung breakdown, the Pinel sleep chapter), so you learn it cold, not just recognise it. The six domains follow the syllabus exactly, in its order, with the heavy core (biopsychology, advanced statistics, psychopathology) taught hardest. Two appendices add the depth off your own Amity paper. Read it cover to cover and you walk in ready. The exhaustive syllabus, in order 1 · Biopsychology & Advanced Neurosciences 2 · Advanced Statistics, Psychometrics & Research Methodology 3 · Psychopathology & Clinical Syndromes 4 · Psychological Assessment & Psychodiagnostics 5 · Psychotherapy & Clinical Interventions 6 · Foundational Psychology, Lifespan Development & Social Dynamics Appendices (off your own paper) Appendix A · PYQ Depth: Off Your Own Paper Appendix B · Indian Psychology (off your own paper) How this book is built The six domains map one-to-one onto the exhaustive master syllabus, down to the micro-concept. Each topic is taught the same way: what it is , the theory or mechanism , the names and exact criteria or numbers , a worked example , the way it shows up in the paper , and the trap . Coloured boxes flag what matters most: Definition (memorise this), High-yield (near-certain to be tested), Exam trap (the distractor built to catch you), and Memory aid (a hook). Nothing is left at a one-liner: every sub-concept is taught to the same floor. The two appendices are not on the formal syllabus: they are the concepts your own Amity paper actually tested (your Master Concept List, and the Indian-psychology cluster), kept because they are real and high-value. 1 · Biopsychology & Advanced Neurosciences This section teaches the physical machinery of the nervous system from the membrane up: how a single neuron holds a charge, fires, and recovers; how that signal jumps across the synapse; what the neurotransmitters are and how the drugs you will be questioned on act on them; and finally how the cortex and the deep brain are organised into the maps and loops that the examiners love to test. Biopsychology is the most fact-dense domain in the whole entrance, and it rewards the candidate who knows exact numbers (the resting potential is roughly −70 mV, threshold is −55 mV, the pump moves 3 sodium out for 2 potassium in) and exact names (Synaptotagmin, the Nucleus Basalis of Meynert, Brodmann area 17). Read it once for the story, then again for the numbers. Every distractor the paper throws at you is a near-neighbour of a true fact, so we will pair each mechanism with the trap that sits next to it. A. Membrane Dynamics & Electrophysiology A neuron at rest is not electrically dead; it is a charged battery held away from equilibrium by metabolic work. Understanding the resting potential, how it is built, and how it collapses into an action potential is the foundation for everything else in this section, so we build it ion by ion. Resting Membrane Potential: the gradients and the driving forces The resting membrane potential (RMP) is the steady voltage difference across the neuronal membrane when the cell is not signalling, conventionally about −70 mV (the inside is negative relative to the outside). It exists because four ions are unequally distributed across the membrane and because the membrane is selectively permeable to them. The key players, with their characteristic gradients, are: Ion Where concentrated Equilibrium potential (approx.) Resting permeability Potassium (K + ) High inside −90 mV High (leak channels open) Sodium (Na + ) High outside +60 mV Low at rest Chloride (Cl − ) High outside −65 to −70 mV Moderate Organic anions (A − : proteins, phosphates) Trapped inside n/a (impermeant) None Two forces act on every ion. The chemical (concentration) gradient pushes an ion from where it is concentrated to where it is dilute. The electrical gradient pulls an ion toward the oppositely charged compartment. The combination is the electrochemical driving force . For potassium, the concentration gradient pushes K + out (it is concentrated inside), but as positive charge leaves, the inside becomes more negative and the electrical gradient begins pulling K + back in. The voltage at which these two forces exactly balance, so there is no net flux of that single ion, is its equilibrium (reversal) potential . Because the resting membrane is far more permeable to K + than to anything else, the RMP sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential, near −90 mV, but is dragged a little more positive (to about −70 mV) by the small resting sodium leak. The Nernst equation: equilibrium for a single ion The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for one ion species from its concentration ratio across the membrane. In the form usually quoted for body temperature it is: E ion = (61 / z) × log 10 ( [ion] outside / [ion] inside ) millivolts, where z is the ionic charge (+1 for Na + and K + , −1 for Cl − ) and 61 is the constant RT/F converted to base-10 logarithms at 37°C (the value 58 to 62 is used in different textbooks; learn 61). Worked example: for potassium with roughly 5 mM outside and 140 mM inside, E K = 61 × log 10 (5/140) = 61 × log 10 (0.0357) = 61 × (−1.447) = about −88 mV. That is why the resting cell, dominated by K + permeability, rests near −90 mV. Definition The equilibrium potential of an ion is the membrane voltage at which the electrical force exactly cancels the chemical force, producing zero net movement of that ion. The Nernst equation gives it for a single ion; the GHK equation gives the resting potential when several ions are permeable at once. Exam trap Nernst handles one ion in isolation. title: RML Clinical Psychology, CET-166 · Study Material from Scratch
text: RML Clinical Psychology, CET-166 · Study Material from Scratch ABVIMS & Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital · MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) via GGSIPU · the whole entrance syllabus taught from zero, tuned to how the RML paper actually behaves. Built for Sihan, 2026-07-02. You flagged RML as the emergency, so this is the first RML drop: a complete, from-scratch study text that covers every concept the CET-166 clinical paper tests, built off the syllabus in your RML Task brief and off how past RML / IPU clinical papers actually behave. Read it top to bottom and you have covered the subject core. Every theorist is given by full name (not just a surname), every test names its author, and every therapy names who developed it, because that is exactly what this paper rewards. Now expanded to the full syllabus neighborhood (2026-07-03): not just the PYQ hot topics, but the foundational build-up, the related theories, and the adjacent subtopics the examiner can swing into, so the high-yield material still gets the most room while nothing is left as a blind spot. Every one of the 12 sections gained new ground: the surrounding reasoning types and the full mental-health-law stack, sensation and cognition and language, brain-imaging methods and behaviour genetics, prenatal-to-ageing-to-death development, the self and social cognition and attraction, biological and cognitive and Indian personality models, the history of abnormality plus culture-bound syndromes, the mental status examination and rehabilitation psychology, group and play and specific behavioural therapies, Indian test adaptations and clinical rating scales, qualitative methods and ANOVA and non-parametric statistics, and the six darshanas with Yoga and Buddhist psychology in depth. Entrance CET-166 (GGSIPU) Split 70% test + 30% interview Format large MCQ block, no negative marking 12 sections · from scratch Full-syllabus expanded 2026-07-03 6-year PYQ map 2020–2025 Companion mocks 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 How to use this. This is a teaching text, not a cheatsheet: each section builds a topic from the ground up, then flags the exact traps and matching-items RML fishes for. The green Key boxes are the must-knows, the red Trap boxes are the confusions the paper exploits, the teal Who → what boxes are the theorist / founder pairings, and the purple RML tilt boxes tell you how this specific paper phrases the question. Read the 6-year PYQ map first to set your priorities, then after each section sit the matching part of any of the six live PYQ mocks ( 2020 , 2021 , 2022 , 2023 , 2024 , 2025 ) and the weak spots map straight back here. What makes the RML paper different, baked into every section below: (1) lean harder on Indian Psychology , tested past AND present; (2) treat abnormal as ICD-deep and factual , including the older signs and eponyms DSM has dropped; (3) drill who developed which therapy and the acronyms (REBT, DBT, ACT, EMDR, MI) until reflexive; (4) by the six-year PYQ count the paper is actually carried by General/basic psychology, Assessment & tests, Statistics/Research methods, Abnormal, and Biopsychology (the top five = 65% of marks; see the PYQ map ); (5) no negative marking, so attempt everything . The syllabus, 13 sections: ★ The 6-year PYQ map (read first) 1 · Reasoning, Research Aptitude & General Awareness 2 · General & Basic Psychology 3 · Biopsychology 4 · Developmental 5 · Social 6 · Personality 7 · Abnormal (ICD-deep) 8 · Clinical Psychology 9 · Counselling & Psychotherapy 10 · Assessment & Tests 11 · Research Methods & Statistics 12 · Indian Psychology 13 · Social Work (the RML 2020 strand) ★ What actually repeats: the 6-year PYQ map (2020–2025) Everything below this heading is built from the real RML papers, all six of them : 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, which is 570 actual questions (100 each year except 2023, which had 70). Every one of those questions was tagged to a topic, the topics were counted across the six years, and the concepts that keep coming back were pulled out. So this is not a guess about what the examiner likes; it is the paper's own track record. Read this section first, let it set your priorities, then go into the twelve teaching sections knowing exactly where the marks actually live. How the marks distribute. The single table below is the whole weighting in one view: how many questions each topic drew in each of the six years, the six-year total, its share of the 570 marks, and which teaching section covers it. The bottom four rows of the ranking (cognitive, social, schools, and the rest) are still worth marks, but the top five topics, basic/general, assessment, statistics, abnormal, and biopsychology, are 65% of the entire paper on their own. That is the order to study in. Topic 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 6-yr Share Taught in General & basic psychology 3 4 10 17 38 20 92 16.1% §1–2, sensation, perception, memory, motivation, emotion, intelligence, learning Psychological assessment & tests 9 15 19 3 6 22 74 13.0% §10 Research methods & statistics 8 19 6 21 6 12 72 12.6% §11 Abnormal / psychopathology 19 13 15 1 14 8 70 12.3% §7 Biopsychology 9 6 7 7 18 18 65 11.4% §3 Developmental & child 9 18 14 2 3 8 54 9.5% §4 Counselling & psychotherapy 8 11 15 0 13 1 48 8.4% §9 Cognitive psychology 9 3 6 9 0 10 37 6.5% §2 Social psychology 16 8 8 2 2 1 37 6.5% §5 Schools & systems / applied 10 3 0 8 0 0 21 3.7% §8, §2 Every paper 100 100 100 70 100 100 570 100% the whole book Attack order, straight off the six-year data: (1) General & basic psychology and (2) Assessment & tests and (3) Research methods & statistics are the three biggest buckets, about 42% of the paper between them, and they are the most learnable (definitions, who-built-which-test, stats vocabulary), so bank them first. (4) Abnormal and (5) Biopsychology are the next tier and together add another 24%. Only after those five are solid should you spend heavily on (6) developmental, (7) therapy, (8) cognitive, (9) social, and (10) schools/systems. Personality looks like a zero in the table only because RML rarely labels a question "personality"; its content (Sigmund Freud's structure, Raymond Cattell's 16PF, Hans Eysenck's dimensions, the Big Five) is tested inside the general, abnormal and assessment buckets, so section 6 is not optional, it is spread across the others. RML tilt, confirmed by the data: two things carry across almost every year, so make them reflexive. First, "who developed what" : the paper repeatedly names a test, therapy, or theory and asks for its author (Hermann Rorschach, Henry Murray, Lee Cronbach, Albert Ellis, Aaron Beck, Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson). Second, the projective tests and the defense mechanisms , which appear in four of the six years each. If you drill only two things, drill those. The rest of this section is the concept-by-concept breakdown, topic by topic, ordered biggest bucket first. Each callout names the concept, the years it actually appeared, and the exact fact or distinction the paper fishes for. Every recurring item here has a fuller treatment in the numbered teaching sections below. Schools & Systems of Psychology, 21 questions over six years This is a small but revealing bucket. It is not "systems of psychology" in the textbook sense (structuralism, functionalism, and so on live in the General bucket). Here the recurring core is organisational / industrial behaviour, systems & family therapy, and, from 2023 onward, research software (Excel and SPSS). Learn the named theories and the named theorists, because RML asks them by name. Repeats (2020, 2023): Organisational & industrial psychology is the steadiest thread here. 2020 probed dysfunctional organisational cultures and case management premises; 2023 asked about a decentralised, empowerment-focused structure (the flat / organic structure) and about Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory. Know the two families of motivators at work. Who → what: Frederick Herzberg → Two-Factor (Motivation-Hygiene) Theory. Motivators (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement) drive genuine job satisfaction; hygiene factors (salary, supervision, working conditions, company policy) only prevent dissatisfaction and never satisfy. The 2023 question keys on "motivators that lead to job satisfaction," so pick the growth-of-the-job factors, not pay. Repeats (2020): Group development ran across several 2020 items. Bruce Tuckman's stages are the must-know: forming → storming → norming → performing → adjourning . The 2020 stem "struggle with each other over leadership and group definition" = storming ; "clarified its purpose and strategy for achieving its goals" = norming . Also seen: common group properties, formed-group characteristics, and William Shulman's group-role language. Who → what: Gregory Bateson → the double-bind theory of schizophrenia. The 2021 mother-and-son vignette (she stiffens at his embrace, then blames him for withdrawing, with no escape from the contradiction) is the classic double-bind illustration: conflicting messages on different logical levels with no way to comment on or leave the situation. The 2021 "individuals, families, and cultures given different power as creators of their realities" stem points to constructivist / narrative family therapy. Repeats (2023): Research software is a 2023 cluster worth easy marks. SPSS = the standard statistical-analysis package (tabulation, graphing, statistical tests) in psychology research; MS-Excel uses PivotTables for tabulating data and the AVERAGE function for a mean of a range. Expect one or two verbatim "which software / which function" items. General & Basic Psychology, 92 questions over six years (the biggest bucket) This is the single largest slice of the RML paper and the most scatter-shot: research methodology, motivation, memory, perception, learning, the schools of psychology, stress and health, cognitive biases, and Indian psychology all live here. The good news is that it is theorist-heavy and fact-checkable, so a map of the repeats converts directly into marks. Each year has a centre of gravity: 2022-2023 lean research methods, 2024 is a memory-perception-learning avalanche, and 2025 is almost entirely motivation, schools, and Indian psychology. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2023): Research methodology and design is the largest recurring theme in this bucket. Recurring hooks: the double-blind design (controls both participant and experimenter expectancy), confounding variables (the barbecue-vs-plain-chips flavour and the radio-on/off items both test uncontrolled confounds), sampling methods ( stratified = divide into subgroups then sample each; cluster = sample whole groups), field vs lab experiments, the literature review, hypothesis formulation, plagiarism, and referencing / citation ethics. Trap: Deductive vs inductive reasoning is asked repeatedly (2023, 2024) and students flip them. Deductive = theory first, then test with observations, general → specific; its conclusion's validity depends on the truth of its premises . Inductive = gather data, find patterns, then build a theory, specific observations → broad generalisation (qualitative research leans inductive). If the stem says "starts with a theory," it is deductive. Repeats (2021, 2024, 2025): Motivation theory is a top-three repeat and dominates 2025. Know each by its one-line signature. Abraham Maslow 's hierarchy (self-actualisation = realising full potential; belonging / love must be met before esteem) appears in both 2021 and 2025. Theory & theorist Core claim (RML one-liner) Hierarchy of Needs (Abraham Maslow) Lower needs first; self-actualisation = full potential at the top Self-Determination Theory (Edward Deci & Richard Ryan) Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness; intrinsic motivation = internal reward & growth Expectancy Theory (Victor Vroom) Effort → performance → outcome, and the outcome must be valued (valent) Goal-Setting Theory (Edwin Locke) Specific and difficult (challenging) goals motivate best Drive-Reduction Theory (Clark Hull) Motivation reduces internal tension to restore homeostasis Incentive Theory Behaviour pulled by external rewards / incentives Social Cognitive Theory (Albert Bandura) Self-efficacy and observational learning drive motivation Trap: Self-Determination Theory's three needs are autonomy, competence, relatedness . The 2025 "which is NOT one of the three needs" item plants a decoy (often "achievement" or "esteem"). Achievement belongs to McClelland, not to SDT. Repeats (2020, 2024): Memory is the 2024 heavyweight and links back to 2020. The founders are the answers, so memorise the name-to-concept map below. The 2024 paper alone tests the magic number, the serial-position effect, decay theory, filter / attenuation theories, tip-of-the-tongue, the PQRST study method, and the method of reconstruction. Concept Theorist (the answer) "Magic number" 7 ± 2 (span of short-term memory) George A. Miller Primacy-recency / serial-position effect Hermann Ebbinghaus Filter theory of attention Donald Broadbent Filter-attenuation theory Anne Treisman Self-reference effect T. B. Rogers (Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker) Decay theory of forgetting Edward Thorndike (law of disuse) RML tilt: "Tip of the tongue" is a retrieval failure (the trace is stored but momentarily inaccessible), not encoding or storage. In the PQRST study method (Preview, Question, Read, Self-recitation, Test), S = Self-recitation (actively recalling in your own words). And the 2020 "what do Hermann Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share" item keys on their common contribution to the early study of memory / association . Repeats (2024): Perception and Gestalt organisation form a dense 2024 block. Dark adaptation = the eyes growing more sensitive to light (dim light) over time; closure = the Gestalt tendency to complete an incomplete figure; the Stroop effect = interference / selective-attention breakdown (colour word vs ink colour). Depth cues recur as a mini-family (below). 2024 depth-cue stem Monocular cue Rail tracks appear to converge Linear perspective Density of stones increases with distance Texture gradient Painted stripes on a freeway off-ramp Relative size / texture gradient Repeats (2024, 2025): Learning and conditioning span both years. Insight learning (sudden "aha" grasp of a solution) is Wolfgang Kohler's Gestalt work; shaping = reinforcing successive approximations; extinction = weakening a habit by removing all reward; stimulus generalisation vs discrimination (the furry-black-cat vs short-haired-tabby item = discrimination); a token that must be traded (five stickers) is a secondary / conditioned reinforcer . 2025 names the parent school directly: stimulus-response conditioning = behaviourism . Repeats (2020, 2024, 2025): The schools of psychology and their history recur across three years. 2020 asked who first used "clinical psychology" in print ( Lightner Witmer , 1896-1907, who also opened the first psychology clinic). 2024 asked who gave "folk psychology" / Volkerpsychologie ( Wilhelm Wundt ). 2025 asked you to name whole approaches from a description. Approach (2025 stems) Signature & key figures Behaviourism Learning via stimulus-response conditioning; John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner Psychodynamic / psychoanalytic Unconscious forces & early childhood; inner drives beyond control; Sigmund Freud Humanistic Free will, growth, self-actualisation; Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers Comparative psychology Study of animal behaviour Structuralism / founder of the field Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, 1879); "folk psychology" Repeats (2024): Stress and health cluster in 2024. Hans Selye 's General Adaptation Syndrome runs in strict order: alarm → resistance → exhaustion . Type A behaviour is the pattern most directly linked to higher coronary-heart-disease risk. Distinguish an acute stressor (short, sharp, time-limited) from a chronic one. Trap: 2024 mixes several cognitive-bias / problem-solving terms that look alike. Functional fixedness = seeing an object only in its usual use; hindsight bias = the "I knew it all along" overestimate of past predictability; a heuristic = a rule-of-thumb shortcut for efficient search. Do not swap functional fixedness for mental set. RML tilt: Indian psychology is a live 2025 theme (five questions) and is easy to underprepare. Core points: it is rooted in Vedanta and the Indian philosophical traditions and centres on consciousness and the self ; Atman = the true self / soul (distinct from ego); it treats mental health holistically (mind-body-spirit, practices such as yoga and meditation) rather than through a purely Western symptom-and-diagnosis lens. Assessment & Tests, 74 questions over six years This topic is dominated by a handful of named tests and the reliability-validity vocabulary: the Rorschach, the MMPI, the TAT and projective logic, the reliability and validity families, and the IQ line reappear in year after year, so the recurring names below carry most of the marks. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): The Rorschach inkblot test is the single most-repeated item. Built by Hermann Rorschach (Swiss psychiatrist, 1921), it has 10 cards total : 5 achromatic (black and grey), 2 black-and-red, and 3 fully multicoloured, so 5 cards are coloured . It is a projective test of personality and unconscious process. RML also asks its procedure: the Enquiry (Inquiry) Phase is the second stage where the examiner returns to each blot to ask what was seen and what made it look that way (location, determinants). Who → what: Hermann Rorschach → inkblot test; Henry Murray & Christiana Morgan → Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), 1930s (1935), Harvard; Starke Hathaway & J. Charnley McKinley → MMPI; John Buck → House-Tree-Person test; Edgar Doll → Vineland Social Maturity Scale; Lee Cronbach → coefficient alpha; Alfred Binet & Theodore Simon → first intelligence test (1905); David Wechsler → WAIS/WISC. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022): The MMPI (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) is asked almost every early year. It is an objective, self-report inventory that measures psychopathology and personality (clinical scales plus validity scales), NOT a projective test and NOT an intelligence test. That objective-self-report identity is the fact RML fishes for. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): Projective tests and their techniques. A projective test uses ambiguous stimuli to draw out unconscious thoughts, motives and personality. Learn the technique labels the paper uses: the Rorschach is an association technique ; the TAT is a construction technique (the participant constructs a story); word-association is also association-based. The TAT's stories are analysed to infer needs, motives and inner conflicts (Murray's need-press theory). Trap: TAT vs Rorschach. Both are projective, but the Rorschach uses inkblots (perception/association) while the TAT uses picture cards of people in scenes and asks for a story (apperception/construction). RML asks directly for the "key difference" and for how many TAT cards are used: the full set is 31, and roughly 20 are shown in a typical session. Who → what: the reliability family. Test-retest = same test, same people, two occasions (stability over time). Inter-rater = agreement between two scorers/observers. Split-half = correlate two halves of one test, best split by the odd-even method and corrected by Spearman-Brown. Cronbach's alpha ( Lee Cronbach ) = internal consistency across all items. RML has asked each of these by definition in 2021, 2022 and 2025. Repeats (2021, 2024, 2025): Validity types. Face validity = looks like it measures the trait, on the surface. Content validity = covers the whole domain. Criterion-related validity splits into concurrent (against a criterion measured now) and predictive (against a future criterion). Construct validity = the test truly captures the theoretical construct. Trap: the 2024 and 2025 items ask which type is NOT criterion-based. Only concurrent and predictive are criterion-based; construct and content validity are separate categories, so they are the correct "NOT criterion" answers. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2025): Intelligence and IQ. Memorise the ratio-IQ formula IQ = (Mental Age ÷ Chronological Age) × 100 (MA 8, CA 10 → IQ 80). Know the test-to-author map: WAIS/WISC are Wechsler individual intelligence scales; Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices measure nonverbal fluid intelligence; the first intelligence test was built by Alfred Binet (with Theodore Simon, 1905). RML tilt: RML likes attitude-scale and rating-scale wording. A Likert scale ( Rensis Likert ) is a summated rating scale : agree-to-disagree items are summed into one score. It appears in 2020, 2022 and 2023 phrased as "summated rating scale," "attitude measurement scale," or "a Likert scale is best described as." Research Methods & Statistics, 72 questions over six years Stats repeats cluster tightly on five spines: sampling methods, scales of measurement, the ANOVA/F machinery, central tendency, and the correlation-is-not-causation logic, with hypothesis testing errors and research ethics close behind. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2023, 2025): Sampling methods, the top stats repeat. Split probability from non-probability. Convenience/accidental (whoever is easy to recruit), snowball (participants refer others), and quota/purposive are non-probability . Systematic sampling = selecting every nth person from a list. Random sampling matters because it gives every member an equal chance and makes the sample representative, which is what licenses generalisation. Repeats (2023, 2024, 2025): Scales of measurement (S.S. Stevens). Nominal = unordered categories (car colours). Ordinal = ranked. Interval = equal intervals but an arbitrary/no true zero (temperature). Ratio = equal intervals plus a true zero and counting (number of books). Trap: zero is the discriminator. The 2024 "arbitrary zero" item is the interval scale; the 2023 "equal intervals AND a true zero point" item is the ratio scale. Do not answer ratio when it says arbitrary zero. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2025): Measures of central tendency are mean, median and mode ; standard deviation is a measure of dispersion, NOT central tendency (a common "which is NOT" answer). In a negatively skewed distribution the order is mean < median < mode , so the mean sits to the left of (below) the median. For skewed data such as anxiety scores, the median is the preferred summary because it resists outliers. Who → what: the ANOVA family (2021, 2022). Ronald Fisher → ANOVA and the F-ratio , where F = between-groups variance ÷ within-groups (pooled/error) variance, so the denominator is the pooled within-group variance . As chance (error) variance falls, F rises . Post-hoc tests (Tukey's HSD, Scheffe, Duncan's multiple range, Newman-Keuls) are run only after a significant ANOVA . ANCOVA adds one assumption ANOVA lacks: a covariate statistically controlled for. Repeats (2021, 2025): Correlation is not causation. A correlational or observational study (regularly exercising adults being less depressed, meditators being less stressed) cannot establish cause because there is no manipulation and no random assignment , so third variables and reverse causation stay open. This exact reasoning is RML's favourite "why is this conclusion not appropriate" item. Who → what: matching a test to the data. Pearson's r → two continuous variables (stress vs sleep). Biserial/point-biserial → one continuous and one dichotomous variable. Non-parametric equivalents (2023): Mann-Whitney U → independent-samples t-test; Kruskal-Wallis → one-way ANOVA (3+ independent groups); Friedman → repeated-measures design. Repeats (2022, 2023): Hypothesis-testing errors. A Type I error = rejecting a true null (false positive, controlled by alpha). A Type II error = failing to reject a null that is actually false (false negative). The 2023 stem "fails to reject the null when it is actually false" is by definition Type II . RML tilt: two smaller but reliable repeats. Informed consent (2021, 2025) = telling participants the study's purpose and procedures so they can freely decide to take part. And the normal-distribution line (2021, 2022): the z-table is derived from the standard normal curve, and the bell curve was first described by Abraham de Moivre and popularised by Carl Friedrich Gauss (hence "Gaussian"). Abnormal & Psychopathology, 70 questions over six years This is the single heaviest cluster on the CET-166 paper, and it rewards flat memorisation over reasoning. RML sits close to the ICD text, loves the older eponyms and signs (Bleuler, Schneider, Janet), and returns to the same handful of anchors every year: Sigmund Freud's defense mechanisms, schizophrenia signs, the anorexia-versus-bulimia contrast, mood disorders, and dissociation. Learn these as fact lists, not as concepts to derive under time pressure. Repeats (2020, 2022, 2024, 2025): Defense mechanisms are the number-one recurring item, almost always as a clinical vignette ("name the mechanism"). Sigmund Freud's ego defenses you must recognise on sight: sublimation (channeling an unacceptable urge into an acceptable outlet, e.g. anger into kickboxing), projection (attributing your own unacceptable thoughts or impulses to others, asked twice in 2025), displacement (redirecting a feeling from a threatening target to a safer one, e.g. yelling at the dog when angry at your partner), repression (involuntary blocking of painful material from awareness), and rationalisation (excusing failure by blaming an external cause, e.g. Clare blaming a co-worker for being fired). Mechanism Core move Paper cue Sublimation Urge → socially valued outlet Anger → kickboxing class Projection Own impulse attributed to others "attributing unacceptable thoughts to others" Displacement Feeling shifted to a safer target Yells at dog / argues with husband Repression Involuntary blocking from awareness Cannot bring anxiety-provoking material to consciousness Rationalisation Self-serving excuse for a failure Blames co-worker for being fired Splitting All-good / all-bad, no middle Seen in borderline personality disorder Projective identification Melanie Klein, paranoid-schizoid Ego defense "in paranoia" Who → what: Sigmund Freud → structural model ( id runs on the pleasure principle, ego on the reality principle, superego is morality) and the topographic model (the preconscious holds accessible memories recalled at will). Asked in 2020, 2022 (Freud on alcohol dependence = oral-stage fixation) and 2025 ("component that operates on the reality principle" = the ego). Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Schizophrenia recurs every one of those years. Know the positive versus negative symptom split (positive = added experiences: delusions, hallucinations; negative = lost function: flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia), identical-twin concordance of roughly 50 percent , and expressed emotion (EE) = a family climate of criticism, hostility and emotional over-involvement that predicts relapse. RML also asks the ICD inclusion/exclusion criteria directly. Who → what: Kurt Schneider → First-Rank Symptoms of schizophrenia (2022 "who gave the concept", 2024 "which is NOT a first-rank symptom"). The list: audible thoughts / voices commenting or arguing, thought withdrawal-insertion-broadcasting, made (passivity) feelings, impulses and acts, and delusional perception. Anything negative-symptom (e.g. flat affect) is the classic "NOT first-rank" trap answer. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Eating disorders, always framed as anorexia-versus-bulimia. Shared feature = intense fear of weight gain plus disturbed body image; the discriminator = anorexia nervosa carries markedly low body weight (and, in older criteria, amenorrhea = absence of menstrual periods), whereas bulimia nervosa runs at near-normal weight with binge eating plus compensatory behaviour (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, fasting, over-exercise). Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022, 2024): Mood / affective disorders. Bipolar is the disorder where mood "swings from one extreme to another"; a manic episode's core pair = elevated/expansive mood plus increased energy or activity. Major depressive disorder is cued by loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) and appetite change, NOT euphoria or specific phobias. Dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder) = milder but longer-lasting than MDD. Depression is the one the paper nicknames the " common cold of psychiatry " and the usual cause of pseudodementia . Repeats (2022, 2024, 2025): Dissociative disorders. Multiple distinct personalities within one person = dissociative identity disorder (DID). Psychodynamic theory reads dissociative symptoms as defense against trauma; dissociative amnesia is usually localised or selective, whereas generalised amnesia wipes the entire life history. RML pairs this with hysteria/conversion signs (see eponyms below). Repeats (2023, 2025): The diathesis-stress model asks the same thing twice: mental disorders arise from the interaction of a predisposing vulnerability (the diathesis, genetic or biological) with environmental stress, not from either alone. Repeats (2021, 2022, 2025): Personality disorders. They are stable, long-term, pervasive patterns. Antisocial PD = manipulation, lack of remorse, irresponsibility; obsessive-compulsive PD = driven by a need for order and control (not the same as OCD). RML tilt: The 2024 paper in particular is dense with eponyms and older signs , so bank them cold: "ambivalence" (one of Eugen Bleuler's four A's) was coined by Eugen Bleuler ; "la belle indifférence" in hysteria is attributed to Pierre Janet ; delusion of infidelity = Othello syndrome (delusional jealousy); First-Rank Symptoms = Kurt Schneider ; kleptomania is a classic French-alienist eponym. RML rewards knowing the name attached to the term, not just the term. Counselling & Psychotherapy, 48 questions over six years The therapy section is built around two obsessions RML returns to every year: who developed which therapy (founder attribution) and the mechanics of behaviour therapy and CBT . Learn the acronym-to-founder map below cold; it converts several guaranteed marks. Note that ego defense mechanisms reappear inside this section too, so the Freud grid above is doing double duty. Who → what: This is the paper's favourite therapy question type (2021, 2022, 2024 all ask it). Memorise the founder map: Therapy / concept Developer (full name) Cognitive therapy / CBT, Socratic questioning Aaron Beck REBT and the ABC model Albert Ellis DBT (distress tolerance) Marsha Linehan ACT (acceptance & commitment) Steven Hayes EMDR Francine Shapiro Motivational Interviewing (MI) William Miller & Stephen Rollnick Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) Gerald Klerman & Myrna Weissman Client-centred therapy Carl Rogers Self-efficacy Albert Bandura Systematic desensitisation Joseph Wolpe Progressive deep muscle relaxation Edmund Jacobson Individual psychology, inferiority complex Alfred Adler Collective unconscious Carl Jung Repeats (2021, 2022, 2024, 2025): The cognitive family. Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy is drilled through its methods (Socratic questioning, collaborative identification of cognitive errors such as overgeneralisation and arbitrary inference, thought records for depression). Albert Ellis's REBT is drilled through the ABC model : Activating event → Beliefs → Consequences. Keep Beck (errors/distortions) and Ellis (irrational beliefs, ABC) separate in your head; the paper baits you to swap them. Repeats (2020, 2021, 2022): Behaviour therapy built on relaxation. The technique where a patient relaxes while visualising a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking scenes (the public-speaking vignette in 2021) is systematic desensitisation , developed by Joseph Wolpe on the principle of reciprocal inhibition / counterconditioning; the relaxation half is Edmund Jacobson's progressive deep relaxation. Repeats (2021, 2022): Operant-based methods. "Behaviour analysis" and "functional analysis" (asked verbatim, twice each) rest on the principles of operant conditioning (B.F. Skinner): behaviour is shaped by its consequences. Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations; the "Lovaas programme" = applied behaviour analysis for autism. Who → what: EMDR (2021, 2022) → Francine Shapiro, and it was developed specifically for PTSD / trauma ; the technique pairs recall of the distressing memory with bilateral eye movements. DBT and its distress tolerance module (2024) → Marsha Linehan. Trap: Defense mechanisms show up inside the therapy section, not just abnormal (2024 asked four in a row). Match them precisely: displacement (harassed at work → argues at home), projective identification in paranoia (Melanie Klein), isolation / undoing / reaction formation in OCD, and splitting in borderline personality disorder. Also do not confuse OCD's exposure treatment ERP (exposure and response prevention) with EMDR. Biopsychology, 65 questions over six years Biopsychology is the single biggest physiological load in the RML paper, and it repeats along a small set of predictable axes: which neurotransmitter goes with which disease, which lobe or structure does which job, and how the classic theories of emotion order the events. Learn the tables below cold and you clear most of the section on recognition alone. Repeats (2022, 2023, 2024, 2025): Neurotransmitter → function/disease is asked almost every year. Memorise the pairings: acetylcholine loss → Alzheimer's dementia (2022), dopamine degeneration in the substantia nigra → Parkinson's disease (2023), endorphins are the "feel-good" neurotransmitters (2024), and alcohol acts as an agonist at GABA receptors (2022).
