Neurotransmitter Signature link RML tests Acetylcholine Deficiency → Alzheimer's disease; muscle activation Dopamine Degeneration → Parkinson's; blocked by neuroleptics GABA Main inhibitory NT; alcohol is an agonist Endorphins "Feel-good" NT, pain relief and pleasure Serotonin / Dopamine Mood; targets of antidepressants and antipsychotics Repeats (2020, 2024): Lobe → function is a perennial. The frontal lobe handles cognitive/intellectual functioning and voluntary movement (2020, 2024), the parietal lobe interprets sensory information (2024), the occipital lobe processes vision, and the temporal lobe processes hearing and language. Lobe Main domain Frontal Voluntary movement, planning, intellect, personality Parietal Somatosensory, interpreting sensory input, spatial sense Occipital Vision Temporal Hearing, language comprehension, memory Repeats (2020, 2023, 2024, 2025): Subcortical structure → job is tested constantly. Fix these: hippocampus → consolidation of long-term memory and the site damaged in anterograde amnesia (2023, 2024); amygdala → emotion, fear and aggression, the "seat of emotion" (2023, 2025); hypothalamus → hunger/satiety centre and homeostasis (2021, 2024); medulla (brainstem) → breathing and heart rate (2023); pineal gland → melatonin and the circadian sleep-wake clock (2022, 2023). Structure Function RML fishes for Hippocampus Long-term memory consolidation; damaged in anterograde amnesia Amygdala Fear, aggression, emotional modulation of memory ("seat of emotion") Hypothalamus Satiety/hunger centre, homeostasis, links to pituitary Medulla oblongata Vital autonomic functions: breathing, heart rate Pineal gland Melatonin; circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycle Trap: The "satiety centre" is the ventromedial hypothalamus (destroy it and the rat overeats), while the lateral hypothalamus is the hunger/feeding centre (destroy it and the rat stops eating). RML has flipped these both ways (2021, 2024). Who → what: Theories of emotion recur every cycle (2020, 2025). William James and Carl Lange (James-Lange theory): stimulus → bodily/physiological arousal → then the felt emotion ("we are afraid because we tremble"). Walter Cannon and Philip Bard (Cannon-Bard theory): arousal and emotion occur simultaneously. Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer (two-factor theory): arousal plus a cognitive label, which explains misattribution of arousal, feeling attraction when actually just aroused by fear (2020, 2025). Who → what: Paul Ekman is tied to the six universally recognised basic emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust (2025 asks which one is NOT on the list, so anything like "contempt", "pride", or "love" is the answer). Repeats (2021, 2022, 2024): Alcohol-related amnesia recurs. Chronic alcoholism → Korsakoff's syndrome (thiamine/B1 deficiency), classically involving profound retrograde amnesia and confabulation (2021, 2024). Distinguish anterograde amnesia (cannot form NEW memories, hippocampal damage) from retrograde amnesia (loss of OLD memories). Who → what: Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) describes stress in three stages: alarm, resistance, exhaustion (2020). Pair this with the fight-or-flight response, run by the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system with the adrenal glands (2024). Repeats (2022, 2024): Sleep architecture appears repeatedly. A normal night runs in roughly 90-minute cycles, giving about 4 to 6 NREM-REM cycles per major sleep period (2022, 2024). Know the NREM to REM progression and that REM is when vivid dreaming occurs. Who → what: Aphasia (loss of language) is the umbrella term (2020), and RML repeatedly probes Broca's aphasia: slow, laboured, non-fluent, telegraphic speech using only keywords, from damage to Broca's area in the left frontal lobe (2022, 2025). Contrast Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech, comprehension lost). Prosopagnosia is the specific inability to recognise faces (2024). Repeats (2024, 2025): Sensory systems and thresholds recur. The vestibular system (semicircular canals of the inner ear) senses spin and balance (2024); rods are the receptors for scotopic (dim-light) vision (2024); the human ear responds to roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (2024); and the absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detectable 50% of the time (2025). RML tilt: The 2024 and 2025 papers lean on split-brain and imaging facts. Cutting the corpus callosum severs communication between the two hemispheres (Roger Sperry's split-brain work); the left hemisphere is typically dominant for language and analytic processing. For imaging, EEG gives the highest temporal resolution, while CT/MRI are used to view brain structure after a head injury (2025). RML tilt: The pituitary is repeatedly framed as the "master gland" that controls the other endocrine glands and regulates growth (2024). Neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drugs treat psychosis/schizophrenia and can cause tardive dyskinesia as a long-term side effect (2022, 2025). Cognitive Psychology, 37 questions over six years Cognitive Psychology in RML clusters tightly around three areas: the architecture of memory (stores, working memory, memory types), how and why we forget, and perception with its named theorists and biases. Almost every named-psychologist question in the section comes from perception or decision-making, so bind each name to its one idea. Who → what: The stage/multi-store model (Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin) runs sensory memory → short-term/working memory → long-term memory. Sensory memory holds information for the shortest duration (2020), and RML asks which store is NOT part of this model (2025). Encoding is the process that moves new information into memory (2025). Store Duration / capacity Sensory memory Shortest, under ~1 second; large raw capacity Short-term / working ~15-30 sec; ~7 items (George Miller) Long-term memory Potentially unlimited and long-lasting Who → what: Working memory (Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch) is a repeat favourite. Know its four components: the central executive (attention controller, disrupted by a demanding secondary task, 2022), the phonological loop (verbal/auditory), the visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buff

title: SGT University · MA Clinical Psychology Entrance · Study Material from Scratch
text: SGT University · MA Clinical Psychology Entrance · Study Material from Scratch Shree Guru Gobind Singh Tricentenary University, Gurugram · MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) · the whole general-psychology core taught from zero, packaged as one deep readable book. Built for Sihan, 2026-07-04. RML is in the bag, so this is the SGT drop. Here is the honest starting point: SGT does not publish a syllabus PDF the way RML's CET-166 does. The official line is that the entrance "syllabus will be as prescribed by SGT University as per the guidelines of the UGC," which in plain terms means a general psychology aptitude test drawn from the standard PG-psychology core, followed by a personal interview. So this book is not built off a leaked topic list; it is built off the seven areas a UGC-guideline general-psych test actually pulls from, the same base you have been grinding all cycle, just gathered into one place you can read top to bottom. Every theorist is given by full name, every test names its author, every therapy names who developed it, because that is exactly what a general-awareness paper rewards. Read it end to end and you have covered the subject core for SGT, and for every other general-psych entrance on your list. Entrance SGT MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) Two stages written test → interview No published syllabus UGC-guideline general psych 14 chapters · from scratch Exam ~11 Jul 2026, Gurugram campus Tracker SGT pattern & dates How to use this. This is a teaching text, not a cheatsheet: each chapter builds a topic from the ground up, then flags the exact traps a general-psych paper fishes for. The green Key boxes are the must-knows, the red Trap boxes are the confusions the paper exploits, the teal Who → what boxes are the theorist / founder / test pairings, and the amber Why boxes explain the mechanism so it sticks. The book now runs to fourteen content chapters: the seven core subject areas plus full stand-alone chapters on learning, memory and cognition, motivation and emotion, social psychology, personality, and intelligence, since a general-psychology paper samples every one of these. Read Section 1 first to set your priorities, then work the chapters. Because SGT has no negative-marking guidance published, treat every question as answerable and never leave a blank. Contents: 1 · How the SGT paper behaves 2 · Biopsychology & physiological 3 · Developmental 4 · Abnormal & clinical 5 · Assessment & testing 6 · Psychotherapy & counselling 7 · Statistics & research methodology 8 · General awareness & history 9 · Learning & conditioning 10 · Memory, attention & cognition 11 · Motivation & emotion 12 · Social psychology 13 · Personality 14 · Intelligence 15 · The attack plan & the interview 1 How the SGT paper behaves, and how to prep it Before any content, get the shape of the thing right, because half of prepping an entrance is knowing what you are walking into. SGT University runs its own offline entrance for the MA Clinical Psychology (RCI) programme at its Gurugram campus, in two stages: a written test followed by a personal interview . Unlike RML's CET-166, there is no standalone syllabus document, no published breakdown of number of questions, marks per question, duration, or negative marking. SGT's own pages say only that the syllabus follows UGC guidelines. That is not a gap in your prep; it is the design. A UGC-guideline general-psychology aptitude test means the paper samples broadly and shallowly across the whole PG-psychology base rather than drilling deep into one niche. Key. No published SGT syllabus is not a reason to panic; it is a reason to prep breadth over depth. The paper rewards the person who can recognise a term, a theorist, or a test from any corner of psychology, not the person who has memorised one topic to the bone. The seven areas the written test draws on Mapping the "UGC-guideline general psychology" wording onto how these general aptitude papers actually behave, the written test pulls from seven areas. This book has one section per area, in this order: # Area What it samples 2 Biopsychology / physiological Neuron, action potential, neurotransmitters, brain structures, endocrine, sensation & perception 3 Developmental Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson, Lev Vygotsky, attachment, moral & lifespan development 4 Abnormal / clinical DSM-5-TR & ICD-11, the major disorders, etiology, case vignettes 5 Assessment / testing Reliability & validity, intelligence & personality tests, projectives, Indian adaptations 6 Psychotherapy & counselling Psychoanalytic, behavioural, CBT, humanistic; who developed which therapy 7 Statistics & research methodology Descriptive & inferential stats, designs, sampling, ethics 8 General awareness / aptitude History & schools of psychology, learning, memory, social psychology, key theorists Why this order. Biopsychology and developmental are the highest-density "recognise the fact" areas in any general paper, so they lead. Assessment and therapy are where the "who made this" questions cluster, so full names are non-negotiable there. General awareness is last because it is the catch-all that ties the schools and theorists together once you have met them in the earlier sections. Trap. Do not confuse SGT's general aptitude test with a deep clinical M.Phil paper. A general-psych entrance will ask "who proposed the hierarchy of needs" far more often than it asks a fine-grained ICD-11 sub-code. Prep the recognisable landmarks of every area, not the deep cuts of one. How to spend the days you have Breadth pass first. Read all fourteen chapters once, front to back, so no area is a blank. That alone clears most of a general aptitude paper. Second pass on the founder boxes. The teal Who → what boxes are the single most exam-efficient thing here; a general paper is dense with "match the theorist / test / therapy to its author." Use your existing mocks as the drill. Everything on the site (the PYQ mocks, the common-section work, the bio and diagnostic sets) is the same base SGT samples. Sitting any of them is valid SGT practice. Prep the interview in parallel (Section 9): the second stage is a real gate, and it is the cheapest marks to secure because it rewards clarity about why you want clinical psychology, not more recall. 2 Biopsychology & Physiological Psychology Biopsychology (also called physiological psychology, biological psychology, or behavioural neuroscience) asks one question: how does the physical machinery of the body, above all the nervous system, produce behaviour, thought, emotion, and experience? To answer an entrance paper on this topic you must be able to build the brain from its smallest working part upward. We therefore start with the single cell, the neuron, and end with whole-brain imaging. Nothing here needs prior biology; every term is defined as it appears. 2.1 The Neuron: The Unit of the Nervous System The nervous system is built from billions of specialised cells called neurons (nerve cells) that receive, integrate, and transmit information as electrical and chemical signals. A neuron is not like an ordinary body cell; it is shaped for communication, with parts that collect signals at one end and pass them on at the other. Parts of a neuron Soma (cell body): the metabolic centre. It holds the nucleus and keeps the cell alive. Incoming signals are summed here. Dendrites: short, branching fibres that spread out from the soma like the branches of a tree (the word means "little tree"). They are the receiving surface; they collect signals from other neurons. Axon: a single long fibre that carries the outgoing signal away from the soma toward other cells. One neuron has many dendrites but usually just one axon (which may branch at its end). Myelin sheath: a fatty white insulating layer wrapped in segments around many axons. It speeds up signal conduction and stops the signal leaking. Myelin is why "white matter" is white. Nodes of Ranvier: the small unmyelinated gaps between segments of myelin. The signal jumps from node to node (see saltatory conduction). Terminal buttons (axon terminals, end feet): the swollen tips at the end of the axon branches. They store and release chemical messengers onto the next cell. Why. The neuron's shape is a receive-integrate-transmit pipeline: dendrites in, soma decides, axon out, terminals hand off. Every fact about signalling maps onto this direction of flow, so memorise the direction, not just the parts. Glial cells (neuroglia): the support staff Neurons are outnumbered by glial cells ("glia" means glue), which support, feed, insulate, and protect neurons. They do not fire signals themselves but are essential. Astrocytes: star-shaped cells that hold neurons in place, supply nutrients, mop up excess chemicals, and help form the blood-brain barrier. Oligodendrocytes: make the myelin sheath in the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). One oligodendrocyte myelinates several axons. Schwann cells: make the myelin sheath in the peripheral nervous system (nerves outside the brain and cord). One Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one axon, and Schwann cells help peripheral nerves regenerate. Microglia: the immune cells of the nervous system; they clean up dead cells and fight infection. Trap. Papers love to swap myelin-makers: oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS, Schwann cells myelinate the PNS. If a question mentions the brain or spinal cord, the answer is oligodendrocyte; if it mentions a peripheral nerve, the answer is Schwann. The neuron doctrine: Golgi versus Cajal In the late 1800s scientists argued whether the nervous system was one continuous web (the "reticular theory") or a set of separate cells. Camillo Golgi , an Italian physician, invented a silver-staining method (the "black reaction") that made single neurons visible, yet he believed the network was continuous. The Spaniard Santiago Ramon y Cajal used Golgi's own stain to show that neurons are separate, individual cells that merely communicate across tiny gaps. Cajal's view, the neuron doctrine , won. Who → what. Camillo Golgi → the silver stain that revealed neurons (but he backed the continuous-network theory). Santiago Ramon y Cajal → the neuron doctrine (neurons are discrete cells). They shared the 1906 Nobel Prize despite disagreeing. 2.2 Resting and Action Potentials: How a Neuron Fires The resting potential A neuron at rest is electrically charged, like a tiny battery. The inside of the axon is about −70 millivolts (mV) relative to the outside; this is the resting membrane potential . It exists because charged particles (ions) are unevenly spread across the membrane: sodium (Na+) is concentrated outside, potassium (K+) inside, and the inside carries a net negative charge. Key. Resting potential = about −70 mV, inside negative. The neuron is "polarised" and ready to fire. This imbalance is maintained by the sodium-potassium pump , a protein in the membrane that constantly pushes 3 sodium ions out for every 2 potassium ions it pulls in, using energy. Because it moves more positive charge out than in, it helps keep the inside negative. The action potential (the nerve impulse) When enough incoming signals push the membrane past a threshold (about −55 mV), the neuron fires an action potential , a rapid electrical spike that travels down the axon. It has clear phases: Depolarisation: sodium channels open, Na+ rushes in, and the inside shoots up toward +30 to +40 mV (briefly positive). Repolarisation: sodium channels close, potassium channels open, K+ flows out, and the charge drops back toward negative. Hyperpolarisation (undershoot): the charge briefly overshoots below −70 mV before the pump restores the resting state. Key. The all-or-none law : a neuron either fires a full action potential or none at all. The strength of a stimulus is coded by how often the neuron fires (frequency), not by making a bigger spike. Every spike is the same size. Refractory periods Absolute refractory period: immediately after firing, the neuron cannot fire again no matter how strong the stimulus (sodium channels are inactivated). Relative refractory period: shortly after, the neuron can fire again but only with a stronger-than-usual stimulus. Why. The refractory period forces the impulse to travel in one direction (down the axon, not backward) and sets an upper limit on firing rate. Saltatory conduction In myelinated axons the impulse does not crawl smoothly; it jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next (Latin saltare , to leap). This saltatory conduction is much faster and more energy-efficient than conduction along an unmyelinated fibre. Trap. When myelin is destroyed (as in multiple sclerosis), conduction slows and fails; saltatory conduction cannot occur without intact myelin and nodes. Do not confuse the nodes (bare gaps) with the myelin (insulation): the impulse jumps to the nodes because the myelinated stretches are skipped. 2.3 Synaptic Transmission: How Neurons Talk to Each Other Neurons do not touch. Between the terminal button of one neuron and the dendrite of the next lies a microscopic gap, the synapse (synaptic cleft). The signal crosses this gap chemically. The action potential reaches the terminal button of the presynaptic (sending) neuron. Calcium enters and causes tiny sacs called synaptic vesicles to move to the membrane. By exocytosis the vesicles fuse with the membrane and dump their neurotransmitter (chemical messenger) into the cleft. The neurotransmitter drifts across and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic (receiving) neuron, like a key in a lock. This opens channels and changes the postsynaptic cell's charge. The signal is then cleared by reuptake (the presynaptic neuron sucks the transmitter back in for reuse) or by enzymes that break it down. Excitation and inhibition EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential): the transmitter makes the postsynaptic cell more likely to fire (depolarises it toward threshold). IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential): the transmitter makes it less likely to fire (hyperpolarises it away from threshold). Why. A neuron is a voting machine: it constantly adds up EPSPs and IPSPs arriving on its dendrites and soma (this is "summation"). Only if excitation outweighs inhibition past threshold does it fire. Behaviour is the net result of this balance across billions of cells. The discovery of neurotransmission Who → what. Otto Loewi → first proof of chemical neurotransmission. In a famous 1921 frog-heart experiment (reportedly designed in a dream) he stimulated the vagus nerve of one heart, collected its fluid, applied it to a second heart, and slowed that heart too. He named the substance "Vagusstoff" ("vagus substance"), later identified as acetylcholine , the first known neurotransmitter. Charles Sherrington → coined the term "synapse" and described reflex integration. 2.4 Major Neurotransmitters Different chemical messengers do different jobs, and many disorders and drugs work by changing one of them. Learn the function and the clinical link for each; entrance papers almost always test the link. Neurotransmitter Main function Disorder / drug link Acetylcholine (ACh) Muscle movement, learning, memory, arousal Loss of ACh neurons in Alzheimer’s disease; blocked at the junction in myasthenia gravis Dopamine Reward, motivation, voluntary movement, pleasure Too much (overactivity) linked to schizophrenia; too little (loss of cells) causes Parkinson’s disease Serotonin Mood, sleep, appetite, impulse control Low levels linked to depression and anxiety; SSRIs raise it Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) Alertness, arousal, fight-or-flight Involved in mood disorders and stress; targeted by some antidepressants GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) The main inhibitory transmitter; calms neural activity Low activity linked to anxiety and seizures; boosted by benzodiazepines and alcohol Glutamate The main excitatory transmitter; learning and memory Excess causes excitotoxicity (cell death from over-firing), implicated in stroke and seizures Endorphins Natural painkillers; pleasure and "runner’s high" Mimicked by opiate drugs (morphine, heroin), which bind endorphin receptors Key. Memorise the four highest-yield pairings: dopamine → schizophrenia (too much) and Parkinson’s (too little); serotonin → depression; GABA → anxiety (the calming brake); acetylcholine → Alzheimer’s and memory. Trap. GABA is inhibitory (the brain’s brake) and glutamate is excitatory (the accelerator). Papers reverse these constantly. Also note dopamine is the classic "two-disease" transmitter: excess → schizophrenia, deficit → Parkinson’s, which is why anti-schizophrenia drugs can cause Parkinson-like side effects. 2.5 Organisation of the Nervous System The whole nervous system splits into two great divisions: Central nervous system (CNS): the brain and the spinal cord. This is the control centre and integrator. Peripheral nervous system (PNS): all the nerves outside the CNS that connect it to the body and outside world. The PNS divides again: Somatic nervous system: carries sensory information in and controls voluntary skeletal muscles (moving your arm). Autonomic nervous system (ANS): controls involuntary functions of glands and internal organs (heartbeat, digestion). It has two opposing branches. Situation Sympathetic branch Parasympathetic branch Role "Fight or flight" (arouses, spends energy) "Rest and digest" (calms, conserves energy) Heart rate Speeds up Slows down Pupils Dilate (widen) Constrict (narrow) Digestion Inhibited Stimulated Trap. Sympathetic and parasympathetic are opposites, but both belong to the autonomic system. A common wrong answer treats the sympathetic system as "voluntary"; it is involuntary. Voluntary muscle control is the somatic system. The spinal cord and the reflex arc The spinal cord relays messages between brain and body, but it can also act on its own in a reflex arc , a fast, automatic response that bypasses the brain. When you touch a hot stove: a sensory (afferent) neuron carries the pain signal to the spinal cord, an interneuron passes it across, and a motor (efferent) neuron orders the muscle to pull back, all before the brain even registers the pain. Why. Routing simple protective reflexes through the spinal cord alone saves the time it would take to consult the brain; the brain is informed a fraction of a second later. This is why you yank your hand away before you feel the burn. 2.6 The Brain The brain is traditionally divided into hindbrain, midbrain, and forebrain, roughly from bottom-and-back (older, survival functions) to top-and-front (newer, higher functions). Hindbrain Medulla (medulla oblongata): controls vital automatic functions, heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure. Damage is fatal. Pons: a bridge relaying signals between higher and lower brain; involved in sleep, arousal, and facial movement. Cerebellum ("little brain"): coordinates balance, posture, and smooth, well-timed voluntary movement; also involved in some learning. Damage causes clumsy, jerky movement. Midbrain A relay hub for vision and hearing reflexes and for movement. It contains parts of the reticular formation, a network running through the brainstem that controls arousal, alertness, and the sleep-wake cycle. Forebrain and the limbic system The forebrain contains the most advanced structures. Beneath the cortex sits the limbic system , the emotional and motivational core: Amygdala: the fear and emotion centre; tags experiences as threatening; central to aggression and emotional learning. Hippocampus: forms new long-term memories and supports spatial navigation. Damage causes an inability to form new memories. Hypothalamus: the body’s regulator; controls hunger, thirst, temperature, sex drive, and it commands the pituitary gland (the link between brain and hormones). Remember the "four Fs": feeding, fighting, fleeing, and sexual behaviour. Thalamus: the great relay station ; nearly all sensory information (except smell) passes through the thalamus on its way to the cortex. Trap. Do not confuse hippocampus (memory formation) with hypothalamus (drives and hormones), or thalamus (sensory relay) with hypothalamus (regulation and pituitary control). Amygdala = emotion/fear; hippocampus = memory. These four are the most-tested structures in the whole section. The cerebral cortex: four lobes The wrinkled outer layer of the forebrain, the cerebral cortex , is where perception, thought, and language happen. Each hemisphere has four lobes: Lobe Location Main function Frontal Front Planning, decision-making, personality, voluntary movement (motor cortex), speech production Parietal Top-back Touch, temperature, pain, body position (somatosensory cortex) Temporal Sides (near temples) Hearing, language comprehension, memory Occipital Back Vision (visual cortex) Language areas and hemispheric specialisation Who → what. Paul Broca → Broca’s area (in the left frontal lobe), for speech production ; damage causes Broca’s aphasia (halting, effortful speech, comprehension intact). Carl Wernicke → Wernicke’s area (in the left temporal lobe), for language comprehension ; damage causes Wernicke’s aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension). Roger Sperry → split-brain research on hemispheric specialisation (Nobel Prize 1981). The two hemispheres are somewhat specialised (lateralisation): for most people the left hemisphere handles language, logic, and analysis, while the right hemisphere handles spatial ability, faces, and holistic processing. They are joined by the corpus callosum , a thick band of fibres. Roger Sperry studied "split-brain" patients whose corpus callosum was cut to treat epilepsy; his experiments showed the two halves could then work independently, revealing what each side does on its own. Trap. Broca = b roken, halting speech (production); Wernicke = w ordy, fluent nonsense (comprehension). Both areas are in the left hemisphere for most people. Also: each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body (contralateral control). 2.7 The Endocrine System Alongside the fast electrical nervous system runs a slower chemical one: the endocrine system , a set of glands that release hormones directly into the bloodstream to act on distant organs. Pituitary gland: the "master gland", sitting under the hypothalamus. It releases hormones that control the other endocrine glands (and it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus). Adrenal glands: release adrenaline (epinephrine) for fight-or-flight and cortisol for stress. Thyroid gland: releases thyroxine, which sets the body’s metabolic rate. Pineal gland: releases melatonin, which regulates sleep and the day-night (circadian) cycle. The HPA axis and key hormones The stress response runs on the HPA axis : the H ypothalamus signals the P ituitary, which signals the A drenal glands to release cortisol. This is the body’s slow, sustained stress system. Cortisol: the main stress hormone; mobilises energy but harms health if chronically high. Adrenaline (epinephrine): the fast surge that races the heart in an emergency. Oxytocin: the "bonding" hormone; released in childbirth, breastfeeding, and social attachment. Thyroxine: controls metabolism and energy use. Melatonin: promotes sleep and tracks the light-dark cycle. Why. Nervous versus endocrine is a speed-versus-duration trade-off. The nervous system sends fast electrochemical signals down fixed wires for immediate, brief effects; the endocrine system sends slower hormones through the blood for widespread, longer-lasting effects. The hypothalamus is the bridge that lets the brain command the hormones. Trap. The pituitary is the "master gland", but it takes orders from the hypothalamus (a brain structure, not a gland in the usual sense). So the true top of the chain is the hypothalamus, which is why the same structure keeps appearing in both the brain and endocrine sections. 2.8 Sensation and Perception: The Basics Sensation is the raw detection of a stimulus by a sense organ; perception is the brain’s interpretation of that sensation into a meaningful experience. Sense organs first perform transduction : converting physical energy (light, sound, pressure) into the neural signals the brain can read. Thresholds and psychophysics Absolute threshold: the smallest amount of a stimulus a person can detect 50% of the time (e.g. a candle flame seen far away on a dark night). Difference threshold (just noticeable difference, JND): the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected. Who → what. Ernst Weber → Weber’s law: the JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount (adding one candle to ten is noticeable; adding one to a hundred is not). Gustav Fechner → founded psychophysics and extended Weber’s work into a law relating physical stimulus strength to perceived sensation. The visual pathway Light enters the eye and lands on the retina , which holds two kinds of receptor cells: Rods: many, at the edges; work in dim light; see in black and white; give night vision. Cones: concentrated in the centre (fovea); work in bright light; give colour and sharp detail. Signals leave the eye by the optic nerve and travel to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Two classic theories explain colour vision: Who → what. Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz → the trichromatic (three-colour) theory: the retina has three cone types tuned to red, green, and blue, and all colours arise from their combined activity. Ewald Hering → the opponent-process theory: colour is coded by opposing pairs (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white); one member of a pair is excited while the other is inhibited. Trap. The two colour theories are not rivals; both are correct at different stages. Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) operates at the cones (retina) ; opponent-process (Hering) operates later , in the retinal ganglion cells and brain. Opponent-process best explains afterimages (stare at green, look away, see red). Auditory basics Sound waves enter the ear, vibrate the eardrum, pass through three tiny bones, and reach the fluid-filled cochlea in the inner ear. Hair cells in the cochlea transduce the vibrations into neural signals sent along the auditory nerve to the temporal lobe. Pitch corresponds to the frequency of the wave and loudness to its amplitude (measured in decibels). 2.9 Research Methods in Biopsychology To study a brain we cannot open, biopsychologists use recording, imaging, and damage-based methods, plus genetics to separate nature from nurture. Recording and imaging techniques Method What it does Shows structure or function? EEG (electroencephalogram) Records electrical brain waves from scalp electrodes; excellent timing Function (activity over time) ERP (event-related potential) Averages EEG responses time-locked to a specific stimulus to isolate the brain’s reaction to it Function (precise timing) CT (computed tomography) X-ray scan giving a still picture of brain anatomy Structure PET (positron emission tomography) Tracks a radioactive tracer to show which areas use most glucose/blood Function (metabolic activity) fMRI (functional MRI) Tracks blood-oxygen flow to map active regions; good spatial detail Both, but prized for function Lesion studies Observe behaviour after a brain area is damaged or removed to infer its function Function (by loss) Trap. Sort methods by their strength: EEG and ERP have superb temporal resolution (when) but poor spatial detail (where); fMRI and PET have good spatial resolution (where) but slower timing. CT gives structure only; fMRI and PET show function. Lesion evidence shows what a region is needed for, not everything it does. Behaviour genetics Behaviour genetics studies how much of a trait comes from genes versus environment. Twin studies: compare identical (monozygotic, 100% shared genes) with fraternal (dizygotic, ~50% shared) twins. If identical twins are far more alike on a trait, genes matter more. Adoption studies: compare adopted children with both their biological and their adoptive parents to separate genetic from environmental influence. Heritability: the proportion of the variation in a trait across a population that is due to genetic differences. It ranges from 0 to 1. Trap. Heritability is about variation within a population , not about a single individual. A heritability of 0.5 does not mean "half of your intelligence comes from genes"; it means half of the differences among people in that group trace to genetic differences. This distinction is a favourite trick question. Recap. Neuron = dendrites (in) → soma (integrate) → axon/myelin (out) → terminals; oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS, Schwann cells the PNS; Cajal’s neuron doctrine beat Golgi’s network (they shared the 1906 Nobel). Resting potential −70 mV kept by the sodium-potassium pump; the action potential is all-or-none (depolarise, repolarise), jumps node to node (saltatory). Otto Loewi proved chemical transmission (acetylcholine, "Vagusstoff"). Key transmitter links: dopamine → schizophrenia (excess) and Parkinson’s (deficit), serotonin → depression, GABA (inhibitory) → anxiety, glutamate (excitatory) → excitotoxicity, ACh → Alzheimer’s. CNS vs PNS; somatic (voluntary) vs autonomic (sympathetic fight-or-flight vs parasympathetic rest-and-digest); the spinal reflex arc bypasses the brain. Brain: medulla (vital signs), cerebellum (coordination); limbic amygdala (fear), hippocampus (memory), hypothalamus (drives + pituitary), thalamus (sensory relay); four lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital); Broca (speech production) vs Wernicke (comprehension), both left; Sperry’s split-brain work. Pituitary is master gland under the hypothalamus; HPA axis releases cortisol. Weber-Fechner thresholds; rods (dim, night) vs cones (colour, detail); Young-Helmholtz trichromatic (cones) plus Hering opponent-process (later, explains afterimages). EEG/ERP = timing, fMRI/PET = location, CT = structure; twin and adoption studies define heritability as population-level variation, not an individual’s fixed fraction. 2.10 Sleep, consciousness and biological rhythms Consciousness is the awareness a person has of their own thoughts, feelings and surroundings at any given moment. It is not a single fixed state but a continuum that shifts across the day and night, from alert wakefulness through drowsiness into the various stages of sleep. Sleep is not simply the switching off of the brain. It is an active, organised, rhythmic process that the body drives on a roughly 24-hour schedule, and studying it reveals how deeply behaviour is governed by biology. Biological rhythms and the circadian clock A biological rhythm is any cyclical change in a bodily process that repeats over a regular period. The most important for behaviour is the circadian rhythm , from the Latin circa (about) and dies (a day), meaning a cycle that lasts about 24 hours. The sleep-wake cycle, body temperature, and the release of many hormones all follow a circadian pattern. Rhythms shorter than a day are called ultradian (for example the stages of a single sleep cycle repeating through the night), and rhythms longer than a day are called infradian (for example the roughly monthly menstrual cycle). The internal clock that keeps the circadian rhythm running is a tiny cluster of cells in the hypothalamus called the suprachiasmatic nucleus , usually shortened to the SCN. It sits just above the point where the optic nerves cross, which is why it can receive information about light directly from the eyes. Even with no external cues the SCN keeps ticking on a cycle close to, but not exactly, 24 hours. External cues that reset the clock to the true day are called zeitgebers , a German word meaning time-givers . Light is the most powerful zeitgeber. Who → what. The SCN was identified as the master circadian pacemaker through animal lesion studies in the 1970s: destroying it abolished the regular sleep-wake and hormonal rhythms, showing that this one small structure sets the body's daily timing. When light falls on the retina, signals travel to the SCN, which then instructs the pineal gland , a small structure deep in the brain, to adjust its output of the hormone melatonin . Melatonin promotes sleepiness. In darkness the pineal gland releases more melatonin, and in bright light it releases less. This is the chemical bridge between the light of the outside world and the felt urge to sleep. Key. Light → eye → suprachiasmatic nucleus (the clock) → pineal gland → melatonin (the sleep signal). Darkness raises melatonin; light lowers it. The sleep cycle: NREM and REM Sleep is measured chiefly with the electroencephalograph , or EEG, a device that records the electrical activity of the brain through electrodes on the scalp. As a person falls asleep and moves through the night, the EEG traces out characteristic patterns of brain waves that let researchers divide sleep into distinct stages. Sleep falls into two broad kinds: NREM (non-rapid-eye-movement) sleep and REM (rapid-eye-movement) sleep. Under the modern scheme, NREM sleep is divided into three stages, N1 to N3, followed by a period of REM. One full pass through these stages takes roughly 90 minutes, and the cycle repeats four to six times a night (an ultradian rhythm). As the night goes on, the deep NREM stages shorten and the REM periods lengthen. Stage N1 (light sleep): the brief transition from wakefulness into sleep. Brain waves slow from alpha toward theta. The person is easily woken and may experience sudden jerks. Stage N2: a deeper light sleep marked on the EEG by short bursts of activity called sleep spindles and single large waves called K-complexes . Most of a night is spent here. Stage N3 (slow-wave or deep sleep): the deepest sleep, dominated by large slow delta waves. It is hardest to wake someone from this stage, and it is thought to be the most physically restorative. Sleepwalking and night terrors, when they occur, arise here. REM sleep: after the deep stages the brain returns to a fast, active pattern resembling waking. The eyes dart rapidly beneath closed lids, and the body's voluntary muscles are effectively paralysed. Most vivid dreaming happens here. EEG wave patterns Each state of consciousness has a signature brain-wave pattern, described by its frequency (how many cycles per second, measured in hertz) and amplitude (how tall the waves are). As a rough rule, the more alert and active the brain, the faster and smaller the waves; the deeper the rest, the slower and larger the waves. Wave Frequency Typical state Beta Fast (about 13 to 30 Hz) Alert, awake, actively thinking or concentrating Alpha Moderate (about 8 to 12 Hz) Awake but relaxed, calm, eyes often closed; drowsy onset Theta Slow (about 4 to 7 Hz) Light sleep, stages N1 and N2 Delta Very slow (below about 4 Hz), high amplitude Deep slow-wave sleep, stage N3 Trap. Do not confuse fast small beta waves (busy waking mind) with slow tall delta waves (deepest sleep). A common exam catch is that REM sleep shows a fast, waking-like EEG even though the person is deeply asleep and hard to wake; this mismatch is why REM is called paradoxical sleep . REM, paradoxical sleep and dreaming REM sleep is called paradoxical sleep because the brain looks awake on the EEG while the body is at its most still, the large muscles being temporarily paralysed (a state called atonia that stops us acting out dreams). Rapid eye movements, irregular breathing and heart rate, and vivid narrative dreams all belong to REM. People woken from REM report dreaming far more often and in more detail than those woken from NREM. Newborns spend a very large proportion of sleep in REM, which has led to the idea that REM supports brain development and the consolidation of memory. Theories of why we sleep There is no single agreed answer to why sleep evolved, but two broad families of theory dominate. Restorative theory: sleep serves to repair and restore the body and brain. During sleep, especially deep NREM, the body releases growth hormone, repairs tissue, clears metabolic waste, and the brain consolidates memories. On this view we sleep because sleep does necessary maintenance. Evolutionary or adaptive theory: sleep evolved to keep an animal safe and to conserve energy during the hours when it cannot forage or defend itself effectively. On this view sleep is an adaptation that reduced risk and saved calories, and different species sleep in patterns suited to their ecological niche. Common sleep disorders in brief Insomnia: persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting restful sleep, despite adequate opportunity, causing daytime distress or impairment. Narcolepsy: a neurological disorder marked by overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden uncontrollable sleep attacks, sometimes with sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy) triggered by emotion, reflecting intrusions of REM-like states into wakefulness. Sleep apnoea: repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, often because the airway collapses, which briefly wakes the person again and again and leaves them unrefreshed and sleepy by day. 2.11 Behavioural genetics and evolution Behavioural genetics is the field that studies how much of the variation in behaviour and psychological traits across people can be traced to inherited biological factors versus the environment. It is the modern, evidence-based way of examining the old nature-versus-nurture question. Genes, chromosomes and DNA Inside the nucleus of almost every cell in the body are chromosomes , thread-like structures made of a molecule called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). Humans normally have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs, one of each pair inherited from each parent. DNA carries the coded instructions for building and running the body, and a gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a particular product or trait. Genes are the basic units of heredity passed from parents to offspring. Key. DNA is the molecule; a gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for something; chromosomes are the long packaged strands of DNA. Genes sit on chromosomes; chromosomes are made of DNA. Genotype versus phenotype The genotype is the full set of genes an individual carries, the inherited genetic blueprint. The phenotype is the set of observable characteristics that actually appear, such as eye colour, height, or a behavioural tendency. The phenotype results from the genotype interacting with the environment. Two people can share a genotype for a trait yet differ in phenotype because of different experiences, nutrition, or circumstances. Dominant and recessive Genes often come in alternative versions called alleles . An allele is dominant if a single copy is enough to express its effect in the phenotype, and recessive if its effect appears only when two copies are present (one from each parent). This is why a recessive trait can skip generations, hidden in carriers who possess one copy but do not show it. Heritability Heritability is a statistic, expressed from 0 to 1 (or as a percentage), that estimates how much of the variation in a trait within a population is due to genetic differences among its members. It is one of the most misunderstood ideas in psychology. Trap. Heritability is about variation across a group, not about a single person. A heritability of 0.5 for a trait does NOT mean half of one individual's trait is caused by genes. It means about half of the differences between people in that population are associated with genetic differences. Heritability also depends on the environment studied and can change if conditions change. Twin and adoption studies Because we cannot ethically control people's genes or upbringing, behavioural geneticists use natural experiments. The two main designs are twin studies and adoption studies. Monozygotic twins (identical twins) develop from a single fertilised egg that splits, so they share essentially 100 percent of their genes. Dizygotic twins (fraternal twins) develop from two sepa

title: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators
text: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators One consolidated lookup for every named effect, phenomenon, illusion, theory, complex and the people behind them. The five old sweeps overlapped heavily (an "effect" carries an originator; a theory carries a theorist), so each item now lives in exactly one entry: the definition, who coined it, the classic study, and the confusable lookalike, together. Drill it both directions: cover the "Who" column and name the person; cover the description and name the term. High-yield NIMHANS / MET ask this two ways. (1) Name the "____ effect / theory / complex" and ask who proposed it (answer = a person). (2) Describe a scene/finding with no name and ask you to name it (answer = the effect/theory). Almost every trap is a same-family lookalike (halo↔horn, Pygmalion↔Golem, placebo↔nocebo, James-Lange↔Cannon-Bard, McCall's T↔Student's t). Always learn each item with its twin. In this reference Named effects (grouped) Phenomena, illusions, biases & clinical signs Theories & models (by domain) Named complexes & syndromes Who originated what — theorists Psychometrics, statistics & standard scores 1. Named effects Every named "____ effect," its originator, and the one-line hook. Grouped by domain so the good-twin / bad-twin pairs sit together. 1.1 Memory & learning effects Effect Who What it is Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik Interrupted / unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones. Von Restorff (isolation) effect Hedwig von Restorff The odd-one-out item in a list stands out and is recalled best. Serial position effect Ebbinghaus (named by Murdock) First + last items in a list recalled best (= primacy + recency together). Primacy effect — First items recalled well (rehearsed into long-term store). Recency effect — Last items recalled well (still in short-term store). A delay/distractor kills recency, not primacy. Spacing (distributed practice) effect Ebbinghaus Spread-out study beats cramming for long-term retention. Testing effect — Retrieving (self-testing) cements memory better than re-reading. Generation effect Slamecka & Graf Info you generate yourself is remembered better than info you just read. Self-reference effect Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker Material related to yourself is encoded and recalled better. Misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus Post-event misleading info distorts the original memory (eyewitness work). Picture superiority effect Allan Paivio (dual-coding) Pictures are remembered better than words. Encoding-specificity / context effect Tulving & Thomson Recall is best when retrieval cues match the encoding context (state/context-dependent memory). Levels-of-processing effect Craik & Lockhart Deeper (semantic) processing → better memory than shallow (visual/acoustic). Trap Remove the delay/distractor and it's the recency end that vanishes (STM decays); primacy survives. Zeigarnik = unfinished remembered; von Restorff = distinctive remembered — don't merge them. 1.2 Attention & perception effects Effect Who What it is Stroop effect J. Ridley Stroop Slower to name ink colour when the word spells a different colour (automatic reading interferes). Cocktail-party effect Colin Cherry Selective attention to one voice in a crowd, yet you still catch your own name. McGurk effect McGurk & MacDonald What you see the mouth do changes what you hear (audio-visual speech fusion). Ventriloquist effect — Sound is mislocated toward a plausible visual source. Troxler effect (fading) Ignaz Troxler Fixate steadily and unchanging peripheral stimuli fade from awareness. Motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) — After staring at motion, a static scene appears to drift the opposite way. Bouba/kiki effect Köhler (later Ramachandran) People map "bouba" to round shapes, "kiki" to spiky ones (sound symbolism). Tetris effect — Heavy repeated activity intrudes into imagery/dreams. Trap The phi phenomenon and autokinetic phenomenon are labelled "phenomena," not "effects" — they live in §2.1. Same content, the label decides where the examiner files it. 1.3 Social & expectancy effects Effect Who What it is Halo effect Edward Thorndike One good trait (e.g. looks) bleeds into an overall positive judgement. Horn(s) effect — The negative mirror of halo: one bad trait darkens the whole impression. Pygmalion (Rosenthal) effect Rosenthal & Jacobson High teacher/leader expectations → the person actually performs better (self-fulfilling prophecy). Golem effect — Low expectations → worse performance (the dark twin of Pygmalion). Hawthorne effect Elton Mayo (Western Electric studies) People change behaviour because they know they're being observed. John Henry effect Saretsky A control group tries extra hard because it knows it's the comparison (a research artefact). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure alone increases liking (also a persuasion lever: familiarity breeds liking). Bystander effect Latané & Darley More onlookers → less likely any one helps (diffusion of responsibility). After Kitty Genovese. 5-step decision model: notice → interpret → take responsibility → know how → act. (Theory form in §3.6.) Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person effort drops as group size grows (precursor to social loafing). Pratfall effect Elliot Aronson A competent person becomes more likeable after a small blunder. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice you. False-consensus effect Lee Ross Overestimating how many people share your views/choices. Lake Wobegon / above-average effect — Most people rate themselves above average (illusory superiority). Cheerleader effect — Faces look more attractive in a group than alone. Overjustification effect Lepper, Greene & Nisbett Paying for an already-enjoyed activity kills the intrinsic motivation. Boomerang effect Hovland tradition (akin to Brehm) Persuasion backfires, shifting the attitude the opposite way (cousin of reactance, §3.6). Trap Same-study, different name: Pygmalion = Rosenthal & Jacobson

title: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options
text: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options For when plain definitions aren't enough and the trap is a near-identical distractor. Each block is one confusable pair: what's the same (why both look right), what differs (line by line), and the one tell — the single thing in the stem that splits them. Read the tell, not the whole block, on exam day. Built 2026-05-25. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. The examiner picks two real, correct-sounding terms and bets you can't split them. Don't re-derive both definitions. Find the tell word in the stem (added vs removed? up vs down? before vs after? thought vs act?) and the option falls out. These are the pairs that actually bleed marks on MET/NIMHANS. Jump to: 1. Learning & conditioning 2. Developmental 3. Sensation & perception 4. Memory & cognition 5. Stats & research 6. Abnormal / clinical 7. Defense mechanisms 8. Therapy 9. Social 10. Intelligence 1. Learning & conditioning Classical conditioning vs Operant conditioning Same: both are associative learning; both show acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination. Classical (Pavlov) Operant (Skinner) Behaviour Involuntary, reflexive (salivation, fear) Voluntary, emitted (lever press) Association Stimulus → stimulus (CS–US) Behaviour → consequence (response–reinforcer) Learner Passive, responds to a cue Active, operates on the environment Reinforcer timing Comes before/with the response Comes after the response The tell: Is the behaviour automatic and triggered by a cue that comes first (classical), or voluntary and shaped by what happens after (operant)? Any "reward / consequence / punishment" in the stem → operant. Negative reinforcement vs Punishment Same: both are operant procedures and both usually involve an aversive/unpleasant stimulus, so they read alike. Negative reinforcement Punishment Effect on behaviour Increases it Decreases it What happens Removes an aversive stimulus (take painkiller → pain gone) Adds aversive (positive) or removes pleasant (negative) "Negative" means Subtraction, not "bad" — The tell: Did the behaviour go up or down ? Up = reinforcement (negative = the bad thing was taken away ). Down = punishment. "Negative" is about removal, never about being unpleasant. Positive punishment vs Negative punishment Same: both decrease a behaviour. Positive punishment Negative punishment Operation Add something aversive (scolding, spanking) Remove something pleasant (take phone, time-out, fine) Other name — Response cost / omission The tell: Positive = something was added ; negative = something was taken away . Both still reduce the behaviour, so judge by add vs subtract, not by good vs bad. Primary reinforcer vs Secondary reinforcer Same: both strengthen behaviour when they follow it. Primary Secondary (conditioned) Why it reinforces Innately satisfies a biological need (food, water, sex, warmth) Learned value through association Learning needed? No Yes (money, tokens, praise, grades) The tell: Does it satisfy a body need directly (primary) or only because you learned it stands for something else (secondary)? Money is the classic secondary reinforcer. Shaping vs Chaining Same: both build complex operant behaviour using reinforcement. Shaping Chaining What's reinforced Successive approximations to one target behaviour Linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours Picture it Refining one act closer and closer Step 1 → step 2 → step 3 as a chain The tell: One behaviour polished step-by-step (shaping) vs several separate behaviours joined in order (chaining). Stimulus generalisation vs Stimulus discrimination Same: both describe how a conditioned response transfers (or doesn't) across stimuli. Generalisation Discrimination Response to similar cues Yes — spreads to stimuli like the CS No — only the exact CS triggers it Little Albert Feared all furry white things Would fear only the rat The tell: Response spreads to lookalikes (generalisation) vs narrows to one exact cue (discrimination). 2. Developmental Assimilation vs Accommodation (Piaget) Same: the twin processes of adaptation ; both are how a schema deals with new information. Assimilation Accommodation Schema Stays the same — new info forced into it Changes / a new one is created to fit reality Example Calls a whale a "fish" Learns a whale is a mammal, makes a new category The tell: Did the existing schema stay put (assimilation) or did it have to change (accommodation)? If the child updated their mental category, it's accommodation. Piaget vs Vygotsky Same: both constructivists; both say the child actively builds knowledge rather than passively absorbing it. Piaget Vygotsky Engine of development The individual child exploring; cognition leads language Social/cultural interaction; language leads cognition Signature terms Stages, schema, assimilation/accommodation, egocentrism ZPD, scaffolding, More Knowledgeable Other, private speech The tell: Is the driver the child alone (Piaget) or a guiding social other / ZPD (Vygotsky)? Any "scaffolding" or "zone of proximal development" → Vygotsky. 3. Sensation & perception Sensation vs Perception Same: both are stages of taking in stimulus information. Sensation Perception What it is Raw detection by sense organs + transduction Brain's organisation & interpretation of it Direction Bottom-up (data in) Top-down (meaning added) The tell: Detecting the raw signal at the receptor (sensation) vs making sense of / recognising it (perception). Interpretation, meaning, recognition → perception. Absolute threshold vs Difference threshold (JND) Same: both are psychophysics thresholds (Weber/Fechner). Absolute threshold Difference threshold (JND) Detects Minimum intensity to detect a stimulus 50% of the time Smallest detectable change between two stimuli Law — Weber's law: JND is a constant proportion The tell: Detecting that one stimulus is present (absolute) vs detecting a difference between two

There are no links out to other pages, nothing to chase, all the content lives right here. Study from this page only tonight. Ataxia = loss of coordination/balance ; apraxia = can't sequence learned movements Neuro Who is Kitty Genovese? 1964 NYC murder, allegedly many witnesses, none helped → launched bystander research Social Type D personality? Negative affectivity + social inhibition ; poor cardiac prognosis Abnormal Escape vs avoidance learning Escape terminates an aversive stimulus already on; avoidance prevents its onset Therapy Object relations meaning Internalised mental representations of self and others Therapy Memory: what/where/when of an event Episodic memory Memory Spearman → factor analysis, Wundt → ? Introspection (structuralism's method) Founders MHCA 2017 + minors Minor can appoint a nominated representative; views considered age-appropriately Acts OR / RR of 1 No association. >1 increased risk, <1 protective Biostats NNT 1 / ARR. Lower NNT = better drug Biostats "Data" singular or plural? Plural in formal use ("data are…"); datum is singular Language ★C. Common-Section Concept Pack high-yield general psych · the foundations · the bits that quietly cost marks This is the section that is bleeding your marks. The subject blocks above are your strong ground; the common section is general psychology, and it punishes shaky foundations and confusable pairs more than raw facts. So this pack is built differently: every block ends in the exact distinction the examiner uses to separate the two options that look identical. Read it for the contrasts, not the trivia. If you can run the cover-and-test set at the very end (C.11) clean, the common section stops costing you. C.1 The schools of psychology (the "isms"), in order Almost every general paper has one "who founded / what method / which school" item. Learn them as a story: each school is a reaction to the one before it. School Core claim Method Key names Structuralism Break consciousness into its basic elements (sensations, feelings) Introspection Wundt (first lab, 1879), Titchener Functionalism Why does the mind do what it does; its purpose and adaptation Observation, applied focus William James, Dewey, Angell Gestalt The whole is different from the sum of its parts; perception is organised Phenomenology Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler Psychoanalysis Behaviour is driven by the unconscious and early conflict Free association, dream analysis, case study Freud, later Jung, Adler Behaviourism Study only observable behaviour; the mind is a black box Controlled experiment, conditioning Watson, Pavlov, Skinner, Thorndike Humanistic People are growth-oriented and free; the "third force" Phenomenology, client report Maslow, Rogers Cognitive Mind as an information processor; mental processes are real and studiable Experiment, modelling, reaction time Neisser (coined it, 1967), Miller, Broadbent Biological Behaviour reduces to brain, neurochemistry, genes Lesion, imaging, twin studies Sperry, Hebb Evolutionary Behaviour was selected because it aided survival/reproduction Cross-species, adaptationist reasoning Buss, Tooby & Cosmides Positive Study strengths, well-being and flourishing, not just pathology Empirical, intervention trials Seligman, Csikszentmihalyi TRAP: Wundt = structuralism + introspection (the first lab). James = functionalism . Neisser = cognitive . Watson named behaviourism but Wundt is "father of experimental psychology"; Lewin is "father of social psychology"; Wundt is NOT a functionalist. Gestalt is a perception school, not a therapy (do not confuse it with Perls' Gestalt therapy ). title: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes
text: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes Every concept you got wrong, guessed, or flagged across all the mocks (MET Mock 1, the NIMHANS PYQ-based mock, the diagnostic-baseline drills, and the MPhil/PEP sets) consolidated into one corrective read, organised by topic, not by which mock it came from. Where a miss recurred across mocks it is marked as a persistent weak spot. This is where you fix what tripped you. Nothing is cut: every corrected answer, distractor analysis, mnemonic, and exam trap from the originals lives here, merged so each concept appears once. In this book The recurring weak spots (read first) Exam-day execution rules Biopsychology & neuroanatomy Neurochemistry, endocrine & pharmacology Famous cases & amnesias Assessment, IQ history & tests Research methods & biostatistics Psychotherapy: who founded what Abnormal psychology & classification Social psychology & the self Developmental psychology Cognitive: memory, learning, psychophysics, creativity Language & verbal reasoning MPhil layer: ethics, law, culture, MSE The recurring weak spots (read first) Across every mock the same clusters bled marks. These are your real syllabus, ranked by how often and how badly they recurred. Each links to its full fix below. Weak spot Where it recurred The fix in one line Pituitary / hypothalamus / endocrine axis NIMHANS mock (3 of 6 biopsych wrongs), diagnostic baseline FLAT PiG anterior pituitary; melatonin is pineal; cortisol is adrenal cortex , not medulla; hypothalamus integrates endocrine + autonomic Neuroanatomy: tracts, lobes, basal ganglia MET Mock 1 (6 biopsych wrongs) Corticospinal crosses at medullary pyramids; right parietal → left neglect; red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia Therapy school attribution MET Mock 1 (4 wrongs), NIMHANS (3 wrongs) Match technique → school → founder by trigger word; empty chair = Perls, musterbation = Ellis, therapeutic community = Maxwell Jones Standard scores & WAIS structure Both mocks, diagnostic Subtest scaled M=10 SD=3; index M=100 SD=15; +1 SD = 84th pct; VCI + PRI = 3 core subtests each Reliability statistic ↔ concept NIMHANS, MET, diagnostic (Cohen's kappa missed twice) Kappa = inter-rater categorical; alpha/KR-20 = internal consistency; ICC = inter-rater continuous Sampling: stratified vs cluster vs non-probability MET Mock 1 + NIMHANS (quota/cluster swapped) Stratified = sample within strata; cluster = whole clusters; "can't compute sampling error" = non-probability (quota) ICD vs DSM durations NIMHANS (schizophrenia), MET (dysthymia, PTSD clusters) NIMHANS leans ICD: schizophrenia ≥1 month (ICD) vs ≥6 months (DSM); read which classification the stem names Named social-psych concepts NIMHANS (Genovese, Type D, anomie all wrong) Pure trivia: learn the named effect + its discoverer + its two-factor mechanism Sleep architecture (REM vs delta) Diagnostic (twice), MET Mock 1 (elimination) REM = atonia + wake-like EEG (paradoxical); delta/N3 = slow wave + normal tone; parasomnias (sleepwalking) are N3 "NOT / EXCEPT" negation-blindness Every mock — careless misses Underline the negation before reading options; this is your most expensive avoidable error High-yield Your self-notes are the syllabus. Every "wtf is X" / "never read this" / "don't know shit about this" you wrote on a question is a topic you had not opened. The same notes recurred across mocks, which means a gap left unfixed reappears. The NIMHANS mock sat at 71.25 vs an 80 cutoff (gap 8.75 = roughly 9 wrongs to convert); 6 of those wrongs were in biopsych alone, so fixing that one section clears the line. On MET Mock 1 your attempted-accuracy was 92% (49 right, 4 wrong) but you skipped 47 — there the gap was coverage, not accuracy. PYQ analysis of 300 NIMHANS questions (2023–25) shows Therapy + Abnormal + Biopsych together = ~49% of marks; that is where to spend time. Trap Your guessing is luck-loaded. On the NIMHANS mock you guessed ~17 times and got 14 right; that regresses toward ~50% on the real paper, so plan against a score nearer 68 than 71. A guess is only worth it on MET-style scoring (+4/−1) once you have eliminated 2+ options. Exam-day execution rules Underline NOT / EXCEPT / LEAST / ALL in the stem before reading options. Half your "knew it but got it wrong" misses are negation-blindness (the ACTH/melatonin pituitary question, the Bandura "not required" question). ~20% of NIMHANS PYQs are NOT-stems. On a NOT-question, pick the outlier , not the most familiar item. On antonym / odd-one-out items, find the outlier first. If 3 of 4 options agree in meaning, the 4th is almost always the answer (gregarious: 3 synonyms + reclusive). Read the relationship in the stem — synonym? antonym? part-whole? cause-effect? — before scanning options. Eliminate extreme-word options on RC main-idea questions: "every, always, never, all, none, only, must" are usually too strong. Pick the most general statement the passage actually supports. Hedging language ("can," "may," "in some cases," "a range of") → tone is "supportive but qualified," not absolute. If the stem names ICD, give ICD durations; if DSM, give DSM. If unspecified on NIMHANS, default to ICD (Indian exam). MET often leans DSM. Don't guess on biostats unless the RR/OR/HR/NNT table is firm. You were guessing 4–5 of 10 biostats questions — a coin flip on ~20% of NIMHANS marks. Pacing: 100 Qs / 90 min ≈ 54 sec/Q. Over 90 sec → mark and skip, return later. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason. Last 5 minutes: never leave a blank where there is no negative marking; with −0.25, only answer if you eliminated 2 options. Length of options is not a reliable tell on the real paper — don't lean on it. NIMHANS uses heavy case-vignette stems; practise extracting the diagnostic core fast. Biopsychology & neuroanatomy This was the single biggest leak: 6 wrong on each of the two full mocks. You are not weak on biopsych in general — you are weak on where structures are , which side does what , and endocrine/neurology trivia . Lock

title: History of Psychology
text: History of Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) History of Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Source pp. 3–7 Founding lab Wundt, Leipzig, 1879 Themes Western timeline · Greek & 17th-c. philosophers · schools & founders · Indian psychology India Sen Gupta, Calcutta 1916 · NIMHANS What this covers. The full history of psychology as a discipline: the Western chronology from the first psychology course (1875) through positive psychology (1998), the Greek theorists (Hippocrates' humoral theory, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle) and the 17th-century philosophers who framed the mind, the major schools of psychology with their founders and "forces," the parallel history of psychology and clinical psychology in India, and the Indian systems (Yoga, Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism, Sufism) that form Indian psychology. Contents: 1 · Western Timeline 2 · Greek Theorists 3 · 17th-Century Philosophers 4 · Major Schools of Psychology 5 · Psychology in India 6 · Clinical Psychology in India 7 · Yoga Psychology 8 · Indian Psychology 1 · Western Timeline The chronology below tracks how psychology developed as a formal discipline, from its first course and laboratory to the emergence of each major school. Year Milestone 1875 First psychology course, by William James on Physiological Psychology at Harvard 1879 Wilhelm Wundt established the first psychological laboratory at the University of Leipzig, Germany 1892 American Psychological Association (APA) established 1896 Structuralism 1896 Functionalism 1900 Psychoanalysis 1912 Gestalt psychology 1913 Behaviourism 1940s Existentialism 1954 Humanistic psychology 1956 Cognitive psychology 1998 Positive psychology Key: Wundt (1879, Leipzig) founded the first psychology lab — the conventional birth of psychology as a science. James taught the first psychology course (1875) and later founded functionalism. 2 · Greek Theorists The Mind–Body Argument Monists: mind and body are a single entity. Dualists: mind and body are separate entities. Hippocrates — Humoral Theory Hippocrates was a dualist . His humoral theory linked four bodily humors to four temperaments. Humor Temperament Character Black bile Melancholic Sad, depressed, poetic and artistic Yellow bile Choleric Fiery, energetic, and passionate Blood Sanguine Warm-hearted, cheerful, optimistic, and confident Phlegm Phlegmatic Slow, quiet, rational, and consistent Socrates Dualist. Focused on morality . Explained eudemonia : long-lasting contentment, peace and happiness comes from building virtues like honesty, generosity, kindness, altruism, etc. Plato Dualist. Allegory of the cave and allegory of the chariot . Tripartite theory of the soul: rational (mind), emotional (spirited), and appetites (pleasures). Theory of forms: forms are universals and are the purest representation of things that actually exist. Aristotle Monist. Gave the first theory of cognitive sciences ; described sensation and perception — special sensible and common sensible . Theory of associationism : law of contiguity, law of frequency, law of similarity, law of contrast. Trap: Hippocrates, Socrates and Plato were dualists ; Aristotle was a monist . The four laws of association (contiguity, frequency, similarity, contrast) belong to Aristotle. 3 · 17th-Century Philosophers René Descartes Famously stated "cogito, ergo sum" ("I think, therefore I am"). Innatism: the mind is born with ideas and knowledge. Dualist. Believed the pineal gland to be the seat of the soul. John Locke Empiricism: all knowledge comes from the senses. Tabula Rasa: individuals are born as a blank slate and all knowledge is acquired from the external world. Rejected innatism . Immanuel Kant Rejected the soul as the subject matter of psychology. Types of knowledge: A priori knowledge: innate knowledge — rationalism. A posteriori knowledge: empiricism. William Dilthey Best known for the way he distinguished between the natural and human sciences . Wrote Ideas for a Descriptive and Analytic Psychology (1894). Who → what: Descartes → innatism + "cogito, ergo sum" + pineal gland; Locke → empiricism + tabula rasa; Kant → a priori / a posteriori knowledge; Dilthey → natural vs. human sciences. 4 · Major Schools of Psychology Each school is defined by its founder(s), method of study, and central focus. Several are tagged as a "force" in psychology. School (year) Founder(s) Description Structuralism (1896) Edward Bradford Titchener Aimed to discover the structural elements of the mind. Method: introspection . Emphasized basic conscious elements. Functionalism (1896) William James Assumed that thinking, like the senses, developed because it was adaptive — it contributed to our ancestors' survival. The role of consciousness is adaptation . Psychoanalysis (1900) Sigmund Freud Two levels of reality: conscious and unconscious. Unconscious instincts: eros (life instincts) and thanatos (death instincts). Parts of personality: id, ego, superego. 1st force in psychology. Gestalt (1912) Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler Method: phenomenology . Studied conscious experience and mental processes. Focus on holism . Behaviourism (1913) John Watson; most famous behaviourist: B. F. Skinner Focus on behaviour only and discredited mental processes. 2nd force in psychology. Existential (1940s) Rollo May Method: phenomenology . Focus on freedom, meaning, and death. Martin Heidegger's Dasein: Umwelt (nature), Mitwelt (people), Eigenwelt (oneself), Uberwelt (spirituality). Humanistic (1954) Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow Method: phenomenology . Focused on the potential of individuals and highlighted each person's subjectivity, consciousness, free will and other special human qualities. 3rd force in psychology. Cognitive (1956) Ulric Neisser Focused on cognition and mental process. Analogy of the brain as a computer . Transpersonal (1960s) Abraham Maslow and Victor Frankl Concerned with the study of humanity's highest potential, and the r

title: Research & Statistics
text: Research & Statistics — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Research & Statistics Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Type I vs Type II error Parametric vs non-parametric Reliability & validity t-test / ANOVA / factor analysis Research designs What this covers. Core research methodology and statistics for the exam: key terms, the research process, variables and designs, descriptive and inferential statistics (central tendency, dispersion, t-tests, ANOVA family), factor analysis and regression, reliability and validity (with threats), standard scores, and research ethics. Contents: 1 · Terms to Know · 2 · What is Research (Steps & Types) · 3 · Variables · 4 · Research Designs · 5 · Descriptive Statistics · 6 · Inferential Statistics: t-test & ANOVA · 7 · Factor Analysis & PCA · 8 · Regression & Correlation · 9 · Reliability · 10 · Validity & Threats · 11 · Standard Scores · 12 · Research Ethics 1 · Terms to Know Random assignment: giving every participant an equal chance of being in an experimental or control group. Internal validity: extent to which an experiment investigates what it is supposed to. External validity: generalisability. Demand characteristics: factors that influence a participant's behaviour based on what they think the purpose of the experiment is. Observer expectancy effect: experimenter communicates expectations unintentionally (Pygmalion / Rosenthal effect). Descriptive statistics: the branch of statistics which deals with descriptions of obtained data. Inferential statistics: deals with drawing conclusions about a large group of individuals on the basis of observations of a few participants. Parameter: a measurable characteristic of a population. Confidence interval: the mean of your estimate plus and minus the variation in that estimate. Null hypothesis: the claim that the effect being studied does not exist. Alternate hypothesis: statement that suggests there is a relationship between the variables being studied. Significance level: the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, i.e., the probability of making a Type I error. Effect size: a quantitative measure of the magnitude of the experimental effect. The larger the effect size, the stronger the relationship between the two variables. Skewness: a lopsided and asymmetrical curve because of extreme data. Kurtosis: the term used to identify the degree of steepness or shallowness of a distribution. Post hoc test: "like a post mortem." Requires two conditions: a directional hypothesis and a significant F ratio. Trap: Type I error = null hypothesis is true but we reject it (alternate is false but we accept it) → "false alarm." Type II error = null hypothesis is false but we accept it (alternate is true but we reject it) → "miss." The significance level is the probability of making a Type I error. Key: Test power is the probability that the test will reject the null hypothesis when the alternate hypothesis is true, i.e., it will not make a Type II error. Feature Parametric test Non-parametric test Assumptions Generalizable; normal probability curve; uses mean; homogeneity of variance; probability sample; large sample size Assumption-free test Test power Higher Low test power Data type Interval / ratio Nominal data only Example t-test, ANOVA Chi square 2 · What is Research (Steps & Types) Research is a systematic, controlled, empirical, critical investigation. Steps Identify a research problem Review of literature Formulate a hypothesis Research design Collect data Analyse data Interpret data Report findings 3 · Variables A variable in research is a characteristic, number, or quantity that can be measured or counted and can take on different values. Type Description Independent variable (IV) Manipulated. Dependent variable (DV) Not manipulated; changes with change in IV. Extraneous variables Controlled. Confounding variables Uncontrolled extraneous variables that affect results. Stimulus variable e.g. light (always IV). Organismic variable e.g. age. Behavioural / response variable e.g. response rate (always DV). 4 · Research Designs Experiment Experiment (lab): complete control on secondary (error) variance, e.g. lab experiment. Field experiment: secondary variance just greater than lab experiment; happens in a real setting; difficult to control extraneous variables. Quasi experiment: secondary variance greatest; no random assignment; non-equivalent groups, e.g. ex post facto studies. Correlation Not causation established; only helps us understand association. Gives us the direction of the relationship. Can't control extraneous variables. Generalization is possible. Types: positive, negative, zero. Trap: Correlation is not causation. It shows association and direction but cannot control extraneous variables. Observation Can be naturalistic or controlled . Can be participant or non-participant . Special Designs Longitudinal design Involves taking a single group and studying it for a long period; the group is called a cohort . Founder note: Lewis Terman — eugenics. Prospective study: looking at the future. Retrospective study: looking at the past. Cross-sectional design Various age groups are compared at the same time. Cohort-sequential (cross-sequential) Cross-sectional + longitudinal; also known as cross-sequential. Survey Uses questionnaires and observation; usually used to check attitude towards something. Tools used: survey, interviews; can be participant or non-participant. Who → what: Lewis Terman — associated with eugenics and long-term longitudinal cohort study. 5 · Descriptive Statistics Measures of Central Tendency Measure Definition Scale Mean Average; sensitive to extreme data; parametric.
