Interval / ratio Median Mid point. Ordinal Mode Most frequent data point. Nominal Key: Empirical relationship: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean . Frequency is measured by: Ogive curve, Histogram, Bar graph. Variance / Dispersion How the scores are spread around the mean.

title: Biological Basis of Behaviour
text: Biological Basis of Behaviour — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Biological Basis of Behaviour Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes 4 lobes · limbic system · basal ganglia 7 neurotransmitters 12 cranial nerves Endocrine glands & hormones Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic What this covers. Development and organization of the nervous system; the forebrain and its four lobes; the limbic system and basal ganglia; diencephalon, midbrain and hindbrain; meninges and ventricles; important Broadmann's areas; techniques to study the brain; dysfunctions of the brain by region; neurotransmitters, hormones and the endocrine glands; glial cells; the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves); and the autonomic nervous system. Contents: 1 · Development & Organization of the Nervous System · 2 · The Forebrain & the Four Lobes · 3 · The Limbic System · 4 · The Basal Ganglia · 5 · Diencephalon: Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Epithalamus · 6 · Midbrain (Mesencephalon) · 7 · Hindbrain: Cerebellum, Pons, Medulla, ARAS · 8 · Meninges & Ventricles · 9 · Important Broadmann's Areas · 10 · Techniques to Study the Brain · 11 · Dysfunctions of the Brain · 12 · Neurotransmitters · 13 · Hormones & the Endocrine Glands · 14 · Glial Cells · 15 · Peripheral Nervous System & Cranial Nerves · 16 · The Autonomic Nervous System 1 · Development & Organization of the Nervous System The Nervous System is divided into the Central Nervous System (CNS) and the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) . Central Nervous System (CNS) — the Brain and the Spinal Cord . Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) — includes the Autonomic Nervous System (with its Sympathetic and Parasympathetic divisions) and the Somatic Nervous System (with its Afferent and Efferent nervous systems). Enteric Nervous System — controls the smooth muscle and glandular tissue in the digestive system. Development from the neural tube The brain develops from the neural tube , forming the following divisions: Primary vesicle Sub-division Becomes Forebrain (Prosencephalon) Telencephalon Cerebral hemispheres / four lobes Diencephalon Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus Midbrain Mesencephalon Midbrain Hindbrain (Rhombencephalon) Metencephalon Pons and cerebellum Myelencephalon Medulla Don't confuse. Afferent nerves carry sensory information toward the CNS; Efferent nerves carry motor commands away from the CNS. Similarly, the Sympathetic system drives "fight or flight" while the Parasympathetic system drives "rest and digest." 2 · The Forebrain & the Four Lobes The forebrain contains the neocortex , which contains the primary and association cortexes . Key. In the cerebral cortex, grey matter is outside and white matter is inside . Lobe Functions Frontal Lobe Executive functioning; association; motor cortex; Broca's area (left hemisphere); metacognition Parietal Lobe Sensation; haptic memory; proprioception; the " where " pathway Occipital Lobe Awareness of visual stimuli Temporal Lobe Auditory cortex; Wernicke's area (left hemisphere); part of the hippocampus; stores declarative memories; olfactory bulb 3 · The Limbic System Key structures of the limbic system, their functions, and dysfunctions: Name Function Dysfunction Amygdala Fear and rage; emotional and flashbulb memory; sense fear and aggression in others; recognize learning, memory consolidation of emotional memories Kluver-Bucy syndrome; Hyperorality; Hypersexuality Hippocampus Encoding new memory; shaped like a seahorse; located in temporal lobe Anterograde amnesia; PTSD Septum Pleasure; inhibits aggression Sham rage / Septal rage Thalamus Relay (contralateral); contains LGN, MGN, VLN, Pulvinar Extreme pain in opposite side of the body Hypothalamus Homeostasis; controls endocrine glands; eating (Lateral, Anterior, Ventromedial); sleep (Suprachiasmatic nucleus) Aphagia; Adipsia Cingulate gyrus Memories; regulate aggression — Who → what. Papez (1937) — the Papez circuit: pain information transmission; recollecting pleasant memories. Dysfunction: aggressive behaviour, shyness. Amygdala (detail) Fear and rage center Encodes emotional memories Sense fear in others Hippocampus (detail) Encode declarative memories Role in PTSD Damaged by long exposure to glucocorticoids Cingulate gyrus (detail) Transmission Important in decision making Pain Social interaction Sex Largest part 4 · The Basal Ganglia The Basal Ganglia handle motor coordination and inhibition; they prevent unnecessary motor movements and activity in the white matter of the frontal lobe. Dysfunction: tremors, involuntary muscle movements, abnormal increase in tone, difficulty initiating movements, and abnormal posture. Components of the basal ganglia: caudate , putamen , globus pallidus , substantia nigra , nucleus accumbens , and subthalamic nuclei . Structure Function Dysfunction Caudate Planning; learning; memory; romantic interaction Overactivity Putamen Speech articulation; addiction; motor learning Overactivity Nucleus Accumbens Motivation and action; drug self administration Depression, addiction, anxiety, difficulty experiencing positive emotions Subthalamic Nucleus Regulate voluntary movement Hemiballismus: sudden, large, flailing movements on one side of the body Globus Pallidus Proprioceptive movement Parkinson's disease, dystonia, and gait abnormalities Substantia Nigra Motor movement; reward functioning Motor control issues, most notably seen in Parkinson's disease 5 · Diencephalon: Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Epithalamus Thalamus The largest part of the diencephalon . Nuclei include: Medial Geniculate nucleus Lateral Geniculate Nucleus Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus Pulvinar Hypothalamus Controls homeostasis and the endocrine glands (see the Limbic System section for detail). Epithalamus Penial (pineal) gland 3rd ventricle 6 · Midbrain (Mesencephalon) Tectum — Posterior (roof) Superior colliculi (vision) and inferior colliculi (audition) Orientation Tegmentum — Anterior (floor) Substantia nigra : black substance,

title: Psychopathology
text: Psychopathology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychopathology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Biggest chapter (PDF pp. 25–55) DSM-5-TR (2022) & ICD-11 (2022) based Full disorder coverage, every duration cutoff MSE + all diagnostic groups + named syndromes Psychopharmacology appendix What this covers. The complete psychopathology core: the 4 D's of abnormality and the history of clinical psychology; the six approaches to treatment; case history and the full Mental Status Examination (MSE); the DSM and ICD classification systems and how they differ; then every major diagnostic group in DSM-5 order — neurodevelopmental, anxiety, OCD-related, depressive (mood), bipolar/mania, schizophrenia spectrum, trauma/stressor-related, dissociative, somatic, feeding/eating, sleep-wake, sexual/gender/paraphilic, personality, substance-related, and neurocognitive disorders — plus named eponymous syndromes, culture-specific syndromes, and a psychopharmacology reference. Contents: 1 · Foundations & Approaches · 2 · Case History & MSE · 3 · DSM & ICD Classification · 4 · Neurodevelopmental Disorders · 5 · Anxiety Disorders · 6 · OCD & Related Disorders · 7 · Depressive (Mood) Disorders · 8 · Bipolar & Related Disorders · 9 · Schizophrenia Spectrum & Psychotic Disorders · 10 · Trauma & Stressor-Related Disorders · 11 · Dissociative Disorders · 12 · Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders · 13 · Feeding & Eating Disorders · 14 · Sleep-Wake Disorders · 15 · Sexual Dysfunctions, Gender Dysphoria & Paraphilias · 16 · Personality Disorders · 17 · Substance-Related & Addictive Disorders · 18 · Neurocognitive Disorders · 19 · Named / Eponymous Syndromes · 20 · Culture-Specific Syndromes · 21 · Psychopharmacology Reference 1 · Foundations & Approaches to Psychopathology Different Terms Abnormal: outlining atypicality. Abnormality depends on the intensity and frequency of behaviour. Psychopathology: part of abnormality — the medical angle of the abnormal (involves neuroimaging, aetiology, diagnosis, prognosis). Clinical Psychology: application of psychological principles in the treatment of mental disorders. The 4 D's of Abnormality: Deviance (social and statistical), Distress (causing unhappiness), Dysfunction (unable to show adaptive behaviour), Danger (to oneself and others). History of Clinical Psychology Historically the mentally ill were tied, chained and kept in inhumane conditions. 1826 — Philippe Pinel introduced moral therapy . 1802–1887 — Dorothea Dix advocated for humane treatment. APA founded 1892 ; first president G. Stanley Hall . Lightner Witmer — founder of clinical psychology; opened the first clinic. DSM introduced in 1952 ; ICD-6 in 1952 . Current diagnosis is more spectrum-oriented. Named figures. Pinel (moral therapy), Dorothea Dix (humane treatment advocacy), G. Stanley Hall (first APA president), Lightner Witmer (founder of clinical psychology, first clinic). The Six Approaches (with pros & cons) Approach View of abnormality Methods Pros Cons Biological Organic problems, biochemical imbalances Drugs, ECT, surgery Effective for those who don't respond to other treatments Side effects; neglects non-biological problems Humanistic Failure to strive towards one's potential / being out of touch with feelings Client-centred, Gestalt, Existential Recognizes positive human goals, values and needs Unsupportive; limited research Behavioural Reinforcement history, environment Desensitization, aversion, operant conditioning, token economy, modelling, social skills training Research supports effectiveness Not long-lasting; neglects cognitive processes Psychodynamic Internal / unconscious conflicts Free association, catharsis, analysis of resistance / transference / dreams First major alternative to biological treatment; abnormal function rooted in same processes as normal function Depends on therapist's subjective interpretation Cognitive Irrational / dysfunctional thoughts REBT, CBT Considerable research support Dysfunctional thinking may not cause abnormal functioning Sociocultural Dysfunctional society — — — 2 · Case History & Mental Status Examination Case History Four assessment techniques are used: Observation, Conversation, Exploration, Testing . Personal information: name, father's/husband's name; sociodemographic profile (age, sex, education, occupation, socio-economic status, marital status, religion, residence, mother tongue, address); source of referral; type of admission; identification marks. Informant reliability — the 5 C's (SIMS): Contact (between patient and informant), Closeness of relationship, Continuity of the account, Consistency of the verbatim, Corroborativeness between sources. History of Present Illness — the factors Factor Definition Predisposing Factors operating from early life that determine vulnerability to develop a disorder Precipitating Events that occur shortly before the onset of a disorder Perpetuating Factors due to which the disorder is maintained or aggravated Limiting Factors which limit the illness from extensive progress Modifying Factors which modify the natural or expected course of the illness Mode of onset: abrupt, acute, insidious. Course of illness: continuous, episodic, fluctuating. Progress of illness: improving, deteriorating, static. Compliance: the extent to which the patient's behaviour (taking medications, following diets, other lifestyle changes) coincides with medical recommendations. Also covered: treatment history, past history (medical & psychiatric), family history (genogram, consanguinity), personal history (birth & early development, childhood disorders, home atmosphere, scholastic/extracurricular, occupational, menstrual, sexual & marital, forensic), premorbid personality (individualized styles of dealing with the environment characteristic of a person prior to onset), and physical examination (by physician). Mental Status Examination (MSE) The part of clinical assessment describing the sum total of the examiner's observations and impressions of a psychiatric patient at the time of interview. General Appearance & Behaviour Parameter Finding & associations Eye contact Assesses rapport, truthfulness, insight, concentration. Partial (fleeting); Absent — complete loss (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Acute delusional disorder). Depression → lowered eyes; Anxiety → shifting gaze. Dress Appropriate (normal); Shabby (Dementia, Substance abuse); Inappropriate , e.g. rain hood on a dry day (Mania, Histrionic PD). Facial expression Depression → corners of mouth turned down, vertical furrows on brow. Anxiety → horizontal forehead creases, widened palpebral fissures, dilated pupils. May be fixed/wooden (parkinsonian drug side effects) or reflect thyrotoxicosis. Posture Depression → hunched shoulders, gaze downward. Anxiety → edge of chair, gripping sides. Agitated depression → tremulous, picking at fingernails. Mania → restlessness. Catatonia → odd postures. Estimate of age Younger than stated → Histrionic PD; Older than stated → Depression or Chronic Schizophrenia. General appearance Kempt (normal, OCPD); Overtly made up (mania/hypomania, histrionic/narcissistic PD, some schizophrenia); Unkempt/untidy (organic psychosis, dementia, substance abuse, severe depression, schizophrenia); Sickly ; Perplexed . Body-build typologies. Ernst Kretschmer: Pyknics (stocky/rounded), Leptosomes (long/linear), Athletics (broad-shouldered/muscular). Sheldon's somatotypes: Endomorph (round, fat abdomen), Mesomorph (cubical head, muscular), Ectomorph (thin, receding chin, spindly limbs). Attitude towards the examiner Frank and Cooperative / Attentive (normal). Defensive & Guarded (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Delusional disorder). Evasive (Organic psychoses, Substance abuse). Hostile (Paranoid Schizophrenia, Antisocial PD). Seductive . Rapport A bidirectional empathetic relationship. Easily established — normal persons, Mania; Established with difficulty — Schizophrenia, Dementia, Depression; Not possible — Paranoid Schizophrenia, Dementia, Depression. Motor Behaviour (selected signs) Sign Description / association Retardation Slowness of initiation/execution — Depression Hyperactivity Increased motor activity, often with over-talkativeness Mannerisms Unusual repeated goal-directed action (e.g. odd hand movements when shaking hands) Stereotypy Repetitive, non-goal-directed action carried out uniformly Grimace Non-goal-directed facial expression; e.g. Schnauzkrampf (snout spasm) — Schizophrenia Tics Sudden involuntary twitchings — Gilles de la Tourette syndrome (SIMS) Waxy flexibility Person maintains the body position into which they are placed Negativism Verbal/non-verbal opposition to suggestion — catatonic schizophrenia Echolalia Repeating another's words — catatonic schizophrenia Echopraxia Repetition by imitation of another's movements Ambivalence Co-existence of two opposing impulses toward the same thing — Schizophrenia, borderline state, OCD Automatic obedience Undue compliance with instructions — catatonia Waxy flexibility, odd posturing, rigidity, self-injury Catatonia; self-injurious behaviour → Borderline PD Also noted: preoccupied, restless, awkward (apraxia, MR), destructive (catatonic/manic excitement), silly smiling (Mania, Hebephrenia), aggressive, perseveration, dyskinesia, dystonia, chorea, athetosis, hallucinatory behaviour, gestures, touching the examiner. Speech Intensity: excessively loud (Mania, Hypomania), abnormally soft (vocal cord palsy, Depression, Paranoid Schizophrenia). Pitch: monotonous (parietal lobe damage, chronic schizophrenia, depression). Reaction time: increased (hypothyroidism, depression, schizophrenia), decreased (Mania). Speed: very slow (depression, dementia, hypothyroidism); rapid with prolixity/flight of ideas (mania, hypomania, hyperthyroidism). Pressure of speech — increased, accelerated, hard to interrupt (Mania, Schizophrenia, cognitive disorders). Ease: hesitant (head injury, anxiety), mutism (stupor, dementia), slurring (cerebellar damage), stuttering/stammering (severe anxiety, schizophrenia), whispering (pseudobulbar palsy), muttering (schizophrenia, dementia). Deviations: rhyming/punning (mania), talking past the point ( Ganser's syndrome , schizophrenia), clang association (schizophrenia, mania), stereotypy (catatonic schizophrenia), perseveration. Cognitive Functions Orientation (time, place, person), attention, concentration, memory (immediate / recent / remote), abstract ability, intelligence (comprehension, general information, vocabulary, calculation). Thinking style Definition & association Concrete thinking Thinking bound to actual things/events & immediate experience — Schizophrenia, young children Functional thinking Abstraction relating only to functional aspects — Schizophrenia, MR Over-abstraction Excessive manifestation of a concept beyond relevance — Schizophrenia, philosophical preoccupations Mood & Affect Mood = persistent, sustained emotion colouring perception of the world. Affect = present emotional responsiveness inferred from expression. Quality: dysphoric, anxious, irritable, depressed, elevated, euphoric, elated, exalted, ecstatic, euthymic. Intensity: shallow (lack of depth), blunted (greatly diminished, uniform voice), flat (no affect displayed). Appropriateness: Paramimia — lack of unity between modes of emotional expression; Parathymia — expression opposite to what is expected (e.g. laughing at tragic news). Diurnal variation: worse in morning (endogenous depression, headache), worse in evening (anxiety, delirium/ sundowning ), worse at night (uremia). Thought Aspect Key terms Stream Acceleration, pressured speech, flight of ideas (rapid, chance connections still understandable), prolixity (ordered flight, returns to task), retardation/bradyphrenia, poverty of speech (laconic), circumstantiality (reaches point via trivia), tangentiality (oblique, never reaches point), thought blocking (sudden arrest → blank) Form Negative type (loses ability to form concept) vs positive type (false concept by blending incongruous elements): loosening of associations, derailment, neologism, over-inclusion Possession Obsession , rumination , compulsion , thought alienation — insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting, thought echo Content Worry, phobias, impulse, somatic symptoms, religious preoccupations (OCD), magical thinking, depressive cognition (worthlessness/helplessness/hopelessness), suicidal/homicidal ideas, inflated self-esteem, delusion (a false firm belief) Perception Sensory distortion — intensity: hyperaesthesia, hyperacusis, hypoacusis. Quality: Xanthopsia (yellow), Chloropsia (green), Erythropsia (red/pink). Spatial form: Micropsia (smaller), Macropsia/megalopsia (larger), Porropsia (retreat into distance without size change). Sensory deception — Hallucination: perception without an adequate external stimulus (auditory, visual, olfactory, gustatory, tactile). Delusion vs Hallucination. A delusion is a false firm belief (a disorder of thought content ). A hallucination is a perception without an adequate external stimulus (a disorder of perception ). An illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus. Don't conflate them. Other psychotic phenomena. Somatic passivity — belief that outside influences play on the body. Made phenomenon — made act (actions under external control), made affect (feelings not one's own), made impulse (impulse admitted as one's own action but not one's own drive). Judgement & Insight Judgement: social, personal, test. Insight — degree of awareness/understanding of being ill (intellectual vs true emotional insight), rated on a 6-point scale: Insight — 6-point scale: Grade 1 complete denial → Grade 2 slight awareness but denying → Grade 3 attributed to external/physical factors → Grade 4 due to something unknown in self → Grade 5 intellectual insight → Grade 6 true emotional insight. 3 · Classification — DSM & ICD The DSM Emil Kraepelin differentiated dementia praecox (a biological illness from anatomical/toxic processes) from manic depression (an episodic disorder not leading to permanently impaired brain function) as the two forms of psychosis. Edition Year Key features DSM-I 1952 Developed by the American Psychiatric Association; 100 conditions; division into psychosis & neurosis DSM-II 1962 Written in paragraphs as explanations DSM-III 1980 Multiaxial system introduced; symptomatic criteria; started aligning with ICD DSM-IV & IV-TR 1994 Five-axis system fully articulated DSM-5 2013 Multiaxial system dropped; spectrum approach; Roman numerals replaced by Arabic DSM-5-TR 2022 Latest; added prolonged grief disorder The five axes (DSM-III to IV-TR): Axis I clinical syndromes (V codes); Axis II personality disorders & intellectual disability; Axis III general medical condition; Axis IV psychosocial & environmental problems; Axis V global assessment of functioning (GAF). DSM-5 disorder categories Neurodevelopmental; Schizophrenia-spectrum & other psychotic; Bipolar & related; Depressive; Anxiety; Obsessive-compulsive & related; Trauma & stressor-related; Dissociative; Somatic symptom & related; Feeding & eating; Sexual dysfunctions; Gender dysphoria; Paraphilic disorders; Sleep-wake; Disruptive, impulse-control & conduct; Neurocognitive; Substance-related & addictive; Personality disorders. New in DSM-5: social (pragmatic) communication disorder; disruptive mood dysregulation disorder; premenstrual dysphoric disorder; hoarding disorder; excoriation (skin-picking) disorder; disinhibited social engagement disorder; binge eating disorder; central sleep apnea; sleep-related hypoventilation; REM sleep behaviour disorder; restless legs syndrome; caffeine withdrawal; cannabis withdrawal; major NCD with Lewy Body Disease; mild neurocognitive disorder. Eliminated: sexual aversion; polysubstance-related disorder. Criticism of DSM: medicalization (over-diagnosis), pharmaceutical influence, cultural and ethical concerns, comorbidity. The ICD International Classification of Diseases. ICD-6: 1948/49. Essential for standardization, research & epidemiology, healthcare management, resource allocation, global consistency. Block ICD grouping F00–09 Organic mental disorders (neurocognitive) F10–19 Substance use disorders F20–29 Schizophrenia and related F30–39 Mood disorders F40–49 Neurotic, stress-related, somatoform disorders F50–59 Behavioural syndromes associated with physiological disturbances F60–69 Personality disorders F70–79 Intellectual disability (neurodevelopmental) F80–89 Psychological development disorders F90–98 Emotional development disorders F99 Unspecified ICD editions: ICD-9 (1977), ICD-10 (1993), ICD-11 (2022). ICD-11 eliminated acute stress disorder and gender incongruence as a personality disorder (dimensional approach instead of categorization) and added prolonged grief disorder, compulsive sexual behaviour, gaming disorder. ICD vs DSM ICD DSM Origin 1949 1952 Authoring body WHO APA Scope Broader Narrower Outlook Global American Editions 11 5 Similarities: symptoms overlap; both are authoritative guidebooks. Other differences: cultural considerations, billing/insurance, acceptance and use. ICD-10 vs ICD-11 ICD-10 ICD-11 21 disorder groupings 11 disorder groupings No harmonization with DSM Harmonization with DSM Separate grouping for childhood/adolescent-onset disorders Omits a separate childhood/adolescent grouping Categorical approach Categorical, with dimensional expansions (severity, course, specific symptoms) 14,400 codes; no extension codes 55,000 codes; extension (X) codes for signs/symptoms, causes, disorders 28 chapters 22 chapters 4 · Neurodevelopmental Disorders Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) Earlier diagnosable only up to age 7, now up to age 12 ; stays into adulthood if untreated; many comorbidities. Inattention: distractible, loses interest, keeps shifting tasks, doesn't attend to detail, loses things. Hyperactivity: impulsive, can't wait, aggressive, can't wait for turn, squirms, talks excessively. Any 6 symptoms must be met; duration ≥ 6 months. Treatment: Ritalin, amphetamine, dextroamphetamine; behavioural modification, applied behavioural analysis, shaping, chaining, token economy, response cost; Modafinil; Clonidine, venlafaxine, bupropion, SNRI. DDx: oppositional defiant, conduct disorder, aggression, depression, substance use, ASPD; problems with frontal lobe & cerebellum; difficulty copying, rapid alternating movements, right-left discrimination. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD / Pervasive Developmental Disorder) Chromosomes 2, 7, 4, 15, 19 involved. Impairment in social interaction (eye contact, social smile, attachment, expression, making friends, routine). Impairment in communication and language (delayed milestones, articulation difficulty, echolalia, verbigeration, saying "me" instead of "you"). Restrictive, repetitive, stereotyped behaviour, flapping, echopraxia; impaired theory of mind; high pain tolerance; biting/scratching/headbanging; isles of precocity (high skill in something). Treatment: Risperidone, Aripiprazole; behaviour modification. DDx: Fragile X, Phenylketonuria, Rubella, Intellectual disability, Tuberous sclerosis, asphyxia. Rett's Syndrome Losing fine motor skills; head circumference decreases from 5–48 months; stereotyped movement; problems with walk/talk/eat/breathe; 75% seizures ; progressive; mostly in girls; microencephaly. A subtype of pervasive developmental disorder. Normal early development followed by partial/complete loss of speech, locomotion & hand-use skills with deceleration in head growth. Treatment symptomatic. Heller's Syndrome (Childhood Disintegrative Disorder, CDD) Rare; late onset (> 3 years) of developmental delays in language, social function, motor skills. Symptoms age 2–10 years: impaired social skills, language skills, bladder control; stereotyped behaviour; microcephaly. Another neurodevelopmental disorder. Asperger's Syndrome Mild ASD; problems with social interaction; experience emotion but can't express; restrictive, repetitive, stereotyped behaviour. Intellectual Disability (ID) Overlaps with ADHD and Autism before 18 years; IQ below 70; spectrum approach; based on adaptive functioning in conceptual, social and practical domains; onset before 18 years . Type IQ % of ID Features Mild 50–70 85% 6th-grade academic skill; independent life; relationships possible; problem with abstract thinking Moderate 35–50 10% Limited vocabulary; needs help with self-care/social tasks; can handle money; relationships possible but little emotion Severe 20–30 5% May learn simple commands; rudimentary communication Profound 0–20 1–2% All development stunted; low age span Aetiology: genetic abnormality (5%) — chromosomal, cranial anomaly, single-gene disorder, inborn errors of metabolism ( Tay-Sachs, Lesch-Nyhan ); perinatal (10%) — infections, prematurity, birth trauma, hypoxia, kernicterus, placental abnormality, drugs; acquired physical (infections, cretinism, trauma, lead poisoning, cerebral palsy); sociocultural (15%) — deprivation; psychiatric (1–2%). DDx: deaf/dumb, deprived, speech defect, psychiatric disorder, systematic disorder, epilepsy. Global Developmental Delay Delay in development for a patient under 5 years who has not been adequately evaluated; missed developmental milestones. Specific Learning Disability (SLD) IQ is normal but poor academic score. Dyslexia — inability to read/comprehend; Dysgraphia — poor handwriting; Dyscalculia — arithmetic impairment. Tics & Tourette's (Motor Disorder) 1% of young people; family history of tics or OCD. Motor tics, vocal tics, involuntary jerks; stress develops; effort goes into controlling tics. Tourette's: ≥ 2 motor and 1 vocal tic; knee-jerking responses; longer than 1 year. Vocal: barks, clicks, coughs, grunts. Coprolalia — swearing (bad-word) tics. Dopamine antagonists used for treatment. Communication Disorders Language disorder: problems in spoken/written/sign language; expressive & receptive; vocabulary & grammar; speaks slower & less; academic issues; can co-exist with ADHD. Speech sound (phonological) disorder: substituting/omitting sounds (e.g. "ghaspetti" for "spaghetti"); diagnosed only in first language; 2–3% of preschool children. Childhood-onset fluency (stuttering) disorder: difficulty with beginning of words; momentary panic; anxiety/frustration; occurs with consonants and initial sounds; begins 2–5 years; more in boys; ~3% of children; dopamine antagonists used. Social (pragmatic) communication disorder: don't understand what to say where; poor contextual use of speech; less practical language use, convention, turn-taking, non-verbal/implied communication; may be comorbid. 5 · Anxiety Disorders (F40–48) Neurosis — subjective distress; ego-dystonic; insight present; personality & behaviour preserved; absence of organicity; reaction to stress & adjustment; somatoform. Anxiety symptoms. Motor (tremors, restlessness, muscle twitch, fearful face); autonomic/visceral (palpitation, tachycardia, sweating, flushes, hyperventilation, chest constriction, mouth dryness, reduced micturition, mydriasis); cognitive (poor concentration, distractibility, hyperarousal, vigilance); affective (apprehension, fearfulness, inability to relax, irritability, feelings of doom); other (noise sensitivity, insomnia, increased startle response). Trait anxiety ("I often feel anxious") vs state anxiety ("I feel anxious now") — those with trait anxiety also have state anxiety. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Most diagnosed anxiety disorder; free-floating anxiety; for 6 months or more ; constant low arousal of the sympathetic nervous system. DDx: OCD, PTSD, mood disorder, physical causes, realistic anxiety. Treatment: benzodiazepine, SSRI, barbiturates (old), CBT, relaxation, psychodynamic therapy. Social Anxiety Disorder Severe irrational fear of evaluation; dysfunction at work and relationships; ≥ 6 months ; sometimes only due to evaluation of performance. Specific Phobia Defence mechanism: displacement . Irrational, disproportional fear of certain animals, natural environment, situations, blood/injection, others. Fear out of proportion; insight present; inability to control fear; avoidance of the object. Agoraphobia Fear of being in a place where they can't get up and leave; fear of crowded/enclosed places. Treatment: clomipramine, venlafaxine, buspirone. Panic Disorder Feelings of impending doom; hippocampus and amygdala involved; periodic, discrete bouts of panic/terror in the absence of any real threat; feels like a heart attack; should be present for more than a month . Separation Anxiety Disorder Fear that something will happen to the attachment figure if away; can happen in adults; may have vomiting; ≥ 6 months in adults, ≥ 4 weeks in children . Selective Mutism Children remain silent except before close people; normal intelligence; family history of SAD; may develop SAD in adulthood; duration > 1 month ; treatment: social skills training. Other anxiety disorders Substance-induced anxiety disorder (from exposure/withdrawal to a medication); anxiety disorder due to another medical condition ; other specified anxiety disorder (clinician specifies reason for non-fulfilment); unspecified anxiety disorder (clinician does not specify). 6 · Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) Young-adulthood onset; most common in males; family history. Obsessions: ego-dystonic, irrational, absurd, distressing, recognised as one's own idea. Compulsions: to neutralize the obsession; not realistic; irrational; insight present; subjective; may diminish the anxiety associated with the obsession. Major patterns: contamination, pathological doubt, intrusive thought, symmetry (tics). Aetiology. Dysfunction in fronto-striatal brain circuitry ( caudate ). Defence mechanisms: reaction formation, isolation of affect, undoing . DSM specifier: with good/fair insight; with poor insight; with absent insight/delusional beliefs; tic-related. Treatment: clomipramine, antipsychotics, lithium, valproate; Exposure and Response Prevention, aversion therapy; caudectomy, cingulotomy, capsulectomy. Trichotillomania Recurrent pulling out of one's hair resulting in hair loss and bald patches; attempts to control the behaviour. Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder Recurrent skin picking resulting in skin lesions; attempts to control the behaviour. ICD-11: factitious dermatitis. Hoarding Disorder Overwhelming urge to accumulate things; distressed when discarding possessions. Body Dysmorphic Disorder Preoccupied with minor body imperfections. Specify if: with muscle dysmorphia. 7 · Depressive (Mood) Disorders Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Duration ≥ 2 weeks. Mnemonic SIGECAPS: S leep disturbance (REM latency, early-morning awakening); low I nterest; G uilt; E nergy deficit; reduced C oncentration; reduced A ppetite; P sychomotor agitation/retardation; S uicidal ideation. Specifiers/features: with psychotic features (schizoaffective); atypical features (hypersomnia, overeating); melancholic features (in old age); catatonic features. Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Symptoms persist for 2 years ; no suicidal ideation; no hospitalization; symptoms never absent for longer than 2 months. MDD vs Persistent Depressive Disorder. MDD = ≥ 2 weeks, may include suicidal ideation and hospitalization. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) = ≥ 2 years, no suicidal ideation, no hospitalization, symptoms never absent > 2 months. Double depression = MDD superimposed on dysthymia (a poor-prognosis feature). Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) For children and adolescents; a precursor to bipolar ; sudden anger, throwing fits, tantrums; persistent negative moods; sadness translated into complete outbursts. DDx: oppositional defiant disorder. Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) Mood shifts or other dysphoria in the week or two before the menstrual period. Prognosis, subtypes & aetiology Good prognosis Poor prognosis Acute onset; typical clinical features; severe depression; well-adjusted premorbid personality; good treatment response Comorbidity with personality disorder/alcohol abuse; double depression; chronic stress; unfavourable early environment; hypochondriacal features; poor drug compliance Endogenous Exogenous Absence of any precipitating life event Due to a precipitating life event; less likelihood of psychosis; more somatic complaints; less likelihood of suicide Physical signs. Veraguth's fold — triangular fold in the nasal corner of the upper eyelid. Omega sign on the forehead. Beck's cognitive triad — negative view of self, world, future. Also: learned helplessness (Seligman). Aetiology: unipolar depression concordance rate 46%; abnormality in monoamine, acetylcholine and GABA neurotransmitters; hormonal disturbances; neuroanatomical — reduced dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and increased HPA axis. Treatment: pharmacotherapy takes 3–4 weeks; maintained for 6 months (prophylactic). Tricyclic antidepressants (block reuptake of serotonin & norepinephrine, the "-pramines"; anticholinergic side effects — constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, dry mouth). SSRIs / NaSSA / SNRI (side effects: nausea, anxiety, diarrhoea). MAOIs. Antipsychotics. Therapies: CBT, mindfulness, IPT, ECT, TMS, vagus nerve stimulation, deep brain stimulation, sleep deprivation therapy, phototherapy (1500–10,000 lux). 8 · Bipolar & Related Disorders (Mania) Manic episode criteria — mnemonic DIG FAST: D istractibility; I mpulsivity; G randiosity; F light of ideas; A ctivity (goal-directed) increase; S leep deficit; T alkativeness. Bipolar I Requires a manic episode . Major depressive episodes common but not required for diagnosis. Bipolar II A hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode ; there has never been a full manic episode. Bipolar I vs Bipolar II — and Mania vs Hypomania. Mania (Bipolar I): lasts 1 week , accompanied by less intense depression, may have psychotic features, requires hospitalization. Hypomania (Bipolar II): lasts 4 days , accompanied by major depressive episodes, may not require hospitalization, never a full manic episode. Bipolar I needs a manic episode; Bipolar II needs hypomania + ≥ 1 MDE and no full mania. Cyclothymic Disorder Periods with hypomanic symptoms (not meeting full criteria) and depressive symptoms (not meeting full criteria) for at least 2 years , during which symptoms have not been absent for more than 2 months. Specifiers Mood-congruent psychotic features; mood-incongruent psychotic features; catatonia; peripartum onset; seasonal pattern; hypomania; mixed episodes (cycle in 7 days); anxious distress; rapid cycling; melancholic features; atypical features. Aetiology & prevalence. Bipolar disorder is the most genetically influenced disorder (74% if both parents affected). Neurotransmitters: increased dopamine activity. Genetic factors: chromosomes 18q, 22q, 21q. Mania more common in men; depression more common in women; onset 30 years and above; more in divorced/single persons. Treatment: Lithium (side effects: postural tremors [treated with beta-blockers], memory disturbance, intracranial tension, peripheral neuropathy, hypothyroidism, polyuria, diabetes; lithium toxicity — tremors, renal impairment, ataxia, delirium, increased reflexes, convulsions, vomiting, kidney issues), Valproate (acute mania), Lamotrigine (depressive), Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, antidepressants; ECT; therapy. Treatment continued for 2 years. 9 · Schizophrenia Spectrum & Other Psychotic Disorders History. Emil Kraepelin gave the term dementia praecox (1896); his classification: simple dementia, paranoia, catatonia, hebephrenia. Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia and gave the 4 A's : Ambivalence, Autism, Association (disturbance), Affect disturbance . Karl Kahlbaum — catatonia. Symptoms Negative symptoms: affective flattening, avolition, apathy, anhedonia, asociality, alogia. Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms (positive). Audible thoughts (1st person); voices heard arguing (3rd person); voices commenting on one's actions; thought withdrawal; thought diffusion/broadcasting; made feeling; made impulse; made actions; somatic passivity. Also: hallucinations; delusions (erotomania, grandeur, guilt, jealousy, passivity, persecution, poverty, reference, somatic, thought control). Speech disturbances: poverty of speech, echolalia, verbigeration (continual repetition of stereotyped phrases), perseveration. Catatonia (Karl Kahlbaum): agitation, cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness/paralysis), echolalia/echopraxia, exaggerated compliance, grimace, mannerism, mutism, stereotypy, posturing, waxy flexibility. Types (subtypes) Paranoid; Catatonic; Disorganized/Hebephrenic; Undifferentiated; Residual; Simple ( worst prognosis ). Also pfropfschizophrenie — schizophrenia and mental retardation coexisting. Type 1 Type 2 Ventricles Normal ventricles Dilated ventricles Damage No organic damage; no comorbidity — Medication response Good prognosis Low response to medication Duration & the psychotic-disorder family Disorder Duration Symptoms to be met Schizophrenia 6+ months All Schizophreniform disorder 1–6 months All Schizoaffective disorder 2 weeks Schizophrenia + mood disorder Delusional disorder 1 month Delusion Brief psychotic disorder 1 day and 1 night All Schizophreniform vs Schizophrenia (the classic duration trap). Schizophreniform = 1–6 months ; Schizophrenia = 6+ months — same full symptom set, only the duration cutoff differs. Brief psychotic disorder is even shorter (1 day–1 month), and schizoaffective requires both schizophrenia and a mood disorder. Etiology, epidemiology & prognosis Positive symptoms — excess dopamine in the mesolimbic tract (VTA → limbic region). Negative symptoms — dopamine dysregulation in the mesocortical pathway (VTA → prefrontal lobe). Genetic loci: 1q, 5q, 6p, 6q, 8p, 10p, 13q, 15q, 22q. Biochemical: dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, GABA. Epidemiology: 1% lifetime; 0.15–0.25% per 1000; good prognosis in females; bad prognosis with low SES. Good prognosis Poor prognosis Abrupt/sudden onset; late onset; catatonic; in females; positive symptoms present; history of mood disorders Insidious onset; early onset; simple/disorganized schizophrenia; in males; negative symptoms present; history of schizophrenia Treatment. Typical antipsychotics (dopamine receptor antagonists; side effect: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome, NMS) — Chlorpromazine (1950), Haloperidol, Phenothiazines, Thioxanthene, Butyrophenones. Atypical antipsychotics (target 5-HT receptors, partially block D2) — Clozapine (treatment-resistant schizophrenia), Olanzapine, Quetiapine; do not cause tardive dyskinesia. 10 · Trauma & Stressor-Related Disorders Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Occurs after rape, floods, abduction, plane crash, soldiers of war; symptoms don't develop immediately. Was classified under anxiety disorders until DSM-IV-TR. Symptoms: avoidance of situations/places/memories; intrusive flashbacks, re-experiencing, nightmares; arousal (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle); depersonalization & derealization. Diagnosed if symptoms appear within 6 months after trauma; symptoms present for more than a month. Brain regions: hippocampus, amygdala. Acute Stress Disorder All PTSD symptoms for less than 1 month ; also experience dissociation; 9/14 symptoms of PTSD must be present. Acute Stress Disorder vs PTSD. ASD = PTSD symptoms lasting < 1 month (with prominent dissociation). PTSD = symptoms > 1 month, appearing within 6 months of trauma. Note ICD-11 eliminated acute stress disorder as a diagnosis. Complex PTSD (ICD-11) Prolonged exposure to trauma. Disturbances in self-organization — the person must experience 2/3 of: (1) emotional dysregulation, (2) interpersonal disturbances, (3) [disturbed self-perception]. Clinical features: re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, impaired self-perception, difficulty maintaining relationships. Treatment: prevention/disaster management, practical help, SSRIs, benzodiazepines, EMDR. Prolonged Grief Disorder (DSM-5-TR & ICD-11) Intense, persistent grief; difficulty accepting loss; intrusive thoughts/memories; avoidance; emotional numbness; identity disturbance (feeling like we have died with the other person); unable to function for more than 6 months . Treatment: grief counselling, group therapy, SSRIs. Adjustment Disorder Not being able to adjust to a new situation; psychological and physical symptoms (depression, anxiety) for a span of 3–6 months . Specifiers: anxiety, depression, behaviour, conduct. Reactive Attachment Disorder Unable to form reciprocal relationships; faced rejection in childhood; periods of irritable sadness; issues develop before age 5 ; persistent if symptoms last longer than a year . DDx: ASD, depression. Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder Outcome of abuse, insufficient caregiving, neglect, frequent change; shyness; don't check in with regular caregiver; may become excessively familiar with strangers. 11 · Dissociative Disorders A group of normally integrated mental processes become separated from the rest. Clinical features: disturbance in integrated consciousness; sudden onset, temporary course; precipitatory stress; secondary gain; no physical abnormality; affects memory, identity, perception; produced unconsciously by the psyche. Types of gain. Primary — internal psychological motivation to reduce guilt. Secondary — external psychological motivation for assurance/social support. Tertiary — parent's/close person's benefit. Dissociative Amnesia (Psychogenic Amnesia) Types: circumscribed (personal event-specific), selective (forgetting some things), generalized (forgetting everything), continuous (from a stressful event till present), systematized (everything about an event). Dissociative Fugue Wandering/running off; losing old identity and picking up a new one; termination is abrupt. Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder Depersonalization — cutting off/detachment from oneself. Derealization — experience of what is real and not real may be lost. Occurs without overlap with other disorders. Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) At least 2 distinct identities; personality states called alter egos . Other dissociative presentations (ICD-10) Dissociative trance or possession disorder; dissociative stupor; dissociative disorder of movement and sensation ( la belle indifférence ) — physical symptoms due to psychological causes. 12 · Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders Somatic Symptom (Somatoform) Disorder Chronic pain without any physical cause; conviction persists despite negative test results; duration 6+ months ; onset may be due to stress. Clinical features: 4 pain symptoms, 2 GI symptoms, 1 sexual symptom, 1 pseudo-neurological symptom. Treatment: psychotherapy. Illness Anxiety Disorder (Hypochondriasis) Over-concern with normal body function; terribly worried about having a serious illness; symptoms don't remain constant; unconsciously start mimicking symptoms (not psychotic); addicted to internet searches. Subtypes: care-seeking , care-avoidant . Duration 6+ months. Conversion Disorder (Hysteria / Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) Body function is lost due to a psychological issue; primary and secondary gain; psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) ; disturbance of consciousness; la belle indifférence ; duration 6+ months . Factitious Disorder Person wants to stay sick for attention; maintains the sick role; simulates symptoms. Types: for self ; by proxy (Munchausen syndrome) — keeping a child sick. Pseudologia fantastica — telling stories, pathological lying. Person pretends to have non-measurable diseases; "professionals as patients". 13 · Feeding & Eating Disorders Anorexia Nervosa Restricted food intake to markedly reduced body weight; obsessing about obesity/weight gain; distorted self-perception of being overweight. Characteristic symptoms: dis

title: Psychological Testing
text: Psychological Testing — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychological Testing Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Neuropsychological batteries Intelligence & Indian tests Projective & objective personality tests MMPI · 16PF · NEO-PI · EPQ Test → author → what it measures What this covers. A complete tour of psychological tests for the clinical/NET syllabus: neuropsychology foundations and batteries (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska, AIIMS, NIMHANS) plus individual neuro tests (WCST, Bender-Gestalt, Stroop, Tower tests, ROCF, CANTAB, MMSE, PGIBBD, WMS); intelligence tests (Stanford-Binet 5, Raven's, CFIT, Kaufman family, Leiter) and Indian adaptations (Bhatia's Battery, Binet-Kamat, Kulshreshtha, WAPIS, MISIC); and personality tests split into projective (Rorschach, TAT, Rosenzweig, Szondi, sentence-completion and drawing tests) and non-projective objective inventories (MMPI family, MCMI, MBTI, EPPS, Holland, MPQ, 16PF, NEO-PI, EPQ). Every test name, author, age range, subtest and cutoff is preserved. Contents: 1 · Introduction to Neuropsychology · 2 · Neuropsychological Tests: goals, categories, approaches · 3 · Halstead-Reitan Battery · 4 · Other Neuropsychological Tests · 5 · Intelligence Tests · 6 · Indian Intelligence Tests · 7 · Personality Tests: overview · 8 · Projective Tests · 9 · Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic) · 10 · Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic) 1 · Introduction to Neuropsychology Neuropsychology is the study of brain function and behaviour. Neuroplasticity Experience expectant — development according to expected growth pattern. Experience dependent — plasticity dependent on new learning, based on new experiences. History of the mind–brain question Mentalism (Aristotle) — a non-material psyche is responsible for behaviour. Dualism (Descartes) — the body is like a machine (only controls reflex); the mind controls the machine. Materialism (Darwin) — the mind is just our brain; neuroplasticity is based on evolution, the capacity to change. Research findings Florenz and Galls challenged localization: removed the cortex of 3 dogs. Young children can recover fast from brain damage (stem cells migrate). In adults, new neurons (2%) are formed in the hippocampus and striatum. Functioning improves with physiotherapy. 2 · Neuropsychological Tests: goals, categories, approaches Neuropsychological testing allows for an in-depth analysis of functional limitation associated with brain dysfunction, and is required for diagnosis by some diagnostic criteria for neurological disorders. Goals (Schaefer et al., 2023) Establish a baseline. Gauge an individual's cognitive strengths and weaknesses and aid in treatment planning. Assist in establishing diagnoses. Establish lateralization and possible etiology of brain lesions. Track progress in rehab. Determination of disability, return to work/school, driving ability or legal purposes. Categories assessed Abstract · Attention · Daily activities · Emotional Distress · Language · Memory · Motor skills · Orientation · Sensation · Perception · Visuospatial reasoning. Sensitivity and Specificity Key. Sensitivity = a test's ability to correctly identify people who have a disease. Specificity = a test's ability to correctly identify people who do not have a disease. Approaches to Neuropsychological tests Approach Description Example Fixed battery Uses the same battery of tests for every client; maintains a constant testing condition; comprehensive normative data; better psychometric properties; broader empirical base for interpretations. Halstead-Reitan Battery Flexible battery Only those measures directly related to the patient's presenting symptoms should be administered. The administered battery inherently changes with a patient's referral question. Uses a core battery of tests and techniques for clients with various syndromes; tests implemented vary based on the practitioner as well as context. Meyers Neuropsychological Battery Commonly named neuropsychological tests Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) Raven's Progressive Matrices Shipley Institute of Living Scale The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) Proverbs The Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure (ROCF) test The Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) Consonant trigrams Stroop test 3 · Halstead–Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery Founder note. The Halstead-Reitan battery arose from one of the first neuropsychology labs in America; it proposed the theory of "biological intelligence" . Introduction Created one of the first neuropsychology labs in America. First neuropsychological test to have a factor-analytic process. Was made to test head trauma. Created: 1935. Time taken: 6–8 hours. 1956: The Halstead-Reitan Test Battery begins to emerge as the premiere test battery in neuropsychology. Now it can detect tremors, cerebrovascular accidents, infections, degenerative diseases, learning disabilities, neurological disorders. Proposed theory of "biological intelligence". Extra information Total 7 scores. Removed: critical flicker fusion test, time sense test. For ages: 15+. Based on T-score value. 6-point score. Scales / Measures Category test — measures abstract reasoning and concept formation; requires the examinee to find the rule for categorizing pictures of geometric shapes. Tactual performance test (Seguin) — measures kinesthetic and sensorimotor ability; requires a blindfolded examinee to place blocks in the appropriate cutout on an upright board with the dominant hand, then non-dominant hand, then both hands; also tests for incidental memory of blocks (score: total time, memory, location). Seashore Rhythm Test — measures attention and auditory perception; requires the examinee to indicate whether paired musical rhythms are same or different. Speech sound perception test — measures attention and auditory-visual synthesis; requires the examinee to pick from four choices the written version of taped nonsense words. Finger tapping test — measures motor speed; requires the examinee to tap a telegraph-key-like lever as quickly as possible for 10 seconds. Other measures Grip strength — requires the examinee to squeeze as hard as possible; separate trials with each hand. Trail making, parts A, B — requires the examinee to connect numbers (part A) or numbers and letters in alternating order (part B) with a pencil line under pressure of time. Tactile form recognition — requires the examinee to recognize simple shapes (e.g., triangle) placed in the palm of the hand. Sensory-Perceptual Exam — requires the examinee to respond to simple bilateral sensory tasks, e.g., detecting which finger has been touched. Aphasia Screening test — tasks include naming a pictured item (e.g., fork), repeating short phrases. Supplementary: WAIS-III, WRAT-3, MMPI-2, memory tests such as Wechsler Memory Scale-III or Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. 4 · Other Neuropsychological Tests Luria-Nebraska Test Battery Founder note. Luria-Nebraska — started in 1978, standardized by Golden in 1980. The AIIMS and NIMHANS batteries are based on this. 269 items (0, 1, 2 scale); T scores are used. In some areas 2 scores are assigned to the same task: speed and accuracy. Can check any organic damage. Total 14 scales: motor, rhythm, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, writing, reading, arithmetic, memory, intellectual scales, pathognomonic — left and right hemisphere. The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (VABS) / Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) Founder note. Developed by American psychologist Edgar Arnold Doll (1935). Most widely used test to measure adaptive behaviour in existence; can be used from birth until death. For younger children, there is a semi-structured interview with parents. Domains: communication, daily living skills, socialization, motor skills, maladaptive behaviour (optional). Can check for Autism Spectrum Disorder, deficits in adaptation, genetic disorders, traumatic brain injury. Age 7–90: given only 3 subtests (not the motor skills subtest). Age 0–7: given all 4 subtests. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) Founder note. Given by E.A. Berg in 1948 (60 cards); Heaton modified it in 1981 to a total of 64 cards. Order: Colour → Form → Number. Can break rapport if the client is unable to answer correctly. Bilateral prefrontal dysfunction patients are excited to give the test even if they give wrong answers. Checks for perseveration. Scored using Milner's criteria. The Bender-Gestalt Test (BGT) Founder note. Developed in 1938 by Lauretta Bender . Tests: hand-eye coordination, perseveration, prefrontal damage. Involves 13 designs for children less than 8 years and 12 designs for age 8 years and above. Memory recall process; global scoring system. Clients are given a lot of sheets, but asked to draw on only one. Visuospatial difficulties identified (lesions in right parietal lobe). Seguin Form Board Test Founder note. Indian adaptation by J. Bharatraj ; norms by S. K. Goel . Part of the Halstead-Reitan test battery (1947). Client is asked to draw the board from memory. Earlier it was used to test eye-hand / visuomotor coordination. Earlier given as 10 blocks of Gesell figures. The Benton Visual Retention Test (BVRT) Founder note. Developed by Arthur Benton . Currently: 5th edition; includes 10 designs. Clients are required to see and copy 10 designs immediately out of memory. Time taken: 5 minutes. The Seashore Test Founder note. The tests were developed by Carl E. Seashore . Used in the Halstead-Reitan Battery. 3–5 errors considered normal. Measures musical ability and cerebral function. Seashore Rhythm Test — a subtest of the Seashore Measures of Musical Talent that measures generalized cerebral function; age-related problems occur. Stroop Test Test of selective attention, response conflict and inhibition; errors indicate dysfunction. Because of conceptual primacy, colour takes longer to recognize. No age bias. For checking smaller lesions, more items need to be added. Indicative of frontal functioning; biggest test is 4 block/trial. Tower Tests Tests for frontal, planning and executive dysfunction. A measure of means-end analysis. Requires the client to reach the final goal in the least number of moves possible. Test Apparatus Least number of moves possible Tower of London Utilizes balls 5 Tower of Hanoi Utilizes rings 6 Dependent on working backwards; one has to visualize; repeat-state avoidance. Checks for inhibition of conflicting responses and working memory. Prepotent: goal-subgoal conflict. The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test (ROCF) Founder note. Developed by Rey in 1941; standardized by Osterrieth in 1944. Measures visuospatial construction ability, visual memory, and executive functioning by the prefrontal lobe. 3 stages: copy, immediate recall, delayed recall. Uses one-for-one diagram. Checks for: fine motor coordination, visuospatial memory, planning and organization, attention and coordination. Age-related bias may be present. Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) Computerized test. Time taken: 40–45 mins. Checks for dementia; frontal, temporal, hippocampal dysfunction. Checks for organic as well as non-organic damage. Independent of language and not sensitive to gender. Subtests: psychomotor coordination and motor speed; reasoning and planning abilities; spatial memory; attention and vigilance. Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) Basic exam of cognitive screening; 11 items. A score of 23/30 and lesser is considered pathological. Domains: orientation, repetition, verbal recall, attention, calculation, language and visual construction. Made in 1975, standardized in 1995. Time taken: 5–10 mins. Used for people with neurocognitive disorder. Drawbacks: heavily verbal; the test has a "floor effect" (can't tell high deterioration). The Postgraduate Institute of Brain Dysfunction (PGIBBD) Founder note. Given by Prashad and Verma , 1990; 2007. Language: Hindi; available for all. For ages: 20–59 years. 19 domains. 5 subtests: PGI Memory scale: immediate, recent, very short term, long term, verbal, non-verbal. Bhatia short scale: Koh's block design, Alexander Pass Along. VAIS: 1. info, 2. digit span, 3. arithmetic, 4. verbal comprehension. Nahor Benson test: organic brain pathology. Bender Gestalt Test. The Wechsler Memory Scale (WMS) Given for the first time in 1945. 4th edition: 2009. Working memory deficits indicate frontal lobe damage; long-term memory deficits indicate temporal lobe damage. Checks for auditory, visual, visual working, immediate, and delayed memory. Does not check much of: verbal memory or verbal working memory and remote memory. Time taken: 80 minutes. Checks for neurocognitive disorders (Korsakoff). The AIIMS Neuropsychological Battery Founder note. Given by Surya Gupta , 2000 — a Hindi adaptation of the Luria-Nebraska test. Training only given by the author; very expensive. 160 items; ages 15–80 years. Used to assess cognitive function; has versions for younger individuals. Scales: motor, tactile, visual, receptive speech, expressive speech, reading, writing, arithmetic, memory, intellectual processes, left hemisphere, right hemisphere, pathognomonic. The NIMHANS Neuropsychological Battery Founder note. Version used: 2004 by Dr. Rao . Inspired by Luria-Nebraska. The test is available but the manual is not. Developed on the principles of localization and lateralization. Checks for attention, visual search, mental search, psychomotor deficit, working memory (frontal lobe damage). Also checks for temporal (BVRT) and parietal lobe (BGT) damage. Includes 19 tests. Popular tests: tower test, Stroop task, complex figure, finger tapping, WCST. 5 · Intelligence Tests History Anthropometry (Galton) Chronometry — RT test (Fechner) Mental Test (Cattell) Psychometric testing (Binet) Dates and timeline Year Milestone 1890 Cattell — Mental test. 1905 1st psychometric test by Binet to identify children with special needs. 1912 Stern gave the term IQ. 1916 IQ formula; Stanford-Binet test. 1917 Army Alpha and Army Beta test. 1939 Wechsler Bellevue scale introduced deviation IQ. 2003 Stanford-Binet Test-5. 2004 The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC II). 2008 WAIS. 2012 WPPSI. 2014 WISC. Key. Basal age = the last level where we get all answers correct. Ceiling age = the lowest level where we get all answers correct. Stanford-Binet Test-5 Follows Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory; given in 2003. 10 subtests; deviation IQ used; uses factor analysis. Age: 2–85 years. 5 factor scores Fluid reasoning — matrices, absurdities, inductive reasoning. Knowledge — procedural, general knowledge, missing details, vocabulary, difficult words. Quantitative reasoning — arithmetic problem, word problem, counting. Visuospatial reasoning — puzzles, direction problems. Working memory — words, sentences, short visual info. Raven's Progressive Matrices Coloured Progressive Matrices (36 cards). Advanced Progressive Matrices (48 cards). Standard Progressive Matrices (60 cards). Power and speed test; measures Fluid Intelligence. Mean = 100; SD = 15. Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT) Founder note. By Raymond Cattell . Group test; speed and power test; 3 forms; only non-verbal test. Different from other tests in reading, experience, language, speed/tempo, environmental experiences. Can be given in groups. The Kaufman Adolescent and Adult Intelligence Test (KAIT) Founder note. Kaufman tests by Alan Kaufman . Age: 11–85+. Based on Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory (fluid and crystallized intelligence) and some part of Piaget's theory. Culture biased. Cognitive Assessment System-II (CAS-II) Based on PASS theory (Das, Naglieri). Only for adolescents; used for scholarship tests. Contains the Naglieri Nonverbal Aptitude test. Mean: 100, S.D.: 3. The Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children (KABC) Based on PASS theory. 4 global scales: Simultaneous, Successive, Mental Processing, Achievement. Culture biased. The Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test (KBIT) Age: 4–90 years; both verbal and nonverbal. Time taken: 20 minutes. Mean: 100, SD: 15. Culture Fair Tests Draw A Person Test (DAPT) 1926; performance test to measure observation and conceptual thinking. Leiter International Performance Scale Performance test; made for African groups; elimination of verbal instruction; no time limit. Tests: reasoning, visualisation, attention, memory. 6 · Indian Intelligence Tests Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence Given in 1940; normed for ages 11–16 years. Performance test. Includes: Koh's block design — speed and power. Alexander Pass along — speed and power. Pattern drawing — speed and power. Immediate memory: digit span — verbal and power. Picture construction. Different norms for rural and urban population. Can be only administered individually. Not completely culture fair. Binet Kamat Test Bombay Karnataka version of the Binet Simon Scale; based on the 1916 Simon Binet test. Used ratio IQ. Ages: 3–22 years, separate norms. Measures: language, reasoning, conceptual thinking, social intelligence, memory, visuomotor performance. Heavily verbal — can't check subnormal intelligence. Items are not appropriate to current times; easy to administer. Severe and profound mental retardation. Kulshreshtha Intelligence Test 1960; Hindi adaptation of the Stanford-Binet test. Ages: 2–22 years; each age level = 6 items. Verbal and performance tests; uses ratio IQ. Tests based on Wechsler's test Wechsler Adult Performance Intelligence Scale (WAPIS) Founder note. Made by Prabha Ramalingaswami (1974). 11 subtests (from WAIS): 6 verbal, 5 non-verbal. Picture completion and picture arrangement have been modified. Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) Founder note. Arthur J. Malin of Nagpur reformed Wechsler's scales. Ages: 6–15 years; 2–2.5 years. 11 subtests: 6 verbal: i. information, ii. general comprehension, iii. arithmetic, iv. analogy and similarity, v. vocabulary, vi. digit span. 5 non-verbal: i. block design, ii. picture completion, iii. object assembly, iv. symbol coding, v. maze. 7 · Personality Tests: overview Projective tests began in 1800. 1st test: Word Association test — Galton, Kraepelin, Jung . 1916: Carl Jung's first standardized word association test. 1917: 1st objective test — Woodworth's Personal Data Sheet. Types / categories of personality assessment Observational tests — rating scales and interview technique. Rating scales: judgement about personality in some categories. Interviews: structured and unstructured. Personality inventories (self-report: forced choice). Non-projective tests , Observation . Bell's Adjustment Inventory 1934; to diagnose adjustment problems. Home: satisfaction/dissatisfaction; health: shyness, introversion. Student form and occupation form; 140 Qs. Adapted in Indian languages. California Personality Inventory 1957, 1987; work-related inventory. Measures behaviour in the organizational setting. 8 · Projective Tests Association techniques Rorschach Inkblot Test Founder note. 1921, by Herman Rorschach ; he created it while playing klexography. Projective vs objective. The Rorschach is a projective association technique studying unconscious thoughts, unlike objective self-report inventories (MMPI, 16PF). Scoring is subjective and system-dependent (Exner etc.), not criterion-keyed. Administration: 10 cards, 7×10 inches, shown one at a time in sequence. Card Theme i Paranoia ii Violence, communication, dominance iii Sexual preference iv Father card v Hostility, castration complex, schizophrenia vi Intimate relationships vii Mother card viii Emotions / complex situations ix Uncertainty / ambiguity x Life situation / oral fixation Phases: Performance proper. Enquiry: ask what, why, where it was seen. Testing the limits: done to give participants with weird responses another chance. Studies unconscious thoughts. Average number of responses: 20–25; per card: 3–5. Focus on: content of the story, feeling or tone, subject's behaviour apart from the responses. Scoring system: Levey, Beck S., Hertz, Klopfer, Exner (1974). Latest scoring system by Exner : 1993. Scoring based on: location, determinant, form quality, content, popular responses. Blacky's Picture Test Based on Freud's psychosexual stages; for children ages 5 and older; 11 cartoon stimuli. In addition to requesting a story for each card, the examiner also presents multiple-choice questions based on stages of psychosexual development. Word Association Test Founder note. Also known as free association technique. First systematically described by Galton (1879); introduced into the psychological laboratory by Wundt ; first applied to the study of abnormality by Emil Kraepelin ; adapted for use as a projective technique by Carl Jung . Construction tests Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) Founder note. Given by Henry Murray and Christina Morgan (1935, 43); based on Murray's theory of personology. Can be both idiographic and nomothetic. 19 cards, for male, female, boys, girls; total cards that can be given: 20. Blank card: Card no. 16. Bellack's scoring system is used. Analysis: Hero · Needs of the hero · Thema · Outcome. Needs of the hero: Needs motivated by desire for power, property, prestige, knowledge, creativity: achievement, acquisition, aggression, construction, counteraction, dominance, exposition, recognition, understanding. Needs motivated by affection, admiration, sympathy, love, dependence: affiliation, deference, nurturance, sex, succorance. Needs motivated by desire for freedom, change, excitement, play: autonomy, change/travel adventure, excitation/dissipation, play. Miscellaneous needs: abasement, blame avoidance, cognizance, harm avoidance, passivity, rejection, retention, sentience. Presses: Press of deprivation: acquisition, retention. Press descriptive of an empty, alien, or rejecting environment: lack of things/opportunities/friends, human support; loss; rejection; uncongenial environment. Press of coercion and restraint: dominance; imposed task, duty or training. Press descriptive of a hostile aggressive environment: aggression. Press of danger, injury, death: affliction, death of hero, physical danger, physical injury. Press of friendliness, sympathy, respect, dependent, love: affiliation, deference, nurturance, sex, succorance. Miscellaneous press: birth of offspring, claustrum, cognizance, example, exposition, luck. 3 levels of interpretation: descriptive level, interpretive level, diagnostic level. Rosenzweig Picture Frustration Study Consists of 24 cartoon pictures each portraying two persons in a frustrating situation. Responses are scored as to whether, and to what degree, they indicate that the subject exhibits aggression towards the source of the frustration; assumes blame or guilt as the cause of frustration; or justifies, minimizes or denies the frustration. The score is based on a total of nine factors derived from combinations of three types of aggression and three directions of aggression. Three types of aggression: obstacle dominance, ego defense, need persistence. Three directions of aggression: extragression, imagression, intragression. What to ask: current situation; thoughts and feelings of the character; preceding events; outcome. Choice or ordering tests: Szondi Founder note. Developed by Leopold Szondi in 1935. Intended to reveal a person's innermost suppressed traits, the parts of yourself you have pushed down into your subconscious. Number of photos: 48. The test involves looking at a series of 48 photos of people with distinct expressions on their faces. The patient picks the friendliest faces and the unfriendliest, the idea being that a person identifies with like people and that their choices from the pictures would represent traits of themselves. Completion tests Sentence Completion Test Semi-projective. 1940: first given by Rohde and Hidreth . Sack's Sentence Completion Test Founder note. By Joseph M. Sacks . Developed to explore specific clusters of attitudes or significant areas of an individual's life. Number of items: 60. 4 subscales: family, sex, relationships, self concepts — each measured on 15 different attitudes such as fears, guilt, and goals. A rating sheet with the four appropriate stems rearranged under the 15 attitude headings allows a clinician to rate the examinee's responses on a continuum that ranges from no significant disturbance to severely disturbed. Expressive tests House Tree Person Test (HTP) Asks for the drawing of a house, a tree, and a person, in order to evaluate them together and globally. Person: who is the person; how old he is; what does he do best; what does he like least. Tree: what kind of tree it is; how old it is; what season it is; has someone tried to cut it down; who waters it; does it have enough light to grow. Usually administered on children. Draw A Man Test Founder note. Goodenough , 1926. Scoring: Chen-Sea (2000). Patients are given a blank piece of paper (8.5×11) entitled "Draw an Entire Man" and a pencil, and are asked to draw an entire man from memory. Kinetic Family Drawing Founder note. Burns and Kaufman , 1970. Helps assess a child's self-concept and family dynamics. The child is asked to draw a picture of their family, including themselves, "doing something". 9 · Non-Projective Tests (Non Factor Analytic) Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) Founder note. Given by Hathaway & McKinley (1989); ages 18 and above. 567 items. 1943: 1st test of validity scales. 1989: Revision. MMPI-A published in 1992. Uses the criterion keyed method (criterion validity). T scores. Time taken: 40–45 minutes. Validity Scales CNS — cannot say. L — Lie scale. F — Infrequency scale, faking bad (1st half). K — Defensiveness / Evasiveness. Fb — Faking bad (last half). VRIN — Variable Response Inconsistency. TRIN — True Response Inconsistency. F-K — Honesty of test. S — Superlative self presentation. Fp — Faking psychopathology in a clinical setting. Fs — Overreporting somatic symptoms. Why it matters. People scoring high on the K scale show high adjustment, insight, higher socioeconomic status, education. People scoring low on the K scale: masochistic tendencies. Clinical Scales Hs — Hypochondriasis D — Depression Hy — Hysteria Pd — Psychopathic deviate Mf — Masculinity Femininity Pa — Paranoia Pt — Psychasthenia Sc — Schizophrenia Ma — Hypomania Si — Social Introversion Other Scales 28 Harris-Lingoes subscales. Content scales: Butcher, Graham, Williams & Ben-Porath (1990). Content component scales (Ben-Porath & Sherwood, 1993). Personality Psychopathology Five scales (PSY-5; Harkness et al., 2002). Restructured clinical scales (Tellegen et al., 2003). Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory 2 (MMPI-2) Validity scales and clinical scales: same as MMPI. Version Author / Year Age Items Scales MMPI Hathaway & McKinley 18+ 567 Validity + Clinical MMPI-2-RF (restructured form) 2008 18+ 338 50 (an alternative to MMPI-II, not a total replacement) MMPI-A Adolescents 14–18 478 Validity and clinical same as MMPI-2; additionally F1 & F2 scales and other subscales MMPI-3 Yossef Ben-Porath & Auke Tellegen (2020) — 335 52 Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory (MCMI) Founder note. Given by Theodore Millon . 4th edition based on DSM-5. 5th grade reading level; made for age 18+. 195 true or false questions. Time taken: 25–30 mins. Scales 15 personality pattern scales. 10 clinical syndrome scales. 5 validity scales: 3 modifying indices, 2 random response indicators. 45 Grossman personality facet scales. Clinical scales — severe SS — thought disorder CC — major depression PP — delusional disorder A — generalized anxiety H — somatic symptom N — Bipolar D — Persistent depression B — Alcohol use T — Drug Use R — PTS Validity Scales X — disclosure Y — desirability Z — debasement V — invalidity W — inconsistency Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) Founder note. By Isabel Myers and Katherine Briggs ; made by the theoretical method (Carl Jung). Highly used by organizations. Interest inventory: Ipsative (every single option has the same value). Types: extroversion vs introversion; sensing vs intuiting; thinking vs feeling; judging vs perceiving. Criticism: little scientific evidence; weak validity; incomprehensive and vague. Allport, Vernon & Lindzey — Study of Values Scale Ipsative; given in 1931. Based on six value orientations: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political, religious. 240 points; interest inventory. Edwards Personal Preference Schedule (EPPS) Founder note. By Ellen Edwards ; derived from Murray's theory. Interest inventory: ipsative. Validity scales: social desirability, consistency. 225 items; used in vocational training. Based on Murray's needs: Achievement, Deference, Order, Exhibition, Autonomy, Affiliation, Intraception, Succourance, Dominance, Abasement, Nurturance, Change, Endurance, Heterosexuality, Aggression. Holland's Interest Inventory Based on Holland's Theory of Vocational Types or the RIASEC model. Vocational Types: Realistic (R), Investigative (I), Artistic (A), Social (S), Enterprising (E), Conventional (C). Multiphasic Personality Questionnaire (MPQ) Founder note. Developed by Murthy (1964); the Indian version of MMPI-2. Age: 18 and above. 100 statements, forced choice type. 2 validity scales: K scale, Repressor Sensitiser. 7 clinical scales: Anxiety, Manic, Psychopathic deviation, Depression, Paranoid, Schizophrenia, Hysteria. 10 · Non-Projective Tests (Factor Analytic) 16 PF Founder note. By Raymond Cattell ; made using factor analysis. Type of traits: temperamental, ability, dynamic (bipolar). Surface traits are a combination of source traits. Oblique design used for factor analysis. Gave the specification equation R = f(S,P). Identified 11 second-order factors. Used multiple abstract variance analysis to measure heritability of traits. 16 source traits Warmth · Reasoning · Emotional stability · Dominance · Liveliness · Rule conscious · Social boldness · Sensitivity · Vigilance · Abstractness · Privateness · Apprehension · Open to change · Self reliance · Perfection · Tension. Types of data Key. Objective measurement: the participant should not know what is being measured. L data — D, J, K, P factors are a part of L data. Q data T data Global 5 scale — created out of second-order factors. Response style scales: acquiescence; impression management (narcissists will show a lot of social desirability); infrequency. NEO-PI Founder note. By Costa and McCrae ; based on the five factor model / big five model. Year: 1978. No lie scale, no validity scales. Number of items: 240; orthogonal rotation used. Three versions: NEO-PI (1985), NEO-PI-R (1992), NEO-PI-3 (2005). Domains measured by NEO-PI: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness. Each domain has 6 facets. The psychoticism scale of EPI correlates negatively with agreeableness and conscientiousness scales. Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) Founder note. By Eysenck . Theory: Type → Trait → Habit → S-R (smallest). Focuses on nature (biological disposition) only. 108 items; current version: EPQ-R (1985). Can measure 22 personality disorders. Three dimensions (PEN): Psychoticism – Impulse control (gave this dimension after working at Maudsley hospital). Extroversion – Introversion. Neuroticism – Emotional Stability. 4th dimension: Lie scale. Reliability vs validity check. Note the distinct validity-scale families across objective tests: MMPI uses criterion-keyed validity scales (L, F, K, VRIN, TRIN…); MCMI uses X/Y/Z/V/W; EPPS uses social desirability + consistency; MPQ uses K + Repressor-Sensitiser; the 16PF uses response-style scales (acquiescence, impression management, infrequency); NEO-PI has no validity/lie scales, whereas the EPQ adds a Lie scale as its 4th dimension. Don't confuse a validity scale (detects faking) with a clinical/content scale (measures the trait).

title: Psychological Interventions
text: Psychological Interventions — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Psychological Interventions Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Psychodynamic → Freud Behaviour therapy: 3 wings CBT waves 1–3 Humanistic & existential Stress, coping & counselling What this covers. The full sweep of psychological interventions: psychodynamic psychotherapy (Freud, defence mechanisms, transference) and transactional analysis; behaviour therapy across its classical-conditioning, operant and modelling wings; the three waves of cognitive-behaviour therapy (Beck's CT and Ellis's REBT, then DBT, MBCT, MBSR and ACT with other third-wave therapies); EMDR; gestalt therapy and its many techniques; humanistic and existential therapy (Rogers, Jaspers, Sartre, Frankl, Yalom); stress and coping models; and the principles of counselling and guidance. Contents: 1 · Psychodynamic Psychotherapy · 2 · Transactional Analysis · 3 · Behaviour Therapy · 4 · Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy (Waves 1–3) · 5 · EMDR · 6 · Gestalt Therapy · 7 · Humanistic & Existential Therapy · 8 · Stress and Coping · 9 · Counselling and Guidance 1 · Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Psychodynamic psychotherapy → Sigmund Freud. Worked with Joseph Breuer (the case of Anna 'O' ); influenced by Charcot (hypnosis) and Breuer (catharsis). Freud — early life & career Was his mother's favourite child; observed his own life; was attracted to his mother and scared of his father. Started teaching at the University of Vienna in 1873. Died in Britain from jaw cancer.
