Career milestones: cocaine exploration; influence of Charcot (hypnosis) and Breuer (catharsis); movement from resistance to suggestion → concentration technique → free association; publication of Studies on Hysteria . Defence mechanisms Defence Core idea Repression Keeping unpleasant memories or thoughts buried in the unconscious. Primal : innately part of the Id. Proper : unacceptable derivatives of original id impulses. Denial Refusing to recognise an unpleasant reality. Rationalization Creating a socially acceptable excuse to justify unacceptable behaviour. Reaction formation Not acknowledging unacceptable impulses and over-emphasising their opposite. Projection Transferring one's unacceptable qualities or impulses to others. Important processes Process Meaning Resistance Reluctance to discuss certain topics; conscious defence mechanisms. Transference The patient projects feelings meant for others onto the therapist. Counter-transference The therapist develops emotional reactions towards the patient. Working through Discussing emotionally charged material over many therapy sessions. Trap — transference vs counter-transference. Transference = patient → therapist (patient projects feelings for others onto the therapist). Counter-transference = therapist → patient (therapist develops emotional reactions towards the patient). Dreams Manifest content: the clearly identifiable stories, characters, events and actions. Latent content: the unconscious thoughts, desires, fears and conflicts. Dream work Mechanism Function Condensation Condensing multiple thoughts into a single dream element or symbol. Displacement Shifting emotional significance from one object to another. Symbolization Representing an action or idea through symbols. Secondary revision Rationalizing latent content. 2 · Transactional Analysis Transactional Analysis → Eric Berne. Transactional Analysis is a psychotherapeutic method characterised by a creative combination of cognitive and psychodynamically oriented psychotherapy, enriched by aspects of communication therapy and gestalt therapy processes. Types of analysis Structural analysis: individual personality analysis. Transactional analysis: dialogue analysis. Game analysis: saying something and meaning something else (analysis of ulterior transactions). Script analysis: compulsive, rigid transactions that people act out compulsively. Ego states Parent ego — Nurturing parent and Critical parent. Adult ego. Child ego — Free child and Adapted child. Transactions Complementary transactions. Crossed transactions. Ulterior transactions — e.g. saying "You don't love me" while meaning "You love my brother so much!" 3 · Behaviour Therapy Behaviour therapy is the application of experimentally derived principles of learning to the treatment of psychological disorders. Assumptions An empirical approach. Most behaviour is learned and therefore can be unlearned. Maladaptive behaviours are learned in the same manner as adaptive ones. The historical account of the development of a problem behaviour is less relevant than the present factors. It rejects the assumptions of traditional trait theory. Features Focus on present factors. Functional assessment and behavioural analysis. Recognition of individual–environment interaction. Active client participation. Two core features: extinction and counter-conditioning . Goal is to reduce maladaptive behaviours. Applications Used in treating anxiety, depression, PTSD, substance abuse, eating and sexual disorders, and hypertension. Applied across diverse fields: developmental disability, mental illness, education and special education, and community psychology. Techniques based on classical conditioning Systematic desensitization Systematic desensitization → Joseph Wolpe (1958). Based on reciprocal inhibition : the process in which maladaptive responses learned due to prior conditioning with aversive events are eliminated by developing antagonistic responses. Steps: Jacobson's Progressive Muscle Relaxation (JPMR). Development of an anxiety hierarchy and exposure in vitro . Desensitization (Subjective Unit of Distress < 25). Flooding Involves therapist-controlled, prolonged exposure to anxiety-provoking conditioned stimuli (CS), simultaneously blocking the individual's chance of escape and avoidance. Implosion Implosion → Thomas Stampfl (1966). A variant of flooding, but it takes place at the imaginary level. Trap — systematic dese

title: Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws
text: Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Health Psychology, Ethics & Laws Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Health-behaviour models (HBM, TPB, TTM) Levels of prevention APA Ethics Code (Principles A–E) Mental Healthcare Act 2017 RCI & RPWD Acts What this covers. Two linked areas. First, Health Psychology : epidemiology basics, the levels of prevention (primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary), and the major health-behaviour and illness models (Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behaviour, Transtheoretical Model, biopsychosocial model). Second, Psychology in Practice — Ethics & Laws : the APA General Principles and Ethical Standards, and the history of Indian mental-health legislation from the colonial Lunacy Acts through the RCI Act, the disability acts, and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 and its 2022 amendment. Contents: Health Psychology · Ethics & Laws Health Psychology Epidemiology and disease measures Epidemiology is the study of the frequency, distribution and causes of infectious and non-infectious disease in a population. Its core measures are: Term Meaning Morbidity The number of cases of a disease that exist at some given point in time. Incidence The number of new cases at some given point of time. Prevalence The total number of existing cases at some given point of time. Mortality The number of deaths due to particular causes. Don't confuse. Incidence counts only new cases; prevalence counts all existing cases (new + old). Morbidity is about illness; mortality is about death. Levels of prevention Level Focus Primordial prevention Inhibit the emergence of risk factors in the form of environmental, economic, social, and behavioral conditions and cultural patterns of living, etc. Primary prevention Awareness programs, psychoeducation, vaccination, wearing a helmet. Secondary prevention Early detection and treatment; reversal of problems/damage. Tertiary prevention Only management, since reversal is not possible; stopping further progression of problems. Key. Order by when they act: Primordial (before risk factors even appear) → Primary (before disease) → Secondary (early disease, still reversible) → Tertiary (established disease, manage and limit progression). Health-behaviour models The Health Belief Model (HBM) Given by Rosenstock . It explains health behaviour through six constructs : Perceived susceptibility — a person's subjective perception of the risk of acquiring an illness or disease. Perceived severity — a person's feelings on the seriousness of contracting an illness or disease. Perceived benefits — a person's perception of the effectiveness of various actions available to reduce the threat of illness or disease. Perceived barriers — a person's feelings on the obstacles to performing a recommended health action. Cue to action — the stimulus needed to trigger the decision-making process to accept a recommended health action. Self-efficacy — the level of a person's confidence in his or her ability to successfully perform a behaviour. Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) Given by Ajzen ; earlier called the Theory of Reasoned Action . According to this theory, a health behaviour is the direct result of a behavioural intention . Behavioural intentions are themselves made up of three components: Attitudes toward the specific action — beliefs about the outcomes of the behaviour (e.g. "if I change my diet, I will lose weight, improve my health, and be more attractive") and evaluations of those outcomes (e.g. "being healthy and looking good are desirable"). Subjective norms regarding the action — normative beliefs (e.g. "my family and friends think I should change my diet") and motivation to comply (e.g. "I want to do what they want me to do"). Perceived behavioural control — e.g. "I will be able to change my diet". Transtheoretical Model of behaviour change (TTM) Given by James Prochaska . It posits that health behaviour change involves progress through six stages of change : Precontemplation Contemplation Preparation Action Maintenance Termination Biopsychosocial model of health Health and illness are understood as the product of interacting biological, psychological, and social factors, rather than biology alone. Model → author. Health Belief Model → Rosenstock Theory of Planned Behaviour (formerly Theory of Reasoned Action) → Ajzen Transtheoretical Model (TTM) → James Prochaska Don't confuse. HBM's self-efficacy vs TPB's perceived behavioural control — both are about confidence to perform the behaviour but belong to different models. TPB's older name is the Theory of Reasoned Action (which lacked perceived behavioural control). Ethics & Laws APA Ethical Principles and Code of Conduct The American Psychological Association's (APA) Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct consists of an Introduction, a Preamble, five General Principles (A–E) , and specific Ethical Standards . The Ethics Code applies only to psychologists' activities that are part of their scientific, educational, or professional roles as psychologists. Preamble and goal In the Preamble, psychologists are committed to increasing scientific and professional knowledge of behavior, respect and protect civil and human rights, and strive to help the public in developing informed judgments and choices concerning human behavior. Goal of the Ethics Code: the welfare and protection of the individuals and groups with whom psychologists work, and the education of members, students, and the public regarding the ethical standards of the discipline. General Principles (A–E) Key. The General Principles are aspirational in nature; they cannot form the basis for sanctions. The Ethical Standards (below) are the enforceable rules. Principle Content A: Beneficence and Non-maleficence Psychologists strive to benefit those with whom they work and take care to do no harm. title: Cognitive Psychology
text: Cognitive Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Cognitive Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Sensation & perception Attention & SDT Learning & conditioning Memory models & forgetting Intelligence & creativity Thinking · problem solving · language What this covers. The whole cognitive block: how a stimulus becomes a perception (Gestalt organization, constancies, motion and depth cues, colour and sound theories, top-down vs bottom-up perception), theories of attention and signal detection, classical and operant conditioning plus cognitive/social learning, the multi-store, working-memory and levels-of-processing models, forgetting and memory distortion, the major theories of intelligence and creativity, thinking and concept formation, problem-solving heuristics and cognitive biases, and theories of language development. Contents: 1 · Sensation & Perception · 2 · Colour & Sound Perception · 3 · Attention · 4 · Classical & Operant Conditioning · 5 · Cognitive & Social Learning · 6 · Memory Models · 7 · Forgetting & Memory Distortion · 8 · Intelligence · 9 · Creativity · 10 · Thinking & Concepts · 11 · Problem Solving, Reasoning & Decision-Making · 12 · Language Development 1 · Sensation & Perception The perceptual sequence runs stimulation → transduction → sensation → attention → perception . Perception can be driven two ways: Top-down — expectation driven (knowledge and context shape what we perceive). Bottom-up — stimulus / data driven (the raw sensory input drives perception). Top-down vs bottom-up. Top-down = expectation/knowledge driven (constructivist, e.g. Gregory). Bottom-up = stimulus/data driven (direct/ecological, e.g. Gibson). Endogenous attention is top-down; exogenous attention is bottom-up. Gestalt psychology Core dictum: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Key ideas include the Phi phenomenon and the law of Prägnanz — every stimulus pattern is seen so that the resulting structure is as simple as possible. Max Wertheimer — founder of Gestalt perception; described the Phi phenomenon , a type of stroboscopic motion , best seen at a time interval of 30 to 200 milliseconds . Laws of Perceptual Organization Law Principle Proximity Objects physically close together are grouped together. Continuity Stimuli falling along the same plane tend to be grouped together. Closure We fill in small gaps so objects are still perceived as whole. Similarity Stimuli resembling one another tend to be grouped together. Common region Stimuli in a common area or ground are grouped together. Common fate Objects moving in a similar direction are grouped together. Perceptual Constancy Colour / brightness constancy — perceiving colour or brightness as constant despite changes in lighting. Size constancy — perceiving an object as the same size regardless of its distance from the observer. Shape constancy — perceiving an object as maintaining its shape despite changes in orientation. Apparent (Illusory) Motion Perception of motion when there actually is none. Autokinetic effect — a stationary point of light appears to move in a dark room. Found by Muzafer Sherif (1935) . Induced motion — motion of one object causes a nearby stationary object to appear to move (e.g. clouds moving past the moon make the moon appear to race through the clouds). Phi phenomenon — an optical illusion in which stationary objects shown in rapid succession, past the threshold at which they can be perceived separately, appear to move. Temporal threshold: 30–200 ms . Beta phenomenon — similar to the phi phenomenon but usually circular motion. Critical Flicker Fusion Frequency — the frequency at which a flickering light appears steady; the threshold where separate/discontinuous images seem to fuse. Motion parallax — as we move, nearby objects appear to glide rapidly past us while more distant objects move more slowly (extremely far objects such as the moon seem to move away from you). Stroboscopic effect — a rapid succession of still images or lights creates the illusion of motion. Depth & Distance Cues Monocular cues Cue Description Accommodation Change in the lens shape as the eye focuses. Interposition (overlap / partial occlusion) A closer object cuts off the view of part or all of a more distant one. Relative size The closer of two same-size objects casts a larger image on the retina. Texture gradient Closer objects have a coarser, more distinct texture; far objects appear more densely packed / smooth. Aerial / atmospheric perspective Closer objects appear sharper than more distant, hazy objects. Relative height / elevation Objects closest to the horizon appear farthest; the lowest objects in the field of vision seem closest. Linear perspective Parallel lines (e.g. edges of sidewalks) seem to converge in the distance. Relative brightness The closer of two identical objects reflects more light to your eyes. Binocular cues Binocular convergence — depth cue based on the inward movement of the eyes as they focus on nearby objects. Retinal disparity — the slight difference in the images seen by each eye, used by the brain to perceive depth. Vertical disparity — due to the image falling on a different place in the retina. Horizontal disparity — due to the difference in angles at which the eyes are placed. Horopter — the imaginary line at which an object placed there produces no disparity. Eleanor Gibson & Richard Walk — the Visual Cliff depth-perception experiment on 3–6 month-old babies; concluded that depth perception is innate . Perceptual Set Refers to the influence of values on perception. Jerome Bruner & Goodman (1947) — coins were perceived as larger than same-size cardboard discs, and more so by poor children than rich children. Because coin size correlates with value, valuable coins "loomed larger" in perception even when the cardboard was the same size. Top-Down Theories of Perception Constructivist theory (Processing theory) — proponent Richard Gregory (1970) . Perception is a hypothesis based on prior knowledge; we actively construct our perception of reality from the environment and stored information. Higher-order thinking is involved. Template Matching theory — a template is an internal construct that, when matched by sensory stimuli, leads to recognition of an object. "Lock and key" idea of pattern recognition; the object must match the template exactly . Prototype theory — an alternative to template matching. A prototype for each object is stored in memory; a pattern is checked against the prototype and recognised if resemblance is found. Not as rigid as templates. Shortcoming: does not account for exceptions. Bottom-Up Theories of Perception J. J. Gibson — Direct (Ecological) Perception : the information in the stimulus itself is the important element; learning and cognition are unnecessary because there is enough information in the environment to make an interpretation. Constraints — a barrier in the environment that helps perception. Affordance — a mediator in the environment that helps perception. Light feedback — from the reflection of light we decide whether to move forward or backward. Feature Detection theory — object recognition is high-order processing preceded by a step in which complex incoming stimuli are identified according to simpler features. Irving Biederman (1987) — Geon theory (aka recognition by components ): the human information-processing system has a limited number of simple geometric shapes ( geons , "geometric ions") that combine to form meaningful objects. Identifying an object from its geons = the principle of componential recovery ; each geon's unique set of Non-Accidental Properties gives geons the property of discriminability . Oliver Selfridge — Pandemonium Model ("pandemonium" = a very noisy, chaotic place). Four kinds of demons: image demons (sensation) → feature demons (feature separation) → cognitive demons (compare with memory) → decision demons (perception). 2 · Theories of Colour & Sound Perception Vision — photoreceptor cells Rods Cones Vision Achromatic, night vision (scotopic) Chromatic vision (photopic) Number ~120 million ~6–8 million Photopigment Rhodopsin (from vitamin A) Photopsin Activated Only in low-light / scotopic vision Bright light; types L, M, S cones Visual pathway: Photoreceptors → Horizontal cells → Bipolar cells → Amacrine cells → Ganglion cells → Optic nerve → Optic chiasm → Optic tract → Lateral geniculate nucleus → Primary visual cortex. Properties of colour Visible spectrum of light: 380 to 760 nm . Hue — the actual colour seen. Saturation — concentration of colour. Brightness — intensity of light. Young–Helmholtz — Trichromatic theory of colour : the retina has three types of colour receptor, each especially sensitive to red, green or blue ; stimulating combinations produces all other colours. Ewald Hering — Opponent-Process theory : three sets of opponent retinal processes enable colour vision — red–green, yellow–blue, white–black . If one colour of a pair is perceived, the other cannot be. Explains afterimages . Dark vs Light adaptation Light adaptation Dark adaptation Transition Rod → cone dominance Cone → rod dominance Mechanism Photopigment bleaching; pupil constriction Chemical changes in photoreceptors; pupil dilation Photosensitivity Low High Time Takes less time Takes more time (rods must be regenerated) Audition Properties of sound Audible frequency: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz . Amplitude — height of the sound wave; determines loudness. Frequency — waves per second; determines pitch. Timbre — quality of sound. Hermann von Helmholtz — Place theory : we hear different pitches because different sound waves trigger activity at different places along the cochlea's basilar membrane. Best explains high pitches . Rinne & Rutherford (1880) — Frequency theory : the brain reads pitch by monitoring the frequency of neural impulses travelling up the auditory nerve. Does not explain sound sensing above 1000 Hz. Best explains low pitches . Key — Volley principle. Supports frequency theory: neurons fire in alternating rapid succession so that, combined, they achieve a frequency above 1000 waves per second. Auditory pathway: Pinna → Auditory canal → Tympanic membrane → Hammer (Malleus) → Anvil (Incus) → Stirrup (Stapes) → Cochlea → Auditory nerve → Cochlear nerve → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate body → Auditory cortex. Other senses Kinesthetic / Proprioception — sense of body position and movements. Vestibular — sense of head positioning (parietal lobe); semi-circular canals and cerebellum involved. 3 · Theories of Attention Attention is the concentration of mental activity that lets you take in a limited portion of the vast stream of information available from both your sensory world and your memory. Sequence: sensation → attention → perception . Types of attention (source) Exogenous — controlled by the stimulus; bottom-up. Endogenous — the brain internally decides what is important; top-down. Sohlberg & Mateer (1987, 1989) — Hierarchical model of attention : focused → sustained → selective → alternating → divided. Focused attention — ability to focus attention on a stimulus. Sustained attention (vigilance) — ability to attend to a stimulus/activity over a long period. Determinants: sensory factor, temporal certainty, spatial certainty, clarity of stimuli. Selective attention — ability to attend to a specific stimulus in the presence of distracting stimuli. Alternating attention — ability to shift focus between two or more stimuli. Divided attention (multitasking) — ability to attend to different stimuli at the same time. Signal Detection Theory (SDT) Wesley W. Peterson & Theodore G. Birdsall — Signal Detection Theory : detection of a signal depends on sensitivity and response bias . Sensitivity (d′) = number of hits − number of false alarms. Signal present Signal absent Responds "yes" Hit (correct) False alarm (incorrect) Responds "no" Miss (incorrect) Correct rejection (correct) For a liberal participant the receiver-operating (ROC) curve peaks towards the right; for a conservative participant it peaks towards the left. Theories of Selective Attention Selective attention is tested with a shadowing / dichotic listening task. Colin Cherry (1953) — early selection model : no overlap in dichotic listening; we do not understand a stimulus before we perceive it. Donald Broadbent (1958) — Filter model (a bottleneck model): we filter information right after we notice it, at the sensory level. Anne Treisman (1980) — Attenuation model : explains the cocktail-party phenomenon . Instead of blocking stimuli out, the filter merely weakens the strength of stimuli other than the target. Deutsch & Deutsch (1963) — Late Selection model : stimuli are filtered out only after being analysed for both their physical properties and their meaning. Johnston & Heinz (1978) — Multimode attention theory : attention is a flexible system that selects a stimulus at three stages — (1) sensory representations created, (2) semantic representations created, (3) both sensory and semantic representations enter consciousness. More processing requires more mental effort. Lavie & Tsal (1994) — Perceptual Load theory : perception is a limited-capacity process that proceeds automatically until that capacity is filled. Anne Treisman & Garry Gelade (1980) — Feature Integration Theory (FIT) : explains how an individual combines pieces of observable information about an object to form a complete perception. Two kinds of visual search: feature search (fast, pre-attentive, primitive features) and conjunction search (slower, effortful; targets defined by a conjunction of features). Eriksen & St James (1986); Posner et al. — Spotlight theory of attention : people can attend to only one region of space at a time. Inspired by William James , attention has a focus (central area extracting high-resolution information where attention is directed), a fringe (extracts information more crudely, extending over a specified area), and a margin (the cut-off between them). Shortcomings of selective attention Inattentional blindness — people fail to see things that are actually there. Change blindness — inability to detect changes in objects or scenes being viewed. 4 · Classical & Operant Conditioning Key — definition. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour as a result of experience. Two basic kinds of learning Non-associative learning (short term) — learning about a single stimulus: Habituation — a decreased behavioural response to an innocuous stimulus. Sensitization — an increase in a behavioural response to an intense stimulus. Associative learning (long term) — learning relationships among events: classical conditioning and instrumental (operant) conditioning . Classical Conditioning Ivan Pavlov (1897) — first researched classical conditioning: a previously neutral stimulus becomes associated with another stimulus through repeated pairing. Based on three broad principles: Contiguity — nearness in space and time. Contingency — prediction power. Blocking — a CS blocks conditioning with another neutral stimulus. Principles of conditioning Principle Meaning Example (Pavlov's dog) Acquisition CS & US repeatedly paired so CS acquires US properties. Dog learns to salivate to the bell. Extinction CS presented without US; CR fades and disappears. Dog stops salivating to the bell. Spontaneous recovery After extinction & rest, CS again produces a faint CR. Dog salivates again on hearing the bell. Generalization CR shown to stimuli similar to the CS. Dog salivates to other bell-like noises. Discrimination CR shown only to the CS, not to similar stimuli. Dog salivates only to the specific bell. Second-order (higher-order) conditioning — once a CS elicits a CR, that CS can briefly be used as a US to condition a response to a new stimulus. Strength / timing of conditioning Type Timing (CS vs US) Note Delayed Bell rings and, while still ringing, food is presented. Conditioning occurs the fastest . Trace CS, then a short break, then the US. — Simultaneous CS and US presented at the same time. — Backward US presented first, followed by the CS. E.g. taste aversions in pregnancy / chemotherapy. Contiguity and Contingency Robert Rescorla — conditioning involves cognitive components. The CS must be a reliable predictor of the US (contingency); mere temporal contiguity is not enough. Positive contingency — CS predicts the presence of the UCS → excitatory conditioning . Zero contingency — no pattern, so no learning takes place. Negative contingency — CS predicts the absence of the UCS → inhibitory conditioning . Classical conditioning & biological preparedness Animals and humans are biologically prepared to make certain connections more easily (e.g. learned taste aversions can be learnt in a single trial). John Garcia & Robert Koelling (1966) — rats more readily learned certain associations: food more likely to become CS for nausea ; noise more likely to become CS for shock . Key — classical conditioning at a glance. Totally based on reflexes ; response is elicited by the stimulus (also called respondent conditioning ); passive learning; reflexes can be conditioned or unconditioned; magnitude of response matters; it is an S–S type of conditioning. The amygdala (lateral nucleus) organizes emotional responses provoked by aversive stimuli. Operant Conditioning Edward Thorndike — learning theory leading to operant conditioning; used a cat in a puzzle box ( trial-and-error learning ). His theory is called associationism / connectionism . Three laws: law of readiness , law of practice/exercise , and the law of effect (behaviour followed by pleasant consequences is repeated; behaviour followed by unpleasant consequences is stopped). B. F. Skinner (1937) — coined the term operant conditioning . The Skinner box delivers food via a lever/disk; the food is a reinforcer and giving it is reinforcement . Operant/instrumental conditioning = learning the relationship between responses and outcomes (an S–R association). Principles of operant conditioning Acquisition — the rat learns to press the bar for food. Extinction — the rat unlearns the bar–food connection and stops pressing. Spontaneous recovery — after extinction and rest, the rat presses the bar again. Generalization — the rat presses other objects that look like the bar. Discrimination — the rat learns to press only a particular bar. Reinforcement & Punishment Positive (add) Negative (remove) Reinforcement (increases behaviour) Deliver a pleasant stimulus after the response (add pleasant). Remove an unpleasant/aversive stimulus after the response (remove unpleasant). Punishment (reduces behaviour) Deliver an unpleasant/aversive stimulus after the response (add unpleasant). Remove a pleasant stimulus after the response (remove pleasant). Negative reinforcement ≠ punishment. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to increase a behaviour; punishment reduces a behaviour. Don't confuse "negative" (remove) with "punishment" (weaken). Shaping and Chaining Shaping — reinforces the steps used to reach the desired behaviour. Chaining — animals are taught to perform a number of responses successively to get a reward. Reinforcement schedules Two basic types: Continuous (rewarded every time; better for learning new behaviour) and Partial (better once behaviour is learnt; more resistant to extinction ). Schedule Reinforcement provided... Fixed ratio After a fixed number of responses. Variable ratio After a number of responses that varies unpredictably. Fixed interval After a fixed amount of time since the last reinforcement. Variable interval After an amount of time that varies unpredictably since the last reinforcement. Learning and maintaining fear (two-factor) Stage 1 — classical conditioning / escape learning: through repeated pairing of the warning light (CS) and shock (UCS), the animal learns the light predicts the shock and shows a conditioned fear response (CR) to the light alone. Stage 2 — instrumental conditioning / avoidance learning: successful reduction of the aversive stimulus reinforces and strengthens the avoidance behaviour. It gives temporary relief, but the long-run consequences of avoidance are detrimental. 5 · Cognitive & Social Learning Learned Helplessness Martin Seligman — cognitive approach to learning: control over the outcome of behaviour is as important for learning as contiguity and contingency. Experiment — Maier & Seligman (1976): Stage 1: some dogs learn that whether they receive a shock depends on their own behaviour; other dogs learn they have no control over the shock. Stage 2: both groups placed in a shuttle box; a tone signals an imminent shock, and the dog must jump the barrier to avoid it. Found: control dogs learn the response rapidly; yoked dogs do not. They had learned that shocks were uncontrollable, and this non-control made avoidance learning impossible → learned helplessness . Robert Woodworth — S–O–R approach : to predict the response we must know not only the stimulus but also the organism stimulated; human motivations and conscious decisions play an important part in behaviour. Wolfgang Köhler (1925) — Insight learning , studied on chimpanzees: insight occurs when one suddenly realises how to solve a problem. Learning happens in a sudden way due to insight, not gradual strengthening of the S–R connection. Social Learning Theory Albert Bandura — Social Learning Theory (aka observational learning ): learning is achieved by mentally rehearsing and then imitating the observed actions of models. An S–O–R theory. Process of learning (sequence): attention → retention → motor reproduction → motivation. Bobo doll experiment — conditions: model hits doll and is reinforced (vicarious reinforcement), model hits doll and is not reinforced , model hits doll and is punished (vicarious punishment). Key. Learning occurs in all three conditions irrespective of reinforcement; however, reproduction of behaviour was dependent on reinforcement. Tolman's Purposive Behaviourism Edward Tolman — Purposive behaviourism (aka latent learning, expectancy, place learning, sign-stimulus theory). Experiment: Tolman & Honzik (1930) . Group A — reinforced on each trial; Group B — never reinforced; Group C — reinforced only on day 11. Found: Group C had actually learnt the maze without reinforcement ( latent learning ) but showed it once reinforcement appeared. The rats developed a cognitive map — a mental representation of the maze. Components of learning: the significate (desired outcome/goal), the sign (stimulus prompting action), and means–end relations (the learner's internal thought process). Field Theory Kurt Lewin (1930) — Field Theory , based on Gestalt psychology, an S–O–R approach: a person's psychological state affects their social field and vice versa. "Field" = the totality of a person's experiences, needs and topography; field forces (intrinsic or extrinsic) drive behaviour. Types of conflict Conflict Description Vacillation / equilibrium Approach–approach Two goals, both valued. Low vacillation, low equilibrium. Avoidance–avoidance Two goals, both undesirable; running away is more likely. More vacillation and equilibrium. Approach–avoidance One goal has both positive and negative vectors. Highest vacillation; equilibrium stage very long. Double approach–avoidance Multiple goals each with positive and negative vectors. Conflict resolved more easily when equilibrium is less. 6 · Theories of Memory Key — definition. Memory is our capacity to register, store and recover information over time — the persistence of learning over time. It is a complex mental system involving multiple stages of information processing. Early models In the mid-1960s researchers proposed two structures of memory: Primary memory — proposed by William James ; holds temporary information currently in use. Secondary memory — proposed by Waugh & Norman (1965) ; holds information permanently or for a very long time. Sperling & iconic memory George Sperling — iconic memory : a type of visual memory lasting only a fraction of a second. Sensory memory capacity is much larger than believed. In Sperling's test, partial report was more successful than whole report; iconic memory capacity is 9–12× that of STM . Multi-Store Model Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968) — Multi-Store (modal) Model : information passes from one storage system to the next in a fixed order — Sensory memory → STM → LTM . Store Duration Capacity Notes Sensory memory 1–4 sec Limited, but more than STM Subtypes: iconic (visual), echoic (auditory), haptic (touch). Short-term memory (STM) 18–30 sec 7 ± 2 Temporary storage; gate to LTM; prone to forgetting. Long-term memory (LTM) Very long / permanent Unlimited Reached via elaborative rehearsal ; accessed by retrieval. Flow: Sensory memory → (selective attention → encoding) → STM → (maintenance rehearsal keeps it in STM; elaborative rehearsal moves it) → LTM. George Miller (1956) — the magic number 7 ± 2 : the average number of items held in short-term memory. Emphasized recoding / chunking of information. Working Memory Model Alan Baddeley & Graham Hitch (1974) — Working Memory Model : temporarily holds and manipulates information during cognitive tasks. Memory span is determined by the speed with which we rehearse information. Component Role Central executive (master subsystem) Takes information from everywhere and integrates it; determines what goes into LTM. Visuo-spatial sketchpad (slave subsystem) Handles visual and spatial information; aids motor movement (1–2 sec). Phonological loop (slave subsystem) Holds verbal/acoustic information (1–4 sec); the articulatory subsystem performs subvocal rehearsal. Episodic buffer Integrates information across the subsystems and links to LTM (added later). STM vs Working memory. STM (Atkinson–Shiffrin) is a passive store (~7±2 items, 18–30 sec). Working memory (Baddeley–Hitch) is an active system that holds and manipulates information via a central executive plus slave subsystems. Levels of Processing Model Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart (1972) — Levels of Processing model : information is more likely remembered when processed at a deep level. There is only one memory system. Depth Level Type of processing Shallow Structural Physical appearance of the word. Mid-level Phonetic Sound of the word. Deep Semantic Meaning of the word. Deepest Personally relevant Self-referent processing. Short-term memory testing Brown–Peterson task — a test of STM using a trigram ; the trigram was forgotten within 15–18 to 30 seconds when rehearsal was prevented. Tulving's model of Long-Term Memory Endel Tulving (1972) — model of long-term memory; distinguished episodic vs semantic memory within declarative memory. LTM type Subtype About Brain area Declarative (explicit) hippocampus-dependent Semantic Facts Cortex Episodic Events Cortex Non-declarative (implicit) hippocampus-independent Procedural (skills) Motor skills Basal ganglia, motor cortex, cerebellum Conditioning Learned associations Cerebellum Non-associative Habituation, sensitization — Priming (semantic) Facilitated processing Cortex Other memory types Autobiographical memory — LTM related to the self (semantic + episodic). Eidetic memory — photographic memory; children have it better. Flashbulb memory — vivid memory of emotionally arousing, surprising events; a strong autobiographical subtype. 7 · Forgetting & Memory Distortion Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) — systematically tested his own memory of lists of nonsense syllables . Found a huge drop in retention soon after learning that eventually levelled off (the method of savings ); emphasized overlearning / revision . Retrieval types Retrieval Note Recall Without a cue — the hardest . Cued recall Easier than free recall. Recognition Easiest. Relearning The most sensitive measure of learning. Neural basis Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) — persistent strengthening of a synaptic connection lasting minutes to hours; based on the Hebbian principle ("neurons that fire together, wire together"). NMDA glutamate receptors are necessary for memory formation; AMPA receptors — dendrites double their contact surface by splitting in two; terminal buttons release more neurotransmitter after potentiation; nitric oxide acts as a catalyst. In the lab, a high-frequency electric charge is applied to the pre-synaptic neuron. Long-Term Depression (LTD) — long-term weakening of a synaptic connection; prunes unused synapses, trimming unimportant connections and leaving only the salient connections strengthened by LTP. Theories of forgetting Decay theory — forgetting is an automatic process; the engram for the information disappears. Interference theory — supported by the serial-position curve. Serial Position Curve Represents the probability of recall of a word given its serial position in a list. Primacy effect — superior recall of words at/near the beginning of a list (into LTM); disrupted by proactive interference . Recency effect — superior recall of words at/near the end of a list (still in STM); disrupted by retroactive interference . John Bergström (1892) — Interference theory of forgetting . Proactive vs retroactive interference. Proactive — old information learned before disrupts recall of the new item (forward-acting). Retroactive — new information disrupts retrieval of previously learned information (backward-acting). Factors: learning new information unlearns previous; response competition between similar materials. Motivated forgetting Sigmund Freud — motivated forgetting via repression : we unconsciously prevent traumatic events from entering awareness to avoid anxiety or blows to self-concept. The repressed material is not lost, but hidden from consciousness. Encoding specificity Endel Tulving — encoding specificity . Two related types: State-dependent memory — information is better retrieved in similar emotional and physical states to those at encoding. Context-dependent memory — information is easier to retrieve in the place/environment where it was originally learnt. The Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik — the Zeigarnik effect : unfinished, incomplete and unpleasant tasks are not forgotten as easily as completed ones. The Seven Sins of Memory Daniel Schacter (2001) — the Seven Sins of Memory . Transience Absent-mindedness Blocking — blocked by sensory information; e.g. the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon. Suggestibility / misinformation — occurs due to a reality-monitoring error. Bias — five types: consistency, change, hindsight, egocentric, stereotypical. Misattribution — occurs due to a source-monitoring error. Persistence (Also noted as memory failings: encoding failure .) Distorted / manufactured memories Three common factors that contribute to faulty reconstructions: source misattributions , exposure to misinformation , and effects of imagination . Elizabeth Loftus and colleagues (1978) — the misinformation effect : participants watched a film of a traffic accident. Group 1 was asked how fast the cars were going when they " smashed " into each other (implying a severe accident); Group 2 heard " hit " (milder). Those who heard "smash" remembered higher speeds and were more likely to (falsely) report broken glass — there was none in the film. Elizabeth Loftus, James Coan & Jacqueline Pickrell — the Lost in the Mall study : showed how easy it is to implant a fictitious memory of having been lost in a shopping mall as a child. Mnemonic devices Helpful for consolidation: Categorical clustering — organizing a list into a set of categories. Interactive images — creating images that link the isolated words in a list. Pegword system — associating each new word with a word on a previously memorized list via an interactive image. Method of loci — visualizing a walk around a familiar area with distinctive landmarks, linking landmarks to items. Acronym — a word/expression whose letters each stand for another word or concept. Acrostic — forming a sentence (rather than a single word) to help remember new words. Keyword system — an interactive image linking the sound and meaning of a foreign word with a familiar word. 8 · Theories of Intelligence Key — definition. Wechsler (1944): intelligence is the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with his environment. The first theory of intelligence was Binet's unifactor theory ; the second was Spearman's two-factor theory . Spearman's Two-Factor Theory Charles Spearman (1904) — Two-factor theory ; laid the groundwork of factor analysis . Intelligence has a general 'g' factor (an overriding intelligence, almost exclusively inherited) and specific 's' factors (competence in specific abilities such as mathematics, language, music). Spearman used the method of tetrad difference : the tetrad difference should be zero but was not, due to a common g factor. Tetrad equation: r 12 × r 34 = r 23 × r 14 . Cattell — Fluid & Crystallized Intelligence Raymond Cattell — general intelligence = fluid (Gf) + crystallized (Gc) intelligence (aka the investment theory ); used factor analysis and second-order factors. Fluid intelligence (Gf) Crystallized intelligence (Gc) Nature Basic capacity for learning and problem solving, independent of education/experience. Result of the interaction of fluid intelligence and culture; learned knowledge and skills. Development Grows rapidly in adolescence to the 20s, then declines (does not disappear). Keeps increasing until death; created by the investment of fluid intelligence into the environment. Environment Cannot be affected by environment. Strong environmental influence. John Horn — expanded the Gf–Gc model with additional abilities: visual processing ( Gv ), short-term acquisition & retrieval ( SAR / Gsm ), long-term storage & retrieval ( TSR / Glr ), processing speed ( Gs ), auditory processing ( Ga ), reaction/decision speed ( Gt ), quantitative ability ( Gq ), and broad reading–writing ( Grw ). Jensen's view of intelligence Arthur Jensen (1969) — divides intelligence into two sets of abilities (method of study: regression ). Level 1 abilities — memory functions and simple associative learning; equally distributed among the races. Level 2 abilities — abstract reasoning and conceptual thought; White and Asian students showed advantages on Level 2 tests. Carroll's Three-Stratum Theory (1993) A hierarchy: Stratum 3 = general intelligence (g); Stratum 2 = broad abilities; Stratum 1 = ~70 narrow abilities. Broad abilities include: Fluid intelligence (Gf), Crystallized intelligence (Gc), General Memory and Learning (Gy), Broad visual perception (Gv), Broad auditory perception (Gu), Broad retrieval ability (Gr), Broad cognitive speediness (Gs), and Processing speed / RT decision speed (Gt). Vernon's Hierarchical Theory Philip Vernon — hierarchical theory. Level 1: general ability (g). Level 2 (major group): verbal-educational (v:ed) and spatial-mechanical (k:m). Level 3 (minor group): creative abilities, verbal fluency, numerical factors, spatial factors, psychomotor factors, mechanical-information factors. Level 4: specific abilities (s). Thurstone's Primary Mental Abilities (1938) L. L. Thurstone — Primary Mental Abilities (group-factor theory); each primary ability is distinct, rejected the g factor . The seven factors (in order): Verbal comprehension, Verbal fluency, Numerical ability, Memory, Perceptual speed, Inductive reasoning, Spatial visualization. Guilford's Structure of Intellect (SOI) J. P. Guilford — Structure of Intellect : every intellectual task is classified by Operation × Content × Product = 5 × 5 × 6 = 150 factors (per the model dimensions below). Operation Content Product Cognition Audio Units Memory recording Visual Classes Memory retention Symbolic Relations Divergent thinking Semantic Systems Convergent thinking Behavioural Transformations Evaluation — Implications Thorndike's theory of intelligence (1920) Edward Thorndike — classified intelligence into concrete / mechanical , abstract , and social intelligence. Does not believe in a g factor; no factor analysis. Four attributes of intelligence: level (difficulty of a solvable task), range (number of tasks at a given difficulty), area (total situations at each level = summation of all ranges), and speed (rapidity of response). Factors: 6 × 6 × 5 = 180 (third-order factors). Gardner's Multiple Intelligences Howard Gardner — Theory of Multiple Intelligences , in his book Frames of Mind ; qualitative method, no factor analysis . Types: Linguistic, Logical/Mathematical, Musical, Spatial, Bodily/Kinesthetic, Interpersonal, Intrapersonal, Naturalistic, Existentialist. Sternberg's Triarchic Theory Robert Sternberg — Triarchic theory ; no factor analysis, rejected g ; disagrees with Spearman, agrees with Gardner. Intelligence Involves Brain area Analytical / Componential Metacomponents, performance components, knowledge-acquisition components; selective encoding, selective combination, selective comparison; retention components. Occipital, parietal & temporal lobes Creative / Experiential Having insights, synthesizing, adapting to unique situations; selective encoding & selective combination. Frontal lobe Practical / Contextual Everyday tasks and relating to the world (aka "wisdom"); three acts — environmental adaptation, shaping, selection. Brain stem PASS Theory Das, Naglieri & Kirby (1994) — PASS theory of intelligence, based on Alexander R. Luria's research; did not accept the g factor. Components: potential abilities, environmental context, internal motivation. Heritability & the Flynn effect Francis Galton — began the study of heritability of intelligence, inspired by Darwin's On the Origin of Species . In Hereditary Genius he argued children inherit their intelligence from their parents. Flynn effect — the observed rise in average IQ scores over generations. 9 · Intelligence & Creativity Creativity is a group of mental abilities covered by divergent thinking . Components include fluency (swift current of ideas and tendency to alter direction), flexibility (readiness to change), originality (newness), and elaboration (detail). Graham Wallas' theory of creativity (1926) Graham Wallas (1926) — the first theory of creativity ; five steps. Preparation Incubation — unconscious. Orientation Illumination — maximum creative thinking (insight). Verification — evaluation and revision. 4 Ps model of creativity Mel Rhodes (1961) — the 4 Ps of creativity. P Associated theorist Person approach Rogers Process approach Guilford & Torrance Product approach Sternberg Press approach Henry Murray The 4 C model James C. Kaufman & Ron Beghetto (2009) — the 4 C model . Mini-C — only "I" appreciate it. Little-C — everyday creativity; others also appreciate. Pro-C — professional creativity. Big-C — eminent creativity; universally appreciated. Investment (Confluence) theory of creativity Sternberg & Lubart (1995, 1996) — Investment / Confluence theory : creativity requires the confluence of Intelligence, Knowledge, Thinking styles, Personality, Motivation (and environment). Creativity is a superset of intelligence; captured by " buying low, selling high ". Torrance Test of Creative Thinking (TTCT) An open-ended test with verbal and figural components. Figural test Scored on Picture construction Originality, elaboration. Picture completion Fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration. Parallel lines Fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration. Verbal tests include: Asking, Guessing causes, Guessing consequences, Product improvement, Unusual uses, Unusual questions, Just suppose — scored on fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration (flexibility optional in some). title: Personality & Motivation
text: Personality & Motivation — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Personality & Motivation Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Freud · Jung · Horney · Adler · Fromm Humanistic & Existential Murray's Personology Motivation: drive, arousal, need theories nAch · ERG · Self-Determination What this covers. The major approaches to personality — psychoanalytic/psychodynamic (Freud), the neo-Freudians and analytical psychology (Jung, Horney, Adler, Fromm), humanistic (Rogers), existential and transpersonal approaches (Heidegger, Rollo May, Wilber), and Murray & Morgan's personology — followed by the theories of motivation (instinct, arousal, drive-reduction, and the need theories of Maslow, Alderfer, McClelland, Deci & Ryan, and Zuckerman). Contents: 1 · Psychoanalytic & Psychodynamic (Freud) · 2 · Neo-Freudian & Analytical Psychology · 3 · Humanistic Approach (Rogers) · 4 · Existential & Transpersonal Approaches · 5 · Personology (Murray & Morgan) · 6 · Theories of Motivation & Emotion 1 · Psychoanalytic & Psychodynamic (Freud) Theory → Theorist. Psychosexual / psychodynamic personality theory → Sigmund Freud . Freud — the psychodynamic model Freud used a topographical model of the mind and held that behaviour springs from innate instincts and unconscious conflict. Life and death instincts — both are innate: Life instinct (eros) — libidinal energy that pushes us to function; survival-related instincts. Death instinct (thanatos) — instincts to hurt; destructive energy. The Id, Ego and Superego Structure Principle Develops in Id Pleasure principle — seeks immediate gratification Oral phase Ego Reality principle Anal phase Superego Morality principle Phallic stage The superego consists of two parts: Ego ideal — rewards ideal behaviour. Conscience — punishes with guilt. Three types of anxiety (Freud) Anxiety Nature Description Realistic anxiety Realistic fear The fear of an actual item. Moral anxiety Social fear Fear of punishment; represented by shame and guilt. Neurotic anxiety Nervous fear The fear of being overwhelmed; feeling that you are about to lose it; fear of the id taking over. Defence mechanisms Repression — keeping unpleasant memories or thoughts buried in the unconscious. Primal: innately part of the id. Proper: unacceptable derivatives of original id impulses. Denial — refusing to recognize an unpleasant reality. Rationalization — creating a socially acceptable excuse to justify unacceptable behaviour. Reaction formation — not acknowledging unacceptable impulses and over-emphasizing their opposite. Projection — transferring one's unacceptable qualities or impulses to others. Displacement — diverting one's impulses to a more acceptable target. Sublimation — channelling socially unacceptable impulses into acceptable activities. Regression — reverting to immature ways of responding. Identification — enhancing self-esteem by imagining or forming alliances with others. Intellectualization — ignoring troubling emotional aspects by focusing on abstract ideas or thoughts. Suppression — actively choosing to ignore something to do what is better and more important at the moment. Key. Id = pleasure principle (oral); Ego = reality principle (anal); Superego = morality principle (phallic), made of the ego ideal (rewards) and conscience (guilt). Repression is the "primal" defence; suppression is conscious, repression is unconscious. 2 · Neo-Freudian & Analytical Psychology Jung — Analytical Psychology Theory → Theorist. Analytical psychology → Carl Jung . Point of difference Freud Jung Role of libido Sexual energy Broad psychic energy Forces that influence personality Present in the past only Present in the past as well as the future The unconscious Personal unconscious Personal and collective unconscious Structures of the psyche: Ego — is in control of itself; the conscious mind. Personal unconscious — accessible once in a while; personal memories that have lost their intensity. Collective unconscious — shared memories (patterns of behaviour), motifs, primordial patterns. Contains complexes , formed if a collective unconscious element completely takes over our personality. Energy principles: The principle of opposites — every wish or feeling has its opposite. The principle of equivalence — there is a constant amount of energy in our psyche. The principle of entropy — redistribution of energy within our psyche. Four functions: thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting. Psychological types — attitudes: introversion / extraversion; rational / irrational. Archetypes and the anima/animus: Anima — the female archetype in the male psyche. Animus — the male archetype in the female psyche. Syzygy — anima and animus together. Self — finding a balance between the different aspects of ourselves. Persona — a mask, a facade to meet society's demands; a compromise between your needs and society's demands. Shadow — deepest, darkest instincts; comparable to the id. Other major archetypes: Joker , Wise Old Man , Hero , Witch , Villain . Horney Karen Horney gave the concept of womb envy . When children are born they have basic anxiety ; if they are met with love and care this anxiety subsides and a healthy personality develops. In the neurotic personality there is a huge difference between the ideal and the real self, because of a rigid ideal self. Neurotic needs — three orientations: Orientation Normal Neurotic Needs Towards people Friendly Compliant Seeks acceptance and help all the time; need for affection and approval; need for a partner who will control their life. Against people Competitive Aggressive Need for power, prestige, personal achievement; need to exploit other people; need to compete all the time. Away from people Autonomous Detached Need to move away from people; independence; self-reliance; perfection; narrow limits. Adler — Individual Psychology Theory → Theorist. text: Social Psychology — Study with Psycho Didi (MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF) Social Psychology Study with Psycho Didi · MPhil Clinical / UGC NET JRF notes Attribution & biases Cognitive dissonance Persuasion & social influence Conformity · Compliance · Obedience Helping · Proxemics What this covers. The core of social psychology as it appears in MPhil Clinical and UGC NET JRF papers: a timeline of landmark thinkers and studies, attribution theory and its many biases, Kelley's covariation model, cognitive dissonance and attitude change, the Elaboration Likelihood Model, the three types of social influence (compliance, conformity, obedience) with their techniques and classic experiments, social norms, prosocial helping (the decision stage model), and proxemics (personal space zones). Contents: 1 · Timeline of Social Psychology · 2 · Attribution & Attributional Biases · 3 · Kelley's Covariation Model · 4 · Cognitive Dissonance · 5 · Attitude Change (Elaboration Likelihood Model) · 6 · Social Influence: Compliance, Conformity, Obedience · 7 · Social Norms · 8 · Prosocial Behaviour & Helping · 9 · Proxemics (Personal Space) 1 · Timeline of Social Psychology Key figures and landmark studies that shaped the field, in chronological order. Year Figure Contribution 1917 John Dewey The need for social psychology 1935 Muzafer Sherif Conformity studies 1940s — Field theory 1950s Solomon Asch Conformity study 1954 Gordon Allport Nature of prejudice 1959 Goffman Presentation of self 1961 Serge Moscovici Social representation 1963 Milgram Obedience study 1965 William Glasser Choice theory 1968 Zajonc Mere exposure effect 1971 Zimbardo Stanford Prison experiment 1971 Elliot Aronson Jigsaw classroom 1972 Spence and Helmreich Attitude towards women 1977 Brown and Kulik Flashbulb memories 1994 Ignacio Martín-Baró Liberation psychology 2 · Attribution & Attributional Biases Attribution refers to the way in which people assign responsibility for certain outcomes. Typically attribution falls into two categories: Dispositional (individual) — assumes that the cause of a behaviour or outcome is internal. Situational — assigns the cause to the environment or external conditions. Watch the biases. Several attributional biases are easily confused. The fundamental attribution error is about judging others , while the actor–observer bias and self-serving bias concern how we explain our own actions. Learn the direction (internal vs external) each one pulls. Types of attributional bias Flexible attribution — a general label for the shifting, motivated way people assign causes. Fundamental attribution error — when judging the behaviour of others, people are more likely to overestimate the role of dispositional attributes and to underestimate the role of the situation. Self-serving bias — seeing the cause of actions as internal when the outcomes are positive and external when the results are negative. Actor–observer bias — we tend to attribute our own actions to the situation. Optimism bias — we like to believe that bad things happen to other people, but not to ourselves. Just-world belief ( M. J. Lerner ) — a belief that the world is essentially fair and just (leads to victim blaming). Self-fulfilling prophecy — because person A expects person B to achieve or fail, person B is likely to do just that. Positive: Rosenthal / Pygmalion effect Negative: Golem effect 3 · Kelley's Covariation Model Covariation model → Kelley (1967). Explains whether we make an internal or external attribution based on three kinds of information: consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness. Information Internal attribution External attribution Consensus Low High Consistency High High Distinctiveness Low High 4 · Cognitive Dissonance Cognitive dissonance → Leon Festinger. Cognitive dissonance refers to the tension that results from holding conflicting beliefs, attitudes, opinions, or values, or when our actions do not coincide with these cognitions. Key — minimum justification effect. Dissonance is experienced when external rewards are not adequate to justify behaviour. Therefore: Large reward = small attitude change Small reward = large attitude change Types of cognitive dissonance Free choice — when you liked both options. Forced choice — when you dislike both options. Methods of reducing dissonance Changing one's attitude Changing one's behaviour Trivialization 5 · Attitude Change (Elaboration Likelihood Model) Elaboration Likelihood Model → Petty and Cacioppo (1986). Route Audience Processing Duration of change Central route Motivated; analytical High effort Long-lasting Peripheral route Unmotivated; non-analytical Low effort Temporary 6 · Social Influence: Compliance, Conformity, Obedience There are three main types of social influence: Compliance — behaviour change based on a request. Conformity — behaviour change based on social pressure. Obedience — behaviour change based on instruction from an authority. Don't confuse the three. Compliance follows a request , conformity follows social pressure (peers/group), and obedience follows an authority's instruction . The source of the influence is the key distinction. Compliance — Principles of Persuasion Principles of persuasion → Robert Cialdini. Principle Techniques Friendship / liking Ingratiation (flattery and praise to get others to like you) Commitment / consistency Foot-in-the-door; Lowball technique Scarcity Deadline technique; Playing hard to get Reciprocity Door-in-the-face; That's-not-all Social validation — Authority — Obedience Teacher–learner experiment → Stanley Milgram (1963). Factors impacting the level of obedience: Distance between experimenter and subject Distance between teacher and learner Expertise of the experimenter Signs of authority of the experimenter Conformity Line judgement task (1951) → Solomon Asch. Stanford Prison experiment (1971) → Philip Zimbardo and colleagues — studied role conformity and the effects of deindividuation. The autokinetic effect experiment (1935)

title: Your Therapeutic Style — interview-ready
text: Your Therapeutic Style — interview-ready This is your clinical voice, pulled straight from your own YourDOST session work. Every quote in a purple box is something you actually typed or said to a real client; every blue box is an answer you can give out loud in an interview, built from that same material. Nothing here is textbook-borrowed. When they ask "what's your therapeutic approach?" you don't have to perform a school you don't practise: you have a real, distinctive style and the language to describe it. Source + method are at the bottom. The one-line answer: you're an integrative, state-driven therapist with a person-centred relational base and a CBT / behavioural spine : you stabilise before you explore, validate before you intervene, and you pick the technique off the client's emotional state in the moment rather than off a manual. Your caseload line (say this with confidence): "I've carried hundreds of clients over the past year on YourDOST." That is your real number, and now it's documented, not a guess. The whole export was re-read end to end this time, every chat in the YD project, and 254 distinct named clients were individuated from it (plus another 79 real client sessions where the platform didn't preserve a usable name), across 473 session-instances. The earlier "~30" was never your caseload; it was just how many the first quick pass could separate. The real, evidenced floor is 254 named clients. So you no longer have to split "the number from you, the evidence from the sessions." Both come from the sessions now: say "hundreds over the year," and if they push for a figure, " over 250 individual clients , the full list is documented." The full client roster is the receipt: name, presenting focus, the techniques you used, session count, risk flag, all of it. 1 Your approach 2 Go-to interventions 3 Specific techniques 3b Named techniques — mechanics + PI lines 3c Most difficult case — walkthrough 4 Relationship + formulation 5 Strengths & growth edges 6 Interview answers 7 Source & method 1 · Your approach / modality, as the sessions actually show it You are not a single-school therapist, and that's a strength, not a hedge: the sessions show a deliberate, repeatable logic for when you use what . The spine is cognitive-behavioural (you name automatic thoughts, loops, triggers, and you set small behavioural homework), the relational stance is person-centred (validate first, collaborative, never directive), and you reach for ACT/compassion/solution-focused moves when they fit the moment. The defining feature: you're state-driven, not modality-driven. You don't run "CBT clients" and "person-centred clients." You read the client's level of overwhelm and switch: • Overwhelmed / flooded → containment + supportive holding • Stuck in a thought → gentle CBT / ACT reframing • Ambivalent about change → motivational interviewing (roll with resistance) • Functionally stuck → behavioural activation + problem-solving • Self-critical → compassion-focused ("what would you tell a friend?") You've actually codified this. Your own session framework is built on two named gears: A) DEFAULT MODE (use when client is stable enough to talk) … B) CONTAINMENT MODE (override default when client is overwhelmed) … Goal: Stabilize the nervous system, not solve the problem. your YD session framework, written out for yourself The CBT spine is unmistakable in your own words to clients: Sometimes our thoughts and emotions follow an automatic loop over time and it becomes important to break that loop. We can definitely look into it to Akashdeep (anxiety) For now, the goal is not to stop the voice, but to change your response to it. When it shows up, pause and say (even mentally) — "This is my old critical voice, not reality." to Vaisakh (inner critic / self-worth) It would be important to identify certain automatic thoughts that we may have that doesnt allow us to accept these thoughts. to Levi But it's always delivered on a person-centred footing: warmth and validation come first , the cognitive work comes after the client feels understood. I understand.. Feel free to start wherever you would like to. We can also start with what is bothering you the most at the moment as well if youd like to Levi — letting the client lead Why this is the honest read: across the transcripts the constant isn't a technique, it's the sequence — validate, normalise, then explore, then reframe, then one small action. You reuse the moves of several schools, but you sequence and simplify them around the client's capacity in the moment. That is textbook integrative, humanistic-CBT practice, and you can say so with examples. 2 · Your go-to interventions These are the moves that recur in almost every session, in roughly the order you deploy them. Validation + normalisation (your most frequent move) You lead with it, every time, in plain undramatic language. Thats completely understandable… anyone in that situation would feel tired. recurring across clients The care and responsibility you showed during such a difficult period speaks about your empathy and strength to the marriage-distress client Strength-spotting / restoring agency You consistently hand the client back evidence of their own competence, and you reframe "failures" as data. The relapse is actually evidence that you can change the pattern, and one relapse doesn't erase that progress. to Akashdeep I don't see those six years as foolish. You stayed because you believed it would work. to Nuzhat (breakup) despite loss and pressure, you still have a strong drive for self improvement and growth, that part of you hasn't disappeared, it's just been waiting. to the identity/career client Psychoeducation — simple, relevant, never a lecture You translate the mechanism into everyday language so the symptom stops feeling like a personal failing.
